Pogacar set to equal Tour record as Carapaz wins stage

BBC News Sat, 25 Jul 2026 16:25:59 GMT

Pogacar is set for a fifth Tour win - but Carapaz, right, will take the king of the mountains polka dot jersey

Tadej Pogacar is set to secure a record-equalling fifth Tour de France after a dramatic stage 20 saw Ecuador's Richard Carapaz clinch victory on Alpe d'Huez as Sepp Kuss crashed twice while leading in the last few kilometres.

If Pogacar avoids a race-ending crash on Sunday's final stage to Paris, in which the overall standings are traditionally not contested, he will become the joint-most successful rider in the Tour's history alongside Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault and Miguel Indurain.

Pogacar, 27, of UAE Team Emirates-XRG, finished the three-week Grand Tour's 'queen' stage in fourth place after helping his 22-year-old Mexican team-mate Isaac del Toro provisionally seal third place on the overall podium and the young rider classification's white jersey.

The pair crossed the line together with their arms around each other's shoulders after Pogacar paced a suffering Del Toro up the final climb.

Pogacar will claim his fifth overall yellow jersey in Paris by six minutes and 26 seconds over Belgium's Remco Evenepoel of Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, after Evenepoel finished the stage in second, 26 seconds behind Carapaz, after a late charge.

"I did my best to help Isaac," said Pogacar afterwards. "Massive respect for what all the guys have been doing in the past three weeks. I finally experienced [being a domestique] myself and I already before appreciate [the] work of team-mates, but now it's like another level.

"It was goosebumps [as we crossed the line together]. [It] was fantastic and one for the memories."

On his future, he added: "I definitely will not be doing this for too much [of a] long time, I think. Isaac showed great potential, but we don't put any pressure yet on Isaac."

Race organisers ASO announced during the stage that Sunday's finale will have its distance reduced from 133km to 89km after the redirection of emergency services to help tackle devastating wildfires in the south-west of the country.

Traditionally, the final stage sees the sport's sprinters battle for the line on the famous Champs Elysees cobbles, but a new section over Montmartre allows riders with more sustained power the potential to steal a breakaway win.

Sepp Kuss crashed twice and nearly fell off a cliff

Mountain GOAT: Pogacar has won 26 stages of the Tour overall

Caparaz's explosive riding looks to have earned him the polka dot jersey

Pogacar and Del Toro crossed the line together

Riders took big risks on the descents of the mountains

1 of 5

The most demanding stage of the whole race was left to the penultimate day, in which riders had to climb 5,450 metres across three hors category climbs covering 170.9km to finish in the iconic Alpe d'Huez ski-resort for a second time in two days.

American Kuss of Visma-Lease a Bike was part a large early breakaway which contained riders looking for a stage win, and attacked alone with about 25km to go.

The 31-year-old looked to have found the strength which helped him win the Vuelta a Espana in 2023 and seemed set to hold on to a slender lead for victory.

But the often unflappable Kuss was on the ragged edge and crashed coming out of a tunnel approaching Alpe d'Huez town.

He maintained his lead, but soon after crashed again on a right-hand corner after getting his line wrong, his rear wheel sliding on dust at the edge of the road before coming to a stop, half off his bike and leaning into safety netting which prevented him from falling down a sheer drop.

The tenacious Carapaz, of EF Education-Easypost, swept past Kuss and into the lead - the 2019 Giro d'Italia winner, eventually taking his second stage win in three days and also securing victory in the king of the mountains competition.

"[I was] not really scared," Kuss told TNT Sports afterwards. "I was just annoyed because we drove down it this morning and I looked at that corner and thought: 'Ah that's a pretty descent corner, no problem in the race,' so I took it pretty full-on.

"It was a bit more of a corner than I expected. My wife won't let me race my bike anymore - she always tells me not take risks on the downhills, but you've got to have a little adrenaline rush every once in a while."

Typically, on a stage such as this one in the French Alps, Pogacar would be expected to deliver yet another masterclass but he held back to help Del Toro, who at one point was starting to struggle on the Col du Galibier, to defend his white jersey and third place overall from French sensation Paul Seixas of Decathlon CMA-CGM.

The 19-year-old Seixas finally ran out of energy on the final mountain of the race and is set to finish fourth in the general classification, 11 minutes and 56 seconds down on Pogacar's overall time.

Britain's Tom Pidcock of Pinarello-Q36.5 finished the stage 16th, nine minutes and three seconds down, and will finish ninth overall in the GC.

Denmark's Mads Pedersen of Lidl-Trek will win the green points jersey in Paris on Sunday just by finishing as he leads Belgium's Jasper Philipsen of Alpecin-Premier Tech by an uncatchable 82 points.

Tourists tell BBC how their holiday turned into race to escape fires

BBC News Sat, 25 Jul 2026 14:18:32 GMT

Families have relived how their tranquil holidays in France turned into a race to escape raging wildfires.

Tourists told the BBC of emergency alerts in the middle of the night, desperate drives just metres from six-storey high flames and the sight of people flocking to beaches with their suitcases.

Huge forest fires in south-west France and central Spain have displaced more than 220,000 people, with the French military drafted in to help and the Spanish government declaring a national emergency.

Winds and continued heat are still helping to fan the flames with some tourists reporting smelling acrid smoke like a "bonfire" far outside the affected areas.

Flights to Bordeaux and Madrid, the closest cities to the blaze-hit regions, are currently not affected. Earlier on Saturday, a French foreign minister described the fires as a "tragedy" but urged tourists not to cancel their travel plans.

Among those caught up in the crisis is Zac Morrison, who arrived in Cap Ferret - a popular peninsula blanketed with pine trees 40 miles (65km) south-west of Bordeaux - on Thursday.

The 21-year-old from London, who is on holiday with 10 members of his family, woke up to two text alerts at 04:00 and 06:00 local time ordering him to evacuate "by all means necessary".

"We had the gendarmerie [French military] going door to door," he told BBC Your Voice. "It was something like out of a movie - we had to take everything."

Since experiencing "panic" before a "well organised" operation to clear out the entire peninsula, he said he received four different evacuation alerts from the authorities - the most recent at 17:00 on Friday - after "we moved away from one fire to only get put into the crosshairs of another".

His family took shelter on a beach in nearby Arcachon before a relative came to their aid with a place to stay. His brother Nate, 11, is still coming to terms with having seen the flames.

"Other people have been sleeping in schools and warehouses and the beaches have had people just waiting for the go ahead," Morrison added. "There's people on the beach here with their suitcases."

He said the family was awaiting instructions on whether they can continue their holiday until mid August.

"It rained last night but we are hearing that electricity may be cut out over the peninsula, especially as the ash clouds go towards Bordeaux... I've heard about houses burning in just an hour, it's scary but sadly people here are getting used to it."

David Morton, a headteacher, had enjoyed most of his week-long trip to Cap Ferret with his wife and two teenage sons in the forests under baking sun.

But the mixture of "tinder dry" pine and intense heat helped upend things on day five when the family was awoken on Friday morning.

"Our phones were all flashing and bleeping; there was a message saying we had to evacuate immediately and drive on the one road out of the [Cap Ferret] peninsula," the 53-year-old said.

"We literally threw everything into our suitcases and within 15 minutes were in the hire car."

He said they came within 500m of the main fire. "The flames were higher than full-size forest pine trees, so five or six storeys high, and it was clear this was a fire that was out of control at that point."

The family, from Gloucestershire, has stayed with friends until their flight home from Bordeaux on Saturday.

Others are still stranded. Rebecca Papin, a French-American visiting her holiday home in the commune of Biscarrosse, near to the Cap Ferret peninsula, saw a large plume of smoke in the distance on Thursday.

Just three hours later when she arrived home that night, "there were water planes in the sky dropping water, firefighter helicopters in the sky and the entire distance was just a wall of flames," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

"It was quite far away from my house but I could see it very clearly from the upstairs level of my home."

She said the authorities appeared "overwhelmed with trying" to fight the fire and issued no evacuation order, so she slept alongside her young children with her earplugs in - meaning she missed the sound of the evacuation overnight.

"When I woke up in the morning we were almost alone in the city because the city has been evacuated and I'm still here," she said.

"The main roads are closed because they're on fire - the police advised me on Friday at 07:30 to stay in my home, to not leave my home under any circumstance; there was ash falling from the sky like snow."

Some British families told the BBC they had moved 100 miles away to other parts of France to continue their holidays.

Mark Dorey, from Leeds, decided to drive to the Dordogne with his wife and three children after being evacuated from a campsite near Parentis-en-Born.

"You wouldn't believe it, but me and my two boys were watching a Queen tribute act at the campsite bar - straight after a rendition of Bohemian Rhapsody someone stopped them to say we were being evacuated at about 22:00," he said.

Before heading to the Dordogne the family spent a night with hundreds of other evacuees in a gymnasium.

Dorey, 42, said he feels lucky to be looked after and safe, but is thinking about holidaying "closer to home" next year.

And BBC South's Joanna Kent, who was on holiday in the Cap Ferret peninsula earlier this week, recalled seeing her campsite deserted after two van loads of police told tourists they had 30 minutes to get out.

While the wildfires show no sign of abating soon, the UK Foreign Office is currently not advising against travel to France or Spain.

Éléonore Caroit, France's minister for international partnerships, advised tourists on Saturday: "You have entire areas that are fine, you're seeing similar phenomena in Spain and other countries.

"I'm in Paris and nothing is happening, and most other regions are OK, so do please come to France and do not cancel your travel plans.

"But wherever you are, please do be advised as to what might be happening."

In Madrid the fires are in the wider region far outside the city centre - and authorities are battling to stop different fires merging.

But the flames have already shut down a facility for US space agency Nasa 37 miles (65km) west of the city.

Madrid's regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso described the fire there as the "worst fire in the history of the region", with the area facing a "perfect storm" of high temperatures, relentless wind and merging fire fronts.

Twenty firefighters taken to hospital after explosion

BBC News Sat, 25 Jul 2026 13:16:49 GMT

Twenty firefighters were taken to hospital after a blaze ripped through an industrial unit and spread to a fertiliser store, triggering a major explosion.

The fire service declared a major incident on Friday, as more than 100 firefighters tackled the flames at Highlands Farm, near the village of Rettendon, Essex.

Three fire engines and two fire service cars were destroyed in the blaze.

Speaking at a media conference on Saturday, Rick Hylton, Essex's chief fire officer, praised the "remarkable professionalism, courage and commitment" of the fire crews.

He said the incident was "one of the most challenging and complex incidents Essex County Fire and Rescue Service has responded to in recent years".

Of the firefighters taken to hospital, four had minor injuries. Sixteen were checked as a precaution for issues such as hearing loss after the explosion.

All of them had been discharged from hospital, Hylton said.

The fire service was called at about 16:50 BST on Friday to reports of a fire involving industrial units and surrounding land at the farm, on Southend Road between East Hanningfield and Rettendon.

Firefighters were confronted by a large and "quickly developing" blaze, Hylton said.

At 17:46 a unit housing fertiliser exploded.

Witnesses told the BBC it sounded "like a bomb" and compared it to a "sonic boom".

Others described hot debris falling from the sky.

On Saturday, about 25 firefighters remained at the scene dampening down. An investigation into the cause of the fire is under way.

Hylton said the fire service was also working on recovery operations for businesses affected.

Six men have been arrested on suspicion of murder after a 22-year-old man was fatally stabbed in Clapham, south-west London, the Metropolitan Police has said.

Police were called at 04:37 BST following reports of a man attending hospital with a stab wound. He later died in hospital, the force said.

The incident is believed to have taken place around Tremadoc Road and Clapham High Street.

Police said four of the suspects also attended hospital with stab wounds and are continuing to receive treatment, although their injuries are not believed to be life-threatening or life-changing.

Alongside the four men in hospital – three aged 22 and one 24 – officers also arrested two further men, aged 27 and 23, at the hospital on suspicion of murder. They remain in police custody.

The Met said it understood the fatally injured man was stabbed at about 04:20. It added that officers were carrying out inquiries in and around Tremadoc Road and Clapham High Street to establish the full circumstances around the incident.

Det Ch Insp Sarah Lee, who is leading the investigation, said those in the area would continue to notice an increased police presence throughout Saturday.

The family of the man who died have been informed and are being supported by specialist officers.

Supt Mark Gallacher, a policing lead for the area, described the incident as "tragic".

"We understand that this will cause concern among the local community and specialist detectives are doing everything possible to determine what has happened," he added.

The Met urged witnesses or people with information about the incident to contact police on 101, quoting reference 1474/25July.

Information can also be provided anonymously to independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

It's the cocktail taking young drinkers by storm - but the packaging is 'unrecyclable'

BBC News Sat, 25 Jul 2026 06:14:54 GMT

Cleaning up after pre-drinks, Aédén Rooney puts his empty BuzzBallz in the recycling.

"It's plastic and metal, so I'd just assume it's recyclable," he said.

The company behind the bright, pre-mixed cocktails that have taken Gen Z by storm said they were recyclable on its website, but experts say this is not true.

BuzzBallz cannot be recycled as the PET plastic ball cannot be separated from the aluminium lid, global environmental action body WRAP said.

"It's greenwashing. I'm shocked," Aédén said.

BuzzBallz blamed a website error for claiming they were recyclable via Terracycle, a US-only scheme, but did not comment on its now-deleted FAQ that said they were recyclable where UK councils allow.

Rooney, 21, is a student at Cardiff University and drinks at least two to three BuzzBallz every week during term time.

He's far from the only one.

BuzzBallz was named the fastest-growing alcohol brand in The Grocer's Britain's Biggest Alcohol Brands 2026 ranking.

Rooney thinks they are popular because they are "strong, they're cheap for the amount of alcohol and the price you're paying - it's a no brainer".

BuzzBallz was founded by teacher Merrilee Kick, but was bought by the Sazerac Company, whose CEO is Jake Wenz, in 2024.

BuzzBallz's UK's mission statement, which was deleted after the BBC contacted the company about this story, said it "loves our planet as much as we love a good cocktail" and partnered with TerraCycle to ensure its packaging gets recycled.

However, TerraCycle, which involves consumers collecting packaging and sending it to be recycled, only runs the BuzzBallz scheme in the United States.

BuzzBallz's UK FAQs, now also deleted, stated: "Yes, our packaging is recyclable. Please recycle your empties where local facilities allow."

But no local facilities anywhere in the UK allow BuzzBallz to be recycled, said Adam Herriott, the head of packaging at WRAP.

"They're a mix of two very recyclable materials that put together makes an unrecyclable format.

"No local authorities will accept these at the kerbside.

"If they end up at a sorting facility, they could end up contaminating the plastic stream because of the metals in there and that could be very problematic for plastics recyclers that get into the machinery."

But why should people care if their drink packaging is not recyclable?

"Plastic is a finite resource, and it's traditionally from a fossil-derived product as well, it comes from oil," Herriott said.

Recycling aluminium, which can be done infinitely, means less is being extracted from bauxite mines, which have huge impacts on communities and the environment from habitat destruction, contamination of soil and harm to human health.

Even the shape of the BuzzBallz make it harder to be recycled because they can roll on the conveyor belts at the sorting facilities, said Herriott.

Among the machinery used, scanners can identify it in one position, but by the time air jets are used to separate it into the right recycling stream, it could have moved, meaning it could contaminate other streams.

"It's definitely one of the villains of recycling," said Ambarish Mitra, co-founder of Greyparrot, a waste analytics company which helps recovery facilities.

He said BuzzBallz have "no recovery route in the current system" and are a "huge pet peeve for our customers and us".

After analysing a plastic recover facility in Manchester with a processing capacity of 35,000 tonnes of plastic a year, for six months, the company found that BuzzBallz contaminated recycled plastic 66% of the time.

"Once in the plastic stream, the aluminium reduces the quality of the recycled plastic, while the colour pigments can lower the recycled plastic bale's value.

"This isn't a recycling problem. It's a packaging problem."

BuzzBallz refused to comment.

Environmental scientist and campaigner Laura Anderson, known online as LessWasteLaura, said most people would assume Buzzballz could be recycled.

Anderson said consumers were unlikely to find clear advice, even if they tried: "When you go to your council's recycling website there isn't a drop-down option for a plastic-metal can. How am I supposed to figure that out?"

Anderson described the company's messaging as "misleading" and "greenwashing".

"I would rather they just said, 'this can't be recycled widely, please just put it in the bin'. Because actually that is really probably what most people should be doing with them.

"If a company cared about sustainability, they could make these products in a fully aluminium can and still have the colours, the branding and the quirky design."

James Piper, co-host of the Talking Rubbish podcast, co-owner of Ecosurety, said he dislikes BuzzBallz because of how difficult they are to recycle.

"Every stage of the recycling journey has been designed around predictable packaging," Piper said. "When people come along and say, 'I'm going to make something different for marketing reasons', they are automatically making it more difficult for the recycler.

"There's nothing environmentally positive about mixing packaging types."

He said the BuzzBallz 'biggies' which have a plastic screw top lid is completely recyclable.

"Anyone can say on their website 'this is recyclable where your council allows'. But if no council allows it, then it doesn't mean anything," he said.

BuzzBallz said: "We very recently went through a global website update and the information pertaining to TerraCycle recycling for BuzzBallz was incorrectly copied and does not apply to the UK market as of today.

"We apologise for the oversight and have since updated our website to reflect the correct position for UK consumers."

The company refused to comment on the now-deleted UK FAQs stating its packaging was recyclable.

Gangs, violence and dumped dead animals: The hidden world of illegal hare hunts

BBC News Sat, 25 Jul 2026 05:00:21 GMT

On a remote Cambridgeshire farm, where his nearest neighbour is half a mile away, Mathew Latta was making lunch when the peace was shattered by the sound of loud exhausts.

Latta ran to the window to see a convoy of more than a dozen 4x4s heading towards his farm. His iron gates were cut open with an angle grinder and concrete blocks were shifted out of the way to clear the convoy's path.

The vehicles drove right over his fields at speed, tearing up the crops and skirting the fence by the family's garden. Then more than 70 people got out of the vehicles, men dressed in military fatigues and balaclavas, cheering and playing music.

Dogs were brought out on leads and began to hunt hares.

"They were all stood up on their cars with binoculars," says Latta. "I would say this is 100% a properly organised coursing event, with competitors and competitive dogs. People watching the course - and watching and betting on that sport. It was quite terrifying."

Warning: This story contains images of dead animals

Latta and his family were trapped in their home. They kept calling the police, but nobody came. His daughter, then aged seven, was terrified and kept asking: "Are these men gonna come inside, daddy?"

More than three hours later, the bloodsport was finally over and the crowd dispersed. They left behind four cars, one of them a burnt-out wreck. It emerged that, earlier that day, the convoy had rampaged through an area 20 miles (32km) long in the county, forcing other cars off the road and even robbing a petrol station.

This is the modern reality of hare coursing. It is an ancient sport where dogs such as greyhounds or lurchers are used to hunt hares, which the coursers usually scare out from the wild. Points are awarded for the number of times the dogs force the hare to twist and turn as it runs - as well as for the kill.

The sport reached a peak of popularity in the 19th Century, but went underground after it was banned in the UK in 2005.

We began investigating this underworld for the BBC Radio 4 podcast Dead Rabbit after the bodies of dead hares and other animals were mysteriously dumped in two picturesque Hampshire villages in 2024.

In Awbridge, more than 20 carcasses - mostly hares and rabbits, along with a muntjac deer with a severed head - were strewn outside a primary school. Children were in tears when they arrived for lessons and found a horror-movie scene.

About seven miles north, in Broughton, about 50 hares were scattered near the entrance of the village's community shop, with blood smeared on the doors and a dead barn owl and kestrel tied to the door handles.

What our investigation found was a hidden world of highly organised illegal bloodsport events taking place in rural areas, often by lamplight in the dead of night, with trophies, big money prizes, valuable hunting dogs and sometimes even international gambling.

And it is all kept secret by organised crime gangs using intimidation and violence.

There have been almost 9,000 reports of hare coursing across the UK in the past three years, according to police responses to Freedom of Information Act requests by the BBC.

The figures are not definitive - some incidents may have been reported more than once, while others may not have been reported at all - but in the absence of official crime figures for illegal hare coursing, they give us an indication of the scale of the problem.

Cambridgeshire Constabulary says it was "very stretched" on the January day last year when Mathew Latta's farm was invaded, and the force says it did not respond the way it would have wanted. Supt Ben Martin tells us that the coursers had rampaged through the county deliberately, to distract police and send them to the wrong places.

Having been caught out, the force stepped up its efforts to investigate who was behind the illegal event, eventually arresting more than 40 people and charging 25, several of whom have now been convicted.

As officers tracked down the coursers, it turned out they had come from all over the country: Lincolnshire, Leicestershire, Berkshire, north Wales. "People had come hundreds of miles to be there that day," says Martin. "It was a proper operation."

Then, after searching an address belonging to one of the arrested men, police found the trophy the coursers had been competing for - the Super 8 Cup, etched with images of dogs and hares, standing maybe 2ft (61cm) tall, about the size of the FA Cup.

The invasion of Latta's farm had been a highlight of the illegal hare coursing calendar, a recurring cup competition whose previous winners are engraved on the base of the trophy - both the owners and the dogs, which had names such as "Beyoncé" and "Bunny".

A scene after the cup final last year, captured on video obtained by the BBC, shows how hare coursing involves serious money. A group of eight men can be seen drinking pints in a pub and shouting, as they haggle over a lurcher standing on the table before them. The dog was the Super 8 Cup champion of 2025 and sold for £55,000.

It is not the only evidence of the cash that flows through the illegal bloodsport: we were told the Super 8 Cup prize was about £50,000, while the entry fee for the competition was £1,000, as revealed by a seized phone belonging to one of the kingpins. Police say this cash funds the prize money and covers expenses, such as a pool of vehicles and even court costs in case the hare coursers are raided.

Ch Insp Kevin Lacks-Kelly, head of the UK National Wildlife Crime Unit, tells the BBC that money had also flowed into the illegal sport through livestreams for gamblers in China on one or two occasions. But he says the gangs in the UK did not need overseas bets to fund their illicit hobby.

Hare coursers were linked to crimes involving significant sums of money, says Lacks-Kelly, not "minimum-wage crimes". "Some of these lads are making a fortune. You've got some of the country's best organised criminals," he adds.

There are some localised events that still just involve a handful of men and dogs, Lacks-Kelly says, but the level of organisation in bigger events "has increased tenfold" with the influx of organised crime.

"They've got the advantage in numbers. And they will go anywhere and do anything and commit this crime at all costs," he says.

"They're like a small army, just do what they want, don't they? Turn up en masse, block roads off, drive over fields, cause damage, dump the cars, burn the cars out. Mass participation events that are designed to overwhelm."

Lacks-Kelly says his team has homed in on 27 of the country's worst offenders for hare coursing and all but five of them have links to organised crime.

"These are violent criminals that abuse people, animals, women. Carry weapons, firearms, and make threats. These are not the people that you want in your community," he says.

The BBC contacted members of the Country Land and Business Association, which represents 30,000 rural landowners and businesses in England and Wales, to ask about their experiences with hare coursing.

About 50 responded, nearly all of them saying their land or property had been damaged. Someone in Cheshire said it happened every week, a farmer in Essex said it had happened more than 100 times, while one in North Yorkshire said 150 times.

And 29 of the respondents said they had been threatened with violence.

According to the survey responses, hare coursers had threatened to kidnap farmers' dogs, shouted that they would burn their buildings down, had thrown bricks through windows, made anonymous phone threats to stab them in the neck, used catapults to fire ball-bearings at them, rammed and damaged vehicles with people inside, and warned the farmers that they knew where they lived and where their kids go to school.

Wiltshire farmer David Lemon showed us his 3,000-acre farm, where hare coursers have previously torn up the fields with miles of tyre tracks. He has tried to fortify the land, closing off gateways, putting in concrete blocks or piles of logs, and digging rows of deep ditches to make it undrivable. But they still get in and, when he has tried to confront them, he has been threatened.

In his vast, isolated farm, a confrontation at night means "no-one's gonna hear you scream", he says.

"First thing you see is a face with a balaclava on, with a catapult in his hand with ball bearings in," he says. "That's one eye gone. And is it worth the struggle?"

He fears that someone will get killed before long - either because a farmer overreacts to the intrusion or the hare coursers take their intimidation tactics too far.

"You get red mist when you see them trashing your years' work and this is all you've got. And they're just trashing it," says Lemon. "This is not fair. You can't be hostage in your own home. This is our farm. This is our home."

Elsewhere in the county, a woman who called police on hare coursers at her father's farm received rape threats on social media as a result, according to Wiltshire Police and Crime Commissioner Phillip Wilkinson.

One gamekeeper was run over and badly injured when he tried to confront hare coursers on land he managed, says Tim Weston from the National Gamekeepers' Organisation.

"He broke both his legs, pelvis, ruptured lungs." Weston says. "They left at high speed, potentially could have left him for dead." Fortunately, the man is now back and work and recovering, he said.

As we talked, it turned out that Weston, who is now based in Wiltshire, grew up in a village near Broughton in Hampshire, where the animals were dumped outside the shop. In 2024, he was working in deer management on an estate where he suspects the dead hares had been killed.

The night before they were dumped, there had been wheel marks across the estate, he says. The local gamekeeper had stopped the hare coursers three or four times.

Weston says the abandoned animals were a message to say: "We've been. You didn't catch us this time."

Using dead animals to taunt landowners is common, Weston says. In our survey of farmers and landowners, 35 of the respondents said animal bodies had been deliberately left on their land.

It is a message to the local community that "we can do what we want because no-one's going to police it", Weston says.

Hampshire Police did arrest a man over the dumped animals at Broughton community shop, however. The force commissioned a forensic analysis of the dead kestrel and barn owl left on the doors and took DNA samples. James Kempster, a man who police say had a prior record of wildlife crimes, was arrested as a result.

At trial, Kempster denied he had abandoned the animals. CCTV footage of two men casually tossing dozens of dead hares outside the shop - one of them ripping one of the bodies in half to smear its blood around - were not clear enough to reveal their identities.

Kempster was convicted of handling the dead birds, a crime in itself because they are protected species. But he was found not guilty of criminal damage - the charge that related to abandoning the carcasses.

So was the incident really a warning or a taunt to the local community from hare coursers? With the perpetrators still unidentified, their motive cannot be known for certain.

One police officer recalls an arrangement of dead animals' whose message seemed undeniable, however. He tells us how he had sometimes found bodies strung over speed limit signs and street furniture in villages or left outside people's houses.

Once, he says, he had seen them laid out in the road, the corpses spelling out the words: "Catch me".

Birthmark no barrier for young footballing TV star

BBC News Sat, 18 Jul 2026 06:00:50 GMT

The family of a teenage footballer born with a rare skin condition have spoken of their pride after he landed a role in CBBC show Jamie Johnson FC.

Ethan, from York, has congenital melanocytic naevus (CMN), a genetic condition that can result in large birthmarks covering up to 80% of the body.

However, his parents, Tom and Abbi, said the 14-year-old's birthmark had "never defined him" and that his achievements were a reflection of his "determination and strength".

Jodi Whitehouse, from CMN charity Caring Matters Now, said: "Seeing Ethan on screen means so much, not only to our CMN community but to every young person who has ever felt different because of how they look."

Ethan's new role saw him join the ranks of aspiring players at fictitious football academy Hawx United for season four of the show.

He was selected to feature in the series while he was with York City FC Academy.

His audition involved playing a football match against the TV show's existing actors to show off his skills, after which he was cast as a squad member.

Executive producer Sam Talbot said Ethan's role on the series reflected "something that is hugely important to us as a show".

"We want all children to see themselves represented on screen and to feel that they belong in the stories we tell," he said.

"Creating a world that reflects the diversity and individuality of our audience will always be at the heart of what we do."

Although a non-speaking role, Ethan still got plenty of screen time and a few close-ups, which, for someone with no acting experience could be surreal, he said

"It was the first time, it was all pretty much new to me," he said, adding the main issue was keeping a straight face and not laughing.

Representing those with visible skin differences "never really crossed his mind" - for him, the focus has always been playing football.

Tom and Abbi said they "couldn't be prouder" of their son.

His stint on TV, alongside his burgeoning football career, has helped with "confidence building", according to them.

"He's just is who he is," Abbi said.

"I think just getting out there, people are accepting of it. Everyone we know just treats Ethan as Ethan."

With filming finished and the series now available to watch on BBC iPlayer, the teen is turning his attention back to his beloved sport.

However, he said he'd "definitely go [back] for another" season of the show.

"It was really fun and I enjoyed all of it," he said.

Ethan currently trains with Leeds United scout and coach Callum McKenzie, and has been selected to play in a PYE Elite team at an international tournament in Sweden.

"You've got to take the opportunities as [they] come," his dad said.

"To go and put yourself in positions like being on TV or putting yourself out there playing football at quite high levels, it's good for him."

Over the years, the family have raised money and attended events run by CMN.

Charity CEO, Whitehouse said: "Positive representation has the power to change perceptions, build confidence and help children realise they don't have to hide or change who they are to achieve incredible things.

"Confidence isn't about looking a certain way.

"It's about believing in yourself, embracing who you are and not allowing your appearance to define your ambitions."

Listen to highlights from North Yorkshire on BBC Sounds, catch up with the latest episode of Look North.

Long overdue, life-changing or frivolous? Your thoughts on wedding rule changes

BBC News Fri, 24 Jul 2026 23:31:11 GMT

The day Sam and Courtney Scholey became husband and wife didn't feel like their wedding day.

There was no walking down the aisle, no rings exchanged, no wedding dress, and no music.

That all came several days later, when the pair had a bespoke ceremony led by a celebrant who knew them, at a venue in the Oxfordshire countryside. It was their dream wedding - but it wasn't legal in England and Wales.

And so in April, they forked out hundreds of pounds to quietly sign papers at a library in Buckingham.

"For us, that day was as insignificant as possible," Courtney told the BBC. "It was just the words we had to say to make it legally binding."

The Scholeys are one of a growing number of couples who feel the rigid rules around weddings are making getting married more stressful, more expensive and less meaningful.

But under new proposals announced this month - described by the government as the biggest shake-up of wedding laws in 200 years - couples in England and Wales could have the freedom to hold official marriage ceremonies in a wider array of unconventional locations, from forests to beaches, as long as the location is approved by a registered officiant.

It's welcome news for Nicky Brown, who said she wants to exchange vows in a wildly picturesque corner of Wales, with just her mum and her partner's mum as witnesses.

"I'd be quite happy to get married in a field full of sheep," the 57-year-old told the BBC.

But some say the sacred tradition of marriage is being perverted.

Currently, a marriage or civil partnership ceremony in England or Wales must take place at an approved venue to be legally binding – and many exert control on elements of the wedding such as vows, headcounts or music.

There are also tight restrictions on who can officiate a wedding and how. Authorised religious figures can, but – with few exceptions – only in places of worship.

Registrars can conduct a wedding, but it can't have any religious content. And celebrants can't legally marry people at all.

A Law Commission report in 2022 concluded that these marriage laws, which date back to the 18th and 19th Centuries, were "complicated, inefficient, unfair and needlessly restrictive".

David Lammy, then deputy prime minister, said marriage laws in England and Wales had "not kept pace with the social and cultural changes that have shaped modern Britain".

He added: "Some feel forced to pay for two different ceremonies, one legal and one belief based. Some enter into a marriage that isn't legally recognised. Others feel they have little choice but to marry in a way which doesn't reflect their beliefs, marring what should be a joyous occasion."

Scotland and Northern Ireland relaxed their rules years ago.

Though the exact shape of the new rules is still under public consultation until September, these changes will take regulations from a "buildings based" regulation model to an "officiant based" one.

Brown said she and her partner had put off getting married because there was no legal and affordable version of a wedding that reflects them.

She said she didn't want bells and whistles - or even a wedding dress. "I just want somebody to marry us and in a beautiful setting that isn't just going to cost the earth."

Brown went on to explain that she'd been scared her mum - who is 86 and unwell - would miss out on her wedding day. But these proposals had given her hope: "The laws are now, what, 200 years out of date?"

Miranda Allard, 66, agreed that change is long overdue.

When she got married 40 years ago, she had to jump through hoops to get permission to hold an interfaith ceremony in her parent's garden - and finds it astounding couples today face the same obstacles.

"We applied for a special licence... [and] explained how we did not want to put my Jewish mother-in-law through a church wedding," she said.

"I, on the other hand, was brought up in a Christian family and would not 'feel married' if doing so in a registry office."

It took letters from the couple, their parents, the local bishop, the village vicar and more to convince authorities to allow the ceremony.

"We also combined our legal Christian service with Jewish prayers and tradition, like breaking the glass. Totally unheard of then and ever since," she said, adding the nuptials even made the paper.

Father John, who didn't provide his last name, wrote in to BBC Your Voice to say he'd like to be able to perform ceremonies like this too.

"Marriage is about the lifelong commitment made before God for me, and for some couples the setting can make that sacred moment even more personal and memorable."

Brian Bracher, 65, from Chichester in West Sussex, said he cannot believe the UK is still debating these changes.

"It is ridiculous that, in this modern era, a small minority are still trying to exert control and make decisions about what is frivolous and not acceptable. Just let people, that love each other, marry in a way that suits them."

The proposals will be a welcome change for Christians from the LGBT community, said 33-year-old Isabel Sinagola.

She added: "[They] currently cannot have the wedding they might want, as they cannot marry in the Church of England, but also cannot have religious content in the only option available to them: a civil ceremony."

Others are hopeful this provides more affordable wedding options.

Carl Jones said he and his partner of 20 years haven't wed because even the simplest weddings are too expensive.

"We want to get married but won't, as it costs too much. It's cheaper if we just have two witnesses, but why should our [12-year-old] daughter not be allowed to attend... It's wrong."

But sceptics say this will do little to lower the cost of weddings, which according to wedding planner app Hitched has jumped to £21,990 on average.

Reverend Tom Kennar said it isn't marriage that is expensive, it's the extras most modern couples like to add.

"[It] is the costs of the reception, vehicles, booze, photographers, clothing, food, cars etc," he said.

Other critics of the proposal say they fear it will dilute the significance of marriage.

"Marriage is a gift from God to secure society. Not an opportunity to set new standards and styles," said Donald Tosh, from Glasgow, who wrote to BBC Your Voice.

"It's now not a life decision, it's a temporary decision. And now with this, a very temporary frivolous decision," said Oliver, from Kent.

However, celebrant Zadie Ward told the BBC the changes could enhance the meaning of a wedding for many couples.

"[Critics] are saying it's a solemn promise and it's about the serious commitment, but how can you ask someone to make a serious commitment in words that mean nothing to them and ways that are meaningless to them?"

She says the changes won't take anything from those who still want traditional weddings – it simply gives couples who don't more options.

"You've got blended families, mixed cultures, traditions that are changing even within those cultures.

"Modern relationships deserve modern ceremonies."

The government has stressed there will be safeguards to guarantee the dignity of marriage is preserved.

Ceremonies deemed to be "gimmicks" that risk trivialising the legal act of marriage would not be allowed. Activities "such as skydiving, white-water rafting, roller coasters or other amusement rides" would "fall short of the standard".

"Every couple deserves to start their journey together with an unforgettable day that reflects their beliefs, their personalities and the lives they plan to build together," Lammy wrote.

"This Government's changes will bring weddings law into the twenty-first century."

Additional reporting by Mary Litchfield and Rozina Sini

Claudia Winkleman's chat show ended after one series - can anyone replace Graham Norton?

BBC News Fri, 24 Jul 2026 23:27:38 GMT

When Lisa Kudrow appeared on The Claudia Winkleman Show earlier this year, she was visibly delighted to meet Linda from The Traitors.

The Friends actress, probably the most famous guest the programme had during its seven-week run, said it was "thrilling" to meet one of the reality show's breakout stars, who she revealed had even inspired one of her own recent performances.

As host of The Traitors, Winkleman was ideally placed to introduce the pair, resulting in the kind of wonderfully bizarre meeting of minds normally seen on The Graham Norton Show.

But Winkleman's own chat show did not last long enough for any more unusual guest combinations on its teal sofa. The presenter quit last week after just one series, saying she was simply "too nervous to enjoy it".

It had made sense for the BBC to commission The Claudia Winkleman Show, given the presenter's popularity on programmes such as Strictly.

There's a different level of pressure, however, hosting a show with your own name above the door.

"Everyone thought she could pull it off because she's smart and funny, but a chat show with multiple guests is very difficult to handle," the Telegraph's arts and entertainment editor, Anita Singh, tells BBC News.

"You have to marshall the conversation, give each guest equal time, help them to plug whatever they're plugging, then cue in whatever anecdote they've agreed beforehand with the researchers. Graham Norton makes that look deceptively easy."

She adds: "I think if Claudia had done a couple more series she would have become better at it. But she's at her best when she's being spontaneous, and the format allows very little space for that."

Winkleman's decision to quit surprised many. The viewing figures were lower than Norton's, but still respectable. The reviews from critics were mixed, rather than universally bad.

The BBC confirmed it was Winkleman's decision to stop, and implied that they would've happily commissioned a second series - and possibly already had.

"My understanding is they had made a deal beyond one season," says Deadline's Jake Kanter, who has reported on the talk show throughout. "How formal that was, I don't know. But there was an intention for it to continue."

He adds: "I wholeheartedly believe her that this perhaps didn't work out because of her own concerns and anxiety around the hosting."

Former BBC One controller Peter Fincham, who hosts the TV podcast Insiders, likens it to the Davina McCall chat show he commissioned in 2006, which also ended after one series.

"You have to remember, particularly chat shows where the presenter's name is in the title, it's very exposing for them," he tells BBC News.

"Had Claudia Winkleman wanted to carry on with her chat show, it could have been a slow burn," he reflects.

"But what she's done is rare, actually, for somebody to say, 'hmm, didn't really enjoy that, don't think I'll do it again'.

"That says something very positive about her that you don't often see among presenters."

Many considered Winkleman, 54, to be chat show emperor Graham Norton's presumptive successor - not least because he seemed to be ushering her through himself.

So Television, which Norton co-owns, also produced Winkleman's show, and it could have been a neat way for the company to retain work when Norton does eventually quit.

Admittedly, Norton's show is not vanishing any time soon - he signed a new three-year deal with the BBC in 2025. He has also taken on several new projects, including a podcast, more novels, and a short-lived ITV game show, The Neighbourhood.

But Norton, 63, has also spoken openly in recent years about working less. He reduced the number of chat show episodes he presents in 2022, and also stepped down from his Virgin Radio show two years later.

The short life of The Claudia Winkleman Show could make the Norton succession plan a key issue for the BBC's incoming entertainment chief, Ed Havard.

"This does leave the BBC with a problem if and when Graham decides to retire, because if Claudia can't do it, I don't know who can," says Singh.

"Graham doesn't want to do 52 weeks a year," Fincham notes, "so I'm sure the BBC would have been delighted to have another long-running chat show that you can balance with his, and they may have another try."

Dozens of presenters would love the gig and many would be perfectly capable - Jack Whitehall did a solid job when he stood in for Norton previously, or Alan Carr could probably be tempted to return to his Chatty Man days.

But the TV landscape is also littered with examples of cancelled chat shows. As well as Winkleman and McCall, Lily Allen and Charlotte Church also hosted series which didn't last long.

A cynic might say that the short life of Winkleman's series will have shown both her and the BBC that launching a new chat show is harder than it looks.

But Kanter has a more nuanced interpretation, reflecting: "My instinct is that this was always a bit of an experiment.

"Clearly it was something that Claudia wanted to do, and when you have a presenter at the peak of her powers, I think it's just good talent management to try and work together with that presenter on their dream project."

He adds: "I'm sure all sides will walk away with their heads held high, and it was worth giving it a crack, I think."

Personalities aside, there's the more existential question of whether the BBC even needs a new talk series, when there are now hundreds of other platforms where celebrities can go to promote their product.

Stars can just as easily appear on YouTube strands such as Snack Wars or Hot Ones as a TV chat show, or spend as much time at press junkets being interviewed by TikTokers as legacy media outlets.

Talent agents know that seeing Hollywood stars talking to a lovable and sweary East London pensioner known as Grime Gran, or playing a game of Would You Rather with LadBible, is just as likely to generate publicity as traditional interviews.

Singh highlights that clips from programmes such as Norton's often go viral too, but adds: "I don't think the public is craving another TV chat show.

"Think back to the most memorable encounters from the heyday of chat shows," she says. "They were one-on-one: Parkinson with Muhammad Ali; Wogan with George Best or David Icke.

"Those long-form interviews have moved to podcasts now, where celebrities find it easy to be open and essentially treat them as an extended therapy session.

"And the most entertaining celebrity interviews around are on Amelia Dimoldenberg's Chicken Shop Date. Compared to content like that, a chat show in a TV studio seems quite old-fashioned."

Norton's show clearly still delivers huge value for the BBC, and Kanter says the "chat show format remains strong" and is a "really important part of the BBC One schedule".

"It sprinkles a bit of stardust, it's appointment to view, I think people enjoy that it's a Friday night and they can tune in for some entertainment, it performs well online, it's an engine for clips and viral moments, and that's something that's to be valued in this attention economy," he notes.

And, speaking from experience, Fincham concludes he is "not a big fan of succession plans" anyway.

"I ran BBC One between 2005 and 2007," he recalls, "and at that time, a regular conversation was 'What's the succession plan for David Attenborough?'

"That was 20 years ago, and I can't help noticing he's still presenting programmes today. So beware of the assumption that a succession plan is needed.

"And Graham Norton, if he chooses to continue, has got plenty more in the tank."

ADHD has rewired the workplace. This is what it means for bosses and workers

BBC News Fri, 24 Jul 2026 23:23:53 GMT

Taking one of the UK's biggest grocery chains to an employment tribunal was something that Ryan Toghill says almost took over his life.

"It was all I could think about for 18 months and more," he says.

The deputy store manager at Lidl, who'd told his bosses he'd been diagnosed with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), was called to a disciplinary meeting after breaking company rules by using equipment he hadn't been trained to use. After that meeting, Ryan was dismissed for gross misconduct.

He successfully appealed the decision and was offered a lower-paid role. He rejected it and took his case to a tribunal. Eventually, he was awarded more than £45,000 when the judge found his former employer hadn't fully taken his ADHD diagnosis into account during the disciplinary process.

The judgement found reasonable adjustments during the process hadn't been offered to him, such as additional breaks.

He'd been described by a manager as showing "a lack of remorse," something the tribunal found was clearly linked with his communication differences associated with having ADHD.

"I don't show a lot of emotions," Ryan explains. "I could be incredibly happy, angry, upset, or remorseful, and my facial expressions and tone of voice would essentially remain the same."

The tribunal upheld part of his claims for unfair dismissal, wrongful dismissal and a failure to make reasonable adjustments. Lidl says it's "committed to ensuring that everyone receives the reasonable adjustments, clear communication and support they need to thrive."

Campaigners, lawyers and HR teams say cases like this highlight a shift that businesses should be paying attention to.

Thousands of people have been diagnosed as neurodivergent in the last few years, an umbrella term that covers autism, ADHD and other conditions such as dyslexia and Tourette's syndrome.

Since the pandemic in particular, diagnosis rates for ADHD and autism have been rising, and they're featuring more regularly in disputes in employment tribunals.

While many people who are neurodivergent don't consider themselves disabled, the Equality Act 2010 may give them protection by recognising their condition as a disability, regardless of whether they have a formal diagnosis. They're entitled to reasonable adjustments if they can show that their condition has a substantial and long-term adverse effect on their ability to do normal day-to-day activities. These are widely defined and aren't limited to work tasks.

Cases going to tribunal can be around employers not making those adjustments, but they can also be about how people are treated at work.

For example, a 2025 tribunal found a software engineer who had ADHD had faced discrimination because a manager sighed and made other expressions of "non-verbal frustration" towards him.

"What we're seeing in tribunals is rarely the result of deliberate discrimination," says Lutfur Ali, a diversity and inclusion adviser at the Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development, the professional body for HR.

"Cases commonly stem from reasonable adjustments being overlooked, performance processes that were never designed with different thinking styles in mind, and managers lacking confidence because they haven't been given the training or the time to have the right conversations."

So, while awareness of neurodivergence has never been higher, why are more cases like this ending up in the legal system? And are businesses struggling to keep up with the needs of the workforce?

Irwin Mitchell is one of the biggest law firms in the UK, and its lawyers say their caseloads increasingly include grievances linked to neurodivergence at work.

Using the Ministry of Justice's online judgments database, the company identified 517 employment tribunal cases mentioning neurodivergent conditions in 2025, up from 265 in 2020. The most commonly cited conditions were autism and ADHD.

The live database is limited and gives only a partial picture. The Ministry of Justice says the figures should not be considered official statistics.

Diagnosis rates of ADHD and autism have soared, and waiting lists for assessments on the NHS in England are at record levels, with lists even closing in some areas due to the huge demand. Irwin Mitchell says those long waits have an impact on workplaces too. "Anecdotally, we're seeing a lot of people that are either threatening to bring claims or actually bringing claims, that don't have formal diagnoses," says Jo Moseley, a legal director at the firm.

Research from University College London suggests nearly a 20-fold increase in the number of UK adults diagnosed with ADHD between 2000 and 2018. Diagnosis rates for autism were eight times higher in 2018 than in 1998.

Despite these rises in diagnosis and referrals, some studies suggest both ADHD and autism are actually underdiagnosed.

In June, the Lancet Regional Health Europe journal published research suggesting that while around 1.2% of adults in England had an ADHD diagnosis, international prevalence data estimates it affects 3-5% of people. The authors of the study said this indicates it could still be under-diagnosed, particularly in older age groups.

Similarly, research by King's College London last year suggested that around 90% of autistic people over 40 remain undiagnosed.

Diagnosis levels aside, there has been a huge increase in awareness of the challenges neurodivergent people can face - whether it's in communication preferences, personal organisation, or sensory needs. In workplaces, many describe "masking," a term which means trying to hide their traits in order to fit in - something which can put a huge strain on the person's wellbeing.

"Society is playing catch-up," says Ben Branson, an entrepreneur who runs a charity called The Hidden 20%, which campaigns for better understanding of neurodivergence. He was diagnosed with autism in 2022.

"The recognition of adult neurodivergence has exploded," he says. "But we have always been here, we are just not hiding anymore, and there are millions of people finally understanding why they kept moving jobs, why they didn't fit, why they kept burning out and why they felt so exhausted, who are no longer willing to struggle in silence."

This year's City and Guilds Foundation's Neurodiversity Index found that while employers think they're "doing better" when it comes to inclusion, neurodivergent employees say they are seeing only small improvements.

The study found employers' confidence levels in their own "neurodivergent readiness" averaged between 70-75%. However, the proportion of employees who reported feeling psychologically safe telling their employer about their diagnosis, and who believed their organisation understood the impact of their condition, was between 32-38%.

This disconnect between managers and staff is something employment lawyer Jodie Hill is familiar with. Her firm, Thrive Law, specialises in workplace wellbeing and works with both employees and businesses. She set it up in 2018 after getting her own ADHD diagnosis at the age of 35.

"In the last three months, I've seen more than I've ever seen before in terms of enquiries," she says.

So, what are some employers doing that leads to successful action being taken against them? Hill says one thing that comes up a lot is bosses asking for proof of a formal diagnosis, when this isn't the legal test. Another issue can be an employer looking to dismiss someone over performance before considering a possible disability. Both of which could leave them exposed to claims of discrimination.

In the training sessions she carries out for businesses, she says she hears from the employer's perspective that it can feel like "every other conversation is about people wanting support".

Fears over cost, and concern that doing something for one member of staff means they have to do it for all of them, can lead to what Hill describes as an "initial dismissiveness" from some employers. But that, she says, comes from a lack of understanding over what can be an "internal and invisible" struggle.

"There's a mindset from employers that it's very linear… and that all the symptoms are the same every day," she says.

Another challenge can be determining what constitutes a "reasonable adjustment," a sticking point which can be what ends up being decided in a tribunal.

Hill says some employers "don't know where to start" and wrongly assume that making reasonable adjustments means doing whatever the employee asks.

Some tribunals have shown the limits of what's "reasonable." In one case, an autistic claimant had requested extensive changes to the recruitment process at the Judicial Appointments Commission (JAC), including simplified questions and advance access to test questions. The JAC had already offered extra time and assistance from a friend and denied the extra requests. When it went to tribunal, the judge found the adjustments the person had asked for were "clearly going beyond what was necessary or reasonable".

While there isn't a check list for employers, lawyers stress that they have to be able to justify why they're saying no to something, and show they've looked at alternative options.

Jo Moseley from law firm Irwin Mitchell explains that when it comes to judging what is "reasonable", a tribunal would take into account factors like the person's role, and the size of the business.

"Big employers will certainly be expected to do more than small employers," she says, stressing that many adjustments can cost nothing or very little, such as looking at how meetings are structured, offering regular breaks, or somewhere quiet to work.

In one tribunal last year, the pub chain Greene King was found to have failed to make reasonable adjustments for a chef who was dyslexic and struggled with reading orders.

He'd asked for a Bluetooth headset. The tribunal found that the company's failure to provide this adjustment had led to his employment ending. He was awarded £24,000. A spokesperson for Greene King said it respected the tribunal's decision and that it was committed to upholding the highest standards of employee welfare.

"Ultimately, the purpose of an adjustment is to facilitate good performance, not to lower the standard of performance," says Prof Nancy Doyle, an occupational psychologist.

"Employers are anxious of challenge, anxious about saying or doing the wrong thing," she adds.

She explains that employers are not expected to keep someone in a job where they're risking safety or delivering less than their peers, but that in some workplaces, managers end up "covering for neurodivergent staff," leaving them in a situation where they are "dependent on kindness, which may ebb away over time."

Daniel Rickman, who runs glazing business Structura, decided not to wait for individuals to ask for adjustments - but instead offer them to all staff.

The company introduced flexible working, fidget toys in meeting rooms, and red or green "busy lights" on desks, that allow staff to indicate whether they're happy to be disturbed.

He says it means the business is "getting the best out of everybody" and he is retaining skilled staff. However, showing the polarisation around the topic, he says he has also been criticised for being "woke."

As awareness of neurodiversity has grown, some businesses such as Microsoft and BAE Systems have created targeted hiring programmes to attract neurodivergent candidates, aware of the skills they can bring to their organisations.

Making neurodiversity a part of how workplaces are designed is what Prof Amanda Kirby believes is needed.

She's heading up the government's expert panel, set up to look at improving the job chances of neurodivergent people, and says a "medical" model of providing adjustments is inadequate.

"Nobody fits into neat boxes", she says, adding that training focused on doing x for dyslexia or y for ADHD is "never going to work."

"It's not neurodiversity over here, mental health over here, unemployment over there," she says, pointing out that those who are not in employment, education or training, and those moving through the justice system are less likely to have a diagnosis and more likely to be neurodivergent.

Kirby's report is yet to be published, but it's part of the government's wider plans to tackle stubborn levels of economic inactivity that remain higher than before the pandemic.

A Government report in 2024 found autistic graduates are twice as likely to be unemployed after 15 months as non-disabled graduates, and last year, the government's ADHD Taskforce estimated that "unsupported" ADHD was costing the economy £17bn a year.

The latest official figures show the number of people receiving Personal Independent Payments topping 4 million, the number of those with ADHD as their main condition was around 100,000 in April, up by 30,000 in the last two years. Just over half of these were aged 16 to 24.

The government is investing £3.5bn into personalised employment support for disabled people and those with health conditions in order to address problems with employment levels.

A Department for Work and Pensions spokesperson told the BBC: "For too long disabled people and those with a neurodiversity condition have been left behind, ignored, and not given the support they need to get into work."

As well as costly, these tribunal claims are becoming increasingly drawn out as the UK's tribunal system creaks.

Figures from the Ministry of Justice put the number of open claims at a record high of 531,000.

Jenna Ide, a partner and employment law specialist at Thomas Mansfield Solicitors, says that the backlog adds pressure on employers.

"It can take several years for a case to reach a final hearing," she says. "In the meantime, employers are often required to make difficult judgement calls without knowing where a tribunal would ultimately draw the line," she adds.

Law firms say some tribunals are now being listed for 2030 and the backlog is expected to grow with the Employment Rights Act. From January 2027, this will give workers protection against unfair dismissal after six months instead of only after two years.

"Most people, even conservatively, think that there's going to be a huge explosion just in unfair dismissal claims," says Irwin Mitchell's Jo Moseley.

Not only could this backlog create problems in terms of access to justice, but according to Kirby, rising numbers of tribunals could have another troubling effect.

"Some employers will go, 'these people' are potentially going to cause us lots of problems," she says, adding that this could lead to a "hidden bias" in recruitment, where employers consider it too risky to take on someone they believe to be neurodivergent and so find a reason to give the job to someone else.

Ryan Toghill, who says he hasn't worked since leaving Lidl because of poor health, says his experience has left him conflicted over whether he would tell a prospective employer about his diagnosis.

But despite the challenges, his hope is that workplace changes will "trickle through businesses" in time.

"You've got to manage people differently if they're neurodivergent," he says. "You can get the best out of them, if you adapt a little bit."

The pop band who went from playing for rescue dogs to selling out arenas

BBC News Fri, 24 Jul 2026 23:01:10 GMT

Every band has to earn its stripes. Some have it harder than others.

At AC/DC's first gig, the club owner cut the power because they were too noisy. Sam Smith started at barn dances, singing on top of a haystack. At Robert Smith's first concert, he got so drunk that he sang David Bowie's Suffragette City while the rest of the band played Jimi Hendrix's Foxy Lady.

But LA pop trio Muna can top them all.

At the start of their career, the band got a call from their record label. We know you've just flown overnight from London, they said, but you have to get to Las Vegas.

Why? Because they'd been booked to play Pet-A-Palooza, a dog adoption festival sponsored by the local radio station. If they turned up, the station would support their new single.

"We were all sick, so it was doomed from the start," recalls guitarist Josette Maskin.

"It was an acoustic set, but we didn't have a sound guy, and the guitar started feeding back."

The noise, according to singer Katie Gavin, was like an unholy screech.

"The dogs were getting upset," says Maskin, wincing at the memory. "They just howled the whole time.

"We were mortified, but looking back, it is so funny. And I've gotten to share those experiences with some of my best friends, and that's what life is really about."

Nowadays, that canine catastrophe is a dot in Muna's rear-view mirror.

Over the past decade, they've become one of the most compelling live bands around – a little bit punk, a little bit electronic, a little bit 80s, eminently watchable and endlessly impressive.

Fans include Harry Styles and Taylor Swift, who handpicked the trio (completed by guitarist/producer Naomi McPherson) to support them on tour.

They were won over by sing-along anthems like I Know A Place, a great big exuberant hug for the LGBTQ community; and the more introspective Stayaway, where Gavin locks herself in her bedroom to avoid anything - friends, music, drink - that could tempt her back into the arms of an ex.

In 2020, all their momentum nearly came to a crashing halt when RCA Records dropped the band, citing pandemic-era cost-cutting.

"That's obviously one where we had to put our heads together and be like, 'OK, we want to continue doing this. Let's just make an album and we'll figure it out'," says McPherson.

That album, simply titled Muna, was eventually released by indie star Phoebe Bridgers, who swooped in to sign the band to her Saddest Factory label in 2021.

"Phoebe's manager had made it very clear that if we were ever single, she'd be interested in working with us," Gavin told the BBC at the time.

Bridgers also provided guest vocals on Silk Chiffon, a freewheeling sapphic love song that became Muna's breakthrough single.

It pegged the band, in its members' own words, as "the queer joy mini-skirt rollerblade" crew - but their music has always dug deeper than that.

I Know A Place, for example, was written as a response to the 2016 Pulse nightclub shooting, acknowledging the fragility of the communal LGBTQ spaces it celebrated.

Their fourth album, Dancing On The Wall, is their most powerful yet.

The music is darker. The lyrics hit harder. Ostensibly anchored to the dancefloor, it's a record that uses dance music to shake the listener out of complacency.

"I think it was a response to a feeling of helplessness in this moment in time that can lead to paralysis," says Gavin.

"Movement is what we need right now, and we also need to feel powerful and to connect to our sources of energy. The tempo of this album helps with that."

The standout, lyrically speaking, is Big Stick. A critique of American imperialism, it's written from the perspective of Big Brother, who "can make you want anything that I want you to" – from war in Gaza to the militarisation of US police forces.

"And If you've got a problem with it, you could end up in jail," Gavin seethes as militaristic synths patrol the beat.

"I think sometimes people want to go to concerts to feel a brief reprieve from the horrors of the world around them, but right now the horrors are so pervasive that what I found myself wanting was a container to express my anger together with other people," says the singer.

"It's an emotional release that I think we are often denied because we have to read tragedies in the news every day and then keep our heads down and work."

Given the polarised state of political discourse in the US, did they have any misgivings about releasing the song?

"Maybe this is actually stupid, but I don't think it was a big decision for us," says Maskin.

"We have always been a political band, and we've always been super open with what we believe in, so it really wasn't a question."

Elsewhere, the album transports the listener to sweaty, laser-lit nightclubs, where unyielding rhythms fuel feelings of "horniness and heartache".

The title track is full of thwarted desire, as Gavin tries and fails to get the attention of a girl who constantly leaves her dangling. Wannabeher, meanwhile, is a sticky, sleazy track about being so completely besotted with someone that you start to blur the boundaries between where your personality ends and theirs begins.

"I think that's a canon gay experience, where you don't know whether you want to be with someone or you actually want to be them," laughs Maskin.

Eastside Girls, meanwhile, is a tender depiction of Muna's neighbourhood, lovingly lampooning the staples of LA hipster culture – astrology, polyamory, roommate dramas and "negronis with the nice gin".

"It's a city that's run by sunshine," says McPherson, who moved to LA from her native San Diego.

"It's bohemian but it's also populated by some of the richest people in the world. It's a strange dichotomy."

The song's chorus is a masterclass in melody and, in Maskin's words, "smacks you in the face". It takes its place among Muna's most irresistible hooks (see also, Number One Fan, Stayaway, What I Want) – which all stem from Gavin's love of classic pop.

"She's been writing songs since she was eight years old, so it's a well-honed skill," says McPherson.

"I think it's a benefit of my obsessive personality, honestly," says Gavin.

"I am constantly searching for the next big chorus, and will probably always be. Also, once I have a seed in my head for a song that feels promising, it really has a hold on me and won't let me go until I feel I've done it justice." (Wannabeher, McPherson reveals, is the final version of a song that began 11 years ago.)

"I will say," Gavin adds, "one random tip is writing in motion - walking, driving, rollerblading, anything like that."

That explains why Muna's music always feels propulsive. "If you're not sweating after the first song, come on," laughs McPherson.

With an ever-growing fanbase, they'll play their biggest ever tour this autumn, titled the Gets So Hot Tour after the album's opening track – although the band previously joked it would be called "The Midwest Princess, Midnight Sun and the Eras Tour as Well", before abandoning the idea for copyright reasons.

A decade into their career, they're playing to "crowds we could never have imagined", while witnessing the genre labelled as "queer pop" expand into the mainstream, with artists like Chappell Roan, Renée Rapp, Lil Nas X and Troye Sivan all achieving crossover success.

"I do feel we were at the cusp of the reclamation of the word 'queer'," says Maskin.

"To us, it's actually a celebratory term, because it's inclusive, it includes everybody in the LGBTQI+ community.

"It came from academia first, the idea of queer theory," says McPherson, who admits the band were initially divided on whether to be open about their sexuality.

"We were reticent to come out of the closet in the hipster Pitchfork era of 2010 and 2011. We wanted to be mysterious and be closeted, and Katie was the one who encouraged us not to, and to just be ourselves. And we've only become more ourselves."

Even so, the label can be restrictive. Muna want their music to be universal.

"The subject matter we write about is queer in its essence, and so are our life experiences," says McPherson.

"The issue that we struggle with is wanting that to also be accepted as just a human experience, as well – especially in these times of great repression."

If anyone can do it, Muna can. Just don't let them play for your pets.

This El Niño will be the hottest by a huge margin

New Scientist July 23, 2026

The planet-warming super El Niño now developing will almost certainly be the strongest ever, breaking the record by an unprecedented margin.

Out of hundreds of simulations by 14 forecast models, 90 per cent predict the tropical Pacific will reach a sea surface temperature anomaly that hasn’t been seen in 150 years of observations, according to the California non-profit organisation Berkeley Earth. It is expected to peak at 3.6°C above average, far above the 2.75°C record set in 2015-16.

Zeke Hausfather at Berkeley Earth says this is one of the few times a climate forecast has truly shocked him.

Advertisement

“Even the median of all the models expects we beat the record by 0.8°C,” he said at a media briefing on 23 July. “If this does end up occurring, it really would be record-shattering and unprecedented.”

El Niño happens when easterly winds weaken in the tropics, allowing water they’ve pushed into the Western Pacific Warm Pool to wash back towards the eastern Pacific. Rainfall shifts eastward, weakening easterly winds further in a self-reinforcing feedback loop. Although it’s a natural cycle, it delivers a jolt of heat on top of 1.4°C of global warming, setting off extreme weather around the world, according to Berkeley Earth.

Already, this El Niño is revving up faster than any previous event. Sea surface temperatures in the central-eastern Pacific have reached 2.1°C above average, vastly outpacing the 1.6°C increase seen at this time of year during the 1997-98 El Niño, the previous record-holder for speedy development.

Why El Niño’s impacts on the UK are hard to predict

This “explosive onset” has already put the event in very strong or “super” El Niño territory, only a month after it started. And once you consider that El Niño doesn’t peak until late autumn or winter, it really does look like the world is facing a “Godzilla” El Niño, the name given to those that increase temperatures past a rise of 3°C.

Within a few months, the huge swathe of warm water across the Pacific will heat up the rest of the world. Global temperatures in 2027 are likely to reach 1.7°C above the pre-industrial average, smashing the record set in 2024, when temperatures were 1.5°C above the average. The El Niño is coming on so fast that there’s even a chance 2026 will break that global temperature record first, as some have predicted.

As a result, the 20-year temperature average will likely exceed 1.5°C by 2029, failing the goal set by the Paris Agreement, said Robert Rohde at Berkeley Earth in the briefing.

“We’re already over 1.4°C, so there’s very little margin left,” Rhode said.

Free newsletter

Different regions will see different extreme weather. Densely populated southern China could experience heavy rainfall in the spring and summer, raising the risk of flooding on the Yangtze river, forecasters have warned. The 1997-98 super El Niño caused flooding on the Yangtze that killed more than 3000 people.

The north-eastern US tends to face drier conditions during El Niño, while the southern US gets wetter, which can unleash mudslides in places like California. Australia tends to dry out, raising the threat of bushfires like those seen during the “Black Summer” of 2018-19.

India, southern and central Africa and parts of Central and South America all face drought risks, which could push up the price of commodities like rice, coffee and chocolate even in less-exposed countries like the UK.

How extreme heat affects the body – and the best ways to cope

“We might get lucky and have smaller reduction in rainfall in Africa or India, but generally… the damages scale with the strength of the El Niño,” said Hausfather.

Strong El Niño events also cause harm to ecosystems, such as widespread coral bleaching, which is expected this year as well.

While some research suggests El Niño events are getting stronger, other studies disagree. What is clear is that the impacts will get worse as global warming accelerates.

“It’s something we need to start preparing for today and make sure we have systems in place to deal with drought conditions,” said Hausfather.
