Extremely basic AI prompt cracks decades-old maths problem

New Scientist July 23, 2026

A long-standing mathematical conundrum has been solved by ChatGPT in a few hours, with only a few simple prompts.

The Dinitz-Garg-Goemans conjecture is a 30-year-old question in graph theory, but a counterexample posted on X by Dmitry Rybin, co-founder at AI start-up Autokernel, has shown that it is false.

A golden age of maths is dawning and mathematicians are freaking out

Rybin entered just four prompts into ChatGPT 5.6 Pro: an initial one instructing the AI to “do a breakthrough and find a structured counterexample”, followed by three others simply urging it to continue searching. All four prompts added up to fewer than 60 words, and the AI took a total of 5.5 hours to crack the problem.

Advertisement

Graph theory is the study of networks made up of nodes, or vertices. The Dinitz-Garg-Goemans conjecture can be thought of as a logistical challenge: imagine shipments from a warehouse to multiple locations can be split into much smaller deliveries that can be sent on different routes. The conjecture states that this scenario can be converted into another where shipments cannot be split, and that the total cost of shipping will not increase.

Rybin didn’t respond to a request for comment, but said on X: “I know counterexamples to old conjectures are becoming a meme at this point. But I really cared about this problem and spent many weeks thinking about it.”

Free newsletter

Chris Bowman-Scargill at the University of York, UK, says there’s a running joke in mathematics that every conjecture in graph theory is false, just as the Dinitz-Garg-Goemans conjecture has now been proved to be.

“In fields like number theory or algebra, patterns that hold for small rank [simple situations] often hold for a long time,” says Bownman-Scargill. “Whereas in graph theory, structural behaviour can shift dramatically once you add just one or two vertices… which is how these conjectures continue to be made. You can see how people miss these things.”

AI has made rapid advances in mathematics in recent months. In May, an OpenAI model cracked a decades-old conjecture by Paul Erdős, causing a stir in mathematical circles. Earlier this week, an AI found a counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture, which had stood for nearly a century. Today, other AI users claim to have solved a Graffiti conjecture and a second graph theory problem. A website has even sprung up to catalogue the AI findings and list them by the model that was used.

Mathematics is undergoing the biggest change in its history

Abhishek Saha at Queen Mary University of London says current AI models seem particularly well-suited to problems like the Dinitz-Garg-Goemans conjecture, but there are limits to what is currently possible – and the problems solved by AI so far are of limited complexity.

“AI is really good, and at least at some mathematical tasks, already superhuman,” says Saha. “There is a fair bit of low-hanging fruit out there. Some conjectures can now be proved or disproved by AI with very little human input; the main challenge is simply pointing the system in the right direction. On the other hand, I don’t think AI is yet at a place where it can build the theory needed to prove some of the deepest open conjectures people care about.”

But there are signs that AI is here to stay and will become a vital tool for mathematicians. Alexander Yong at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign says AI’s growing role in mathematics will empower researchers to discard dead ends and instead push in promising directions.

“Counterexamples to old conjectures are never quite as impressive as finding a sequence of interlocking arguments that constitute a proof,” says Yong. “However, I’d expect that AI will soon prove many conjectures by a combination of their inherent superhuman energy in knowing the literature and trying many things at a prompt. Those conjectures that survive AI scrutiny will be the genuine goals for human innovation.”

One of NASA’s crucial links to deep space is at risk of burning down

New Scientist July 24, 2026

NASA’s ability to communicate with its distant spacecraft is in jeopardy. We send commands to spacecraft beyond Earth’s orbit and receive data from them using the Deep Space Network (DSN), which consists of three enormous sets of radio antennae: one in California, one in Spain and one in Australia. A wildfire has consumed the area around the radio dishes in Spain, and the level of damage to the facility itself is not yet clear.

UN space database aimed at easing global tensions is mysteriously down

Wildfires have been raging across Europe all month, driven by a heat wave and intense droughts. On 24 July, a fire near Madrid intensified and burned through the Madrid Deep Space Communications Complex (MDSCC) in the town of Robledo de Chavela. This is “the worst fire in the history of the region”, said Madrid’s regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso, and Robledo and surrounding areas were evacuated.

According to a statement from NASA, all employees at MDSCC were able to evacuate safely, but the antennae themselves have not been evaluated yet. “Any potential damage will be assessed when it is safe to do so,” the statement reads.

Advertisement

Damage to the dishes in Spain could be disastrous for NASA. The DSN is already drastically oversubscribed, which slows down the process of getting commands to spacecraft and data back down from them. With one dish out of commission, this problem could get even worse – and with the Artemis lunar programme just ramping up, demand is only going to increase. If the oversubscription gets severe enough, it’s possible that some data will never make it back to Earth.

The other problem comes from the way the three stations of the DSN are set up. “These stations are designed to cover about a third of the sky, such that at any given time we can use two to track and communicate with spacecraft way out beyond Earth’s orbit,” says Paul Byrne at Washington University in Missouri. “As a function of geometry, there will now be times of the day when certain spacecraft are out of touch when they otherwise wouldn’t have been.” That is particularly a problem for extremely distant spacecraft, such as Voyager 1 and 2.

According to the NASA statement, for the time being, “the agency has seamlessly transitioned support for mission operations to the Goldstone Deep Space Communications Complex in California, ensuring continuity of service and uninterrupted support for spacecraft communications”.

That is a temporary bandage on the problem, though, and it is inevitable that if MDSCC were damaged, there would be effects on spacecraft. “This isn’t great,” says Byrne.

Clothes made from living fungi can clean and repair themselves

New Scientist July 24, 2026

A parasitic fungus that grows on caterpillars has been turned into a dress designed to be able to repair itself if damaged.

In the video game and TV series The Last of Us, Cordyceps fungi evolve to infect humans and turn them into zombies, but in reality they are harmless to humans.

How our ancestors used mushrooms to change the course of human history

Using the fungus Cordyceps militaris as a base, Ke Li at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and her colleagues created a living textile that can be “programmed” with different properties using various microbial components.

Advertisement

It feels denser and less fibrous than cotton, says Li, and is closer to a soft, non-woven sheet or a flexible leather-like material.

“After washing and processing, the material does not have a strong mushroom-like smell,” she says. “A slight biological or fermentation-related odour may be detectable in freshly prepared samples, but this can be greatly reduced through cleaning, drying and post-treatment.”

Free newsletter

The fungus is made up of thin filaments known as hyphae. Li and her colleagues first grew the fungus as small, spherical pellets in liquid culture, then washed them and placed them into moulds where they formed a sheet.

To prevent the resulting textile from becoming brittle, it was soaked in glycerol, which acts as a “plasticiser”, making the naturally rigid fungal structure softer and more flexible.

“We do not use a conventional fabric, polymer mesh or other external supporting scaffold,” says Li. “The Cordyceps militaris mycelial pellets themselves serve as the structural building blocks, and their intertwined hyphae form a continuous, self-supporting sheet.”

To add colour to the material, the team introduced yeast cells that were engineered to produce orange, blue and purple pigments. “These cells can be applied to the fungal textile so that the colour is generated biologically, rather than through conventional synthetic dyes,” says Li.

The researchers also showed they could change the properties of the textile by adding other fungi, for example making it clean itself by repelling water droplets. For UV protection, they added Aspergillus niger, a mould that commonly grows on fruit and vegetables. This forms a dark layer on the surface of the material containing melanin pigment, which absorbs ultraviolet radiation.

How our ancestors invented clothing and transformed it into fashion

If the textile is damaged, then fresh, wet fungal pellets can be applied to the area that needs repair and the fungus simply grows over the breach.

Under dry conditions, most biological activity is greatly reduced, and the cells may remain inactive or dormant, says Li.

But under humid conditions with nutrients present, some cells can become active again. This latent biological capacity is what enables functions such as regrowth and repair, and also means that the material is readily biodegradable, showing near-complete visible degradation in soil after just over 40 days.

Li and her colleagues created a dress out of their fungal material, but so far no one has worn it. “We’ve treated it as a rather precious display piece, and it was made in a small size,” she says. “Perhaps next time we should find a few petite and adventurous volunteers to try it on and see how it looks in motion.”

Justin Beardsley at the University of Sydney, Australia, says the biodegradability of the dress is amazing compared with what we currently have in terms of getting rid of waste from fast fashion.

But that is also a drawback because you don’t really want to be wearing something that is too easily biodegradable, as “it’ll break down while you’re wearing it”, he says.

As the textile is alive, Beardsley envisages one day being able to change its qualities in real time. “If there was some way that you can make it water-repellent for a while, becoming less breathable during rain, that would be fantastic, and then you can revert to the more breathable, less water-repellent version afterward,” he says.

Earth is heating up faster than at any time in its history

New Scientist July 24, 2026

As Europe bakes in what could be its hottest and driest summer on record, the rapid transformation of our climate is harder than ever to ignore. But how much hotter will it get, and what will that mean for life on Earth?

To get a picture of our future, we can either use computer models or look to episodes of rapid climate change in the geological record. While models are invaluable in terms of tracking where our world may be heading, peering back into deep time provides unrivalled information about cause and effect; about how the climate has changed in the past and what the consequences were. There is no guesswork involved, as the evidence is all laid out for us in the sediments and rocks, in the ice sheets and in the remains of ancient life.

Europe’s heatwave is the hottest and most humid ever

Looking back in time also helps us to put human-caused global heating in context by making comparisons with past episodes of rapid temperature increase, and when we do this, the news isn’t good. It isn’t so much the degree of heat that is the issue – our world has been much hotter than it is today for much of its 4.6-billion-year history – but the speed of change.

Advertisement

Perhaps barring the immediate aftermath of the dinosaur-obliterating asteroid impact 66 million years ago, atmospheric carbon dioxide levels have never risen as quickly as they have in the last couple of centuries. Even worse, nowhere in the geological record is there evidence for the average temperature of our world climbing as quickly as it is now. This means 10 times faster than during the Palaeocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum, which marked extreme hothouse conditions 56 million years ago, and at least 20 times faster than at the end of the last glacial period.

Judicious analysis of past climates also permits us to recognise potential analogues for where our world is heading in the decades and centuries to come. Over the last 50 million years or so, the planet’s climate has followed a broadly cooling trend, which we are now rapidly rewinding – a process, if you like, of prehistorification. Deciding how far back we will end up is still within our gift, but it is a given that our grandchildren will grow up in a climate different to any experienced during the tenure of human civilisation.

Free newsletter

Modelling studies suggest that if – and it’s still a big if – emissions peak by 2040 and then fall quickly, we will rewind the climate clock 3 million years and bequeath to our descendants a Late Pliocene climate. Then, atmospheric CO2 levels were much lower than today, at 330 to 400 parts per million (ppm), but the temperature was between 2.5ºC and 4ºC above the pre-industrial average, and sea level 15 to 25 metres higher. Pliocene conditions could start to appear in the continental heartlands as soon as the 2030s and spread out from there.

If we fail to rein in emissions fast enough, or if natural feedback effects drive more heating than expected, then a further rewinding of the climate clock back to the Miocene becomes more likely; to a time 15 million to 17 million years ago, when CO2 concentrations, at 400 to 600 ppm, were a bit lower to moderately higher than they are today. At 6ºC to 8ºC above the 1800s, however, the temperature was far higher than expected for such CO2 levels, suggesting the involvement of other heating factors that we don’t yet fully understand. Sea level was maybe 50 metres higher than it is today.

Collapse of AMOC ocean current may already be locked in

But this may not be the end of it. The current high rate of heating documented by satellite observations and borne out by Earth’s rapidly escalating energy imbalance implies that rewinding the climate clock back fully 50 million years remains within the bounds of possibility, eventually reprising the blistering heat of the early Eocene hothouse. Such conditions would make most of our world uninhabitable for humans, and severely test the capacity of our species to prevail.

As the Persian poet and mathematician Omar Khayyam observed almost 1000 years ago: “When I want to understand what is happening today, or try to decide what will happen tomorrow, I look back.” They are words that serve us well as we contemplate our future climate, and that we ignore at our peril.

Bill McGuire is professor emeritus of geophysical and climate hazards at University College London. His book, The Fate of the World: A history and future of the climate crisis, is published by HarperNorth.

Having a young biological age could help with weight loss

Being biologically younger than your actual age may lower your risk of heart disease, cancer and dementia. A new discovery suggests it may also aid with weight loss, possibly by making the body more efficient at switching from using food for energy to using stored fat.

In February, a review of existing research concluded that intermittent fasting – such as the 5:2 diet, where you eat as normal on five days a week and restrict calories on the other two – is probably no more effective for weight loss than doing nothing at all. But fasting can also involve eating no, or very little, food for a single, continuous stretch of time, which is sometimes done for religious reasons.

There are only a few anti-ageing supplements that actually work

Focusing on this type of fasting, Steve Horvath at the University of California, Los Angeles, and his colleagues recruited 32 volunteers with no known health conditions, who consumed just 200 to 250 calories a day in the form of fruit juice, vegetable broths and honey for 12 days. “This is not something to try at home,” says Horvath. “It was a medically supervised inpatient programme at a specialist clinic, with clinical monitoring throughout.”

Advertisement

These calories were consumed in three windows: 7am to 9am, 11.30am to 1pm and 6.30pm to 8pm. This put the participants – who were aged between 25 and 72 – in a fasting metabolic state, says team member Robin Mesnage at King’s College London, which occurs when the body shifts from burning energy from food to energy stored in the body.

The team used 12 different epigenetic clocks to estimate and track the volunteers’ biological ages over the course of the study. These mostly work by looking at patterns of chemical tags on DNA, which change in predictable ways with age, but can also be altered by our lifestyle, such as how much we exercise.

Free newsletter

The clocks varied in their responses to the fast. Some ticked upwards to an older age, suggesting that the extreme fast put negative stress on the body. But one clock, which was built to detect changes in body mass index, went down.

Incongruous results are a known issue between different epigenetic clocks. But one finding was fairly consistent: the participants who were generally deemed to have a young biological age, relative to their chronological age, at the start of the study lost more weight than those who were biologically older.

The researchers weren’t expecting this result, according to Hovarth. “Honestly, we don’t know the mechanism,” he says. But he thinks the most likely explanation is that biologically younger people have better metabolic adaptability, which means they can swiftly switch from using food for energy to stored fat when calories are scarce.

This is plausible, because biologically younger people tend to have more efficient mitochondria, which leads to faster switching to fat burning, says Paulina Correa-Burrows at the University of Chile.

A clinical trial to reverse age-related vision conditions using stem cell treatment could finally deliver on the promise of a major discovery in ageing and regeneration made 20 years ago, says columnist Graham Lawton

Biologically younger people may also have better pathways for sensing nutrients in cells, which could also enable more efficient switching between fuel sources to burn fat. But Correa-Burrows cautions that the group of volunteers was small, so the results are inconclusive.

Horvath now wants to see investigations into whether biologically younger people also lose more weight under less restrictive diets. “A 12-day medically supervised fast is not a long-term diet and it isn’t meant to be one,” he says.

In the meantime, a healthy lifestyle can help lower our biological age. “The habits with the strongest evidence for healthy epigenetic aging are the familiar ones: do not smoke, [do] physical exercise, keep a healthy body weight and maintain good relationships,” says Hovarth.

Do not change your diet without first speaking to a doctor.

10 of the best pictures of solar eclipses throughout history

New Scientist July 24, 2026

A total eclipse occurs somewhere in the world about once every 18 months on average, and that has been the case for all of human history. For millennia, humans have been documenting their views as the moon moved between Earth and the sun, blocking out the sun’s light and revealing its swirling outer layers.

The earliest confirmed written record of a solar eclipse comes from the 13th century BC, when scribes in China wrote that the sun had been “eaten”. Scientific and religious texts continued to document eclipses up until the present day, and researchers now use these texts to study both how eclipses have changed in the intervening centuries and how human views of them have evolved throughout time. This particular petroglyph, carved into stone by the early Pueblo people in New Mexico, is thought to represent a total solar eclipse that occurred on 11 July 1097. The swirls around its perimeter bear a resemblance to the corona of the sun, which is only visible when the moon hides the rest of the solar disc.

More recent art depicts religious and scientific figures observing eclipses directly. This watercolour from the late 17th century shows a group of French missionaries observing a solar eclipse with King Narai of Siam and his court in April 1688. They can be seen using the projection method to avoid looking directly at the sun: the light passes through a telescope and projects the shape of the eclipse on a screen beneath it. This technique is still commonly used today, with pinhole cameras or even just the gaps between shadows cast by leaves on the ground.

Advertisement

Scientific sketches of eclipses proliferated as science became more of a formal, professionalised pursuit. This drawing, by astronomer José Joaquín de Ferrer, depicts an eclipse that occurred over New York on 16 June 1806. Watching this event led de Ferrer to give the outermost layer of the sun, the corona, its name. He was among the first people reported to have hypothesised that the corona must be part of the sun, not the moon, because of its incredible size – it can stretch to as much as 20 times the width of the main disc of the sun, as he sketched here.

The first photograph of a total solar eclipse with enough detail on the corona to be scientifically useful was taken on 28 July 1851 by Julius Berkowski at the Royal Observatory in Königsberg, Prussia. With help from the astronomers at the observatory, he attached a small telescope to a device called a heliometer, a specialised instrument for measuring the sun. This daguerreotype was an 84-second exposure taken through the telescope. Not only is the corona visible, but several eruptions can be seen blasting from the sides of the sun over the edge of the moon.

After Berkowski’s image, the ability to take photographs of eclipses became more widespread around the world. These images were taken by William and Frederick Langenheim on 26 May 1854 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Without access to the scientific tools Berkowski used to magnify the light from the eclipse, they were forced to use small cameras to create these miniature daguerreotypes, the largest of which is just 7.2 centimetres tall and the smallest less than half that size.

The total solar eclipse that swept over parts of Africa and South America on 29 May 1919 proved to be one of the most important eclipses ever observed. This image comes from the expedition that astronomer Arthur Eddington made to the African island of Principe. He and his team photographed several stars located close to the sun to compare their apparent positions in the sky before and then during the eclipse. In this image, the stars are marked with horizontal lines. The comparison proved that the gravity of the sun bent the light coming from those stars, providing some of the first evidence for Albert Einstein’s theory of general relativity and creating a new understanding of the workings of the universe.

Eclipses became popular photographic targets for scientists and non-scientific photographers alike. This image, taken by Frederick Goetz on 24 January 1925, shows an effect called the diamond ring, or Baily’s beads. This effect occurs just at the beginning and end of totality, when the edge of the moon is nearly, but not quite, covering the entire disc of the sun. Ridges and craters on the moon’s surface let through only a few rays of sunlight, creating the glare that earned Goetz’s inscription of “Signs and Wonders”.

Modern images of solar eclipses, such as this one taken in California on 11 July 1991, display the corona in much more detail than has ever been achievable before. Past observations revealed an astonishing mystery: the corona is about 300 times hotter than the sun’s surface. Eclipses provide prime opportunities to try to figure out how and why it gets so hot, plus research how we might be able to predict solar activity someday to mitigate its potential effects on satellites, astronauts and even electrical grids on Earth.

The sun itself is, of course, not the only thing that researchers study during eclipses. As seen in this image taken in Chile on 2 July 2019, during a total solar eclipse the sky darkens almost completely. Temperatures drop precipitously. Birdsong ceases almost entirely. Through studying how animals react, researchers try to decipher what they may be feeling and thinking, and how they perceive the unexpected darkness.

When viewing an eclipse from the ground, it can be hard to imagine the scale of it. These images of an 8 April 2024 eclipse, taken by NASA’s Deep Space Climate Observatory (DSCOVR) satellite, show that handily. The dark spot moving across the planet in these pictures is the shadow of the moon. People standing within that spot witness totality, and those along the edges see only partial eclipses.

Our ability to image and understand these phenomena has come a long way since petroglyphs in stone walls – imagine what we’ll be able to see in another few thousand years.

Most neurons seem to be jacks-of-all-trades, not specialists

New Scientist July 24, 2026

For decades, scientists have been discovering neurons with seemingly unique jobs. There are place cells that fire in response to a particular location, mirror neurons that may help us interpret behaviours and even neurons that respond to all things Jennifer Aniston. These discoveries have encouraged a picture of the brain as a collection of highly specialised cells.

But a new discovery suggests that most neurons are actually jacks-of-all-trades. “These [earlier] neurons are really the exception, not the rule,” says Stefano Fusi at Columbia University in New York. And the more abundant, generalised cells “can be as important or more important than the good-looking [specialist] neurons we isolated in the past”, he says.

How healthy is your brain? We now know how to find out

In a 2013 study, Fusi noticed “mixed selectivity” neurons – cells that respond to multiple different task-related inputs at the same time – in the brains of monkeys. But it was unclear how widespread they are in the mammalian brain.

Advertisement

Now, Fusi and his team have turned to the International Brain Laboratory. This holds information on the activity of individual neurons throughout the brains of more than 100 mice while they did a decision-making task. The task involved the mice looking for an image on the left or right side of a screen and moving it to the centre by quickly turning a wheel.

The researchers found that the only areas with specialised neurons were those in dedicated sensory cortices, such as the primary visual cortex. Instead, the neurons in most areas of the brain responded to various aspects of the task. For instance, those outside of the visual cortex also seemed to be involved in processing the image, as well as deciding which side of the screen it was on and generating the movement to turn the wheel. “The important thing to stress is that there are specialised neurons [such as place cells],” says Fusi. But these are not the norm, he adds.

Free newsletter

The researchers also found that most neurons didn’t respond in the same way to the same stimulus. For example, the somatomotor areas, which are regions associated with planning movements, responded strongly to licks and whisker movements. Other areas still responded, but not as strongly. This suggests that while specialism exists, individual neurons generally aren’t myopically focused on one type of information.

“The problem is if you’re arguing there’s no [specialisation], somebody can always say: ‘You just needed [to study] a few more neurons [to uncover it],’” says Ben Hayden at Baylor College of Medicine in Texas. “This [study] is a giant smack in the face saying: ‘Fine, we got 14,000 neurons and we still didn’t find it [for the most part].’”

Having a collection of neurons that respond to the same stimulus in slightly different ways may maximise the amount of information the brain can process. This may mean that these generalised neurons contribute to a plethora of tasks, including memory, cognition, decision-making and perception.

Around a third of people are able to almost fully rebuild their brains after a stroke and uncovering why is pointing the way to better treatments for everyone

The researchers point out that the mice’s task wasn’t particularly complex. A complicated, multidimensional set of tasks could shed light on when individual neurons focus their responses on one aspect of such tasks versus another, says Fusi.

He and his team are now collaborating with researchers who study non-human primates and patients who are conscious during open brain surgeries, such as those treating epilepsy, to see if the findings in mice apply to people.

With all these projects, Fusi hopes to shift the emphasis from looking at the role of individual neurons to patterns of activity across many cells in the brain. “It’s very difficult to draw conclusions by looking at one neuron at the time,” he says. “Instead, we [should] look at all the neurons together. That’s the perspective of the brain because each neuron in the brain doesn’t [get input from] one single [other] neuron. Each neuron in the brain looks at 10,000 other neurons that are connected on its dendritic tree.”

Nature DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10668-4

We now know how a black hole can be flung across the universe

New Scientist July 24, 2026

Two supermassive black holes smashing together can create another supermassive black hole that recoils at such high speeds that it launches out of its galaxy. Though this would only happen in rare instances, it provides an explanation for the recent possible sighting of such a runaway black hole.

In 2023, researchers noticed a thin, line-like shape in an image that the Hubble Space Telescope took of a patch of space about 7.5 billion light years from Earth. Based on further analysis, including images from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and studying the line’s light, Pieter van Dokkum at Yale University and his colleagues concluded that the line was a consequences of a never-before-seen cosmic event – a supermassive black hole flying out of a galaxy at supersonic speeds and leaving a chain of young stars in its wake.

Not everyone agrees with this analysis, but Tousif Islam at the University of California, Santa Barbara and his colleagues have now uncovered what it would take for a supermassive black hole to behave this way.

Advertisement

This physicist is hunting for the biggest black hole in the universe

Informed by observations and large-scale simulations of the universe, the team built a mathematical model that could take the idea and properties of a runaway black hole (RBH) and reveal its origin story. “It’s similar to fossil analysis, we are working backwards to see what the past looked like,” says team member Digvijay Wadekar at the University of Texas at Austin.

The team found that an RBH like the one posited by van Dokkum and his colleagues would have had two parent supermassive black holes, where one was spinning quickly and was six times more massive than the other. These would have violently merged about 70 million years ago, creating a recoiling RBH.

“When we do simulations of binary black hole mergers… almost every time there is a recoil kick, but in most of the cases the recoil kick is much smaller,” says Islam. The team estimated that a large enough recoil to match the proposed RBH could happen in fewer than 10 per cent of black hole mergers.

“As a mathematical exercise, it’s very interesting, because the physical mechanism to produce a runaway supermassive black hole is there. Now, the chances that this happens in reality are very low,” says Jorge Sánchez Almeida at the Institute of Astrophysics of the Canary Islands in Spain.

Since 2023, he and his colleagues have argued for a less exotic interpretation of the original images. According to their analysis, the line represents a galaxy, full of star-forming regions, viewed edge-on.

Free newsletter

Analysing light from these regions is subtle and it can easily be mistaken for a consequence of a fast-moving RBH, says Sánchez Almeida. He says that several other measurements are consistent with the edge-on galaxy interpretation, including the relationship between the mass of the stars and their rotational velocity, which fits the Tully-Fisher relation, a known fingerprint of a disc-shaped galaxy.

The team, however, stands by the RBH view. “There are competing explanations and this seems like the least unfavourable, or you can call it most favourable,” says Wadekar. Islam says that he learned about the RBH when his university hosted a conference about black holes, and it was speaking with astronomers there that convinced him that its existence and past were compelling to study.

This debate could be resolved by future observations. Sánchez Almeida says that the JWST already has the capability to image this region of space further and definitively identify the edge-on galaxy. The team wants to use its model to predict gravitational waves that the merger of RBH’s parents would have produced, which could be detected by near-term instruments such as the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA), says Islam.

There are only a few anti-ageing supplements that actually work

New Scientist July 24, 2026

I’m a big fan of the New Scientist podcast Change Your Mind, on which my erstwhile colleagues Cat de Lange and Helen Thomson discuss “all the brain health advice you really need to know”. One recent episode is well worth a listen if you’re interested in keeping your brain healthy. Cat and Helen invited JoAnn Manson, who is head of preventive medicine at Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Massachusetts, to the podcast to discuss her research on multivitamin supplements and brain health. She described how she and her colleagues found that people over 60 who take a daily multivitamin show significantly slower cognitive decline and age-related memory loss over two to three years.

The only four skincare ingredients that have been proven to work

For me, that was a marmalade dropper. On the issue of supplements, I’m a hardened sceptic. Based on a New Scientist feature I edited many years ago, as well as a recent update by another ex-colleague, Alison George, my informed opinion is that very few supplements work and some are positively harmful. I make an exception for vitamin D because I live too far north to make enough on my own from the feeble winter sunshine. But once the clocks have gone forward, I stop taking it. I would also take folic acid if I were female and trying for a baby (I’m neither), long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids if I didn’t eat oily fish weekly and vitamin B12 if I were a vegan. But as for the rest, I don’t waste my money.

For people who are willing to shell out for supplements, there are myriad opportunities. One of the thriving markets is in anti-ageing. Although very few if any have been scientifically validated, I’m slightly less sceptical. A few years ago, I took an anti-ageing supplement called alpha-ketoglutarate for six months for a story I was doing. I had my biological age measured before and after, and it went down. But that is hardly solid data of the sort you get from a clinical trial.

Advertisement

Of that, there is plenty, and it doesn’t cast anti-ageing supplements in a good light. I found a gold mine of information in an academic book published earlier this year called Supplements and Drugs for Healthy Longevity. Under the guidance of the eminent biogerontologist Suresh Rattan at Aarhus University in Denmark, an expert panel rated the evidence for more than 250 compounds with supposed anti-ageing effects. These ranged from vitamins and minerals to plant extracts, traditional medicines, probiotics and hormone supplements, plus some much-hyped compounds I often hear bigged up in anti-ageing circles: NAD+, coenzyme Q10, spermidine and D&Q, or dasatinib and quercetin. Interestingly, they didn’t look at the evidence for alpha-ketoglutarate.

Suffice to say that none of them met the highest standard of evidence, which Rattan defines as “solid, reproducible and trustworthy”. A few reached a secondary level, but, on the whole, the authors recommend obtaining these compounds from food. “At present using one or more nutritional and other supplements… is mostly an act of faith and hope”, rather than being based on strong scientific evidence-based data, the book concludes.

Suddenly feeling old? Evidence now suggests that rather than a long, steady decline, we dramatically age around three specific times in our lives. Might it be possible to stay younger for longer?

But it also says that more research is needed. So, I had a look at Manson’s. Her results come from a clinical trial she and her colleagues ran between 2015 and 2023 called COSMOS (Cocoa Supplement and Multivitamin Outcomes Study). The trial recruited more than 21,000 people aged over 60 and gave one group of them a daily multivitamin plus cocoa extract, which contains flavonoid compounds thought to be beneficial for some age-related conditions. Other groups received just a multivitamin, just cocoa extract or nothing. The principal goal of the trial was to test whether the multivitamin/cocoa cocktail would reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease and cancer. It didn’t, but the researchers still found nuggets of useful information in the data.

One of these was the effect on brain health, as discussed on the podcast. Another, which was published earlier this year, looked at the effect on ageing in general. A subgroup of 958 participants had their biological age measured at the start of the trial and then again two years later. Those who received the daily multivitamin aged, on average, more slowly than those who did not (the cocoa extract had no effect). The effect was relatively modest – a month or two over the two years – but over the course of longer periods that could really add up.

Free newsletter

Another study adds weight to the idea that supplements can slow down ageing. Last year, a team including researchers at the University of Zurich in Switzerland published a study on omega-3 fatty acid supplementation in people aged 70 to 91. The traditional verdict on these supplements has been that they aren’t worth taking unless your diet is deficient in the main sources of omega-3, which are oily fish, flaxseed, chia seeds and walnuts. The Zurich research challenges that. Over the course of three years, the people who took the supplement aged biologically three months less, on average, than those who took a placebo. Adding vitamin D and strength training increased the benefit to four months.

So, have I changed my mind about supplements? Not yet. Both studies rely on biological age measurements, which are notoriously unreliable. Neither found any meaningful change in the health of their participants, and slowing down biological ageing doesn’t necessarily correspond to what really matters: an increase in healthspan. It is also possible, Manson told the podcast, that the participants in her study were deficient in one or more vitamins, and the multivitamin supplement merely corrected for that.

But it’s a start. As Daniel Belsky and Calen Ryan at Columbia University in New York wrote in response to the multivitamin study, “Evidence that simple multi-vitamin supplementation can slow aging, even slightly, would have substantial implications, including for public health guidelines.” We’re not quite there yet, but if and when we are, I’m heading to the pharmacy.

Magnesium has been called the “super mineral of the moment”, hailed for its supposed benefits for the brain and body. But columnist Alice Klein finds that the evidence is lacking for many of these claims

Flaxmere family of 11-year-old Emma-Jane Kupa ‘relieved’ as driver denied parole

New Zealand Herald July 25, 2026

Emma-Jane Kupa's (right) family felt relief after Terina Pineaha (left) was denied parole for killing their daughter. The woman has been sent to prison for more than four years for her manslaughter. Photos / Rafaella Melo/RNZ/Supplied

The mother of 11-year-old Emma-Jane Kupa says her family felt “relief” when they learned the driver jailed for killing their daughter had been denied parole.

But their fight for what they believe is a tougher justice system is far from over.

Terina Pineaha was sentenced to four years and five months in prison in July last year after pleading guilty to the manslaughter of Emma-Jane, who was killed while cycling along Chatham Rd in Flaxmere on January 30, 2025.

Pineaha had been drinking, using methamphetamine and driving at nearly twice the speed limit on the wrong side of the road when she struck Emma-Jane.

She also admitted dangerous driving, excess breath alcohol, failing to stop and wilful damage.

On Thursday, mother Shannon Davis, father George Kupa and two of their sons travelled from Hawke’s Bay to Wellington for Pineaha’s parole hearing.

The hearing came two weeks after what would have been Emma-Jane’s 13th birthday, on July 10.

Davis said returning for another stage of the justice process was “emotional”.

“We wanted to go there to have our say to make sure she doesn’t get out,” Davis said.

Pineaha was not present at the hearing.

The family travelled back to Hastings without knowing whether she would be released.

About 4pm, shortly after they arrived home, a phone call brought the news they had been waiting for: parole had been declined.

“We were in pain. It was a relief.”

The New Zealand Parole Board said its decision was not yet publicly available and that Pineaha’s next hearing was scheduled for July next year.

“We’re just happy knowing she will remain in prison for now,” Davis said.

“Every time she applies for parole, we’ll be there to make sure that she does not get out. To make sure that she serves her time in prison.

“No matter what, I will continue to fight for my baby.”

Davis said the sentence remained a source of anger.

“Four years and five months for a child’s life? A child’s life here in New Zealand doesn’t matter.”

The family, who had been campaigning for change since Pineaha was sentenced, launched a 5000-signature petition calling for action over what they claim was an inadequate prison term.

The campaign was not only about Emma-Jane.

“I don’t want another family to go through the same thing that we are.”

Emma-Jane’s two brothers, now aged 18 and 8, travelled with their parents to Wellington for the hearing.

Her youngest son still did not fully understand what had happened, and became upset when his parents did not explain why the family was at the hearing.

Davis said they were trying to protect him until they felt the time was right.

“My baby, he does have nightmares about it, and I just don’t want to trigger anything.”

Emma-Jane was riding her bike alongside her older sister, who was on a scooter, when she was struck.

At Pineaha’s sentencing last year, Davis told the court her older daughter was left with the memory of the screeching tyres and seeing her sister being hit.

She said her daughter would always be remembered as “just a beautiful innocent girl”.

“Forever 11.”

Rafaella Melo has more than 10 years of experience as a journalist in Brazil. She has worn many hats, from radio and TV presenter and producer to magazine editor before joining the Hawke’s Bay Today team as a multimedia journalist.

Backbencher pub-owner Alistair Boyce to stand for NZ First in Hutt South

New Zealand Herald July 25, 2026

Outspoken Backbencher pub owner Alistair Boyce is running for Parliament for New Zealand First, saying society has become too uptight. Photo / Ethan Manera

Wellington publican Alistair Boyce has spent his career “taking the piss” out of politicians, now the Backbencher pub-owner wants to cross Molesworth St and become one himself.

The self-styled raconteur and satirist has announced he’s running for New Zealand First in the hard-fought Hutt South seat, although admits he’s “probably not” going to make it into Parliament.

“But I’m doing it for the right reasons”, 60-year-old Boyce tells the Herald, sipping a pint in the dockway of the famous political haunt.

Business is tough, the “lanyard class” is destroying Wellington, and society has become too uptight, he believes.

“You’ve got to remember, being offended is a choice,” Boyce said.

“I called Jenny Shipley ‘Jenny the Squid’, it was a calamari dish but Jenny was really upset. I used to call politicians on the dessert menu tarts.”

Asked if he stands by his past inflammatory remarks, Boyce is unapologetic.

“I’m not going to be scared of calling someone a tart or two,” Boyce, or “Boycie” as he’s known, said.

It is not his first attempt at politics: in 2023 he threw his hat in the ring for the National Party candidacy for Wellington Central, but ultimately lost to lawyer Scott Sheeran.

During candidate selection, Boyce said he was asked by National Party officials about his stances on issues like co-governance and mainstream media, and that was the moment he realised he was no longer aligned with National.

“I thought I was in a conservative style party, I wasn’t - I was in a centrist to even centre left party, so it wasn’t the fit.”

Socially he’s conservative, but economically interventionist, making New Zealand First a natural fit.

“The markets aren’t working,” he declares, taking a sip of his Steinlager, a beer he’s been drinking since age 14 when working at the Kings Cross Hotel Cobb & Co.

“I‘m all about breaking up the power companies, breaking up the banks, breaking up the supermarkets, even extending [it] to the insurance monopoly.”

Things have simply got too expensive for most people, Boyce said, noting he himself can only afford third party insurance for his car, a purply-blue 1999 Saab.

After ditching National, Boyce became involved in heading up the controversial Better Wellington campaign group for last year’s local body elections.

The group, led by Ray Chung, became embroiled in scandal after an earlier unsavoury email sent by Chung about Tory Whanau became public, sparking widespread condemnation.

“We had no idea about Ray’s email and his description of those events and Tory. Ray’s a very sincere and naïve politician and we couldn’t correct that,” he believes.

Boyce is comfortable labelling the email - which detailed gossip about the former mayor’s sex life - as sexist, and admits there were other moments during the chaotic campaign that “crossed a line”.

Asked about a social media post by the group that likened another councillor to “mental, extreme communist trans-loving ... Green Party retards”, Boyce said he did not approve, calling it “unnecessarily offensive”.

“I wouldn’t put retards on a menu because I want them to eat the food,” he laughs.

There is a line, he insists, “I just don’t think that should be in the lexicon of normal conversation”.

Asked about some of his would-be colleagues’ controversial comments, Boyce has mixed views.

Shane Jones’ “butter chicken tsunami” line? “really funny”, he says.

Jones’ knee pads remark? Fine, Boyce says, “that appeals to me as a satirist [...] his oratory is unmatched.”

This week’s Stuart Nash text? Boyce takes a more diplomatic approach, “it’s not for me to say” he says.

The typically forthcoming and opinionated Boyce would not be pushed for a view, “I’m going to plead the fifth on this one, you can quote me on that ‘Boycie pleads the fifth.’”

He is perhaps reluctant to fall offside with Winston Peters, who he compares to Jesus Christ when parting crowds at the Parliament anti-mandate occupation in 2022 (though it was Moses who parted the Red Sea in the Bible).

Boyce is less concerned about ruffling feathers with his opponents in the Hutt South electorate, declaring Chris Bishop seems “a bit sad”, and appears to have “given up” on the race, after Bishop told reporters this week it it would be ”highly unlikely" he would retain his electorate seat on current polling.

Ginny Andersen, Boyce believes, is “probably ahead” in the race, but not being from the Hutt counts against her.

“She’s from Waiheke,” he claims. “I’m a Hutt boy - at least Bish is a Hutt boy.”

Anderson moved to the Hutt at age 26 from Christchurch, but told the Herald she has never lived on Waiheke.

“Hutt is my home,” Boyce says, adding he would move back there from his actual home in Khandallah if elected.

While less operationally involved in the pub these days, which he helped set up in 1990, Boyce spends most of his days at his coffee roastery in the Ngaio Gorge.

“I’m not thinking that I can necessarily win out in the Hutt,” Boyce concedes.

Asked if he was instead expecting to be elected on the party’s list, he says “probably not”.

On the chance he is elected, he promises not to turn the famous Backbencher into an unofficial New Zealand First headquarters.

“I always wanted it as a neutral space, all politicians should be safe here.”

Ethan Manera is a Wellington-based journalist covering Wellington issues, local politics and business in the capital. He can be emailed at ethan. manera@nzme. co. nz.

Mortuary makeup: Inside the art, science and tricks of makeup for the dead

New Zealand Herald July 25, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Foundation, fillers, orange peel and tints are part of the toolkit used by morticians to make dead bodies look more lifelike. Jane Phare investigates the secrets of mortuary cosmetology.

There’s no escaping the death of an elderly family member. The hours, sometimes days, spent in a family vigil, waiting for the final, drawn-out breath. And when that comes, there is just stillness, a sallow, sunken complexion and an open mouth. Nothing like the mother, father or elderly relative you have known and loved all your life.

We were all there in Tauranga Hospital to farewell an elderly family member last year. A week later, we gathered at Purewa Cemetery in Auckland to meet the funeral director who had driven her up from Tauranga.

He slid back the coffin lid so the family could say a last goodbye, and there she was, transformed. She looked pretty and sweet, as though taking a peaceful nap before popping out for a high tea. Her makeup and pink lipstick were perfect, her hair neatly styled, her dress immaculate.

Elise Williams, from Hope Family Funerals in Tauranga, is pleased to hear that. She was most likely responsible for the result.

Williams, 35, has been a funeral director, specialising in makeup, for the past four years, leaving behind a 12-year career as a beautician.

“I had always wanted to be a funeral director because it’s such a special time for families.”

When Williams was 12, she lost three close family members within two years. She remembers that time, meeting new relatives and learning about the childhoods and early lives of those she’d known only as elderly.

“It was really special. It ends up being a bit of a family reunion sometimes.”

Williams has a Bachelor of Social Work but, after joining Hope Funerals, trained on the job. She’ll often ask the bereaved family for a photograph of their loved one so she can get the details correct, including how they like their makeup done and which side their hair is normally parted.

Older women often don’t wear much makeup so she’s careful not to overdo the look, she says. And she uses a less-is-more routine with men, sticking to moisturiser and adding light foundation only if necessary.

“If it is some Kiwi bloke, you certainly don’t want him looking like he’s all covered in makeup.”

Some families elect not to have the body embalmed - there are no rules saying they have to. At Fountains the “professional fee” is the same, whether or not the body is embalmed and has makeup done.

Some other funeral homes charge separately for embalming and makeup. Funeral costs can range from $3000 for cremation up to tens of thousands of dollars for a more elaborate event.

Many families and cultures prefer a more natural, less chemical approach. Others don’t want makeup used - or injuries or bruising concealed. But for those who do, there are tricks of the mortuary cosmetology trade.

Even if the family doesn’t want to see the body of their loved one before the coffin is sealed, funeral directors say people can change their minds at the last minute, so each body is presented with care.

The first step is to wash the body and embalm it in the mortuary. The embalmer will set the features, making sure false teeth are in, and the eyes and mouth are closed.

To overcome the sallow greyness of a complexion, embalmers will add tints to the embalming fluid. An open mouth is gently sutured shut from the inside until the lips meet naturally.

Because the body loses fluid after death, sunken eyes are covered with little curved caps placed beneath the eyelids, which are then sealed shut with glue or gel. The body is dressed in clothes provided by the family and hands are placed either by the person’s sides or across their chest during the embalming process.

Embalmer Mary Shilling, 38, has her own bag of tricks, some of which she shares, while keeping others a mortician’s secret.

She’s been an embalmer for 13 years after completing a diploma in embalming. Now working for Fountains Funerals in Papakura, she’s left the industry a couple of times to pursue another career but has always been drawn back.

Does she love it?

“I actually do, I really do love embalming. I’m one of those weirdos that really just loves it.”

At school she was fascinated by the way ancient Egyptians prepared their dead for burial through mummification.

“Even now, I’m so interested in the science and the art behind it.”

Shilling’s 14-year-old son is not so keen.

“My son absolutely despises what I do. Thinks it’s disgusting.”

In a social setting, when people ask Shilling what she does as a job, the answer either brings a barrage of curious questions or an awkward silence.

“They’ll either want to know more, or the conversation stops there.”

Shilling has her own palette of dyes she adds to the embalming fluid to give the body a natural colour and glow. And she has her own methods to plump out sunken cheeks.

“I will use a solution, and I get a needle and a syringe and pretty much give them fillers.”

Getting the skin to look right is an art. She’s even used an airbrush in the past for fine detailing. To recreate pores in a man’s face, smoothed out in the embalming and makeup process, she’ll use a technique with a sponge or press the skin with an orange.

Red patches are covered with a green base before the foundation is applied. Purplish blue is disguised with a yellow base. A heavier mortuary foundation is used to cover bruises or grazes, although some families don’t want them covered.

Wendy Bygrave has been a funeral director at Fountains Funerals for 24 years, managing both the Papakura business and the Pukekohe branch. She always wanted a career that involved helping people; she considered the police force, but couldn’t run fast enough. She’s worked in a hospital in the past and was always interested in the mortuary.

“It’s something that never bothered or scared me.”

The industry is unregulated, so anyone can become a funeral director, but embalming is a special skill, she says.

“You can embalm a body, and you can embalm a body.”

The three embalmers at Fountains are trained to know how to mix the chemicals depending on the skin colour, whether it’s an elderly person on medication, a child, how long a body needs to be preserved if it is travelling overseas, or someone who has died as a result of trauma.

With a hint of pride, Bygrave, 59, leads a tour of the sprawling Fountains Funerals building, which recently had a major renovation.

The building is, in a tasteful way, death by layers. On the top floor is a large, airy reception room and outdoor deck where guests can gather after a funeral service. Sandwiches, cakes and savouries are laid out ready for a ceremony that is nearly over when the Herald visits.

Downstairs is a large chapel and three viewing rooms (one of which can double as a small chapel) in which family members can visit the body before the coffin is sealed.

The viewing room is warm, the lighting soft. A photo of the loved one shows on a TV screen and below is a memorial book of photos that Fountains prepares for mourners to sign. There are extras: tissues, scented candles, bottles of water. One family wanted to bring their father’s beloved dog for a final goodbye, so Bygrave made sure there was a bowl of water and a bag of doggie treats at the ready.

Down in the basement, the temperature drops considerably. It is here that the work starts, in the mortuary for embalming and next door in the “trim room”. Here, bodies are lined up on trolleys under shrouds, waiting for Shilling and the other staff to work miracles.

In the centre is a large trolley stacked with cosmetics, perfume, makeup brushes and sponges which could belong in any beauty parlour. In the hair salon section are hairdryers, curling tongs, hair rollers, straighteners, and a selection of mousses, gels and hairsprays.

Hair is shampooed, conditioned and dried. If hair regrowth is showing, staff will dash out to a supermarket to pick up some hair dye for a touch-up.

A former hairdresser on staff, now an embalmer, will do a haircut if necessary before styling. Straggly beards and moustaches are trimmed, or shaved off completely at the family’s request.

Beyond the beauty paraphernalia are racks of coffins lining a wall, a reminder of what this business is all about. Outside the trim room are racks of clean duvets, sheets, rugs and quilts. Some families don’t want to see the body in a coffin, so the staff make up a stretcher trolley to look like a bed.

“In winter we make it look really snug, and in summer we just cool it down with more of a fresh cotton blanket,” Bygrave says.

The trick to getting the presentation right is to get as much information as possible from the family. How did she wear her hair and makeup, what was her favourite lipstick colour, what clothes would he or she want to be dressed in, should they be wearing their glasses, she’ll want to know.

“For me, it’s got to be right.”

And she’ll prepare the family for what they’re about to see. Bygrave says she nearly had heart failure on one occasion when a woman arrived to view her mother and said, “That’s not my mum.” For a moment, Bygrave thought there had been a terrible mix-up.

But what the woman meant was that she was used to seeing her mother wearing glasses. Once the missing glasses were added, Bygrave heard the reassuring words, “Now that’s my mum.”

Sometimes family members bring in the person’s own makeup, and some will want to do the makeup and nail painting themselves as a last gesture of care.

Based in South Auckland with a multi-cultural population, the funeral home caters for a “melting pot” of religions, cultures and ethnicities, Bygrave says. She recalls the death of a Mormon woman. Her sisters dressed her in a traditional white gown and white slippers, and did her hair and makeup themselves.

Māori and Pacific families will often dress the body themselves and stay with their loved one. She recalls one Tongan family who decorated the chapel and stayed for nights, singing and sharing memories until midnight.

The hardest part of Bygrave’s job is witnessing families grieve, particularly in cases where a young person has died in a traumatic accident, or a child or baby has died unexpectedly.

“There have been times when my staff and I have had some tears, absolutely, and we don’t hide that,” she says.

Babies are dressed, wrapped in shawls and placed in a bassinet. But before that, Bygrave often finds herself rocking the babies in her arms.

“When you’re holding a baby, it’s something you naturally find you’re doing.”

In cases of trauma, she’ll talk frankly to the family and, in some cases, advise them not to view the body.

“We let them know exactly what they’re going to see so they’re not shocked.”

But she’ll follow the family’s lead. Some don’t want bruises and grazes disguised; they don’t want makeup or to be dressed; some will want to view their loved one no matter what their state.

Brian Barrett, manager at Sibuns Funerals, based in a stately double-storey villa in Auckland’s Remuera, has only been in the industry for two years and talks of it as though he’s already in heaven.

“I love this industry. You don’t get a more rewarding business.”

He’s had an assorted career as a professional cricketer, a businessman and a spell in the corporate world, but found his calling as a funeral director.

It’s hard work, mind you, he says. Sibuns often deals with high net-worth families whose expectations are very high. Or, in a tough financial environment, family members might not agree on how much to spend.

Whoever the person – Sibuns looked after the funerals for gym magnate and former Mayor of Auckland Les Mills this year and Sir Colin Giltrap, founder of the Giltrap Group, two years ago – everyone is prepared with the same care, Barrett says.

If there’s one piece of advice he’d like to share, it’s for people to pre-arrange their funerals rather than leave grieving family members with the burden.

That could include the type of coffin, the outfit, the order of service or readings, and a selection of photos. That circumvents family tensions and arguments at a time of high emotion.

Earlier this year, Barrett was visited by a woman three weeks before her death, which occurred more suddenly than expected.

“We got everything right down to the music that we were carrying her out of the chapel [to], the catering numbers, the photo tribute, we did all of that.”

For Williams, she regards the loss of a loved family member as a time to think and talk about the person when they weren’t old or sick. But it can also be tragic.

“It seems to me that when that sadness is there, all that love comes flooding out and all these stories. Young people in the family learn about someone’s identity from before they were born. You know, they weren’t always a grandmother or auntie, so that’s really, really special.”

Jane Phare is a senior journalist based in Auckland. Her roles at the Herald have included assistant editor of NZ Herald, editor of the Weekend Herald, founding editor of Viva, features editor and deputy print editor.

Squally thunderstorms with gusts up to 100km/h are threatening the top of the country, as southerners wake to a frosty start and sub-zero temperatures for some.

Wet weather swept across parts of both islands yesterday, including Manawatū-Whanganui where torrential downpours combined with a shallow early morning 5.9 earthquake near Taumarunui combined to cause slips blocking State Highway 3 Awakino Gorge and SH43 Forgotten World Highway.

A cold southerly flow remains over most of the country today, and a low crossing Northland and Auckland promised more heavy showers and potentially squally thunderstorms after an already unsettled start to the weekend, MetService meteorologist Ashlee Parkes said.

“When we talk about squally thunderstorms, we’re talking about the potential for strong gusts with those thunderstorms.

“So areas particularly through Northland may see some gusts in the 80 to 100km/h range in the morning with potential thunderstorms.”

The thunderstorm risk continues into the afternoon before conditions ease in the evening, she said.

You. 🫵🥶Yes, you. Stay warm. Look after yourself. 🧤🫂We're in for a cold plunge. ❄️❄️❄️The video below shows cold air sweeping across New Zealand. This blast of cold Antarctic air is being driven north by southwesterly winds. By Wednesday, temperatures begin to recover… pic. twitter. com/qc8aSWdAOl

But the rest of the country was looking relatively fine, although showers weren’t expected to clear out of the central North Island until later this morning, with a mostly fine afternoon.

The South Island was the place to be today, Parkes said.

Sunny weather is forecast across almost the entire island, with only parts of the deep south in line for a touch of wet weather.

However, clear skies also meant a frigid start.

“We’ve just had this big sub-Antarctic air push over the country bringing these cool southerlies. Some places particularly through Canterbury, Central Otago are going to wake up [to] some very cool temperatures … and potentially severe frosts for some places.”

A low of -6C was expected in Twizel, with a biting -4C on the way for Christchurch, Timaru, Ashburton and Alexandra.

“Those temperatures are definitely what we would be looking at for crunchy grass.”

Daytime highs wouldn’t be more than a degree or two below average for the time of year though.

A high of 13C is forecast in Auckland and Tauranga, with 11C in Hamilton, and 9C in the capital, Christchurch and Dunedin.

The chilly start would return tomorrow, with another fine day expected for most of the country – including Northland and Auckland, Parkes said.

A weak front would brush past the southwest of the South Island, she said.

“Unfortunately it’s the usual Fiordland and Stewart Island [that] may see some wet weather, but most other areas should be predominantly fine.”

Letters: Running record achieved on the shoulders of Kiwi giants

New Zealand Herald July 25, 2026

Josh Kerr has broken Hicham El Guerrouj’s 27-year-old mile world record. Photo / Getty Images

The news that British athlete Josh Kerr has broken the world mile record of 27 years should bring a sense of nostalgia to many New Zealanders.

This is because Kerr stands on the shoulders of a few athletes, an illustrious group, who have held this record in the past. They include three New Zealanders: Jack Lovelock, Peter Snell and John Walker.

Lovelock’s record-breaking mile in 1933 was New Zealand’s first track world record. It is worth noting that Snell then broke the record on a grass track in 1962 and not on a modern 400-metre synthetic track. Walker broke the mile record in 1975 and became the first man to go under 3m 50s for the distance.

All of these men were Olympic gold medallists. Snell and Walker were products of an era that revolutionised training through the coaching methods of New Zealander, Arthur Lydiard. New Zealanders should also feel proud whenever this record is broken as an echo of our own past resonates through this event.

Bernard Walker, Mt Maunganui.

Stuart Nash well and truly shot himself in the foot with the appalling comments he made about MP Katie Nimon, his Napier electorate opponent.

Now that his misogynistic views have been made public, it is reprehensible that he served as the Minister of Police for over three years in a Labour Government.

This is the sort of toxic verbiage that is found in the manosphere, and it has absolutely no place in New Zealand politics, or anywhere else.

Lorraine Kidd, Warkworth.

It’s no wonder Shane Jones knows about kneepads. Many of us suspect that’s what he wears when he meets representatives of the mining and fishing industries.

Chris Cottingham, Te Henga.

While somewhat expecting some interesting and provocative statements, prior to the upcoming election, I am rather disappointed that the two main minor coalition partners seem to be taking aim more at their senior coalition partner rather than the Opposition parties.

I am referring to Shane Jones’ comment that PM Christopher Luxon should take off his kneepads. As a Kiwi, I sadly find that statement quite offensive, especially when we have recently had a visit from the leader of the largest democratic country in the world and quite obviously this is where the comment appears to have been aimed.

While National continues to govern, as it should, the coalition partners seem to be constantly endeavouring to undermine it. All I can really say is thank goodness there is at least one adult in the room – and in my view, it is certainly not the leaders of Act or NZ First who currently qualify as that.

Mike Baker, Tauranga.

It’s a pity Prime Minister Christopher Luxon is still so reliant on consistently undermining the previous Labour Government. His endlessly repeated claims that Labour “mismanaged the economy” are at best a matter of opinion and at worst, demonstrably false.

Yes, Labour borrowed a lot to fund our Covid response, and yes, it should probably have been backpedalling faster, as global inflation started rising because of supply-chain issues persisting after Covid, and US and EU sanctions on Russia (and in particular, sanctions on Russian oil).

To blame Labour for that inflation, which was actually a global phenomenon and uniform across the entire Western world – as National’s leaders seemed happy to do before the election and for a long time after it – raises concerning moral and ethical questions.

As to the supposed brownie points this National-led coalition Government has accrued around education, and law and order:

Education: Okay, most people would agree Erica Stanford has done a pretty good job with education.

Law and order: The jury’s likely very much out. Fear-mongering around law and order is bog-standard, right-leaning populism. There was no explosion of crime under Labour. There was a small and relatively circumscribed problem around ram-raiding – yes, a problem that has now reappeared in rural New Zealand.

We are one of the most imprisoned countries in the world – a truly deplorable situation – but under this Government we’ve built more prisons and are locking up more people, for longer.

That’s not only tragic, it’s also a recipe for disaster.

Andrew Joughin, Devonport.

Why has Claire Achmad been removed from her job as Children’s Commissioner, after her outstanding service?

Is it because she’s been speaking truth to power?

I hope to see some questions being put to those responsible for this shoddy treatment of one of our outstanding public servants. It’s outrageous.

I hope the public will listen to her departing message, and her plea that our political leaders of all parties explain why they don’t prioritise the wellbeing of our children. It’s our national shame, and disgrace.

We clearly have the most uncaring and brutal Government in living memory.

Vivien Fergusson, Mt Eden.

Rotorua Mana Aroha shower and laundry service saved with one-year funding boost

New Zealand Herald July 25, 2026

Mana Aroha in Rotorua will remain open for another year, news welcomed by long-time rough sleeper Maria Hohaia (inset). Photos / Kelly Makiha

Rotorua’s homeless will be able to access free showers, laundry services and hot drinks in the central city for another year thanks to the service being thrown a financial lifeline.

Mana Aroha, run by Visions of a Helping Hand Charitable Trust, has been operating on Pukuatua St for six years but funding woes risked its closure.

Te Taumata o Ngāti Whakaue Iho Ake has agreed to pay for the service to remain at reduced hours, news met by one user of the service with a big smile and a “chur”.

Mana Aroha has three showers, six commercial washing machines, four dryers and a second-hand store.

It operated Monday to Friday from 9am to noon and, according to the trust’s website, supported about 120 rough sleepers by providing donated toiletries, lockers, towels, tea, coffee and – for a koha – second-hand clothing.

The trust announced in April it would close the service at the end of June.

Funding it previously received for managing emergency housing motels had dried up as that system wound down and the trust could not afford to continue Mana Aroha.

Te Taumata o Ngāti Whakaue Iho Ake has answered the trust’s calls for help and will pay to keep the service open with reduced hours and days.

Trust acting chief executive Sarah Isaac said it was “extremely grateful” for the support and recognition of the service’s importance to the community.

Isaac said Mana Aroha provided essential hygiene facilities, practical assistance and a place of dignity and connection for the most vulnerable people.

She said it had been operating without dedicated external funding. The trust would try to firm up sustainable funding options during the coming year.

Mana Aroha’s new hours were 9am to 11.15am Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and Friday.

Te Taumata o Ngāti Whakaue Iho Ake has been involved in health, education and social services since 2005. Its housing arm is building a development alongside the Government in Ngongotahā for those in need.

Acting general manager Anahera Waru said it had a long-standing relationship with Visions of a Helping Hand Charitable Trust.

“Across Aotearoa, more people are sleeping rough, despite the basic right that every person deserves a place of warmth, safety and dignity.”

Waru said Mana Aroha provided essential care, the ability to shower, wash clothes and restore dignity.

“We are proud to support the continuation of this service for another year, while continuing to work with others in our community towards long-term housing solutions for our people.”

The landlord of the Mana Aroha building, who spoke on the condition they were not named, was pleased the service would remain.

While there were issues with the behaviour of some homeless in the area, she said the trust kept the area clean and the rent paid.

“From a landlord’s perspective, we are lucky to have a tenant as there are a lot of empty buildings around town. Clearly they need the service because they need to be able to clean themselves.”

Maria Hohaia’s eyes lit up when she talked about the laundry and shower service remaining for another year.

The 51-year-old long-time homeless woman, known on the streets as Sweetie, told the Rotorua Daily Post she had heard it was not closing yet but was not aware who had funded it.

“Ngāti Whakaue? Ah, chur.”

Hohaia said she had been homeless about 30 years and slept in a doorway near Mana Aroha.

She said she did not meet criteria for housing support, “so I don’t have anywhere else to go”.

She said the laundry and shower service were essential to make her feel good and clean.

“When you live on the streets, these are the only facilities we have to use.”

She said the reduced hours would mean she had to use it four days a week.

“We’ve got two hours to get in and get it done.”

Rotorua Mayor Tania Tapsell has been critical of the behaviour of some rough sleepers and supported the Rotorua Lakes Council’s actions to trespass them from the central city.

Police and council staff shut down a makeshift village on Amohia St, around the corner from Mana Aroha, in June last year.

Waiariki MP Rawiri Waiteti called this “inhumane and disgraceful” at the time, but Tapsell said the council had no choice because people were “s***ting, taking and selling drugs, and having sexual intercourse” in public.

Asked for her reaction to the laundry and shower service remaining for another year, Tapsell said Rotorua had made great progress recently to improve inner-city safety and turn around a perception of homelessness.

She said some locals associated homelessness with anti-social behaviour and disruption that impacted nearby workers and businesses.

“I reassure our community that illegal and anti-social behaviour will not be tolerated.

“If issues come up, we’ll continue to support a safe and welcoming city centre and will also encourage providers to explore more suitable long-term options that meet people’s needs while better aligning with our wider vision for the inner city.”

Kelly Makiha is a senior journalist who has reported for the Rotorua Daily Post for more than 25 years, covering mainly police, court, human interest and social issues.
