Nicole Pierce honoured with top MinEx award for quarry leadership

New Zealand Herald July 25, 2026

Waiotahi Contractors Operations Coordinator for Quarries, Nicole Pierce won the MinEx Kristy Christensen Memorial Award at the 2026 Komatsu New Zealand Women in Extractives event and awards ceremony.

Waiotahi Contractors operations coordinator for quarries, Nicole Pierce, was surprised to be named the MinEx Kristy Christensen Memorial Award winner at the 2026 Komatsu New Zealand Women in Extractives event.

The annual awards, hosted by the New Zealand Minerals Council, Aggregate and Quarry Association (AQA), and MinEx, recognise outstanding women across the extractives industry, and celebrate leadership, innovation and commitment.

The award Pierce received carries special weight.

It honours Kristy Christensen, who spent 15 years working in underground coal mining while advocating for workplaces that better support women.

Christensen died of breast cancer at 37, leaving a legacy that continues to shape industry culture and expectations.

Waiotahi colleagues Hollie Atarau and Gerard Hull nominated Pierce for her leadership, professionalism and unwavering focus on people.

Pierce’s pathway into quarrying was anything but traditional.

Growing up in Whakatāne with a passion for horses, she studied tourism and travel at Waikato Polytechnic before building a career in hospitality and food management.

A later role at Farmlands during Covid drew her closer to a rural environment – something she admits felt more aligned with her interests.

In 2021, Pierce started with Waiotahi Quarry as an administrator, then moved into quality assurance, overseeing materials destined for the Ōpōtiki Harbour project.

“That leads to a more environmental role, where I follow the strict environmental code Waiotahi takes so seriously,” she said.

“That includes monitoring dust emissions and ensuring roads and waterways aren’t polluted.”

The variety of work – and the company’s focus on training – keeps her engaged.

“The company is really good at upskilling people, and I love learning new things - that’s what keeps me interested,” Pierce said.

“Whether it’s gaining my wheels, tracks and rollers endorsements or taking on new tasks, there’s always something to build on.”

Pierce is now working toward her B Grade Quarry Manager certification, which Atarau said reflected both her ambition and her commitment to strengthening capability across the wider operation.

Atarau said Pierce stood out for her hands-on, practical leadership style.

“Nicole demonstrates outstanding leadership across quarry operations through a people-focused approach that consistently sets high standards,” she said.

“She’s not afraid to get stuck in and regularly works alongside the team on site.”

Working in a traditionally male-dominated industry, Pierce also played an important role in building a culture where staff feel supported.

With few women on site, she becomes a trusted sounding board, encouraging open communication and helping to create a workplace where people feel safe to speak up.

She places particular emphasis on mental wellbeing – an area she believes is critical to both safety and performance.

“The mental health of the team is extremely important to me,” Pierce said.

“People need to be looked after to be productive.”

Pierce supports the rollout of the UOK BRO NZ wellbeing initiative within the company.

The programme provides free and confidential counselling services, alongside practical support such as budgeting advice.

“In my eyes, it really is okay to not be okay,” she said.

“No one should be carrying the weight of their problems alone, whether that’s work-related or personal.”

Atarau said Pierce’s approachable nature and empathy have had a lasting impact.

“When issues arise, Nicole is proactive and solution-focused, often the first person on site working through challenges and identifying practical solutions,” she said.

“She also steps into leadership when the quarry branch manager is on leave, ensuring continuity and strong performance.”

Alongside her operational responsibilities, Pierce plays an active role in strengthening safety practices across the business.

She is a committed member of the health and safety committee and contributes to ongoing improvements in systems and processes, helping reinforce a strong safety culture within quarry operations.

Pierce also works collaboratively with other quarry managers and the company director, sharing knowledge and supporting wider organisational goals.

Her ability to lead is most evident in complex situations.

One standout example involved the removal of metal stockpiled on private property – a long-running issue that presented logistical and community challenges, including resistance from local residents.

Pierce took the lead in engaging with iwi and landowners, navigating the situation with sensitivity, persistence and professionalism.

Through careful coordination, the material was successfully removed, transported to the processing site and sold – a significant outcome given the complexity of the situation.

She remained on site throughout the process, ensuring operations ran smoothly and safely, while maintaining strong relationships with all parties involved.

Atarau said this reflected the qualities that made Pierce deserving of national recognition.

“Nicole’s professionalism, approachability and strong leadership – combined with her commitment to people, safety and operational excellence – make her a highly deserving recipient of this award," she said.

“She has a very bright future in the quarrying industry, and we are proud to have her as part of our team.”

Why wool could be the secret to healthier plants and vegetables - Kem Ormond

New Zealand Herald July 25, 2026

Wool can take a year to break down but enriches the soil as it decays. Photo / Michael Craig

I have been seeing quite a few gardeners using wool as mulch in their vegetable gardens.

While I don’t bring anything into my vegetable garden due to my chop-and-drop method, I am still interested in seeing if it is making a difference.

There are probably three ways you could use wool fleece: adding nutrients, water retention, and weed control.

A farming friend who has been planting natives and also has access to the old daggy and stained wool said often it was a struggle for natives in their first year because pasture grasses outcompeted them for moisture.

Using wool enables them to have a head start by removing that competition and stabilising soil moisture.

Sheep wool has fantastic water storage properties, and with drier summers on the way, the moisture trapped after rain can be released back to the plants to enable them to survive when the soil gets dry.

The soil gets more aerated when the wool is dug in, becomes more fertile and creates a wonderful, healthy environment beneficial for insects and bugs.

Some gardeners incorporate it into the soil, while others use it as mulch.

For large trees, having it around the base will really only give water retention, as for many trees, the roots will have spread everywhere, so they will not really get as much benefit as putting the wool around young seedlings.

Some put a small amount of wool directly in the hole the seedling is to be planted in, so the wool is directly under the roots.

I like this idea, as it would retain water better and the plant would get some of the nutrients once the wool starts breaking down.

This may not appeal to the impatient gardener, as wool does take a while to break down and release all that fertiliser.

It would work better for seedlings that have been in the ground for a while, not for the quick growers such as lettuce and radishes.

However, wool even laid on top would be beneficial, as would some added to your compost bin.

Most gardeners said that if dug into the vege garden, it took over a year to break down completely, but a lot depends on the thickness you apply.

As a mulch, it takes longer, so that would also work great, as you could use it for both summer and winter mulching.

One thing a few of my gardening friends told me was that it didn’t deter snails; in fact, they sometimes treated it as a home away from home!

It also can be an attraction to dogs if they are that way inclined … just something to think about.

If growing vegetables in pots, for example, tomatoes, you could use wool the same way.

Put some in the bottom of the pot, add the plant and top with your soil, then add wool to the surface and water.

If you are lucky to live on a farm or know someone who does, you have ready access to wool.

If not, you might need to ask around.

Maybe some small local breeders have some waste wool they wish to dispose of.

Wool is a powerful slow-release fertiliser, a slow-decaying mulch, and a water sponge full of micro-organisms, boosting organic matter and is environmentally friendly.

Your plants will love it, and so will your soil and no matter what your gardening beliefs are, it’s something worth considering.

- Kem Ormond is a features writer for The Country. She’s also a keen gardener.

At 18, with a baby, Leah Purcell fled violence with her mother’s book. It became her life’s work

Sydney Morning Herald July 26, 2026

The actor, writer and director says it would be ‘a crime’ not to tell her ancestors’ stories on stage.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

When her mother Florence died at the age of 60, actor Leah Purcell kept two of her prized possessions: a book of Henry Lawson short stories bound in red leather and a purse full of old family photos.

Purcell packed these keepsakes into her yellow Datsun Sunny alongside her baby daughter, Amanda, and at 18 fled an abusive relationship and her home town of Murgon, in rural Queensland. In 1988, she had fallen pregnant at 17, turned 18 in August, given birth to her daughter in September and lost her mother in October. Bound for Brisbane, she was determined to set her life on a new course and pursue her dream of a career on stage.

As a child who hated reading, it was an odd choice to keep a book she’d scribbled in the margins of, to the horror of Florence, an avid reader. But it contained The Drover’s Wife, a childhood favourite she’d beg her mother to read and knew so well she could recite the last line by heart.

1:39

Leah Purcell on The Drover's Wife opera

How the actor, director and playwright has added 'librettist' to her body of work.

Decades later, that battered old book and those faded family photos would become the backbone of Purcell’s body of work as a playwright, actor, novelist, filmmaker and director. Now add librettist to that list – an opera adaptation of her award-winning play The Drover’s Wife opens at the Sydney Opera House next month following a critically acclaimed Queensland premiere in May.

“I’d never in my wildest dreams have thought that when I left Murgon and took that little book, I’d ever turn it into a play, a film, a novel and now an opera,” says Purcell, a Goa, Gunggari and Wakka Wakka Murri woman, like her mother. “It was just something that me and my mum shared.”

Lawson’s story, published in The Bulletin in 1892, is the tale of a woman left alone with her four children, and the drama that unfolds when a black snake enters their bush hut while her husband is droving.

As a single mother of seven, Florence no doubt knew the loneliness of the drover’s wife portrayed by “the people’s poet” Lawson. Purcell’s father, Les Haack, was a white man, a boxing trainer and the town’s butcher, but Purcell was not allowed to acknowledge him as her dad. He had another family, a white family, who lived on the other side of town.

From him, she learnt how to pack a punch. “I always had a good right hook,” she jokes about the sport her boxing father taught her and her brothers.

Some of that story was retold in Box the Pony, the 1997 semi-autobiographical one-woman play she wrote with Scott Rankin. But it was the emotional gut punch in The Drover’s Wife, which she adapted and first performed as a play at Sydney’s Belvoir Theatre in 2016, that lingered with audiences long after she exited the stage.

“At Belvoir, women stayed back in the foyer after performances, drinking champagne and sharing stories,” Purcell says. “Grandmothers would suddenly start talking about things their own mothers had gone through that they’d never spoken about before.”

Purcell, who adapted the play into a novel in 2019 and then wrote the screenplay and directed and starred in the 2021 film version, wove threads of her own experience of domestic violence into her rendering of the Lawson classic. Unlike Lawson, she gave the protagonist a name, Molly Johnson. Molly not only battles isolation, poverty and the Australian bush but also the trauma and threat of male violence.

Inspiration came from Florence and her forebears, three generations of whom worked as drovers or jillaroos and whose images on horseback were contained in the sepia photos in her mum’s purse. The opera is told from the point of view of the son in the story, Danny, who as a 32-year-old reflects on his mother’s ordeal. He’s the one who promises his mother “I won’t never go a-drovin’” – the last line that Purcell remembered so clearly it as a kid. She’s also transformed the threatening “black snake” into an Indigenous fugitive called Yadaka (played in the opera by Marcus Corowa).

“The opera has allowed us to go bigger,” says Purcell. “There’s fantasy, spirituality, dance and an emotional force from the music, some of which is in my grandmother’s language. The opera lets the story breathe in another way. It’s still about a mother’s love for her children and what she will do to protect them – I just sprinkle my black pepper through it.”

Composer George Palmer, a former justice of the NSW Supreme Court, first approached Purcell and her partner Bain Stewart to suggest her script would make a perfect libretto after his wife read Purcell’s novel for her book club. “He put music to my play script first,” Purcell explains. “Then, through workshops, we’d take chunks of dialogue and turn them into arias.”

She describes Palmer’s musical composition as “like a really good doona – it wraps around you and carries the story”.

Purcell first met Stewart, who has an Indigenous father and a white mother and was running a martial arts centre, when she arrived in Brisbane with her baby back in 1988 (they now live with her daughter and two teen grandsons in Sydney’s inner west). She’s probably best known for her acting work in Wentworth, High Country and Redfern Now on television and the movies Lantana and Jindabyne. However, she started as a singer, touring in Bran Nue Dae in 1993, and was once the support act for Shania Twain.

From there, though, it’s quite a jump to her debut as an opera director. And for the first time since she put a name to the character of Molly Johnson, she has handed over the role to her cousin’s daughter, London-trained soprano Nina Korbe. “Her mother and I are like sisters,” says Purcell, adding that Korbe was cautious about taking on the role. “She said, ‘Molly Johnson is you.’ And I said, ‘Not in this one. She’s yours now.’”

Purcell is delighted by the idea of inheritance – of stories passing through generations, from her grandmothers and mother to her cousin’s daughter, just like her mother’s beloved book. And she is thrilled that the opera – set in the Snowy Mountains, which Purcell fell in love with while filming High Country and Jindabyne – received rave reviews when it debuted in Queensland in May.

She is also forever grateful for the friends and family there who shaped her, like the teacher in year 7 who gently encouraged her to write. “I entered a writing competition, but when my teacher handed back my story, it was covered in red-penned corrections,” says Purcell. “I thought I was in trouble, but she told me, ‘We can fix the spelling and grammar. This is a great story.’” She won the Murgon Lions Rotary Writing competition.

She’s thankful, too, to the supervisor at the Murgon meatworks who told her not to come looking for a job there when she finished school. “I thought I’d done something wrong but he said, ‘I saw you in the high school musical. I think you can go far.’ I skipped out of there with an extra bounce in my step.”

The musical was Bye Bye Birdie, in which Purcell played glamorous secretary Gloria. “That was the first time I got a real laugh from an audience,” she says. “I milked it for all it was worth. And I’ve been doing that ever since.”

Above all, though, she’s grateful to her mother. “Molly Johnson is a representation of my mum, her sisters, and the strength of other Aunties within the family,” she says. “I have the opportunity to give voice to their stories, and I’m doing that to show the personal side to something that is always politicised in our country. The death rate from domestic violence is still phenomenal. At this minute, somewhere, a woman is being abused.”

She wishes her mum could be in the opening night at the Sydney Opera House, resplendent in the Christmas decorations she always wore as jewellery as she was too poor to afford the real thing.

“My mum was my hero. She raised seven of her own children and looked after her bedridden mother for 27 years as well as my grandfather and two nephews. There were always extra kids around. She was just amazing, a card, a bit of a performer herself.

“She died at 60 of bowel cancer, which was horrific. She was an Aboriginal woman who was voiceless. A statistic. My grandmother was of the stolen generations, considered subhuman, so for me to not use my talents and chase my dreams and do something positive would be a crime against them.”

Purcell says she hopes this version of the Lawson story helps to keep people talking about difficult subjects. “At the heart and soul of it, the opera, this story, is about celebrating women – all women.”

How a global pandemic helped Olympian Josie Baff clinch gold

Sydney Morning Herald July 26, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Josie Baff won gold at the Youth Olympics in Switzerland and a month later the world descended into chaos.

It was January 2020 – the start of Baff’s HSC year and the start of the COVID-19 pandemic.

As the pandemic worsened, Baff bunkered down at home in Jindabyne and focused on her final year of schooling.

“It definitely helped me focus,” Baff said of the pandemic when reflecting on her final year at Jindabyne Central School, where she was enrolled from kindergarten to year 12.

Baff, who most recently won gold in snowboard cross at the 2026 Winter Olympics, had always enjoyed school, but the 2020 Games were a learning curve in what it took to balance education with elite sport.

“When I went to the Youth Olympics, that was the first time I was away from school a little bit more, and I realised that I had a different career path that I wanted to do,” Baff said.

“That was the first time I actually believed I was going to be a professional athlete.

“I found it a little bit hard [balancing school] just before that, and then I think afterwards the teachers realised that I was pretty serious about sport, and then I got a lot more support around being like more flexible with dates of exams.”

Her success at the Youth Olympics solidified her goal to be a full-time winter-sports athlete, but also made it harder to focus at school.

“It was definitely always important to me to continue it [school], because I was always quite good in school, and I really loved it,” Baff said.

“I was super dedicated, and I am a bit of a perfectionist, so I was always spending a lot of time doing my schoolwork.

“Then when it came to year 11 and 12, after those Olympics, I found it a little bit different to motivate myself to do it, but I managed to do it, and COVID helped.”

Inside Sydney’s neonatal refuge where staff carry panic buttons

Sydney Morning Herald July 26, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Dozens of young women, heavily pregnant or with babies in their arms, arrive at the Wiyanga House in Sydney’s west every year facing homelessness.

Run by Uniting, the refuge is one of a handful of specialist services in the state. The single-storey refuge near Parramatta caters to young women aged 16 to 24 who are expecting or raising children. Some young mothers arrive with suitcases and bags; others come with only the clothes on their backs and their infants.

Nearly all are fleeing domestic violence.

Last October, 23-year-old Jenny* and her son Ben*, 3, were preparing to spend the night sleeping in a park.

Jenny had previously been living in temporary social housing, where agreements required her to actively apply for private rentals to maintain her placement. But she said these requirements were difficult to achieve with a baby and a tight $450 weekly budget, well below Sydney’s median unit rent of $780.

After applying for a rental that exceeded her case-plan budget by just $10, she was evicted for non-compliance. She then found shelter at a motel, only to be evicted again after her weekly rent jumped from $510 to $700.

Carrying suitcases with her infant bundled in blankets, she had nowhere else to go. Jenny was terrified when police and social workers approached them in the park, fearing Ben would be taken away from her.

Instead of being separated, they were brought to Wiyanga.

All five beds at the house are usually filled. In 2025-26, the refuge supported 52 women and their children – a 25 per cent increase from the previous year. But amid increased demand, Uniting is forced to turn away dozens more.

Since arriving at Wiyanga, Jenny has been paired with a financial counsellor, mental health counsellor, parent groups, and Parent Pathways, which offers financial support and employment training. She recently found long-term accommodation and is hoping to re-enter the workforce.

“There were heaps of times that I wanted to give up. Nothing was going the way I wanted it to,” she said. “My message to other mums is don’t give up. We got there in the end.”

How NSW supports vulnerable mothers has remained under intense scrutiny since a woman gave birth to twins, one of whom did not survive, while living in a makeshift camp in the NSW Riverina.

Data modelling from Homelessness NSW estimates up to 80,000 people may be experiencing homelessness in NSW, with nearly 700,000 more at risk. Street counts show the rate of people sleeping rough has doubled since 2022, with 2308 identified during this year’s Homes NSW statewide street count.

Women and children affected by domestic violence make up one third of all people experiencing persistent homelessness in NSW and nationally, according to Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) data.

At the same time, the capacity to provide help is shrinking. In 2024-25, there were 21,500 requests for homelessness services in NSW that went unassisted – a figure that has almost doubled over the past eight years. There is an average of 59 unassisted requests a day.

In 2024-25, Uniting was forced to turn away 91 young people seeking housing due to a lack of space.

Wiyanga is funded under state government specialist homelessness packages. But Uniting’s Jasmine Aspinall said there hadn’t been a substantial increase in over a decade, and the house operates on a shoestring budget.

The house’s weekly grocery budget is $250 for five women and their children, and the centre relies on donations for clothes, formula and other necessities for the mothers.

“It’s so difficult. We really do depend on other services,” Aspinall said.

Aspinall said the centre was in dire need of another case manager to help the women once they transitioned out of Wiyanga.

“A lot of these clients are returning clients. If they had had somebody with the continuity of care, that might be prevented,” she said.

From the outside, Wiyanga House looks no different from other homes on the street. However, the location of this single-storey brick building near Parramatta is kept strictly secret.

Security cameras monitor the driveway, and staff carry duress buttons to alert authorities should violent partners show up. A staff member is present at the six-bedroom cottage 24/7.

If a violent ex-partner does appear, house co-ordinator Shanique Toonen said staff must find the mother alternative emergency accommodation.

“They threaten to put the safety of all our mums and babies at risk,” she said.

One of the first conversations Toonen has with new arrivals focuses on safety, with many women yet to come to terms with their experience of domestic violence.

“We do a lot of work around what is a healthy relationship,” she said.

Termination and contraception are also discussed sensitively, with some women unfamiliar with proper contraceptive use or available options.

Teenage pregnancies make up less than 2 per cent of all births in Australia, according to AIHW data, though Toonen said the women referred to Wiyanga are increasingly skewing younger.

Most are leaving households where there’s violence, overcrowding, or drug issues, realising the environment is unsafe for their child. Many residents are from Aboriginal or non-English-speaking backgrounds, or live with intellectual disabilities.

The home operates with set rules, including a curfew and chore roster, but avoids policing its residents. Staff provide support rather than supervision. Residents pay $210 a week rent.

“We try to be flexible. This is their home,” Toonen said. “Nobody wants to live in a refuge, and they’re not lucky to be here. This is usually the lowest point of their life.”

Noelani*, 20, has been living at Wiyanga for almost three months with her 13-month-old, Eli. She said she was on a “destructive path” before becoming pregnant.

“I was getting into arguments with his father, going into custody, drinking and smoking a lot,” she said.

Noelani has experienced intermittent homelessness since age 14, frequently ending up on the streets following conflict with her mother.

“I was getting by day-to-day with temporary accommodation, motels, frozen meals and then stealing just to get breakfast,” she said.

Her own childhood was marked by domestic violence and adults drinking.

“I wanted different for my son,” she said.

Change wasn’t easy, and it took her a few months to find her feet. After being referred to Wiyanga, she accessed mental health support and feels she is on the right track.

Without Eli, Noelani believes she would still be drinking, “running a muck” and lacking direction.

“Falling pregnant was a blessing in disguise because I’m not just thinking about myself; I have to put him first,” she said.

*Names changed for privacy.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. For crisis support, contact Lifeline 13 11 14 or lifeline. org. au.

Abi Martin snatches Commonwealth bronze for England in gymnastics team final

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 20:58:31 GMT

England pip Wales to secure medal by just 0.900pts

Gabriel Langton discharged from hospital after fall

England held their nerve to claim bronze in the women’s artistic gymnastics team final after a tense final rotation enabled them to edge Wales by less than a point in Glasgow. The defending champions finished with 154.300 points, just enough to snatch third place from Wales, while Australia delivered a dominant display to win gold ahead of Canada.

Australia set the tone from the opening rotation, with Kate McDonald posting the highest uneven bars score of the day at 14.200 as the silver medallists from Birmingham 2022 established an early lead they would never relinquish. England made a solid start on vault through Shantae-Eve Amankwaah, Ruby Stacey, Alia Leat and Abi Martin. However, the uneven bars proved costly. Amankwaah’s excellent 13.500 boosted England’s challenge, but Stacey fell during her routine and her score did not count, leaving England trailing Australia at the halfway stage.

Heading into the final floor rotation, England trailed Canada by just 0.350 points in the battle for silver but also faced the threat of Wales, who watched on after they had set an impressive total earlier in the day.

Amankwaah opened with a stylish routine before a music delay briefly interrupted Shanna-Kae Grant’s Commonwealth Games debut, though that failed to unsettle her as she produced a superb routine, highlighted by a huge double Arabian, to keep England in medal contention. Leat’s 12.150 left England needing at least 12.350 from the final routine to overhaul Wales. Martin delivered under pressure, scoring 13.250 to spark celebrations as England secured bronze by just 0.900 points.

Australia finished five points clear of Wales’ earlier total to reclaim Commonwealth gold, while Canada’s strong final vault rotation, led by Ellie Black’s impressive 13.950, secured silver. Wales were left agonisingly short of a first team medal since Glasgow 2014.

Meanwhile, England’s Gabriel Langton has been discharged from hospital after scans determined no lasting damage from his fall during the men’s team final on Friday. The 19-year-old landed head first off the high bar in the final apparatus. The competition was held up for 20 minutes as he was carried away from the arena on a stretcher.

“Gabriel was transferred to the hospital as a precautionary measure overnight and underwent multiple scans today, with very positive results,” Team England said in a statement. “Thankfully, he has been cleared of any serious injury complications and will be discharged to return to the team hotel this evening.

“He is in good spirits and hugely grateful for the many messages of support and the excellent care provided by the medical teams. He is looking forward to being reunited with the team to celebrate his silver medal.”

Earlier in the day, before the medals were decided, one of the loudest cheers inside the Glasgow International Arena was reserved for a gymnast who would compete for less than two minutes. Two years ago, Tiana Sumanasekera was a United States Olympic alternate, training at the famed World Champions Centre in Houston alongside Simone Biles and Jordan Chiles. Now she is representing Sri Lanka – the country of her parents’ birth – with the aim of making the finals at Los Angeles in 2028.

Sri Lanka achieved a milestone at the Tokyo Olympics when Milka Gehani became their first gymnast to compete at the Games. Sumanasekera’s arrival represents another significant step forward with the 18-year-old boasting the talent to challenge for world championship and Olympic finals on balance beam and floor exercise.

after newsletter promotion

Sumanasekera is a multiple Pan American Games medallist who finished third on balance beam at the 2024 US Olympic Trials; she has long been regarded as one of the sport’s most promising gymnasts.

“I started competing at the elite level when I was 13 years old when I was with Team USA,” she said. “I had been with them for about five years and in 2024 I became an Olympic alternate. It really shifted my perspective on my capabilities.

“From when I was a little girl, I’ve always wanted to compete at the Olympics, so I thought the best decision was to represent my parents’ home country of Sri Lanka. I’m so proud and honoured to be here and doing so.”

But the Commonwealth Games arrived at the wrong time. A shoulder injury forced her to abandon plans to compete in the all-around event. Instead, she entered women’s qualification on one apparatus – balance beam – hoping to make the final despite limited preparation.

Her routine opened with a back dive to chest stand mount, displaying the originality that has made her a fan favourite, but her trademark back handspring layout series came up just short. She lost her balance, the one-point fall deduction ending her hopes.

Rather than unravel, Sumanasekera reeled off a beautifully connected front aerial into a split jump before finishing with perhaps the best moment of the routine – a stuck layout full-twisting dismount that drew applause from the crowd.

It was not enough to secure a place in the final, but Sumanasekera hopes she can build on this before LA 2028. “It was absolutely amazing being out here representing Sri Lanka on one of the biggest stages in the world. I was so grateful to compete.

“It didn’t go my way, but things happen. You live and you learn and you move on, so I’m excited for what’s to come next.”

Millions of people are losing weight using GLP-1s. How do the drugs affect their love lives?

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 20:00:52 GMT

Prescribing doctors often warn of the medications’ potential side-effects – but unexpected impacts on romantic relationships are less understood

For Jennifer, obesity was the obvious culprit for most of her problems.

The litigation attorney told herself it was the reason why she wasn’t being invited to parties, and why she and her husband struggled with physical intimacy in their otherwise “solid” marriage.

“If people excluded me, or if things weren’t going as I wanted them to, I often defaulted to, ‘Well, they don’t like fat people, they don’t want fat people at their event … they don’t want a fat person representing their brand,’” she says.

Jennifer, who is 57 and asked to keep her surname private, had struggled with obesity since she was eight, when her parents divorced. In her 30s she underwent gastric sleeve surgery, only to put the weight and more back on. But that all changed in 2023 when she started using Mounjaro, a drug in the new class of GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) weight-loss medications.

Designed to manage type 2 diabetes by regulating blood sugar, slowing digestion and reducing appetite, GLP-1s are now taken by millions of people across the world for weight loss, with Australian prescriptions increasing almost 10-fold since 2020 and use in the US more than quadruping.

Jennifer’s husband had concerns about well-known potential side-effects, including abdominal pain, but ultimately agreed with her that it was a risk worth taking.

Three years on – and with Jennifer 40kg lighter – the drugs seem to have resolved her lifelong struggle to manage her weight. But while she had hoped weight loss might help with the niggling issues in her relationship, she’s now contending with its fallout on her 30-year marriage, something neither she nor her husband expected.

“I’m glad I had five years of therapy before I started it,” she says. “I am not sure I would have been equipped for the psychological changes otherwise.”

Prescribing doctors often advise patients they might experience well-known potential physical side-effects of GLP-1s, including nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and constipation. What is not as well researched, or understood, are their effects on romantic relationships. Some patients in forums like Reddit and Facebook support groups have shared that they have experienced changes in desire, sexual function and emotional connection.

Early research suggests the GLP-1s could suppress more than just hunger through their impact on brain pathways and hormones.

“A potential unique mechanism with GLP-1s is their impact on the brain in regards to dopamine reward pathways,” says Dr Terri-Lynne South, a general practitioner specialising in obesity medicine. “We see this in regards to reducing the pleasure-seeking around alcohol, nicotine, and potentially sex drives.”

Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads

The evidence surrounding changed sexual function is limited, and mixed. Some studies suggest GLP-1 medications may improve testosterone levels, potentially benefiting sexual health, while a 2025 analysis of US Food and Drug Administration data identified 185 reports of sexual dysfunction, particularly among men taking GLP-1 receptor agonists.

A 2025 Kinsey study showed that 18% of respondents said their sexual desire had increased on GLP-1s while 16% said it had decreased.

“Some of this we do need to tease out,” South says. “Is it weight loss? Is it GLP-1? Or is it some coexisting things that are happening at the same time? For example, a middle-aged perimenopausal female with reduced sexual function.”

What is known is that experiencing major and rapid weight loss alone can significantly affect relationships – a 2018 Swedish study that analysed 1,958 patients who had bariatric surgery found there was an increased incidence of divorce or separation for those in couples, while there was a higher likelihood of a new relationship for those who were single.

Jennifer isn’t sure if the intimacy problems in her marriage are related to her age, or the weight-loss medication she’s on or the new identity she’s now embracing as a result of her changed body.

While she was on a shopping trip, a man offered to take her grocery cart back to the bay for her. Before she lost weight, she says, that never happened. Meanwhile, in professional settings, people who don’t know she used to be heavier make comments about overweight colleagues that leave her stunned.

Her husband is the one who suggested couples therapy after 34 years together once Jennifer did not “magically become more physically demonstrative in the bedroom” after her weight loss. He also commented that she’ had become “meaner”.

“I’m less afraid of our relationship failing, so maybe I hold him to a higher standard than I used to,” she acknowledges.

Without her obesity to blame, Jennifer now realises that her marital problems were “always a two-person problem but my weight was easy to point to because I felt so bad about it”.

Relationship breakdown is complicated and rarely attributable to any single factor.

“Human libido and relationships are complex at their core, so it would be very difficult to extrapolate what it is about these medicines specifically that would have an impact there,” says Dr Mark Mellor, a bariatric doctor and specialist GP who regularly prescribes GLP-1s and says research would be challenging.

As people’s self-confidence soars, Mellor says, that could also play a role in “people perhaps thinking, ‘What am I doing here in this relationship?’”

Glenn Mackintosh, a psychologist and clinical director of Brisbane’s Weight Management Psychology Clinic, says couples who visit the clinic often mention disruption to their old lives before GLP-1s.

“Say a couple who have a shared routine of finishing the day with Netflix and a pack of chips they share – if that eating is part of a shared routine, it will impact the relationship and so there’s a grieving process,” he says.

Sign up to Five Great Reads

Each week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morning

after newsletter promotion

Renewed self-confidence and attention from others can also stir fear in partners.

“It’s like, ‘OK, now my partner is getting more attention, are they going to leave me?’”

These are issues that Mackintosh says he has seen resolved in secure, functioning relationships through communication and acceptance.

“It can really cause friction. What we often say is that weight loss doesn’t cause relationship problems but it can reveal them.”

The social penalties paid by people living with obesity in the dating world are well known. For some on GLP-1s, changes to their bodies can improve their self-confidence in approaching dating – but not without navigating psychological challenges.

After 14 years of singledom, Joanna Wood started dating again last year after losing 25kg taking a GLP-1.

The former Australian diplomat, who is 59, remembers feeling nervous before her date with Bruce Hart, a 63-year-old social worker. She felt all the natural vulnerability that comes with a first date but she also felt shame that she used a GLP-1.

“I used to be a much bigger person and the story around that feels like a character defect rather than science,” she says.

After that initial date – which lasted eight hours – the relationship blossomed, as the couple started hiking together. When Wood finally revealed she’d been on a GLP-1, it didn’t faze him.

“To me, it was such a background issue,” Hart says. “I was more focused on what she was doing and her values and who she was as a person.”

Dr Rebecca Puhl, a psychologist who studies weight stigma at the University of Connecticut and has previously consulted for Eli Lilly, the manufacturer of Mounjaro, says people sometimes hide their GLP-1 use.

“They’re worried that they’ll be viewed as cheating or lacking willpower by a potential partner,” Puhl says. “Even though obesity is recognised as a complex chronic disease ... for some people, internalization of weight stigma can persist even after losing significant amounts of weight.”

Wood, who has heart disease, found the shame hard to shake even though her health has improved drastically.

When she briefly stopped taking the medication, “food noise” returned. She regained 10kg and found herself hiding confectionery from Hart.

She has since restarted the medication, accepting they are likely to be a lifelong treatment.

Having retrained as a counsellor, Wood has developed a program for women over 50 on GLP-1s to navigate the psychological journey of using the drugs.

Jennifer is also sure she’ll be on a GLP-1 for life.

Her marriage is another commitment she expected to last a lifetime.

“Things are stable for now,” she says. “We aren’t fighting and we continue to talk but we aren’t solving anything, either.”

She isn’t sure whether the medication changed her marriage or simply stripped away the explanation she’d relied on for decades. The weight is gone but the questions it once answered are not.

“We will adapt in some way – I am just not sure how yet.”

The moment I knew: We discussed the pill on our first date, kissed on our second. By the third, I knew he was the one

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 20:00:52 GMT

In the 1960s, 19-year-old Anne Ring was set up with Ian and felt an immediate attraction

Find more stories from the moment I knew series

It was June 1961, I was 19, and innocently dating in the ways of that time – I’d had several boyfriends, had my heart broken once and had broken two.

A platonic friend decided I should meet Ian, as we both liked to talk. So he invited Ian – who was 20 – and me to dinner. It was at our friend’s family’s home with Beethoven’s violin concerto playing in the background, and he was right. From the outset Ian and I were totally immersed in our conversation, and I felt an immediate connection and attraction to him. Driving me home, he asked me out the following Saturday.

That first date was to an Indian restaurant in Sydney’s centre. Afterwards, we drove all the way to Palm Beach, about an hour-and-a-half drive. There, we walked and talked until 4am about everything under the moon, including a pressing issue of the day, the pill. We had a lot of opinions in common despite our different backgrounds; my family as migrant Hungarian secular Jews coming from China, his as pioneer-stock Anglo-Australians who had lived in the same house since before Ian was born.

It also turned out that, as we were then living in the same Sydney suburb, we had already noticed each other. Ian had seen me on the bus and had, he said, been much taken by my animated conversations and cheekbones. And I’d slid down in the driver’s seat of our car while driving past a young man – Ian, as it was – washing his car, hoping he wouldn’t see that I was in my dressing gown, worn as a dare by a friend living at the top of his street.

Our second date, a week later, was a visit to one of my childhood homes in Wallerawang, almost three hours away, followed by a picnic in Lidsdale state forest. Walking hand in hand among the pine trees, we had our first kiss. And on the drive home, we sat close to each other on the bench car seats of the day, minus seatbelts.

By our third date, when we’d talked and laughed about the movie that we had just seen – about complicated relationships, in Albert Finney’s Saturday Night and Sunday Morning – I knew that what we had was both uncomplicated and special, that what I felt for him was well beyond any boyfriend of the past. My parents always waited up for me after dates to debrief. When I got home that evening I told them I thought Ian could be the one. That was something that they hadn’t heard before. As loving parents, they were happy because I was so happy.

Soon after that Ian wrote me a beautiful letter about how he felt. We became fully absorbed in our love, spending as much time together as we could, and making good use of the pill – helpfully provided by my enlightened father, a GP.

As our relationship blossomed, Ian was keen on us living together without that “unnecessary piece of paper” but we were both busy studying for our respective degrees. My mother, meanwhile, was absolutely focused on us getting married eventually. During a holiday in the Snowy Mountains with my parents, when Ian was about to start his final year, she badgered my father into asking him – when the four of us were in his old Holden – what his intentions were. It was effectively a proposal, to which Ian said yes.

So that was that, and I never got the one on a bended knee. Instead, we chose a beautiful antique opal ring together, became engaged at the beginning of that year, and married after his final exams. To this day Ian is very glad he accepted my father’s proposal.

We feel so lucky to have had 65 years and counting together, with our lives full of shared pleasures, adventures and challenges, and much travelling. We’ve mutually supported each other’s careers, his in public health and epidemiology, mine in social science research and writing, while having our three wonderful daughters and now, their families too.

We don’t always see eye to eye but we always have each other’s back, in our continuing romance based on love, trust and shared sense of humour.

For Ian, Beethoven’s violin concerto is our song, and I also see it as the overture to our joyful life together.

Dr Anne Ring is a health sociologist, freelance writer and author of Engaging with Ageing: What matters as we grow older, available now through Halstead Press (AU$34.95)

What makes a woman a witch? Financial independence

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 20:00:52 GMT

Women aren’t being burnt at the stake any more, but there is still risk and violence implicit in the label ‘witch’

When Katherine Harrison’s husband passed away, she became the wealthiest woman in Wethersfield, Connecticut. Rather than wallow in her new status as a young widow she decided to run the farm she’d inherited on her own. She took up ranching and a slew of other hobbies including brewing ale, spinning yarn and beekeeping. She traded honey and beeswax for candles. She was by all accounts, headstrong, outspoken and clever.

In many corners of the internet, Harrison’s interests are having a moment. Craft brewers have been spruiking classic ales for years, urban beekeeping is surging in popularity, and people are looking to textile-based crafts as ways to practise mindfulness.

But Harrison was a single woman and mother of three daughters who, in a notable contrast to today’s tradwives, felt she did not need a man. Her independence, wealth – and the fact that she practised astrology – make her hobbies seem less like those of a good wife and more like those of a good witch.

Unfortunately, Harrison lived in the 17th century when fear and paranoia dominated the New England colonies. It was a time when a woman’s refusal to conform to puritanical, patriarchal norms made her vulnerable to accusations of witchcraft. In 1668, more than two decades before the Salem witch trials kicked off 200km north, Harrison was arrested and put on trial for witchcraft.

In 2024 I visited Harrison’s land in Wethersfield, one of the first stops I made on a research trip for my book Good Witch. Over three years, I spoke to dozens of experts, travelled from Connecticut to Massachusetts and then across the seas to Scotland, England, Denmark and the far north of Norway. Each place was touched by the European witch trials that spanned the 15th to 18th centuries, where 80% of the approximately 80,000 to 100,000 people tried were women.

While there were many causative factors in the witch-hunts – patriarchy, economic hardship, and religious and political tensions, to name a few – a woman’s financial independence and power made her vulnerable. Sometimes this independence was realised through inheritance, sometimes her proficiency at work.

Harrison’s initial charges were dismissed, but she was summoned before the court again the following year. The indictment alleged she had “familiarity with Satan … and by his help acted things beyond the ordinary course of nature”. The wide-ranging accusations included divination and healing; people said they’d seen her likeness appearing in their beds at night.

It was alleged she had asked for the devil’s help to make her work more profitable and to hinder the work of her neighbours. More than one witness mentioned being suspicious of her skills as a spinner, several men accused her of bewitching them to impede their trades as weavers and one tailor claimed she bewitched him to incorrectly sew sleeves on a jacket seven times in a row.

During the trial, it was clear her neighbours’ accusations of witchcraft lacked evidence and were mostly based on petty grievances, jealousy and superstition. Although she was convicted the magistrate spared her life, citing weak evidence, and banished her from Wethersfield instead.

Harrison’s case is emblematic of a pattern in the witch-hunts of colonial New England. In an analysis of the trials, the US historian Carol F Karlsen found that, although it was rare for women to inherit property, when they did, they were more susceptible to witchcraft allegations. Women from families without male heirs (Harrison had three daughters) made up 64% of the females prosecuted, 76% of those who were found guilty, and 89% of those who were executed.

The pattern reflects how “these women were aberrations in a society with an inheritance system designed to keep property in the hands of men,” writes Karlsen, in her 1987 book The Devil in the Shape of a Woman.

That Harrison’s business endeavours are prevalent in her trial notes speaks to another pattern. “Like midwives, healers and female religious leaders, women who turned their traditional skills to profit placed themselves in competition with men – and in positions of vulnerability to witchcraft accusations,” writes Karlsen.

Women’s work was a factor in witchcraft allegations in Europe too. A Cambridge University study by Dr Philippa Carter found that women’s employment options in the 16th and 17th centuries – healthcare, food preparation, dairy production and livestock management – all came with a higher risk of witchcraft accusations.

Rather than relying on legal records, which painted a one-sided picture, Carter used the casebooks of a medical practitioner and astrologer, Richard Napier, who recorded at least 1,714 incidents of suspected bewitchment from 1597 to 1634. Work in dairying and medicine were naturally prone to spoilage and disease. These ordinary outcomes were viewed as corruption induced by bad magic: “corrupt blood made wounds rankle and corrupt milk made ill-scented cheese,” she writes.

A woman’s daily tasks would often see her crisscrossing between homes, bakehouses and marketplaces, and these frequent interactions with neighbours also increased the chances of becoming embroiled in conflicts and labelled a witch.

Across Europe, women’s work in medicine would be maligned as witchcraft by institutions – like the church and academia – too. Wise women once enjoyed prominence and reverence in their communities for treating ailments with herbal remedies and prayers, delivering babies, performing minor surgeries and setting bones. But in 1325, Pope John XXII wrote a letter to Bishop Stephen of Paris, warning him that women who were practising medicine without formal education were in fact practising witchcraft and asking him to forbid them from doing so.

In the centuries that followed, regulations concerning who could legitimately study and practise medicine were tightened further. Since women were barred from academic institutions, they were effectively barred from the medical profession too.

Eventually, the marginalisation of and attacks on female healers would culminate in witchcraft prosecutions, like in Scotland when the healer Agnes Sampson – another widow – was put on trial by King James VI in the North Berwick witch trials of 1590.

She was accused of participating in a gathering of witches with the devil, where it was alleged they had cast spells to raise storms and sink the ships of King James as he sailed home from Denmark-Norway with his new bride, Princess Anne. James ordered that Sampson be tortured, and under immense duress she confessed. Of the 53 offences she was indicted with, over half focused on her practice as a healer.

What we see in Sampson’s case is evidence of how society maligned women’s labour as witchcraft and punished women for their feminine power. Accusations of witchcraft were wielded as threats against women like Harrison, who dared to defy the social structures that limited their participation in the workforce, and inheritance structures that kept property in male ownership.

Historically it’s been dangerous for women to reach for financial independence and status. While modern witchcraft, from tarot cards to astrology, has surfaced in the zeitgeist as a dreamy symbol of female intuition and girlhood, there is still risk and violence implicit in the label.

Women aren’t being burnt at the stake any more, but as we saw in June on the billboards across Melbourne depicting Victorian premier Jacinta Allan in a black pointed hat, when people want to take a woman’s power away, they’ll still call her a witch.

Good Witch: In Search of Our Lost Feminine Power by Lucianne Tonti is available in Australia now through Simon & Schuster

Police investigate payments to Reform UK first revealed by the Guardian

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 19:11:21 GMT

Scotland Yard is looking at two £250,000 donations to the party by Britain Means Business before the 2024 election

Payments to Reform UK first revealed by the Guardian are now being investigated by the Metropolitan police.

The inquiry is scrutinising payments made to the party via a company controlled by its deputy leader, Richard Tice.

Scotland Yard is looking at two donations of £250,000 made to the party by Britain Means Business in the weeks before the 2024 general election.

The Guardian revealed earlier this month that Fiona Cottrell made a £1m transfer to Britain Means Business shortly before the donations were made. About half of the funds were then passed to the party.

Cottrell’s son, George, is a convicted fraudster with close links to Reform’s leader, Nigel Farage.

The Guardian reported earlier this month that Fiona and George Cottrell have been interviewed under criminal caution as part of the police investigation.

In response to a query about the investigation from the BBC, Tice said: “This is the first I have heard of it – if true why are the Met police briefing the BBC before contacting interested parties?

“Is the Met leadership now engaged in the widespread politically motivated smear campaign against Reform and its leaders?”

Fiona Cottrell also made two donations directly to the party, each worth £250,000, in May 2024. These are also within the scope of the Metropolitan police investigation.

Tice, who was elected to parliament after the poll, is the sole director of Britain Means Business.

He has previously confirmed that his company received donations from Fiona Cottrell but described reports about the money as a “politically motivated smear campaign”.

The Guardian told how the transfer from Fiona Cottrell to Britain Means Business was reported to the National Crime Agency by bankers via a suspicious activity report.

Suspicious activity reports are not crime reports but exist to identify potential incidents of money laundering.

The Guardian understands that neither the NCA nor bankers have been able to trace the source of the original £1m sent by Fiona Cottrell to Tice’s company. The NCA is seeking help from a foreign partner in its attempts to understand where the money originated.

A Reform UK spokesperson said: “Reform takes pride in its stringent vetting of donations and always ensures that the Electoral Commission guidelines on donations, as set out in the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000, are strictly followed, as has been the case with donations so far.”

Fiona Cottrell did not respond to the Guardian’s attempts to contact her about the donations to Britain Means Business.

When asked about the developments by the BBC on Saturday evening, the Metropolitan police repeated a statement issued earlier this month.

“An investigation was launched in February 2025 after a referral was made to the Metropolitan police by the Electoral Commission relating to donations made to a political party ahead of the 2024 UK general election,” the force said.

“Detectives from the Met’s special enquiry team are investigating alleged offences under section 61 of the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000.

“Early investigative advice has been sought from the Crown Prosecution Service and two people have so far been interviewed under caution. No arrests have been made.

“An offence under this section is not one that the Electoral Commission can investigate and, as such, it is a matter for the police.”

From Haaland love to Mexico’s Merlin: 26 memories from the 2026 World Cup

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 19:00:50 GMT

Norway’s striker left his mark, as did Scotland’s fans in Boston, but Turkey’s dark horses fell at the first hurdle

“I played with him on my PlayStation, and now I’ve scored against him,” Livano Comenencia said after converting Curaçao’s first World Cup goal past Manuel Neuer in their opening match against Germany. The smallest nation ever to qualify for the World Cup went on to lose 7-1 but that goal – their only one of the tournament – will go down in history.

Should Jude Bellingham’s first goal against Norway have been ruled out? Perhaps so given the ball appeared to hit an overhead cable in the buildup. Fifa insisted there had been no such intervention; Norway’s manager, Ståle Solbakken, was sure there had been. “Many on the bench reacted immediately … the ball fell down straight in front of us,” he said, furiously.

“I’d rather be us than them,” said Jesse Marsch after Canada were comprehensively beaten by Morocco in the last 16. “It takes some nerve to say that when you lose 3-0,” said Morocco’s head coach, Mohamed Ouahbi, in response. Marsch also somewhat hilariously overestimated the capacity of BC Place after his side’s 6–0 win over Qatar, saying: “There’ll be 60 million people that said they were here.”

Between 1978 and 2018, only the original Ronaldo had scored more than six goals at a single World Cup (eight in 2002). Lionel Messi and Kylian Mbappé had matched the Brazilian’s tally by the semi-finals this time around, with Mbappé winning the Golden Boot after scoring two goals against England in the third-place playoff.

Scottish supporters marked their return to football’s biggest stage in 28 years by taking over Boston, filling Fenway Park with songs and drinking their pubs dry. With the Tartan Army crowning some of the city’s most recognisable statues with bright orange traffic cones, the “Boston cone” was greeted by Boston’s mayor, Michelle Wu, upon its arrival from Glasgow last week. Scotland’s players may have made little impact in the US this summer, but their fans no doubt left a legacy.

‘CR7’ finally ended his knockout goal drought against Croatia as Portugal squeezed into the last 16. However, joy soon turned to despair when Portugal were eliminated by Spain in the next round. Ronaldo struggled to have any impact on proceedings, managing only 19 touches in what was his final World Cup match. “I gave it all, I gave it my best,” he said afterwards.

The mistaken identity rule was updated for this World Cup to cover situations where a player was booked but the offence was committed by the other team and well and truly took effect during Argentina and Switzerland’s quarter-final in Kansas City. The referee, João Pinheiro, initially issued Argentina’s Leandro Paredes a yellow card for his challenge on Switzerland’s Breel Embolo before the VAR called him to the monitor. Embolo was then ruled to have dived and was punished with a yellow card himself – it was the forward’s second of the game and he was duly sent off. “This rule destroyed the game today,” said Switzerland’s head coach, Murat Yakin, after his side’s 3-1 loss.

Competing against the backdrop of their country’s conflict with the US, Iran’s players faced incredible difficulties before a ball was kicked. With their training base abruptly switched from Arizona to Mexico before the tournament, the team were then only allowed to enter the US the day before their first two matches and had to leave immediately after. Despite that, they only narrowly missed out on the knockout rounds after Austria and Algeria drew 3-3 in the final round of the group stage to send them home on goal difference. “What these players have done should be written in history because the host country treated us very unfairly,” Iran’s head coach, Amir Ghalenoei, said.

Snapchat stories. Stuffed raccoons. Doing next to nothing against Brazil for 79 minutes and then scoring twice in 11 minutes. It’s fair to say Erling Haaland made his mark at the World Cup. “When someone asks me what my biggest fear is but I can’t say being charged at by Haaland at full speed so I just say spiders,” reads a video that has racked up millions of views on Instagram, a reference to how Haaland chased down Iraq’s goalkeeper, Jalal Hassan, for his second goal of the tournament.

Turkey were tipped to go far but, in the end, didn’t even make it out of the group stage. Indeed, they were the second country eliminated from the tournament following back-to-back losses to Australia and 10-man Paraguay. “We should have won these games … everybody’s sad, everybody’s crying,” said Arda Guler, Turkey’s wonderkid after his country’s less-than-wonderful showing.

“I’m going home and won’t be watching any more games from the tournament,” said Egypt’s head coach, Hossam Hassan, after his side’s loss to Argentina in the last 16. “What happened to us wasn’t fair. We should have had a penalty, a goal was disallowed and I don’t know why.” Hassan was not alone in thinking crucial decisions had favoured the world champions in what was arguably the game of the tournament in Atlanta.

It started off as a standard submission for the World Cup’s official track list but was quickly adopted by England’s travelling support as the theme song of their tournament run, Oasis’s 1995 classic creating a genuinely uplifting bond between plays and fans. Harry Kane went as far as describing the post-match ritual of standing alongside his teammates, arms around each other’s shoulders, and facing a wall of happy, singing English faces as one of his “favourite ever moments in an England shirt”.

Lamine Yamal had a great World Cup but not as great as his three-year-old brother, Keyne, who captured hearts worldwide with his wide-eyed, big-grinned expressions of delight whenever his older sibling shone at the tournament. A young star was born on the back of another young star and both look here to stay.

Merlin the duck became a sensation after being spotted at Mexico’s post-game celebrations following their opening World Cup win over South Africa. Indeed, Merlin became so famous that he was granted a meeting with Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum. “We feel very honoured to be here with the president, it is an honour for us to stand before you and for the whole world to see the beautiful side of Mexico.” said Karla Gómez, Merlin’s owner. Sadly, Merlin was unable to watch Mexico in the flesh due to Fifa regulations.

Messi, Mbappé, Haaland, Harry Kane … this has been a World Cup of goalscoring superstars well and truly coming to the fore, and then there has been Mikel Merino. The Spain midfielder came off the bench to score crucial winning goals against Portugal and Belgium in back-to-back knockout games. It was some contribution from the Arsenal player to his country’s World Cup triumph.

“Gordon!” shouted Javier Aguirre at England’s left-sided forward during the first-half hydration break of an epic last-16 encounter at the Azteca, followed by something indistinguishable when Anthony Gordon turned back to look. Keen-eyed internet users later deciphered it as a very cheerful “fuck you!” from Mexico’s manager, with both men subsequently laughing with delight. “I’d just run the full-back down the line,” Gordon said after England’s 3-2 win. “So I took it as a bit of a compliment from him.”

After being named player of the match in Cape Verde’s opening goalless draw with Spain, Vozinha teared up. “My mum didn’t manage to be here because of the visa,” said the 40-year-old goalkeeper. Two days later the House Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries, announced that arrangements had been made to waive the cost of Ana Évora’s visa; she was subsequently in attendance as her son played in a 2-2 draw with Uruguay and became one of the stars of the tournament.

Neil El Aynaoui struck the crossbar. Justin Kluivert’s effort ricocheted off a post. Bart Verbruggen almost saved Soufiane Rahimi’s strike but helplessly watched it squirm under him and into the back of the net. At 2-2, Quinten Timber put his shot well wide, handing Morocco the advantage only for Achraf Hakimi to do the exact same thing. Standing bolt upright, Yassine Bounou saved from Crysencio Summerville before Ismael Saibari put an end to the rollercoaster of a truly remarkable last-32 penalty shootout.

“I’m begging Fifa to change the position of the photographers in the national anthem, because I could not see my team,” Thomas Tuchel said after England’s opening win against Croatia. “It was a very special moment, and I was standing in front of a wall of 50 photographers and I could not see one single player.” It wasn’t the first time at the tournament that England’s head coach made his frustrations clear.

Mexico’s 2-0 win over South Africa kicked off the World Cup and simultaneously almost equalled the 2022 tournament’s tally of red cards in a single match. Yaya Sithole capped off a terrible second half for South Africa by getting sent off just after the break before his teammate Themba Zwane and Mexican defender César Montes were shown red cards within eight minutes of each other.

With the vast majority of the football world rooting for them, Belgium reacted to the suspension of Folarin Balogun’s ban for the USA’s last-16 encounter with the Red Devils in Seattle with a ruthlessly commanding performance. They beat the co-hosts 4-1 and marked the victory with a string of celebrations that made clear what they thought of the controversy surrounding’s Balogun’s presence on the pitch, including an imitation of Donald Trump’s dance moves in the dressing room afterwards and a gleeful tweet from the team’s official account that simply read: “Overturn this.”

There was widespread delight when Paraguay eliminated Germany in the last 32 with a show of togetherness and defiance but their popularity diminished during their subsequent defeat by France on the back of a brutal display of the dark arts. Joe Hart brandished the South Americans an “absolute disgrace” while his fellow BBC pundit Micah Richards thought that the approach was wholly unnecessary, saying: “Paraguay are better than that. Defensively they were so good and they didn’t need to get into these antics.” The Uzbek referee, Ilgiz Tantashev, also faced intense criticism after inexplicably failing to book any Paraguay players.

After Kylian Mbappé scored the first of his two goals against Sweden, he and his teammates ran over to Didier Deschamps and hugged their head coach. The gesture was a response to Deschamps’ return to the touchline following the death of his mother. When asked about the embrace, Mbappé said: “That’s the DNA of this group. The coach has been through certain circumstances, and we’re all with him and will continue to support him.”

In a bizarre twist, the USA’s 2-0 victory over Australia in the group stages had to be stopped for, and not by, the referee, Felix Zwayer, after he collapsed with cramp in the dying minutes of the contest in Seattle. Australia’s midfielder Aiden O’Neill and the USA’s Balogun helped Zwayer stretch out the cramp amid ironic cheers from the crowd.

Croatia had seemingly rescued their World Cup campaign from the jaws of defeat after Josko Gvardiol tapped in at the back post in the final stages of their last-32 encounter with Portugal in Toronto. But then VAR got involved and the goal was ruled out after Fifa’s sensor technology discovered that the cross to Gvardiol had taken the faintest touch off the head of Igor Matanovic. “It was very bad refereeing,” said Croatia’s manager, Zlatko Dalic. “I’m not saying that sometimes VAR can’t be of help, but it kills the emotions, it kills everything.”

Jayden Adams, who featured in all three of South Africa’s group games, passed away just days after returning home from North America. “Today, South African football mourn the loss of a talented player whose passion, dedication, and love for the beautiful game inspired many,” read a national team tribute. A minute’s silence was observed before all quarter-final matches, alongside an outpouring of touching tributes to the 25-year-old midfielder.

The 21-year-old, who studies at Loughborough University, was given a huge roar when he was announced to the crowd. But he was unable to match the pace set by Australia’s Sam Short, the 2023 world champion, who took gold in 3 mins 41.25 as he finished 12 seconds back.

But for McCann, reaching the final at all was a major achievement, especially as he was up against multiple Olympic and world medallists.

“I’m buzzing,” said McCann, speaking after he qualified by finishing fourth in his morning heat. “It wasn’t really an expectation coming in, especially with how strong the field was, but I’m delighted to see I made it.

“I wouldn’t say I felt the pressure but I was certainly nervous with so many people watching and I wanted to do well, not only for myself but Team Scotland as well. I was definitely nervous but I’m glad I produced a decent swim.

“It was amazing, I could hear them the whole way through the race. They spurred me on to really give it my all down that last 100m.”

McCann grew up in England, but qualifies for Scotland through his father, Gerry, who was at the Tollcross Swimming Centre, as was his mother, Kate, to support their son. He and his twin sister, Amelie, were two years old when Madeleine, then aged three, went missing during a family holiday in Praia Da Luz, Portugal, in 2007.

McCann started swimming seriously at Charnwood Triathlon Club when he was eight, and by the age of 10 had joined the high performance City of Leicester club. He has been part of the Scottish swimming programme since his teens.

Asked about his motivation for wanting to swim, he said: “From a young age I really enjoyed competing. That makes all the hard hours in training worth it, coming out here in front of a crowd like this and swimming as well as I can really.

Lando Norris grabs F1 Hungarian GP pole while Hamilton and Antonelli are penalised

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 16:50:54 GMT

Defending champion takes first pole of 2026 by 0.012sec

Hamilton and Antonelli receive three-place penalties

The margins were tiny and for a moment it seemed Lewis Hamilton had finally found his edge in qualifying, only for the seven-time champion to be beaten by but a breath. The defending world champion, Lando Norris, pipped him to pole for the Hungarian Grand Prix in a thrilling, dramatic contest.

Worse was to follow for Hamilton as his very real chance of converting a front-row start to a win in his hugely competitive Ferrari took a severe blow as he was penalised three grid places for impeding McLaren’s Oscar Piastri during their final laps. Hamilton will start from fifth place.

Norris took the top spot for McLaren by one-hundredth of a second from Hamilton’s Ferrari, but the latter’s place on the front row remained in doubt, as he was under investigation by the FIA.

Hamilton said he had been informed by the team that Piastri was closing on him only when the McLaren was already right behind him and that he did not know anyone was still on a hot lap behind him. Nonetheless, after qualifying, the stewards ruled he was at fault and imposed the grid penalty.

“I was told when he was at the apex behind me, so I had no idea he was coming,” Hamilton said. “I thought everyone came out behind me. I was the first out so I thought everyone had finished their lap, and I think Charles was the car that was behind me when I left the pit lane, as far as I was aware. So, yeah, crazy, because it had been clean, and obviously it wasn’t intentional.”

Hamilton’s teammate, Charles Leclerc, was in third, with the championship leader, Kimi Antonelli, in fourth for Mercedes, but the Italian was investigated for failing to slow under yellow flags and also given a three-place penalty. Antonelli leads Hamilton by 45 points and his teammate, George Russell, by 50 points in the championship.

Piastri was fifth for McLaren, Max Verstappen sixth for Red Bull after he spun on his final lap, while Russell could manage only seventh and was told to pull his car off the track after his final lap with a water leak.

The day belonged to Norris, who delivered a superb run for McLaren to claim pole. Given that the team had opened the season off the pace of Mercedes and Ferrari, their upgrades for Miami and further developments added in Canada have proved impressive and they are the first team to deny Mercedes the top spot this season.

It is Norris’s second pole at the Hungarian GP and the 17th of his career, while for McLaren it is another strong result at the circuit. With Norris winning here last year and Piastri in 2024, they may well be in position to make it three in a row at a meeting where McLaren have a record 13 victories.

On the opening laps in Q3 Verstappen made the running but was surpassed by Norris, yet Hamilton nailed his first lap to take provisional pole with a time of 1min 17.219sec, a tenth up on Norris in second, and a chance to take his first pole for Ferrari and a record 10th at the same track.

The track had been steadily rubbering-in throughout the session, the times coming down as the grip increased and the final runs were crucial. Hamilton was sent out early but could not improve on his time and Norris, the last man on track, was on a quick run. Immense through the middle sector, there was nothing in it and he just edged out Hamilton by one-hundredth of a second with a time of 1:17.207.

Given the track was evolving Hamilton felt the decision to send him out early had been an error. “I felt solid throughout qualifying, but for some reason we went out first, which I don’t think was the right call,” he said. “The grip wasn’t there for either Charles or I. We were quickest throughout, so it’s definitely one that got away.”

Aston Martin brought their radically overhauled B-spec car to Hungary in the hope of turning round a disastrous opening to the season. The car was overweight and aerodynamically far from where they had expected to be, while their Honda engine is down on power and suffered from causing severe vibrations early in the season.

The team principal and designer, Adrian Newey, admitted it had been an immensely difficult start. “These first races have been a complete nightmare,” he said. “Hopefully, we can get at least to a point of respectability now, that is the immediate goal.”

In qualifying at least they made a step forward with Fernando Alonso putting an Aston into Q2 for the first time this season, no mean feat given they were two seconds slower than the Cadillacs in Belgium. Alonso ultimately finished in 16th.

The success of the upgrade is considered to be key in persuading Alonso to stay for 2027, with a further development expected for Zandvoort when Honda will also bring their new engine.

The return of the Malaysia to the F1 calendar could be confirmed as early as Sunday, with the meeting arranged after the cancellation of the races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia earlier in the season. It will take place between the rounds in Baku and Singapore on 4 October. The race at the Sepang circuit near Kuala Lumpur is expected to be branded as the Bahrain Grand Prix held in Malaysia, with Bahrain funding the event. The circuit last held an F1 meeting in 2017.

F1 is also understood to be looking into the prospect of hosting the season finale at Imola if the final two rounds of the season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi are unable to be held because of the conflict in the Middle East.
