Wildfires around the Arcachon lagoon near Bordeaux and around Biscarrosse, in the Landes, have destroyed more than 36,000 hectares of forest. This is the third stage of the Tour to be subjected to prefecture intervention, due to wildfires or a heatwave, in this year’s race.

Resources and the lack of them have also been a topic of debate since Pogacar’s astounding win on Alpe d’Huez on Friday. The four-time champion is now expected to secure a record-equalling fifth title in Paris on Sunday evening after Saturday’s 20th stage was won by Richard Carapaz.

A day after setting a record time up the Alpe’s famous hairpin bends to extend his overall lead, Pogacar could afford to concede 39 seconds to his closest challenger, Remco Evenepoel, on Saturday and will start Sunday’s shortened stage into Paris ahead by six minutes and 26 seconds.

However, there was significant fallout after Friday’s chaotic climb, largely due to the dangerous behaviour of some among the thousands at the roadside. Several incidents, which endangered both riders and fans, rebooted the debate over the safety of Tour stages on the Alpe.

In-race motorbikes, blocked by the crowds, stalled an attack from Evenepoel, while a lack of crowd control led to the Movistar climber Einer Rubio abandoning the race after riding into the rear windscreen of a UAE team car. The crash, which led to Rubio being transported by helicopter to hospital in Grenoble, where he was given 20 stitches for facial injuries, was caused by an unruly spectator falling in front of the car, forcing it to suddenly brake.

“If we had been using cars from 20 years ago, the accident wouldn’t have happened,” the race director, Thierry Gouvenou, said, apparently blaming the braking sensors in the car.

More footage of fans wrestling each other over gifts from the caravane publicitaire and climbing over moving race vehicles – including the Guardian’s – further fuelled the notion of a race that was out of control. The French national champion, Romain Grégoire, said spectators were “so drunk that it was more like being slapped on the arse, than getting pushes”. Evenepoel’s Red Bull-Bora Hansgrohe sports director, Klaas Lodewyck, said: “As long as they’re cheering on the riders and creating a good atmosphere, it’s fine. But when they start punching in side mirrors and banging on the windows, that’s crossing the line.”

On Saturday’s final mountain stage, Pogacar the ogre, as L’Équipe called him, worked to protect the interests of his third-placed UAE teammate, Isaac del Toro. Carapaz, stage winner in Orcières-Merlette and third in Friday’s stage to Alpe d’Huez, was again one of the key animators, attacking on the first climb, the Col de la Croix de Fer, as he sought to consolidate his lead in the King of the Mountains classification.

More than 250,000 people flee wildfires in France and Spain

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 16:23:17 GMT

Hundreds of firefighters battle blazes as strong winds drive fires towards Bordeaux and smoke prompts health warnings in Madrid

Unrestrained wildfires in Spain and France have forced more than 250,000 people to flee, authorities from both countries have said, as they struggle to contain the blazes.

About 70,000 people were evacuated from central Spain, while 197,000 people fled in France, including tens of thousands from the wine region city of Bordeaux.

Spain declared a national emergency, the first time the country has ever done so over a wildfire. France’s evacuations constituted “probably” the biggest peacetime evacuation the country has ever seen, its interior minister said.

Hundreds of firefighters have worked to contain the blazes, which have been fuelled by persistent heatwaves and the climate crisis, but were still unable to stop their advance. In Spain, high winds were exacerbating the fires, and two of the three blazes merged on Friday.

France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said a huge military cargo plane, the Airbus A400M Atlas, was being deployed to join 18 other aircraft in the “long and very difficult” battle against wildfires in the Gironde region of south-western France.

The French government has called in the military to help, deploying 1,500 soldiers, and has rushed 1.5m face masks to help protect people from smoke inhalation. Fire crews have also been digging trenches, as well as using retardants, as winds were forecast to push the fires closer to Bordeaux. Wildfires were reported to be about 20 miles west of the city.

The French government ordered people in the path of the fire to evacuate, including those in Bordeaux’s western suburbs. Police went door to door to tell people to leave, with scenes of panic unfolding as residents fled their homes under a smoke-darkened sky.

The Gironde regional prefect, Sophie Brocas, said on Friday that strong winds were driving the fire towards the Bordeaux metro area and that it had grown to “an unprecedented magnitude”.

Officials said the sudden blazes caught residents and authorities off guard. Some people in France had to flee by boat when the flames headed towards coastal towns.

The French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said the fire in Gironde was so strong that it had begun generating its own winds.

“The fires that are hitting our country have reached a level that has never been seen before,” he wrote on X. “Our priority is clear: protecting human lives.” He urged people to obey evacuation orders “without delay”.

The Spanish health minister instructed people in Madrid not to go outside over concern of the poor air quality.

“Avoid physical activity and staying outdoors. If you go outdoors and there is smoke or ash, use a mask,” Monica Garcia said on X.

On Saturday evening, Spain’s interior ministry said a man had died in a fire in Manises, in Valencia. He had been found in a car in a ravine, officials said.

The fire was a separate incident from the major blazes raging west of Madrid, which have so far not caused any reported deaths.

The long, back-to-back heatwaves in Europe have dried forests out, turning them into tinder for wildfires. Fires had already consumed 130,000 hectares (320,000 acres) of forest this year in Spain, about a third higher than the country’s annual average, Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said on Saturday.

In France, fires burned down more than 98,000 hectares, which France’s interior minister said was a “historic record”.

Scientists say climate breakdown is triggering more frequent and more extreme weather events, evaporating soils and waterways, fuelling wildfires and leading to thousands of excess deaths. Europe is heating at about twice the global average rate.

Sánchez said that cooler weather on Saturday gave a “window of opportunity” for firefighters to help contain the blazes. “We are going to have some complex hours ahead because, although the temperatures have gone down, we do not know exactly how the wind will develop, how strong it will be,” he added.

Other European countries were helping both countries fight the blazes, with Croatia, the Czech Republic, Greece, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal and Slovakia sending aid and water-dumping aircraft to France and Spain.

The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, promised more help was on the way.

“Europe stands alongside France and Spain in the face of the devastating wildfires ravaging them. Five planes and two helicopters from the rescue fleet are now deployed in France and four planes are arriving in Spain today,” she said on X.

New North Sea oil drilling faces delay after gear accidentally dropped in sea

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 16:00:46 GMT

Exclusive: Blunder at Rosebank, UK’s biggest undeveloped oilfield, comes as government considers granting licence

Production at Britain’s biggest undeveloped oil and gasfield could be delayed for months after equipment from a rig was accidentally dropped in the North Sea, the Guardian can reveal.

Andy Burnham’s new government is under pressure from the fossil fuel industry to allow oil to be retrieved from the Rosebank site despite opposition from climate campaigners and some Labour MPs.

Rosebank, located about 80 miles north-west of Shetland, was believed to be ready to generate oil before the end of the year, pending ministerial approval.

Adura, the company responsible for Rosebank, now says it anticipates this will happen at some point in 2027. The field is projected to produce 300m barrels of oil over its 25-year lifespan, according to industry estimates.

Some MPs believe enhanced domestic production of oil and gas would help tackle the cost of living, a central focus of the new prime minister, by improving energy security amid global instability, while green campaigners believe the impact on the UK economy of exploiting the fields would be minimal.

However, delays at Rosebank mean production at the field will be unlikely to affect the UK’s energy supply over the winter months. Licences for Rosebank and another site, Jackdaw, were granted under the Conservatives but operations were paused after a court challenge by environmental groups.

The new energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is expected to make a decision on the fields’ future after consultations regarding their emissions conclude in August.

Earlier this week, Adura told the BBC that the Jackdaw site, about 150 miles east of Aberdeen, could produce gas as early as October.

However, preparations for oil production at Rosebank have been hindered by the rig incident, which occurred on 18 April. No workers were hurt, but two central pieces of drilling equipment, including a safety valve, were dropped 1,100 metres on to the seabed.

The platform, hired by Adura from Norwegian company Odfjell Drilling, was taken to a shipyard in Bergen for repairs. It is now back at Rosebank but not yet operational.

Odfjell Drilling said in internal documentation that the rig could be out of action for up to four months. The Guardian understands this means that some oil wells will be completed significantly behind schedule.

Burnham is facing calls from trade unions and opposition parties to ramp up North Sea production. Some Labour MPs say the oil and gas industry, centred around Aberdeen, could face collapse without new investment.

Sally Jameson, a Cabinet Office minister, has also argued that more domestic production of oil and gas would give Britain greater control over the cost of energy. Others fear it would have no real impact on bills, while wreaking untold damage on the climate.

Mike Reader, part of the Labour Environment Campaign, said there was no evidence new drilling would save jobs in the long term.

The Guardian revealed that only 27 direct full-time jobs would be created by Jackdaw, one of the biggest gasfields remaining in the North Sea, according to an environmental impact assessment filed publicly by Adura.

Ed Miliband, the new foreign secretary, previously described the Rosebank proposals as “climate vandalism” when Labour was in opposition. However, in recent weeks talks are believed to have taken place on how to allow new drilling without breaching Labour’s 2024 manifesto commitments, in which it pledged not to issue new licences but honour existing ones.

Several environmental groups are understood to be considering whether they would have grounds to take legal action regarding any government decision to allow new drilling.

Angeliki Papantoniou, a lecturer in environmental law at the University of Hull, said that, while a fresh challenge would be a “long shot”, it would be most likely to succeed if based on “substantive environmental matters” such as the disruption of ecosystems, pollution and potential health impacts.

“It could be argued that those developments cannot reasonably be ignored when taking a decision with likely high environmental effects,” she said.

“In theory, it could be hard for [Fahnbulleh] to claim that [the government] took all necessary precautionary measures without detailed risk assessments on the effects of drilling on the marine environment, climate and human health.”

Areeba Hamid, co-executive director of Greenpeace, which challenged the original decision to grant licences, said approval for the fields would make “zero difference” to energy bills and generate few jobs.

“Despite these meagre benefits, we would be prolonging a polluting industry that’s fuelling heatwaves while sending a disastrous signal to our international allies,” she said.

Odfjell Drilling declined to comment. Adura did not respond to a request for comment.

Wealthy gen Xers stand in the way of a Burnham tax on the super-rich

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 15:00:45 GMT

If the prime minister wants to make the system fairer he will need to upset the professional classes with a land value tax

The professional classes act like a Praetorian Guard for the super-rich.

Having acquired some of the trappings of being rich, they defend the privileges of wealth – land, property and pensions. They do this as if they – company managers, lawyers, doctors, judges, senior civil servants, architects and chartered this and thats – were the main beneficiaries.

Crucially, tax is a hill that many upper middle-income gen Xers and baby boomers are prepared to die on. That is, they will die at some point, and want to take as much money with them, whether as a sign of success, to secure their families financial security or to give to charity. Whatever the reason, they definitely don’t want democratically elected bodies – national or local – to have the money.

It is true they pay a much higher proportion of the government’s tax receipts than they did 15 years ago, hence their reluctance to pay any more.

It is an understandable stance, except that the tax system they now defend is one that is so complex and riddled with distorting incentives that it is slowly destroying the economy. And it allows the super-rich to escape almost all obligations to support the society that gave them huge wealth in the first place.

The professional classes appear to care little that their defence of the current tax system undermines the incentive for work, and especially to work as a salaried employee, or that the current tax system deters business investment.

They have calculated that their high level of wealth will be enough to cash out, hopefully as part of an early retirement package, live on the proceeds for the rest of their days and hand on the surplus to their favoured recipients.

It might seem unfair to pick on a particular group, but wealthy gen Xers – those born from 1965 to 1980 (making them 46 to 61 years old) – and baby boomers born after the war and before the 1960s really began to swing, are the people in charge of pretty much everything; and, as such, are a powerful lobby against changes to the tax system.

Sparks are about to fly because one of the battlegrounds in Andy Burnham’s first months in office will be how to raise funds to support a wide array of measures he hopes will improve living standards.

The new prime minister’s ability to borrow more funds will be limited, leaving his advisers with little option but to raise more tax.

Taxing the rich will fit with his pledge to make the government “more Labour” to please the left flank of his party, which still flexes its considerable muscle despite Jeremy Corbyn’s expulsion.

The tax change that would do more for the economy and would introduce a huge dose of fairness into the system would be a land value tax (LVT). Anyone who wants to read more about how we could ditch council tax and stamp duty – the two main taxes on property – in favour of an annual tax on the value of land can see the latest discussion paper by Dan Neidle’s Tax Policy Associates.

It replaces the £45.2bn raised by council tax and the £11.5bn from stamp duty with a flat LVT rate of 1.28%. Under the Neidle scheme, LVT raises £56.7bn. By his calculation, about 70% of homes pay less than their current council tax. These homes are mostly outside London and the south-east.

The super-rich would be unable to dodge the tax because they cannot shift the land they own overseas.

after newsletter promotion

Economists are almost uniformly in favour. One of the leading proponents, Fred Harrison, has written about how LVT was discussed in the highest circles during the early 19th century, just as wealth was being accumulated and largely untaxed, but defeated by lobbying from the newly minted professional classes.

Burnham has spoken in favour of a land tax, and he could phase in a scheme that replaces council tax and stamp duty, setting England, and possibly the other countries of the UK if they follow suit, in an exciting new direction towards land being used more productively and not as a store of wealth.

In the meantime, he needs extra cash. There are people close to the prime minister lobbying for a rise in capital gains tax (CGT) to match the thresholds for income tax. This would discourage taxpayers from accumulating wealth at the expense of income, which has been a trend for the last 40 years.

Another, possibly complementary idea, focuses on those families with more than £100m in assets, which studies have shown can pay as little as zero tax and have an average tax rate at least half that paid by the bottom 80% of households.

These wealthy families can sidestep CGT because they are so rich they do not need to sell assets and trigger a much higher CGT payout. These initiatives could raise £10bn-plus each.

A tax commission that reported almost six years ago recommended a one-off wealth tax that raised more than £300bn.

Tackling the issue will not be for the faint-hearted. As long as the professional classes remain determined to protect their privileges and luck from 40 years of pension and property accumulation at the expense of economic growth, Burnham’s resolve will be tested.

India’s education minister resigns in victory for Cockroach youth movement protests

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 13:54:33 GMT

Dharmendra Pradhan steps down after demonstrations over exam leak scandal, prompting celebrations among thousands of protesters

India’s education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, has resigned after a week of mass demonstrations, handing a major victory to a new youth movement that has posed an unprecedented challenge to Narendra Modi’s government.

In a statement on Saturday afternoon, Pradhan said he had submitted his letter of resignation to the prime minister after student pressure.

“Considering the situation that has arisen at Jantar Mantar and ‌across the country, so that anti-national forces do not take advantage of this situation … I have sent my resignation letter to the prime minister,” Pradhan wrote in a social media post.

He said he had been “saddened by what unfolded over the last 10 days”, but added: “I deeply respect the aspirations, feelings, and legitimate expectations ‌of the country’s youth.”

During his 12 years in power, Modi has cultivated a strongman image and has maintained his ministers are not accountable to public pressure. This was the first time a mass uprising had forced one of his most loyal ministers to resign.

The protests were organised by a newly formed youth political movement, the Cockroach Janata party (CJP), which has escalated into a nationwide uprising of youth dissent this week.

The core demand of the CJP and its supporters was the resignation of Pradhan over an exam leak scandal that has devastated the lives of millions of students and led to more than a dozen students taking their own lives.

The refusal by Modi to sack his minister over the scandal was widely seen as symbolic of the alleged lack of accountability of the Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) and its repeated failure to address the issues faced by young people, particularly in the country’s flawed education system.

CJP organisers confirmed they had called off their demonstration after Pradhan’s resignation and a meeting with senior BJP ministers on Saturday afternoon.

In a speech to the crowds gathered at the Delhi Jantar Mantar protest site, CJP’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, saluted the “courage” of students who had turned out in huge numbers, even when they were subjected to police violence.

“We have done it,” he said, to cries of “victory to India” and “long live the revolution”. But Dipke also emphasised Pradhan’s resignation was “just the beginning” in the movement’s push for systemic education reform and its fight for democratic rights.

He also cautioned against people making a hero of him. “Do not make this mistake,” said Dipke. “The country has been ruined by making one person a hero.”

Faria Asif, 26, a lawyer who was in the crowd, said: “I am extremely joyous. This is a huge victory, not just for the students, for the constitution and for the entire nation. Being part of this movement has been extremely empowering for all of us. I think it’s the beginning of change.”

The news of Pradhan stepping down was met with ecstatic cheers by tens of thousands of CJP supporters gathered in Delhi, who have been demanding accountability from the government.

“This is one of the most historic days for our country,” said Rochelle Cope, 27. “For the first time in 12 years, someone from the government has been held accountable for wrongdoing. And it wasn’t political parties that did this; it was the people.

“This is a movement of unity, love, solidarity, peace, justice and power. Being here has made me proud to be a citizen of India. This is only the beginning – this government will not be able to rule like it did before.”

For many of those present, this week was the first time they had taken part in a political protest and the movement was described as a “gen Z political awakening” in India.

Among them was 16-year-old Kanishka Dabla, who said she hoped to become a doctor one day. “It’s wonderful that he has resigned,” she said. “It has made us all feel very powerful. And this also feels like justice for those students who committed suicide because of the exam leaks. It’s made me hopeful for my future again.”

In a statement, the CJP said the resignation was a victory for democracy. “We have a free country where we are free to express ourselves, dissent, criticise the government we elect. We will never let anyone take that away from us,” it read.

The statement added: “Remember, do not mess with cockroaches.”

Sonam Wangchuk, the renowned Indian engineer and activist who had galvanised the movement as he went on a 26-day hunger strike, celebrated the “victory of democracy, straight from the streets”.

The CJP demonstrations had taken a dramatic turn on Monday, when hundreds of thousands of young people and students took to the streets of Delhi in the largest youth-led protest seen in years. The police had hit back against the peaceful gatherings with brutality, including teargas and baton charges, leaving hundreds injured.

Widespread anger erupted at the violent police response, prompting more people to come out in support of the movement. Throughout this week thousands had flocked to the CJP’s Delhi sit-in to chant slogans against the government and call for Pradhan’s resignation. Demonstrations also broke out across the country, with hundreds of thousands taking to the streets in Kolkata and Mumbai.

For weeks, the Modi government had ignored the CJP protesters, but as support grew into ahuge mass movement this week, the government agreed to have a dialogue.

Modi had agreed to fast-track justice for the exam leaks, but had made no mention of the CJP’s core demand, the resignation of Pradhan, who was seen as one of his most important and loyal ministers.

However, the CJP’s leadership had made it clear the resignation of Pradhan was a non-negotiable demand for the movement. As more protests erupted over the weekend and negotiations were at a deadlock, the BJP government appeared to be backed into a corner.

Not all those who took part in the protests were gen Z. Annie Raja, 62, beamed as she looked out at the celebrating protesters. “I feel enthusiastic and happy,” she said.

“The young people came out on the streets and they saved our democracy. Previously the government thought they had all the power, and the people were living only in fear. Now the Modi government is scared of us.”

The AI jobs apocalypse probably isn’t coming anytime soon

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 13:00:43 GMT

Artificial intelligence may not deliver on its promise of vast economic opportunity at a price that humanity is willing to pay

In March, Anthropic, the cutting-edge artificial intelligence business that gave us the chatbot Claude, published an analysis on the impact of AI on employment, to help us assess the claim that intelligent robots were about to redefine human existence, ending demand for human labor.

Last year in May, Anthropic’s co-founder, Dario Amodei, claimed AI could wipe out half of all entry-level jobs in one to five years. Last January, he told us AI would probably become a “general labor substitute for humans”. In June he said we risk “a world where the economic trade-off dial is stuck on the hypergrowth, hyper-inequality setting”.

And yet, Anthropic’s report suggests that, so far, AI’s impact has fallen short of expectations: “We find no systematic increase in unemployment for highly exposed workers since late 2022,” the report stated. Deployment of the technology “remains a fraction of what’s feasible”. Claude covers just 33% of all tasks in the computer and math category whereas theoretically it could take over nearly 100% of them.

Spending on datacenters is going through the roof, for sure, but productivity has not been experiencing the galloping gains that the technorati’s epochal prognostications lead one to expect. Labor productivity was, in fact, slower in the first three years of our AI era than during the information technology boom that began in the mid 1990s.

Even OpenAI’s Sam Altman, AI’s most public face, says he now doubts its job-killing potential. “I don’t think we’re going to have the kind ​of jobs apocalypse that some of the companies in our space advocate or talk about,” he said in May. As Massachusetts Institute of Technology economist David Autor noted: “A lot of people have noticed that the world is not changing as fast as they predicted.”

This has opened the public conversation to a less cataclysmic narrative of the evolution of the technology. The emerging new story not only puts more emphasis on the complexity of the relationship between automation and human work across history. It is also raising doubts about the very feasibility of the threatened AI transformation of the universe. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index, which had been propelled almost exclusively by the rise of AI-related stocks, has fallen about 8% since its peak in early June.

One strand of critique of the “AI-will-do-everything” story might be called the O-ring argument. It comes from the mid-flight explosion of the space shuttle Challenger 73 seconds into its flight on 28 January 1986. A lengthy investigation concluded that the demise of the multibillion dollar spaceship was caused by a rubber O-ring that didn’t work at low temperatures.

That cheap O-ring proved critical. The analogy suggests that as long as AI cannot perform every task perfectly, it will increase the value of the remaining tasks. Depending on which the AI takes over, it could increase the value of high skill workers who are relieved by AI of the low-end part of their job, or increase the opportunity of lower skilled workers by taking over the more expert tasks.

As one recent study noted: “despite strong substitution at the task level, overall employment effects are modest, as reduced demand in exposed occupations is offset by productivity-driven increases in labor demand at AI-adopting firms.”

Things could change. As Jed Kolko points out, research on the labor market impact of artificial intelligence is still in its infancy. There are almost four years to go in Amodei’s one-to-five year window. And maybe devastation hits in year six. According to the Federal Reserve, adoption of AI is expanding fast across businesses.

Moreover, Autor argues, AI is getting better. And its progress shows no sign that it will soon hit a ceiling. “Skepticism about the stochastic parrot is behind us,” he told me. The dystopian AI future – utopian, if you get to own and run the AI – is still on the cards.

“Insiders are as gung ho as ever,” noted Daron Acemoglu, the Nobel prize-winning economist. “They still believe artificial general intelligence is around the corner.” Indeed, Elon Musk has not budged from the dream that “AI+Robots will be able to do everything, resulting in universal high income. Work will be optional.”

One may recall the quip by Nobel prize-winning economist Robert Solow in the early years of the computer revolution: “You can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics.” It took another 10 years or so, as businesses reorganized around the new technology. But computers did eventually show up in the stats.

Clouds are nonetheless gathering on the AI horizon. It’s not just that AI may not end all human work. AI may not deliver on its promise of vast economic opportunity at a price that humanity is willing to pay.

The politics have decidedly soured on the project. Seven in 10 Americans oppose building AI datacenters in their area. While this has to do with their insatiable demand for energy, which drives up local electricity costs, AI’s unpopularity is no doubt related to the proposition that it will destroy society as we know it.

There are other bumps in the road. Despite its vast progress, big doubts remain on whether AI can do everything a modern economy needs. “Not everything is a computational problem,” notes Autor. AI is good at replicating language, but it cannot connect language to the reality around it. Despite its progress, it still makes plenty of critical mistakes.

And then there are the impossible economics. Even if AI could eventually solve all our problems, the solution looks expensive. How much of GDP are we willing to invest in AI datacenters, 20%? 30%? 40%? According to some estimates, that is where we are headed. The International Energy Agency estimates that power demand from datacenters will more than double by 2030 to about 945 terawatt-hours, more than the energy consumption of Japan.

The economics look more fragile considering how fast the investment in AI depreciates, as new models overtake those developed just a few months ago. Companies developing AI models “are never going to make money”, Acemoglu said. “They are losing hundreds of billions of dollars every year.”

One may discount Altman’s new modesty as a PR feint. Somebody may have told him that equating the AI revolution with mass joblessness was not smart politics. But misgivings about AI’s vaunted capabilities are more than a marketing twist. The grand, epochal promise may be in trouble. Maybe artificial intelligence can’t deliver at a price society is willing to pay.

‘Really inappropriate’: teachers decry plan for humanoid robot in New York high school

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 12:00:42 GMT

Robot from company that acquired sex doll maker to be introduced in school with large Native American population

A humanoid robot is being introduced as part of a pilot program, along with an AI teaching assistant, at Salamanca high school in Salamanca, New York, located on the Allegany territory of the Seneca nation.

Teachers have criticized the program, deeming it “inappropriate” and claiming it dehumanizes the profession with the introduction of human-like robots. Some local Native American residents have also criticized the pilot program, citing its implementation as “culturally tone deaf”.

The robot, named Sally, was purchased by the Cattaraugus county school district – which includes Salamanca high school – for $57,590. According to a presentation on the program, Sally will be a closed-loop system, but available virtually to students 24/7 for those with access, and offers personalized learning options.

The district will be the first in the US to deploy a humanoid robot and AI teaching assistant, according to a press release by Realbotix.

“The Salamanca pilot also includes deployment of a Realbotix M-Series humanoid robot, which uses natural conversation, facial expressions and real-time interaction to create engaging, hands-on learning experiences,” the press release states.

Realbotix, formerly Tokens. com, a Toronto-based company, purchased Simulacra, a Las Vegas-based company known for realistic sex dolls, for $16.7m in April 2024, marking a pivot for the company from crypto to humanoid robots.

Realbotix has denied ties to the sex doll company, and denied any inferences that the dolls – manufactured by Abyss Creations, a subsidiary of Realbotix – are related to the pilot program.

“The Salamanca teachers’ union as a whole is concerned about the background of the company of Realbotix. We’re very concerned about the security of the software that they’re implementing, and whether or not the data will be stored, how it will be gathered, are the recording capabilities,” said Lacey Pihlblad, president of Salamanca Teachers’ Association and a teacher at the high school.

“We would like to see the school district pause implementing the robot, pause implementing the software aspect of this AI technology until we can have more individuals weigh in.”

She said New York state is currently shifting away from too much technology in the classroom.

“There’s a growing consensus that indicates our students should be exposed to less technology. Placing a humanoid robot into the classroom to interact with our children, I believe, is a massive step in the wrong direction, and I believe that the majority of our teachers feel the same.” she added. “If we’re going to do something of this magnitude, I feel we need to make sure that we do it the correct way, and I’m not sure that that’s currently what’s in place.”

Pihlblad said the union was completing negotiations for a new union contract and intend to include protections around artificial intelligence.

Melinda Person, president of the New York State United Teachers, the parent union of the Salamanca Teachers’ Association, which represents teachers at the high school, told the Guardian that teachers across the state are concerned about the robot program.

“Our members in Salamanca and educators across the state are sounding the alarm that this is really inappropriate,” said Person. “I would say our initial reaction is this is kind of creepy.”

Person said it was “way out of the realm of what we should be doing in our schools”.

“The answer to the challenges in education is not more screens, it’s not more algorithms, not more robots. What we need in our schools right now are more caring adults and more human connection,” she said.

She said teachers were not anti-technology, but rather pro-child, and take positions based on whether something is beneficial for students.

“Putting a lifeless machine in front of students is a bad idea,” she said. “I would say a machine that the intention of it is to simulate a human relationship with young people who are just learning those skills of how to interact, how to be with their peers, how to solve conflicts, and putting a robot that looks like a human that will lead to the dehumanization of the profession of education, is exactly the wrong thing for us to be doing.”

Local residents have also criticized the selection of a high school with a significant Native American population to serve as the testing ground for humanoid robots in the classroom. Nearly 40% of the high school’s student body are Native Americans.

The Seneca nation declined to comment to the Guardian.

“Out of all the schools in New York state, let alone in the US, they chose to experiment on Native American children yet again,” said Sierra May Abrams, a substitute teacher at Salamanca high school and local resident. “Our culture is struggling to stay alive due to the impact of the Native American boarding schools and what they did to our elders. We live on the only reservation located in a city so it’s just absolutely insane that we’re the ones ‘testing it out’.”

Alyson Brown, a community health specialist and local resident and Seneca nation member who graduated from Salamanca, said several students have connections to the traumas of Native American boarding schools.

“Many students have connections to relatives who attended the Thomas Indian school located on our Cattaraugus territory. Many native families are viewing this pilot program as history repeating itself,” said Brown. “I see nothing positive to come from this being introduced in the classroom setting. I worry for the cognitive development of young minds in this exposure.”

A spokesperson for Realbotix did not comment on criticisms from teachers and Native American residents or the call for a pause from the Salamanca Teachers’ Association.

“Realbotix and Salamanca city central school district announced a limited pilot for fall 2026 involving Optio, an AI-powered educational assistant, and one new Realbotix M-Series humanoid unit,” the spokesperson said by email.

“The program is intended to complement, not replace, teachers by giving students supervised access to emerging AI and robotics tools as part of the district’s existing Stem [science, technology, engineering and mathematics] curriculum. The partnership also gives educators an opportunity to evaluate these technologies in a controlled classroom environment under district oversight.”

The Salamanca city central school district and superintendent Mark Beehler did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

The assistant commissioner of public affairs for the New York state department of education, JP O’Hare, said the agency had been in contact with the school district regarding its purchase of a robot “and has raised serious concerns about student privacy, appropriate safeguards, and the risk that the robot could be used to perform functions that should remain the responsibility of trained, qualified professionals.

“Technology can and should support educators and students, but it should not replace the human judgment or accountability essential to a safe and effective learning environment.”

Staff turnover is rampant under Trump 2.0 – with insidious results

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 12:00:42 GMT

A new report shows more Senate-confirmed staffers have left their jobs this time around than in his first term

Donald Trump loves a construction project. He’s building a ballroom, revamping a reflecting pool, and overseeing the construction of a skyline-altering arch in Washington DC. For his next real estate scheme, may I suggest a giant revolving door in the White House? It would certainly get a lot of use: senior officials are leaving Trump’s second administration at record rates.

According to a new report called Quiet Chaos by the nonpartisan Partnership for Public Service, 27 Senate-confirmed officials have left their positions within cabinet departments to date. That’s nearly 150% higher than the 11 departures in the first 18 months of Trump’s first administration. Per the report, it is also “nearly two and a half times as many as Trump’s first administration (11) and over six times as many as the average between the George W Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden administrations (4.3)”.

High-profile departures, like that of homeland security secretary Kristi Noem’s, have had a lot of media coverage. But as the Partnership for Public Service note in their report, there has been “remarkably little public attention” when it comes to overall departures in Trump 2.0. Indeed, the narrative has largely been that while Trump’s first term was a chaotic mess marked by constant personnel changes, his second presidency has been far more stable.

And that narrative isn’t entirely wrong. In Trump’s first term the rapid turnover was a sign that the reality TV host and real estate nepo baby had no idea what he was doing. In Trump 2.0, however, the departures point to something far more insidious. Rather than signaling incompetence, they are fuelinga power grab by a president who seems to think of himself as a king.

“Turnover on this scale does not just thin the government’s leadership ranks – it concentrates power in the president,” Chris Piper from the Partnership for Public Service writes in a blog post. “Each seat left to an acting official is one the president can fill on his own terms without the Senate’s advice and consent: no vetting, no confirmation hearing, no vote.”

Trump himself has said he likes acting officials because the temporary nature of the position gives him more control. “And so, Acting gives you much greater flexibility,” the president said in his first term. “A lot easier to do things.” Last month Trump similarly told the Wall Street Journal that he thought the non-permanent status of Bill Pulte, his incoming acting director of national intelligence and a man sometimes referred to as “Little Trump”, was an asset. “You’re less shackled,” he said. “It sort of gives you more power, you know, for a somewhat limited period of time.”

Power, and the rapid accretion of it in the executive branch, is the overwhelming theme of Trump’s second term. The conservative supermajority in the supreme court, which Trump helped create, has been invaluable to him in this regard. In July 2024, the court ruled that former presidents are entitled to some degree of immunity from criminal prosecution, nullifying the chance of an election subversion case against him before the election. Then, last month, the supreme court gave the president another gift: the power to fire leaders of independent agencies or commissions. The decision in Trump v Slaughter overturned Humphrey’s Executor, a 1935 ruling that the US constitution did not grant “illimitable power of removal” to the president.

Trump doesn’t quite have carte blanche to remove whomever he likes. On the same day as that decision, the supreme court ruled in Trump v Cook that the Federal Reserve was an exception to Trump’s power. Nevertheless, it is hard to overstate the significance of the Slaughter ruling, which upended almost a century of well-settled law curbing executive power. “Today, the court discards that democratic regime in favor of one that distorts the structure of government to fit the majority’s theory of unitary, total executive control. The result is a president who emerges with far greater power than ever before,” justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote in her dissent. Trump, meanwhile, wrote on Truth Social that it was “the Greatest Increase in Presidential Power in the last 100 years”.

I highly doubt that Trump has spent significant portions of his life thinking about the constitutionality of the Humphrey’s Executor decision. But do you know who has? The people at the Heritage Foundation, who are behind Project 2025, which is widely seen as the playbook for Trump’s second term. Overturning Humphrey’s Executor is right there on page 560 of Project 2025. Also in that playbook are steps to interfere with election administration and weaponize the Department of Justice against election officials who make decisions the Trump administration disagrees with. In other words: a strategy for influencing the upcoming election. Make no mistake: the masterminds behind Trump’s second term haven’t overseen “the Greatest Increase in Presidential Power in the last 100 years” just to easily cede that power to a Democratic president at the next election.

Elon Musk has been whining about Christopher Nolan casting Lupita Nyong’o as Helen of Troy for months now. This week, following rave reviews of the Odyssey, Musk announced that his AI image and video generator Grok Imagine would create its own “historically accurate” version of the film. Perhaps Musk should listen to Colman Domingo, who recently said on Jimmy Kimmel Live that he has a message for everyone upset about diversity in The Odyssey: “If you want to see a film with a cast of all white people who are cursed by the gods, the ‘Melania’ movie is currently streaming.”

The senator also suggested women experiencing abuse should simply “not put up with it”.

While violence by Arabs is called “terrorism”, the media tends to downplay attacks by Jewish settlers in Israel by characterizing it as “settler violence”. This violence, enabled by the Israeli military and ignored by many in the US, has been intensifying. Following a deadly settler attack on Friday, Israeli-Palestinian human rights group B’Tselem and 19 other Israeli human rights organisations condemned the international community’s “silence and inaction” and called for “immediate action to stop Israel’s violence and prevent pogroms by settler militias”.

Women are putting the internalized ageism aside and realizing you’re never too old to go out clubbing.

Rule 34 of the internet is that if something exists, there is porn of it. The dystopian machinations of the Trump administration are no exception. Wired has a disturbing piece on the rise of Maga-themed porn.

Meet Jimothy, who appears to be the internet’s new favourite racoon. Seattle-based Jimothy hasn’t won hearts and minds by passing out drunk in a Virginia liquor store like some of his compatriots. Rather, he has gone viral because of his distinctive body shape, which may be the result of a rare genetic condition called short spine syndrome. He looks a bit like a furry goblin, basically. I reckon Jimothy’s lack of a well-functioning backbone means he has a promising political career ahead of him. Perhaps Trump could make him Secretary of Trashury.

Euphoria gave me the courage to come out to my friend – now we’re together

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 11:00:41 GMT

I was uncertain about expressing my queerness, until I saw the way Zendaya and Hunter Schafer’s characters opened up to each other in HBO’s drama

I don’t remember the exact moment when I started catching feelings for my friend Ellen. It might have been when she trusted me to cut her hair into a feathered bob, or when I noticed she’d taken to keeping my favourite tea at her parents’ house. But in the summer of 2019, a month before our final year of school together, I realised I was falling in love.

We were 17 at the time and had been best friends since our first year of high school, both of us part of the same tight-knit group of girls. Ellen and I knew each other well and were quick to make each other laugh, but we were also very different. Whereas Ellen is reserved and gentle, I’m loud and loquacious. So my sudden attraction to her was confusing – especially since neither of us was openly queer.

I had been raised in an accepting, liberal household in Stockholm, where queerness was never frowned upon. And yet, I had always assumed that I was straight. It was the default script that had been handed to me. So, each time Ellen greeted me with her one-dimpled smile, I tried to ignore the fluttering in my chest, thinking it would be too complicated, too daunting. Even as I sensed those feelings might be mutual, I didn’t dare act on them. I was worried it might damage our friendship.

This all changed when I watched the first season of Sam Levinson’s television show Euphoria. Set in suburban California, the show (an adaptation of an Israeli series of the same name) follows a group of high-schoolers as they recklessly navigate adolescence. They abuse drugs, drink alcohol, have sex, watch porn and fall in and out of love.

More specifically, it was the relationship between Rue (Zendaya), a recovering drug addict, and the town newcomer, a transgender girl named Jules (Hunter Schafer), that drew me in. The two meet after a party at the end of the first episode and quickly forge a connection. As their friendship deepens, Rue begins to fall for Jules.

I recall watching the first few episodes at a friend’s house and being enthralled by Rue and Jules’s plotline, and how tender and complex it was. Even though my own world was far removed from the dark, gritty one of Euphoria, I related to the more innocuous parts of their story: the insecurities Rue has about her feelings toward Jules, that flicker of hope each time the line between platonic and romantic love is blurred. It all felt so similar to what I was experiencing.

There was also something refreshing about the depiction of the characters’ sexuality. In the series, there are no major coming-out scenes, no need for Rue or Jules to explain their orientation. When Rue tells her mother she’s in a “relationship” with Jules, her mother simply responds by saying: “It may not matter what I think, but I really like her.” This is not to say that coming-out scenes in fiction aren’t important. But for me, Euphoria was the first show that portrayed queerness as liberating – and it helped me realise I could feel that way too.

Watching Rue and Jules open up to one another gave me the push I needed; when I finally did kiss Ellen, she kissed me right back. And as morning light filtered through the blinds of her bedroom, I knew I had made the right decision.

We have been together for six years. We didn’t settle into a relationship right away; we needed time to figure out coupledom. But slowly, Ellen and I have managed to build a life, furnished with our mutual love of books, movie nights and laughter. She is my bulwark and the person who helps me decompress.

I did try watching the later seasons of Euphoria. And while some viewers may have enjoyed the grimmer tone, I couldn’t make it through the final run. Still, I’m grateful for that first season: it helped wash away my uncertainty and gave me the courage to make the first move. And truly, it was the greatest thing I ever did.

I tried so hard to become a salad eater. Now cyclospora is sending me back to burgers

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 11:00:41 GMT

Between the companies pushing junk food and the bacteria threatening our produce, eating right feels basically impossible

While war and conflict seem to be raging across the planet, the greatest weapon of mass destruction afflicting the United States today is, apparently, a salad – in the sense that fresh produce is now waging battle with our stomachs thanks to the cyclospora parasite. Cyclospora has infested an unknown amount of our food, causing thousands to suffer bowel movements that would make Pompeii look like a gender-reveal party.

This is a tragedy for everyone except the fat cats at Big Toilet. Cyclospora may be spread through human feces getting into irrigation systems in the food supply due to poor worker hygiene. It can’t be killed through usual agricultural sanitation processes. The best we can do is throw all that cilantro away and start from scratch. The FDA is scrambling to find the source of the contamination as soon as possible, going as far as to finger the supplier Taylor Farms with a false positive test that they had to sloppily retract as fast as they declared it. I, for one, am trembling, and not because I’m seconds away from expelling parasitic eggs. I’m terrified because now I don’t know what to eat.

A year-and-a-half ago, I was strongly recommended a diet by a kindly nutritionist that banished carbs and emphasized leafy greens. It brought down my cholesterol levels and blood pressure. I lost 40lbs. I’ve never felt less like a glistening slug, slithering through life trying to avoid getting stepped on by someone fitter than me during a vigorous jog.

I’m not a healthy person, by nature. My son, who is addicted to McDonald’s chicken nuggets, caused me to indulge in fast food. If he’s going for yet another Happy Meal, why not a lovely Big Mac for Dad? When I wrote my first book, my only solace in the lonely days and nights of banging on a keyboard for hours was pizza delivery. Circumstances conspired to unlock my latent gluttony, causing every health marker on my chart to turn a sickly shade of red to denote “strong chance of every organ retiring from service all at once”. Personally, I’d like my body to keep working for another few years, so I took the advice from my nutritionist and gained all the benefits.

Unfortunately, the very food I’m meant to eat to stay alive is now a potential threat. Sure, I could order a salad for lunch, but I also might have to move all my worldly possessions into the bathroom. I feel like I’ve stumbled into a Faustian bargain where, for the price of one prolonged bout of digestive emergency, I can have a summer beach body.

I’d love to continue my journey toward dietary harmony, but as this outbreak continues, I’m starting to wonder if I should pivot back to my customary regimen of fried dough and cheese cones. If my food isn’t barbecued or dipped into hot grease, can I even trust it? Cuts to food safety programs at the federal level last year certainly aren’t helping my belief in the propriety of what I put in my mouth. In 2025, a CDC program quietly trimmed the number of foodborne illnesses it tracked from six to just two. One of the four illnesses axed from the program? Cyclosporiasis. Only salmonella and E coli survived the purge, which are at least two of the most famous illnesses. The Q score for salmonella and E coli has got to be Taylor-Swift-Rihanna levels at this point, making the term “going viral” almost literal.

Yes, I know they are actually bacteria. But there’s an entire world of obscure microscopic bugs out there to contend with, and at least for now, we all need to eat food. Worse yet, we all need to eat good food, if such a thing even exists in our mass-produced, industrial culinary world. To match the voracious demand for sustenance and maximize profits, every step of the food-production process has been degraded. Who knows how many microplastics and pesticides are in my system right now, eager to wreak havoc on my internal systems at a moment’s notice? The answer to my food anxiety probably isn’t to subsist on Pop-Tarts and ranch dressing. The damage might be slower than bacteria would cause, but the bill will come due regardless.

The problem isn’t with me or you or anyone else who relies on the safety of our food supply. It’s on the companies and the government agencies who manufacture and regulate what we eat. At this juncture, it feels less like my tax dollars go to securing our food and more like they’re going directly into my toilet.

Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humorist

Treasure as trinkets: Zendaya’s earrings renew debate on ownership of ancient artefacts

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 11:00:40 GMT

Jewellery made from BC Iran worn at Odyssey photocall throws spotlight on the trade of rare archeological finds

The Odyssey has stormed cinemas, but while its take on the Homeric epic has created ripples among western classicists, it is an actor’s earrings that have made waves further afield.

Zendaya, who portrays the goddess Athena in the movie, provoked outrage when she appeared at a London photocall wearing earrings that were allegedly made from Iranian artefacts dating back to the 1st millennium BC.

According to Barron London, a Mayfair-based gallery and dealer that owns the earrings, the gold medallion plaques are “attributed to the Ziwiye hoard, discovered in north-west Iran in the late 1940s”. They were bought from another London jeweller, Glenn Spiro, who mounted them with diamonds in yellow gold.

But while the Mayfair retailer claims the jewellery celebrates “the remarkable artistry of ancient Persian goldsmiths” and encourages “wider appreciation of one of the world’s great artistic traditions”, academics take a different view.

A petition has been launched calling for Barron London to publish the complete known provenance of the gold plaques, reveal the checks they undertook on the legality of the items, permit examination of the objects, and even suspend sale.

Zendaya is used to the glare of camera lenses, but being the focus of academically qualified antiquarians is something else altogether.

Dr Christos Tsirogiannis, an antiquities expert at the Swiss Federal Office of Culture, said: “Personally, after all these two and a half decades of continued scandals emerging everywhere about all sorts of illicit antiquities … I’m extremely surprised, negatively surprised, that no one among all these people that escort these celebrities said something to protect her.”

Romina Frohar, the founder of the Forensic Archive of Iran, an independent investigative archive documenting threats to Iran’s cultural heritage that set up the petition, said her concern was broader than Zendaya’s decision to wear the items.

“Barron London has described the loan as a celebration of ancient Persian artistry, but cultural appreciation cannot substitute for provenance transparency,” she said. “If these objects are being publicly presented as Iranian cultural heritage, the evidence concerning their origin, export, ownership history and acquisition should be open to scrutiny.”

Even if antiquities were authentic and lawfully possessed, ethical issues may still arise, said Frohar, a PhD researcher at the Glasgow School of Art. “Private custody can be responsible when it is transparent, conservation-led and attentive to public and scholarly access. But legal possession alone does not extinguish the cultural claims of the people whose history the object embodies.”

The earrings’ odyssey from BC Iran to A-list actor involved a trip into the shadowy world of rare treasure trading – an industry in which priceless archeological finds are transformed into high-end luxury trinkets.

Many of the collections of Mayfair dealers, auction houses and private homes would be at home in the glass cases of museums.

Among items currently available to purchase from dealers online is an Egyptian mummy mask made of beads that dates from somewhere between 664BC to 332BC; Hellenistic gold earrings with garnet and agate dating back to the 3rd century BC, and a bronze dress pin with an end resembling an ibex that apparently comes from Iran and could be up to 3,000 years old. Their prices start at about £450.

In parallel, auction houses have put astonishing antiquities under the hammer. In 2018, Christie’s sold a 3,000-year-old relief from the palace of Ashurnasirpal II, a neo-Assyrian king who ruled 800 years before the establishment of the Roman empire, for nearly $31m.

Tsirogiannis is no stranger to such sales. His work has turned up evidence casting doubt on the provenance of numerous antiquities on the market. “About 90% of antiquities in the market one way or another, sooner or later, are proved to be illicit or lacking provenance, lacking documentation,” he said.

If Zendaya’s earrings were authentic, they might also pose another moral conundrum: “Possibly they are coming from a burial. How does she feel that she is wearing an ancient dead woman’s earrings [that may have been] looted?” he said.

Provenance and ownership of antiquities is an issue that has long passed beyond academia. Among the most notorious examples is the Koh-i-Noor diamond, which was surrendered to Queen Victoria by the 10-year-old maharajah Duleep Singh in 1849 as part of the Treaty of Lahore, becoming part of the British crown jewels.

The legalities around establishing who owns ancient items can be complex.

“Most so-called source countries for antiquities now have state ownership laws in place to say that ancient objects discovered belong to the state,” said Simon Mackenzie, a professor of criminology at Victoria University of Wellington (Te Herenga Waka) in New Zealand. “So the act of discovery and looting is essentially a form of theft [from the government].”

“In many countries, including Iran, these laws had been built up over time andwere not retroactive, so legal arguments could be made about what date exactly the theft rule applied from, he said.

Despite the outrage, sprinkling some modern celebrity stardust on the treasures of millennia gone by is not always a bad thing. When bling attracts academic attention, a conversation about provenance can begin.

When Kim Kardashian was snapped posing in a gold dress next to a gilded Egyptian coffin at the Met Gala in 2018, for example, experts in antiquities trafficking took notice.

The Met museum had acquired the 2,100-year-old coffin of a priest called Nedjemankh for $4m and made it the star of an exhibition. However, experts soon revealed it had been excavated by thieves in 2011 and smuggled out of Egypt to Dubai and then Europe, where it was restored and given false documents.

The legal and ethical problems which came with Zendaya’s earrings may never be resolved, but there remains one conundrum that does not require a PhD to spot.

As Tsirogiannis pointed out, the film star’s jewellery put the spotlight on Iran while promoting a film that had nothing to do with ancient Persia.

‘Everywhere there were pitifully injured people’: how a newly unearthed memoir captures the devastation of Hiroshima

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 10:58:40 GMT

In an exclusive extract from his memoir, Kiyoshi Tanimoto describes the terrifying trip across the city to locate his wife and child

‘I didn’t want to be a victim of the bomb’: read an interview with Tanimoto’s daughter Koko Kondo

Most of the people of Hiroshima had neither seen nor heard any plane. They heard no sound of explosion. They had seen only a strange flash in open daylight, or merely felt the reflection of the flash. However, there had been a tremendous explosion.

The parents of Mr Konda, one of our church members, had been waiting for a train at Yokogawa station, located 2km [one and a quarter miles] away from the centre of the bomb’s explosion. They saw a B-29 and a parachute dropping through the air. Before they had time to wonder at the sight, they fell unconscious. Afterward, they could not remember sensing any sound or light. When they regained consciousness, they found themselves lying on the ground, burned and without any clothing. The houses all around had been crushed to the ground. After getting to their feet, they ran toward the suburbs. Other people rushing along the Koi highway had the same experience.

After crossing the Koi and Fukushima bridges, I reached a place about a kilometre away from the explosion. From the suburbs to this spot, houses were heavily damaged but somehow were still standing. However, the houses from here to the centre of the explosion were all flat on the ground, as if they had been toy buildings crushed by a hammer. Painful cries of “Tasukete!” – “Help! – could be heard from under smashed houses.

People seemed to be buried in the ground. I knew full well how hard a job it would be to pull out even one log from a collapsed house, because I had helped with the clearing of houses. Nothing whatsoever could be done, with the strength of only one person, to help the people beneath those houses. Yet there were people buried here and there – everywhere.

After I had stopped to try to do something for these people, the thought that my wife and baby and neighbours must be in the same state flashed through my mind. I was the defence coordinator of my neighbourhood, and there were 120 lives entrusted to me. I had to hurry back to my post. I ran away in tears, saying, “Excuse me, I’m sorry, but excuse me!” I ran like a wild man. At Fukushima bridge, I saw Mr Matsuo, who had been with me when the atomic bomb exploded. He came running up, out of breath. “Mr Matsuo, please excuse me, for I have responsibilities,” I said, and ran on.

I followed the riverbank of the Fukushima river, looking to find a place where the fire was not so furious. Then I came to Nakahiromachi, a northern neighbourhood, where there were many farm fields and not so many houses.

Everywhere there were pitifully injured people. They could no longer keep moving, so they were lying in the streets. The further I moved into the city, the more wounded I saw. I grabbed my panama hat and threw it on the ground. In my heart I cried, “Forgive me!” because I felt no reason for why I had been left uninjured. I thought my wife and baby must be injured like these people and might be buried under our house. I asked their forgiveness for not being there to rescue them.

The usual way home was to take the Misasa Bridge across the Ota River toward central Hiroshima and go out to Hakushima, but the foot of the bridge and the Hakushima district were in flames. Fortunately, the Ushita district, which was on the other side of the river, seemed to be unscathed by fire. If I could get past Ushita, my own neighbourhood of Noboricho would be within a stone’s throw.

In a determined manner, I plunged into the river. It was not that I had confidence in my swimming ability, but there were no other means of reaching my goal. The Ota River varies in water level according to the tides. There was not much water, but the stream was swift. Naturally, I lost control of my limbs. I had already run continuously for about an hour and was dead tired.

I began to swallow water, which ran into my nose and mouth. My body was heavy, and my head started to sink into the water. My gaiters became loose and dangled about my legs. One of my shoes came off. I thought I was drowning. I would not have resented being killed by American bombs, but it seemed regrettable to be drowned. I prayed while sinking, “Oh God, do help me. Protect my body until I can save my wife and child and my neighbours.” Then I calmed myself and became lighter by taking off my gaiters, coat and the other shoe. With all my remaining energy I swam through the water.

Soon I reached shallow water about my height and was saved. When I got to the opposite bank, I could not move any longer and rested for some time with my head on the ground. After I regained some strength, I got on my feet and started walking toward Ushita. I was completely undressed and only differed from others by having no scars from burns.

As the treasurer of my church lived nearby, I went to his house and saw that it was also crushed and deserted. Praying for his safety, I passed through Ushita. I saw no other residents and thought that everybody must have escaped by now.

Mrs Tada’s house, where my wife often stayed overnight, was nearby, and I thought of dropping in. Although she usually was back home by half past six or seven o’clock in the morning, I wondered if she might have stayed until nine or 10 that morning at Mrs Tada’s place and thus would have been saved. Praying, I took a few steps toward the house, and, to my surprise, I found my wife carrying Koko in her arms, in a line of refugees. She was wearing a blood-stained chemise, her hair was hanging about her shoulders, and she had a ghostlike appearance.

I called to her. She turned around, looked at me, and stood quietly with tears in her eyes. I looked away and asked, “What happened to you?”

She said, “Just as I reached home, Mrs Takaki came for a visit. We were both talking at the door when we were buried.”

“And what happened to Mrs Takaki?”

With a miserable expression, she said, “I don’t know.”

I had not experienced the slightest pleasure seeing my wife and child safe. Rather, I was filled with indignation. It was unpardonable that a church member who was paying a visit to the parsonage should be killed during an air raid and the family of the pastor still be saved. Should not the wife of the pastor have died together with the church member? I was filled with accusatory feelings toward my wife.

Afterward, I learned that my wife had been buried under the house in an instant and nearly crushed under the pressure of heavy wood. She could not breathe for a while and began to fall unconscious. However, she was brought to by the screams of Koko, who was still in her arms. She struggled with all her strength to save her baby. Calming herself, she noticed a small hole in the attic. Both of her arms were strongly pinned in the ruins, but she could move a bit and finally managed to stretch out one arm.

She gradually made the small hole wider. Every time she struggled to move, broken pieces of roofing fell on her head. Koko continued to cry loudly. Struggling with all her strength, she enlarged the hole and was finally able to push out Koko. Then she did everything she could to free herself and managed to get out.

By then, the house next door was on fire, and smoke was rising from it. She staggered along the alley with Koko in her arms. She thought of getting someone to help Mrs Takaki, but every house in sight was smashed and already deserted. The fire was spreading, and the smoke was getting thick. With the baby in her arms, she could not return to our house. Finally, she reached the Sentei gardens, after being pursued by the fire and smoke. However, her thoughts were with her neighbour.

This is an edited extract from Hiroshima, 8:15: The Lost Memoir by Kiyoshi Tanimoto. It will be published by Ebury on 6 August. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

‘Shameful’: Pentagon accused of cover-up over US military casualties in Iran war

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 10:00:41 GMT

No press briefing has been held for months, as the defence department belatedly or inaccurately releases figures

The Pentagon is taking a “shameful approach” to releasing information about US casualties in the Iran war, Leon Panetta, a former defence secretary and CIA director, has told the Guardian.

The defence department has not held a press briefing for two and a half months. Officials have faced accusations that they are engaged in a cover-up designed to hide the true cost of Donald Trump’s war of choice in Iran, fearing a public backlash before November’s midterm elections.

Panetta, who held weekly Pentagon briefings during the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, criticised the department for failing to disclose how many people had been hurt in bomb attacks by Iran on US bases.

“There’s a deliberate effort here to basically withhold information from the American people, and I think it represents in many ways a shameful approach to sharing the responsibility that we all have when it comes to fighting a war,” he said by phone.

A fragile ceasefire between the ​US and Iran collapsed earlier this month and both ​sides have been carrying out daily strikes against each other, prompting fears of a quagmire and a betrayal of Trump’s campaign promise to eschew “forever wars”.

The number of US troops killed in the war on Iran ​rose to 18 last weekend, while ‌roughly 430 US troops ​have been injured. The Pentagon said on ​Monday that 100 service members had been injured since 7 July but that 96% had returned to duty. The department initially failed to disclose the figures, according to a New York Times newspaper report, only belatedly acknowledging the casualties in a social media post.

Officials dismissed the Times’ article as “baseless and malicious” and contend that they are not strictly required to publicise injuries if service members are expected to return to duty. But questions intensified when another Times report said the Pentagon’s website had lowered the number of troop deaths from 18 to 14; Sean Parnell, a Pentagon spokesperson, blamed “a temporary data disruption”.

Critics, however, say the information blackout is a calculated political strategy to hide a failing military intervention.

Ned Price, a former deputy to the US representative to the United Nations and former spokesperson for the state department, said: “This goes beyond a run-of-the-mill administration distrust toward and hostility against the press. This is more about shielding the American people from the true and total cost of this war.”

Since the war started five months ago, there has been a tension between the government’s desire for operational secrecy and the media’s demand for transparency on behalf of the public. Even during contentious, unpopular wars in Vietnam and Iraq, the lines of communication were kept more or less open. But since Trump’s return to power in January 2025, the Pentagon – restyled as the Department of War – has been restricting access.

Almost immediately, it ousted major outlets including the New York Times, National Public Radio (NPR) and Politico from their long-held desks, supplanting them with Trump-friendly media such as Breitbart, One America News Network and the New York Post. In May, it imposed restrictions on the free movement of reporters in much of the Pentagon building.

In October, most news outlets turned in their access badges and walked out of the Pentagon rather than agree to new rules that would leave them vulnerable to expulsion if they sought to report on information – classified or otherwise – that had not been approved by Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, for release. In December, the department held a three-day event to usher in newly accredited media organisations, including pro-Trump podcasters and influencers.

In March this year, the Pentagon introduced a rule that required journalists to be escorted on Pentagon grounds by authorised department personnel. In June, it said its press office was now a classified space inaccessible to journalists because it was used by speechwriters who “routinely handle classified material”. The ever-tightening limits have alarmed press freedom watchdogs.

Clayton Weimers, the Washington director for Reporters Without Borders, said: “I don’t think it’s an exaggeration to say this Pentagon has been more hostile to the news media than any other Pentagon in recent memory.”

Mark Schoeff, president of the National Press Club, agrees that such hostility is a historical aberration, saying: “What is happening at the Pentagon is unique in my 34 years in Washington. We’ve not seen these kinds of restrictions on the media at the Pentagon. Even during Desert Storm [during the Gulf war] and the war in Afghanistan, I can’t recall a time when the Pentagon tried to shut down press access like this.”

The current obfuscation is particularly jarring when contrasted with the administration’s earlier posture: in the opening days of the Iran war, Hegseth was a ubiquitous presence, delivering bombastic briefings in which he crowed about annihilating the Iranian military with “no mercy” and restoring the US as a nation of “real warriors”.

The Pentagon then banned photojournalists when images of Hegseth deemed “unflattering” appeared in the public domain. At one briefing, Hegseth compared reporters to the “Pharisees”, describing the media’s coverage of the war in Iran as an “endless stream of garbage”.

Now the bravado has been replaced by a vacuum. While there have been no briefings since May, Hegseth last week announced a screening programme for “testosterone deficiency” among troops, calling it necessary to allow them to operate at their “absolute best”. Such diversions raised suspicions that the war was spiralling out of control.

Joel Rubin, a former deputy assistant secretary of state, said: “When you’re not able to communicate clearly what’s actually taking place on the ground, that means you’re likely not confident or comfortable with what is happening on the ground and how it will play politically and in the policy world here. It’s a pretty obvious thing that there’s a lot of concern about there being casualties in this war right now.”

The war in Iran is already unpopular in the US due to rising gas prices and other inflationary impacts on people’s everyday lives. People who are paying attention know that 18 US service members have died, Price said. “But what they don’t know,” he added, “unless they’re really digging, is the full extent of casualties that our men and women in uniform have suffered as a result of this decision to take our country to war without clear objectives and certainly without a clear off-ramp.

“This is not the sort of thing where a dozen or two dozen service members have suffered low-grade concussion. There are hundreds – by one count, some 500 US service members – who have suffered physically as a result of this war, and the administration probably rightly calculates that, if the economic costs were compounded with the full toll that this is taking on our service members, this war, which is already a politically losing proposition, would drag the administration down even further.”

For veterans and national security experts, the Pentagon’s handling of US casualties amounts to a shameful cover-up. “The Pentagon said 96% of those affected returned to duty but, again, a reminder that we know that modern warfare, like the impacts of an injury, might not be felt or seen until months or years later,” said Janessa Goldbeck, chief executive of Vet Voice Foundation, a non-profit advocacy organisation. “We deserve to know exactly what’s happened and it raises questions about why they wouldn’t be reporting these casualties in a timely manner. My assumption is that it’s about controlling the political narrative before a major national election.”

Although Hegseth has avoided the media, he was obliged to attend a hearing on Capitol Hill this week to defend a war that has already cost the US $37.5bn. During a combative Senate appropriations committee hearing on Tuesday, politicians from both sides of the aisle expressed deep frustration with the administration’s endless demands for money coupled with its refusal to provide straight answers or a coherent strategy.

When the senator Gary Peters, a Democrat, called the administration’s approach a complete “failure”, Hegseth erupted in anger, snapping: “Shame on you and others who call this a quagmire and a failure.” Peters shot back: “You, sir, are the failure. You don’t have a strategy. You don’t have a long-term plan to actually win this war.”

Steven Cash, a former intelligence officer and executive director of the Steady State – an advocacy group of more than 400 former national security officials – warns that the Trump administration and its Pentagon leadership do not view the public or the press as stakeholders to be informed, but as adversaries to be defeated.

“Pete Hegseth and the president of the United States don’t see a real major role for the voters of America or the Congress, so why tell them anything? They’ve made it clear that they don’t see a role for you, the media. You are an enemy,” he said.

The Pentagon denies that it is minimising reports of casualties. Sean Parnell, the chief spokesperson, said in a statement: “The Department of War and US Central Command has consistently provided comprehensive, real-time updates to the world on the United States’ strikes and operations in Iran.

“President Trump and Secretary Hegseth have been constantly providing updates directly to the media and the American people online, delivering clear, unfiltered insight into our objectives and decisive actions.”

Although briefings have dried up, the news has not, and Pentagon beat reporters continue to work their sources and pursue information. Panetta said officials were “trying to tiptoe past the graveyard, so to speak, in the sense that they’re hoping that the less they say, the less controversy they’ll be involved in, but the reality is that the press will only operate that much more aggressively to find out exactly what’s going on.

“In essence what they’re doing is challenging the press to find what’s really happening, and they will. They can dodge, bob and weave, they can hide it, but my experience is that no matter how much you try to hide it, in the end the truth comes out.”
