Lucy Harrison’s father was holding the gun that killed her but was never arrested. Now her mother wants Andy Burnham to take up the case

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 10:00:40 GMT

Eighteen months after her daughter’s death in Texas, Jane Coates hopes new PM can persuade US authorities to reopen case

Lucy Harrison felt that 2024 was her best year yet. The 23-year-old had graduated from university with first class honours, landed her dream job and bought her first house with her boyfriend. She was a “big girl adult” now, Lucy would say. She shed tears of joy seeing her idol, Taylor Swift, at Wembley on the Eras tour that summer. Life could hardly get any better. “All the hard work, all the tears, everything was coming to fruition,” said her mother, Jane Coates, from Warrington in north-west England.

That Christmas, Lucy and her boyfriend, Sam Littler, flew to Texas to spend time with her father, Kris Harrison, who had left the family home when she was two. The pair had a complex relationship – Harrison was a recovering alcoholic – and Littler, 24, did not want them to go. But Lucy enjoyed seeing her two younger half-sisters at their home in Prosper, an affluent suburb 30 miles north of Dallas.

Lucy and Littler were due to fly home to the UK on 10 January 2025 when Coates received a knock on the door. It was Littler’s mother. Lucy had been shot, she said. She was dead.

It was only later she learned that Kris Harrison had been holding the gun. He was never arrested and a grand jury chose not to indict him, based on an investigation by local police.

Eighteen months on, Coates is urging Andy Burnham’s government to encourage US authorities to reopen the case after a Cheshire coroner ruled that Lucy was unlawfully killed.

Coates, a deputy head teacher, raised Lucy as a single parent from the age of two. The pair had an incredibly close bond and would talk about virtually everything. As a child, she was always outside exploring, climbing trees, riding her bike, before becoming engrossed in Harry Potter books – a “comfort blanket” she would turn to time and again into adulthood.

By the age of nine, she was a devout Swiftie, performing a Taylor Swift song at her school leavers’ assembly and later going to three of her concerts. Anyone who knew Lucy knew her contagious laughter. “We call it like the Barbara Windsor belly laugh,” said Coates, 49.

Like many young adults, Lucy went through difficult times. She struggled with the uncertainty of what she wanted to do with her life in her late teens, Coates said. She had counselling to help with the relationship with her father.

But Lucy had never been happier than in 2024. She graduated from Manchester Metropolitan University with a degree in fashion buying and merchandising, began working at the retailer Boohoo and bought a home with Littler, her “soulmate”, five minutes from both of their mothers.

“That final year of Lucy’s was the best year of her life,” Coates said. “She was such a high achiever and she just really wanted the best for herself.”

She soaked up life, both good and bad. But that meant she would sometimes get upset about events happening thousands of miles away.

The murder of George Floyd by a Minneapolis police officer in 2020 was one such event, Coates remembers. “She used to worry. She was an overthinker and used to cry a lot at different things. Sometimes it was with frustration because she was very passionate about things.”

She was vehemently opposed to guns, an issue that caused tension with her father. Harrison, a telecoms executive originally from Liverpool, moved to Saudi Arabia for work when she was a child, later settling in Texas where he married Heather Harrison, an education recruiter, and had two daughters.

Harrison had bought a pistol for $500 (£370) from a colleague two years before Lucy’s death. Gun owners over the age of 21 are not required to obtain training or a licence in Texas, one of the most firearms-friendly US states.

Her inquest in Cheshire was told that Lucy had expressed concern to friends about her two younger siblings being in the house with her father’s Glock 9mm semi-automatic pistol.

On the morning of her death, Lucy and her father argued about sexual assault allegations against Donald Trump, who was about to start his second term as US president.

Littler said Lucy had asked her father: “How would you feel if that was me and then the guy got away with it?”

Harrison had replied that it “wouldn’t bother me that much” because his two younger daughters live with him, Littler said. Lucy “went into floods of tears and ran upstairs”, he added, and sent her father links to news articles about the Trump allegations, denied by the US president.

Littler had been in a relationship with Lucy for five years by that point and had known her since they were 12. “This was the sort of stuff that happened on a regular basis,” Littler said. When he met Harrison in Prosper for the first time a year earlier, he told Lucy he did not want to go back. “You’d feel like you’re on eggshells.”

Coates is keen to stress that Lucy was not shot “because they’d had an argument about Trump”. Passionate debates were not uncommon between Lucy and her father: “It could have been an argument about anything.”

Later that morning, the family were watching children’s television shows and preparing to go to the airport when Harrison took Lucy’s hand and escorted her to his bedroom.

Harrison’s wife, Heather, looked at Littler in surprise and joked: “He never takes my hand like that.” “It was mysterious,” Littler said. “No one knew what was going on.”

Then came the loud bang. Initially they thought it was a prank, then Harrison screamed for his wife. They ran into the room and saw Lucy on the floor. Harrison, in shock, could not say what had happened. The pistol was on the bed. He stammered: “I don’t know, I don’t know. Call an ambulance.”

Bodycam footage shows Harrison telling officers he had shown his gun to Lucy when “it just went off”.

“When I pulled it out, it went off,” he said.

Despite an officer smelling alcohol on Harrison’s breath, he was not breathalysed. He initially denied drinking that day but later told police he had a drink problem and “keeps it going”, an admission an officer understood to mean that Harrison drinks throughout the day.

CCTV obtained by police showed Harrison buying two 500ml cartons of wine earlier that day and discarding one of them outside a shop. He later admitted drinking that morning.

During his police interview, a Texas ranger explained to Harrison that the “gun would only discharge if the trigger was pressed”, according to a report released to the UK inquest. “Kris said ‘OK’,” it noted. Yet authorities said they were unable to arrest Harrison because they could not prove intent.

Coates said she had told a Texas ranger that Harrison must have been pointing the gun at Lucy and pulled the trigger, to which she said he had agreed, but argued: “We just can’t prove it.”

On the same call in March 2025, a prosecutor said they were unable to conclude Harrison pointed the weapon at Lucy “because that implies intent”, Coates said. They told her the most they could say was that the “muzzle was aligned with Lucy’s chest and a trigger was pulled”.

The police case was handed to a grand jury in Collin County, Texas, which decided in June last year Harrison should not be prosecuted. Its reasoning, and the evidence it considered, has not been made public.

Littler was also taken to the police station. While waiting to learn whether Lucy had survived, he said he heard a muffled conversation between officers in which they referred to the shooting as an “accident”.

“The police just took Kris’s word for it,” said Coates. “The investigation was not rigorous or thorough enough.”

She suspects the police would have treated Lucy’s death more seriously had it happened in a less “white middle-class prosperous area”.

Of all the disturbing details they have learned, one of the most painful for Coates is that Lucy’s body was tested for alcohol and other substances – all with negative results – while Harrison was not even breathalysed. “That’s what we find absolutely incredulous,” Coates said. She and Littler have submitted formal complaints to Prosper police department.

In February, the senior coroner for Cheshire, Jacqueline Devonish, ruled that firing a pistol at Lucy from across the room was an act of gross negligence and that her death could not be considered accidental.

Coates said the family had been let down, not just by the Texas authorities but also by the British government. She was told the Foreign Office would not be able to help them because nobody had been prosecuted.

Sarah Hall, the Labour MP for Warrington South, said the family did not have “adequate support” and called on the government to press the Texas authorities to re-examine the case.

Coates hopes the new prime minister, who represents the nearby Makerfield constituency, will take up Lucy’s case with the US. She is keen to meet Ed Miliband, the new foreign secretary, to discuss how the government could better support the families of those killed abroad.

“At the beginning, nobody was there for us apart from Sarah Hall,” she said. “We have got hope that this new cabinet and the foreign secretary will support us, [but] there were no authorities supporting us as British nationals wanting justice for a British citizen who was killed by a British citizen.”

A Foreign Office spokesperson said: “Our thoughts remain with Jane and her family for the tragic loss they have suffered, and we will always look to learn lessons from cases such as this one to improve the consular support we offer to other families in the future.”

What’s behind Maga influencer Laura Loomer’s about-face on Ukraine?

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 10:00:40 GMT

After a Kyiv visit, rightwing firebrand now supports Ukraine – but perhaps it’s just because Trump favors a winner

Laura Loomer, the online Maga provocateur, has never worked in the White House or anywhere else in the government, but her sudden conversion to the Ukrainian cause this week is significant because her social media posts often have real policy implications in the second Trump administration.

The rightwing commentator has spent the last few days in Kyiv, where she announced a newfound sympathy for Ukraine in its long war with Russia, and admitted that she had previously fallen for Russian propaganda.

Loomer – who has previously echoed Kremlin talking points to her 2 million followers on social media – has enjoyed direct access to Trump since the 2024 presidential campaign. During the early months after Trump returned to office, Loomer used her online presence to push for ideological purges of government personnel, including many in the national security arena.

For a time, her power to break careers among foreign policy officials made her seem as if she were Trump’s de facto national security adviser.

It is unclear whether she still has that kind of pull inside the White House, but Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, certainly took her seriously when she arrived this week, holding a private meeting with her on Thursday.

Three days earlier, Loomer posted about experiencing her first air raid, as Russian missiles pounded the Ukrainian capital

“This is everyday for every Ukrainian,” she posting, adding she felt that she had been “an asshole for minimizing the struggle of Ukrainians for the last 5 years”.

“I often said I don’t care. Looking back, that wasn’t very nice of me to say. There are people in Ukraine who have to run to a bomb shelter everyday and some of us had the audacity to say Russia wasn’t wrong because we believed the lie that Ukraine is a country full of Nazi sympathizers. We have been so propagandized by Russia and we don’t even realize it.”

Before their meeting on Thursday, Zelenskyy’s office posted a statement saying: “It is really important that @LauraLoomer is in Ukraine and sees things with her own eyes as they are.”

Loomer’s change of heart is potentially important not only because she is close to Trump, but also because she has long served as a reliable barometer of Maga attitudes.

Loomer has long been disdainful of Ukraine, adopting what could only be described as a pro-Russian perspective. Many in Maga circles have for years held positive views of the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, thanks to Russian propaganda that portrayed him as a bulwark against homosexuality and a defender of fundamentalist Christianity. They became convinced that the Russia-Ukraine war was a proxy fight between Russia’s fundamentalist Christianity and the EU’s western secularism.

Loomer’s shift comes at a critical moment for Ukraine, which recently lost one of its strongest supporters in Washington with the death this month of Lindsey Graham, the Republican senator from South Carolina who had consistently pushed for increased sanctions on Russia to punish Moscow for its invasion of Ukraine.

But Loomer’s change also coincides with what appears to be an important recent shift in Trump’s own views on Ukraine.

Trump returned to office openly hating Ukraine, at least in part because of the 2019 impeachment over his attempt to hold up aid to Ukraine in exchange for dirt on Joe Biden. Early in his second term, Trump humiliated Zelenskyy in an Oval Office meeting, cut off direct the supply of US weapons and forced Ukraine’s European allies to buy American weapons for Kyiv instead.

But Trump likes winners, and even without full support from Washington, Ukraine has been able to slow Russia’s advance. Kyiv has become a global leader in drone technology, and it has taken the war to Russia itself with long-range missile attacks on the country’s oil infrastructure, leading to an energy crisis in one of the world’s biggest oil-producing nations.

Clearly impressed with Ukraine’s performance, Trump announced at the Nato summit in Turkey earlier this month that the US would license Patriot missile technology to Ukraine, allowing Kyiv to produce the advanced air defense missiles on its own.

At the same time, Trump also supported a move in Congress, which had been backed by Graham, to impose new sanctions on Russia, while also seeming to back off an earlier insistence that Ukraine would have to agree to give up large swaths of territory in exchange for any US-brokered peace deal with Russia.

Trump’s policy shifts were modest, but significant; it is possible that Loomer changed her position simply in order to stay in lockstep with Trump.

But her about-face could be even more politically significant if it represents a broader thawing of Maga attitudes towards Ukraine and an awakening to the dangers of Russian propaganda.

Andrew O’Hagan: ‘The worst thing anyone’s said to me? That I was the spitting image of David Cameron’

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 09:00:39 GMT

The author on an encounter with the CIA, an embarrassing moment in church, and longing to hold hands with David Attenborough

Born in Glasgow, Andrew O’Hagan, 58, studied at the University of Strathclyde. In 1995, he published The Missing, a work of nonfiction. His debut novel, Our Fathers, was shortlisted for the Booker prize in 1999; Be Near Me and The Illuminations were longlisted in 2006 and 2015. His recent novels are Caledonian Road and Mayflies. The latter was adapted for BBC television in 2022 and is now a play which will be performed at the Edinburgh fringe from 7 to 30 August. O’Hagan is editor at large for the London Review of Books; he lives in London with his wife and has a daughter.

What is your greatest fear? I can’t say it.

What is the trait you most deplore in yourself? My interest in Los Angeles.

What is the trait you most deplore in others? Making people smaller than they are because of something they can’t handle in themselves.

What was your most embarrassing moment? My first holy communion, where my trousers were too big for me and fell down, a circumstance which earned me both the instant contempt of the girls and the heightened interest of the priests. That’s just how it was in 1975.

Describe yourself in three words Just. Hanging. On.

What makes you unhappy? Reform UK.

What is your most unappealing habit? Deciding a TV drama is crap after 10 minutes of episode one, then building a case against it for the rest of the series.

What do you most dislike about your appearance? My hands are tiny. I need both to lift a cupcake.

Who would play you in the film of your life? Janette Krankie, I fear.

Who is your celebrity crush? David Attenborough. We could just hold hands, like I was a baby orangutan.

What did you want to be when you were growing up? Most days, I wanted to be Albrecht in the classical ballet Giselle, dancing until I dropped dead.

What is the worst thing anyone’s said to you? Somebody once told me I was the spitting image of David Cameron.

What is your guiltiest pleasure? Selling Sunset on Netflix.

Trump forced to play good sport at correspondents’ dinner – but it couldn’t last

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 08:58:57 GMT

President’s speech started well enough but quickly moved to the usual insults, taunts, jokes and grievances

This time, at least, everyone got to finish their dinner.

And any urge to hide under the table was driven not by the barking commands of Secret Service agents on alert against a marauding gunman, but by a desire to escape the tedium of a meandering speech from Donald Trump that strayed quickly and wildly from the matter at hand into the weeds of his normal stump addresses.

For more than two hours at Friday’s rescheduled White House Correspondents’ Association dinner, Trump was forced to play the good sport; smiling and applauding while awards were bestowed on journalistic foes he berates daily as purveyors of “fake news” and plaudits heaped on past presidents he loathes.

But eventually something had to give. Trump had to be Trump, insults had to be hurled, some of them stale and familiar, a few of them funny, all of them grievously petty.

As often happens with his stump speeches these days, the president lost his audience. Phones were gazed at, silence ensued. Never more so than when he embarked on a tiresome bigoted diatribe against the Democratic representative from Minnesota, Ilhan Omar, one of his frequent targets.

Trump was finally getting to deliver his maiden speech as president to the association’s annual marquee gathering that a alleged would-be assassin had denied him by trying to storm the original event in April, before being foiled by Secret Service agents.

Both the association and Trump had decreed such an act of political violence could not be accepted as the final word. So a rescheduled dinner was arranged – but with significant adjustments.

Instead of the vast auditorium at the Washington Hilton – the dinner’s venue for several decades and once the site of an attempt on the life of Ronald Reagan – the Astoria Waldorf was chosen to stage a drastically scaled-down dinner, with just 700 guests attending, compared with the 2,600 who were at the original event in April.

Given the upheaval that unfolded then, the greater visibility of armed security personnel – even for a much smaller guest list – was unsurprising.

Weijia Jiang, the outgoing WHCA president, vowed in advance that the restaged dinner would be “more intimate”.

Trump, when he spoke – after being forcibly humbled by the dishing out of awards to a succession of journalists for their unflattering portrayal of his presidency – quickly established that humility would not feature strongly in his speech.

His first comment on the changed venue was to observe that he had once owned it, when it was the Trump International Hotel.

“This has not been an easy evening. All these awards. Do I have a say?” he asked. “But it’s great to be back at a place that I know very well because I built it, and I’m very proud of it because I built it for $2.9bn less than the Federal Reserve Building, which is a lot smaller, by the way.”

To his credit, he quickly entered the intended spirit by invoking the episode that had caused everyone to be there in the first place.

“Tonight we come back together to answer that heinous attack with unwavering resolve, and every one of us here this evening to show that in America we do not yield to political violence,” Trump said to applause. “So in this country, we believe in freedom of speech. We settle our differences not with bullets, but with open and vigorous debate.”

It seemed an apt response to Jiang’s appeal, based on the event’s theme of “celebrating the first amendment”, to respect and honor the media’s place in American life.

“Many founders [of the US constitution] couldn’t stand the press … but they understood our access is restricted,” she said. “If the media faces government pressure or censorship, it’s the people who end up knowing less. There is a difference, though, an existential difference between criticizing the press and trying to undermine it.”

But that was as high-minded and worthy as Trump was willing to allow.

Sign up to First Thing

Our US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

after newsletter promotion

From there, it was on to the insults, taunts, jokes – and grievances. Some of it was amusing and drew laughter, notably when he jested at the expense of the health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr.

“I hope that everyone finally got to enjoy their entire, very delicious beef tenderloins, very special beef,” he said. “And I want you all to know that Bobby Kennedy, who’s right here, personally ran over the cow and he cut it up, and he brought it here for you to eat tonight. Bobby also suggested appetizer featuring his favorite cut of male raccoon roadkill, but we drew the line at that.”

Adam Schiff, the Democratic senator for California and a particular Trump bete noire, was mocked as “watermelon head because he has the largest head I’ve ever seen with the smallest pencil neck”.

Jimmy Kimmel, Jimmy Fallon and Stephen Colbert, all comedians who have mocked Trump unceasingly, were derided as “people without talent”.

Trump said the speech was much more generous than the one he had planned to give in April before the gunman and would-be alleged assassin, Cole Tomas Allen, stole his thunder.

But what could have been going through his mind as Wolf Blitzer, the veteran CNN anchor who famously witnessed the shooting scenes at the original dinner, announced that the Katharine Graham award for courage and accountability was going to a Wall Street Journal team who had reported on the president’s past relationship with Jeffrey Epstein.

In the event, Trump shook hands with the team’s members, including one journalist whose home address had been disclosed in a $20bn suit he filed against the paper, forcing the reporter’s family to have to move home.

“I hope you all know that I believe in the free press more than anyone in this room,” Trump told the gathering later, overlooking the fact that his administration had filed subpoenas for several New York Times reporters and their relatives after the paper had reported on security breaches on the new Air Force One jet, gifted by Qatar.

“You people have no idea how lucky you are. When I’m gone, you’re all going to be broke. There’s not going to be anybody to report on.”

As he wound up, the sound system blared out YMCA by the Village People. By then, Trump had been talking for 65 minutes, paeans of praise to the founding fathers and journalistic bravery had been forgotten – and there seemed little doubt about whose event it really was.

The perfect books for the beach … picked by Freida McFadden, Mick Herron, Robert Harris and more

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 08:00:36 GMT

From a transporting historical saga to a tale of small-town betrayal, the authors of our favourite page-turners reveal the books they take on holiday – introduced by Jenny Colgan

It is important to follow a balanced diet on holiday. Too many “My Wife’s Sister’s Husband’s Psychopath”, and you’ll get confused and grumpy. Too much sugary romance and your teeth will fall out. Something too big and challenging you’ve been meaning to get round to for ages will make you feel guilty and more liable to give in to scrolling, and if you take too many supposedly upmarket “must reads” of the summer, you will simply prove to yourself just how much overhyped averageness there is out there, when all you want is something satisfying.

You need to be able to chop and change depending on your mood, which means fiction and nonfiction. And finally, you need to be able to throw all of these rules out of the window if you find a sandy old water-stained copy of, for example, James Herbert’s Domain in your holiday cottage and decide to devote yourself to 600 pages of post-nuclear mutant rat-strewn London, or choose to go for a full-on Maeve Binchy sesh.

My top tips for this summer? For the outward journey: Kathy Burke’s smash-hit and brilliant autobiography A Mind of My Own, a reminder of the absolute Britishness you are leaving behind. For that first post-rosé afternoon when you are filled with warmth and benevolence towards the world and everyone in it: Whistler by Ann Patchett.

For a wonderful immersive epic where everyone is also extremely boiling hot all the time: This Is Where the Serpent Lives by Daniyal Mueenuddin. For cruising altitude day four when everyone else has gone to see some stupid boring hot cave and left you alone and you want something quality and capable of being finished in an afternoon: Glorious Exploits by Ferdia Lennon. For the day everyone is doing your head in: Emma Cline’s huge hit from a couple of years ago, The Guest, a thoroughly nasty piece of work and the best of all those “neighbourhood psycho” books.

Nonfiction palate cleanser day: OK, everyone is going to be reading the Maggie Haberman Trump book, but for the love of God could we possibly not think about him for one solitary five-second interval? That would be the definition of a holiday. If annoying Americans are still your bag, try Belle Burden’s Strangers, about a seemingly perfect, rich Wasp marriage unexpectedly going down the toilet.

For queueing at non-EU passport control and cursing Nigel Farage’s £5m: The Impossible Fortune by Richard Osman. Forget the motley crew of celebrity impersonators that squelched along in his wake; Osman’s lightness of touch and genuine comic ability means this slips down more easily than free limoncello. Bonnes vacances!

author of The HousemaidOne of my favourite reads of the year has been The Calamity Club by Kathryn Stockett. I’ve been on a historical kick lately, and this novel set in the southern US during the Great Depression is historical fiction at its best. The audiobook is masterfully narrated and by the last chapter, I had tears in my eyes.

author of YesteryearIn The Shampoo Effect by Jenny Jackson a group of friends in their mid-30s in a tight-knit Massachusetts coastal town deal with secrets, romance and the fallout from a stunning betrayal. It’s frothy and clever and perfect for a vacation.

author of Fleishman Is in TroubleI brought Here in the Dark by my New York Times colleague Alexis Soloski on vacation a couple of years ago. I couldn’t put it down from the minute I started it, even missing a family dinner so I could continue reading. (Sorry, kids!) It’s a modern noir about an acerbic theatre critic who finds herself caught up in a mystery, and I can’t say enough about its voice, its humour, its darkness, its poignancy and the twists and turns that make it a truly original thriller. I loved it.

author of HeartstopperConvenience Store Woman by Sayaka Murata is about a woman whose only dream is to work at a convenience store and, like much of Murata’s work, explores the inner world of a woman who feels deeply uncomfortable about the role she’s forced into by society. It’s short, it’s strange, it’s the perfect read for a trip away this summer – and a great introduction to Murata, if you haven’t dipped in before.

author of the Slough House seriesBeaches are for walking along not reading on, but when the paddling’s done and a sand-free environment’s been found, Daniel Mason’s Country People is a treat. A failed academic and his family relocate to Vermont, where his PhD avoidance strategies involve increasingly alarming immersion in local folklore. An absurd, joyful delight.

author of The MaidThe Paper Palace by Miranda Cowley Heller. August heat, a summer cabin in Cape Cod, and the unravelling of one woman’s secrets. Elle is happily married with three kids, but her whole life is upended by an illicit encounter with a childhood friend. A charged generational saga about love, desire and loss – you’ll need regular dips in the water to cool yourself as you read.

author of None of This Is TrueThe best page-turner I’ve read this year is It’s Not What You Think by Clare Mackintosh. She already lays claim to one of the genre’s greatest twists in her 2011 hit I Let You Go and here Mackintosh is back to deliver multiple twists, short chapters and non-stop reveals in this scintillating read.

author of Call Me by Your NameLondon Falling by Patrick Radden Keefe is about a 19-year-old Londoner who desperately wants to join the world of super-wealthy Russian oligarchs, many of whom live in the capital. He manages to affect belonging to that class until he is finally exposed for who he really is – a smart, resourceful but hapless kid. The story is totally addictive, real, and I couldn’t put it down.

author of The Guest ListThe Wedding People by Alison Espach is an absorbing, transporting book that left me with a serious what-to-pick-next panic after finishing it. I took it on holiday last year and the summer setting makes it perfect: the waterfront hotel, the excursions on boats and in open-top cars, and also the unfurling sense of optimism. It’s a paean to solo travel, to leaving it – quite literally in this case – all behind. But it’s also a book with teeth, poignancy, depth and humanity, all qualities I look for in a top-notch summer read.

author of The Night StairsThe Pinnacle by Abir Mukherjee is a satirical thriller set in a Mumbai skyscraper. A washed-up American actor is accused of killing his Bollywood starlet wife. It’s got everything you could want from a book: belly laughs, unforgettable characters, a thumping plot and simmering political rage.

author of the Ninth House seriesThe Last Baron by Tom Sancton. Thick with loathsome individuals and rich with history, this heavily researched story of a 1970s kidnapping in Paris spans generations. It is wildly juicy, just be prepared for a Succession experience: you’ll struggle to find anyone to root for but you won’t be able to look away.

author of The Midnight LibraryThe Infinite Sadness of Small Appliances by Glenn Dixon is a weird, wonderful book about a vacuum cleaner that becomes sentient after hearing To Kill a Mockingbird read aloud. Said vacuum cleaner renames herself Scout and embarks on a quest to save the human she lives with. It’s highly original and feels like a sign that – in the age of AI – the way out is through vivid human creativity.

author of The NamesA will-they-won’t-they romance is a much-anticipated holiday treat for me, and Annabel Monaghan’s are guaranteed to make my cheeks ache from smiling and keep me reading until 2am. In Nora Goes Off Script, screenwriter and single mum Nora falls for a leading actor when her house is co-opted as a film location.

author of ConclaveGraham Greene has accompanied me on a lot of holidays over the years, especially the novels set in hot climates. I recommend in particular The Power and the Glory, The Honorary Consul and The Quiet American – perfect reading for a sweltering beach, a deserted baggage hall, or a night-time veranda with a sickly blue light zapping the insects.

author of YellowfaceI recently read and loved Anthony Doerr’s Cloud Cuckoo Land. Like David Mitchell’s Cloud Atlas, it’s a testament to ridiculous hope and the power of stories that is also ridiculously, formally ambitious – its crosscutting storylines span centuries and continents. It’s precisely the kind of book I needed to remind me how high human storytelling can soar.

author of On We GoAn MP has been murdered and a taunting message left in binary code: “Catch me if you can.” So begins Body of Lies, the politically and technically prescient conclusion to Jo Callaghan’s unique Midlands-set series featuring Kat and Lock, a human and AI detective pairing. Brimful of big ideas and heart, its action-packed finale is, to put it mildly, as moving as it is thrilling.

author of Claws Out!The Enchanted April by Elizabeth von Arnim. I read this recently and found it completely charming and brilliantly transporting. Four women, bored, lost, lonely and miserable respectively, take a villa in Italy for a month of respite. It’s funny, tender and trots along at pace. But above all else, it’s a novel about women and the community that springs up between them. A perfect beach read.

author of American WifeCrash Into Me by Robinne Lee is the ideal beach read not just because I literally was reading it on the beach earlier this week, though I was, or because the American cover features waves crashing on the sand, but because it’s an irresistible mix of glamorous, thought-provoking and sexy. Jamaican-born, New York‑raised, France-dwelling photographer Cecilia is living temporarily with her famous director husband and kids in LA when she reconnects with Anouk, a model with whom she had a complex encounter 20 years earlier. Now the two women are middle-aged and equally tempted to protect and blow up their lives. This is Lee’s follow-up to The Idea of You, and it’s just as juicy.

author of Witch TrialNonesuch by Francis Spufford is an absolute banger. Historical meets fantastical in this London blitz-set novel. The perfect combination of literary and compulsive page-turner, it reads like a dream. A bonus recommendation for Time to Burn by Ellery Lloyd, which also starts in the blitz but adds a thoroughly contemporary, compelling time-travelling twist.

author of The Burning GroundsMy choice is The Shadow Step by Mark Billingham, the latest in the Blackpool-set series featuring the wisecracking, ballroom-dancing detective Declan Miller. This one sees our hero running an investigation into the murder of a rather despicable young man, which quickly gets derailed by the kidnapping of a student. As with the others in this series, Billingham weaves a fiendish plot but also lets rip with the jokes. An absolute joy to read.

author of The Death of UsI’d recommend Main Characters by Bobby Palmer. Seb and Clara meet in a Soho square, and an epic on-again, off-again romance begins. But their story is narrated by everybody except the main characters. Sometimes it’s a close friend, but we also hear from people‑watchers, neighbours and colleagues. The result has the feeling of a short-story collection, with small, perceptive insights into a vast cast of characters, and the ways lives collide and divert. Make sure you have sunglasses to hand – I wept.

author of The Barbecue at No 9This year, Dead Heat by Sabine Durrant exceeded my unofficial “beach read” criteria of 1) page-turning crime or thriller 2) set in hot weather. This elevated psychological thriller, which takes place over a Greek summer, gave me serious Patricia Highsmith vibes. It’s classy, cinematic and truly thrilling.

author of Getting Away With MurderIn Five by Ilona Bannister, someone on a London train platform will die in five minutes when the train arrives. As the clock ticks down, you meet the characters who might die, and you get to know them intimately. If you want a completely immersive read, this is for you.

author of Karla’s ChoiceIf Lewis Carroll sat down with Mick Herron to write a thriller about memory and nightmare, you’d get There Is No Antimemetics Division by qntm. A funny, gripping and genuinely disturbing counter-espionage monster novel told in beach-friendly episodic style. What’s not to love?

author of The Girl on the TrainFour Terrible Parents by Calla Henkel. Careering towards 40, two rock stars, an artist and a former banker decide the time has come to settle down, get married, and co-parent a child (while also renovating a hotel in South Carolina). Henkel’s comedy-slash-thriller is so fiendishly plotted you might not even notice all she has to say about art, love, friendship and family.

author of The Map of BonesRecently reissued, Fenny by Lettice Cooper – first published in 1953 – is a coming-of-age story set in the Tuscan hills. Dripping with heat, the sound of cicadas and the smell of the pine trees, this is the story of a Yorkshire governess who pitches up at a villa outside Florence in the years before the second world war and falls in love with the country, the light, the Italian pace of life. Heartwarming, atmospheric, a perfect summer read.

author of Just My LuckMad Mabel by Sally Hepworth. You may not have heard of this Australian-born, New York Times bestselling author yet, but I’ve been reading her for years; I love everything she’s written and I’m waiting to see her to blow-up here. Her bittersweet, thrilling dramas are shot through with life-enhancing humour. Somehow Hepworth’s Aussie sunshine floods off the page even when she’s delivering dark twists and murders. In this novel, unapologetically grumpy, fiercely independent 81-year-old Elsie lives quietly in an Australian suburb, except everywhere she goes people die in mysterious circumstances.

author of All InI couldn’t get enough of Some Bright Nowhere by Ann Packer, which is told from the perspective of a husband whose terminally ill wife asks him to move out so her best friends can move in. The literary equivalent of a friend telling an increasingly shocking story, it’s an unexpected and deeply moving read.

To support the Guardian, order your beach reads at guardianbookshop. com/beach-reads

The hill I will die on: Breakfast cereal is for babies – I eat salad in the mornings, like a grownup

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 07:00:35 GMT

There’s no way I could get by on a bowl of Coco Pops – give me sliced tomatoes and cucumber every time

I recently got into a row on X about the unlikely subject of salad. I want to acknowledge that arguing with strangers on social media is definitely for babies and I should know better by now, but I’m a work in progress. And so I mentioned that I had enjoyed how readily available salads had been at breakfast buffets while I had been travelling in Denmark and Sweden this year compared with the UK. Salad has been a part of my breakfast for about a decade now, and I think a lot of people would benefit from it. It’s a pretty easy way of getting a couple of portions of fruit and veg before you have even left the house.

All hell broke loose. Salad for breakfast is “not normal in a northern European climate”, according to one agitated typer in a response to my post about its availability at breakfasts there. In one of the towns we visited, Luleå, we were just 100km south of the Arctic Circle and the sea was still frozen in April. The hotel had an excellent breakfast buffet – a rotating assortment of freshly prepared salad items with fruit that hadn’t even been poured from a can. Someone should alert the authorities.

“Only freaks eat salad for breakfast,” another wordsmith reported. What really took the rice-crispy cake was the person who explained: “It’s the uk [sic], our food is heavy and warm here. Cold island nation that had to be out in the fields with constant rain”, which was presumably typed on a precariously balanced laptop by someone driving a tractor somewhere on Shetland. Obviously the people I worked with in UK offices who I witnessed spooning sugary snack foods into their faces while staring at their computer screens are the outliers here.

Don’t misunderstand me – I love a bowl of Coco Pops. Not as a morning food option but as an after-lunch-and-too-early-for-dinner hangry-management solution. There’s no way I could get through an entire morning on a bowl of crispy rice dusted with cocoa sloshing around in semi-skimmed cow juice.

I need sliced salted tomatoes, a generous handful of fresh assorted leaves, the crunch of a cucumber and, if I am being fancy, thinly sliced mangetout with a handful of finely chopped dill, mint or parsley to set me up for the morning, and ideally I want to have it sitting at a breakfast table. Whatever curveballs might come my way throughout the day, I can start it knowing I have done something for me and by me that was not only healthy but also delicious, and that made me sit down with a knife and fork to actually make time for at least one civilised meal.

So no thanks to the people who told me I could go into a supermarket or McDonald’s and buy salad whenever I like. That sort of misses the point – I want to eat breakfast in the place where I am staying. I don’t want to pick wilted leaves from a plastic bowl with my fingers in the middle of the high street.

Complain all you like, but I’m eating salad as part of breakfast whenever I can. There’s a reason those Scandinavians have colour in their cheeks and live long and healthy lives, and I want in on that. As for the person who responded to the photo of my breakfast of salad, garlic mushrooms and boiled egg on toast with a sophisticated total of three “being sick” emojis, thanks for proving my point – cereal for breakfast really is for babies.

Four types of thinker have been identified. Which one are you?

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 06:00:35 GMT

Investigation finds evidence of distinct groups, from big-picture thinkers to those who sweat the small stuff.

Illustrations by Michael Parkin

An investigation into what people think about has put the spotlight on the modern mind, revealing thoughts dominated by work, the need for coffee and a strong desire to go back to bed.

It also found evidence for four distinct groups of thinkers who spend more time than most either worrying about the world; mulling on household chores and finances; focusing on the mind and body; or the work-hard, play-hard combination of career and pleasure.

The groups are not definitive and people will move between them, but the finding shows how sampling people’s thoughts at random can provide a nuanced view of human thinking patterns, according to the researchers.

Economists at Claremont Graduate University, in California, and Wuhan University, in Hubei, China, explored people’s conscious thoughts after finding a surprising dearth of work on the topic. “So much of what it means to be human is about what’s going on in our head,” said Dr Joshua Tasoff, a senior author on the study. “The fact that we haven’t really looked at that as economists is really quite extraordinary.”

For the study, 258 volunteers aged 19 to 71 downloaded an app that beeped at eight random times per day for two weeks. On each beep, they were required to write down their thoughts, what they were doing and rate their happiness level.

After gathering more than 23,000 real-time responses, the economists saw that people’s thoughts flowed with the rhythms of the day, steered largely towards work in the day and entertainment in the evening. Roughly half of people’s thoughts were intentional, the rest being intrusive or accidental thoughts from mind wandering or reminders.

Sensory information, including feeling tired and sleepy, and mental impressions, accounted for nearly a fifth of all thoughts. Next came work at 17% and food at 14%. About 10% of thoughts centred on hobbies, games, play and art, with a similar amount focused on relationships.

When thoughts centred on what people wanted, nearly half involved food or drink, especially coffee. This chimed with thoughts that mentioned needs, with 29% seeking relaxation, and naps and sleep in particular.

The mind was rarely blank, the study found, with only a fraction of a per cent of responses claiming no thoughts at all. However, even fewer thoughts appeared to be about sex, leading the researchers to suspect reticence. “There may be things people don’t want to share with us. You know: TMI [too much information],” Tasoff said. Perhaps related, a quarter of beeps went unanswered, according to a preprint of the study, which has yet to be published in a peer-reviewed journal.

Part of the study tested an assertion by the Roman emperor and philosopher Marcus Aurelius, who said: “The happiness of your life depends on the quality of your thoughts.” The researchers found that what people were thinking was more predictive of their happiness than anything else they looked at. “Maybe Marcus Aurelius was on to something,” they said.

The authors cautioned against extrapolating the findings to the global population because the psychology of the volunteers, all classified as western, educated, industrialised, rich and democratic – or Weird – could differ dramatically from other populations.

The analysis of people’s conscious thoughts showed they clustered into four groups, but the categories are tentative and people probably move between them. Tasoff said a longer study with more people was needed to confirm the results. The labels were designed to capture the “vibe” of each group, he added.

The groups are based on common themes in people’s thoughts, but are not defined by a person’s background or what they do. People in different groups did similar activities and there were only minor differences in demographics, such as age, income and education, and socioeconomic status.

Worriers thought about world events, politics and social issues about 60% more than average, their minds occupied with concerns over wars, the Covid pandemic when it was raging, and other major events. They thought about their safety and health about 50% more than average. Words that typically appeared in their thoughts included Covid, awake, lonely, pain, hunger and fatigue. Interestingly, the group thought about music nearly twice as often as average, possibly to mitigate the emotional toll of their other thoughts, the researchers speculated.

A group focused more on practical and household matters, domestics devote about 50% more thoughts than average to chores, the home, finances, but also stories through movies, books and TV. The words that often described their thoughts were highly variable, however, including solve, process, debate and document.

No other group thinks more about their senses, feelings and mental impressions of themselves and the world than this one. As a group, bodily thinkers are the youngest, with an average age of 32, and nearly two-thirds are women. They have the highest rate of unwanted, intrusive thoughts, at 28%. Words that appear frequently in their thoughts are therapist, ache and overwhelm. The group might exemplify how people can move from one pattern of thinking to another. The higher proportion of women in this group could be due to the effects of the menstrual cycle. It also reflects people who had physical or mental health issues during the study turning their thoughts towards their bodies, symptoms and care.

Their minds are largely split between work and leisure, thinking about the job 50% more than average, while still thinking about hobbies, games and art about 25% more. The group has the highest income and happiness scores of all the groups and has slightly more males than females. Key words used to describe their thoughts include relaxation, presentation, flight, nail, project and gym.

I grew up near Andy Burnham. This is what shaped the UK’s new PM

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 05:00:37 GMT

In the Warrington suburb of Culcheth, people are hopeful about what one of their own can achieve as the first northern PM in half a century

The Cherry Tree pub is an unassuming local. On a busy road in the Cheshire village of Culcheth, it is a chain-run pub where four shots cost £8, every burger comes with a soft drink, and sport is shown all day on the big screens. It is also a favourite of Andy Burnham, the new prime minister.

Many of the drinkers have a story about – arguably – Culcheth’s most famous son.

“I was at school with Andy,” says Mike Hodgson. “He went to our school, he likes the Smiths … He’s got a good northern sense of person, and he’s done a good job in Manchester.”

Janice Fox chips in: “I used to play with him when we were kids.”

The Cherry is in the opening scene of Burnham’s book Head North. One night in April 1989, in its smoke-filled back room, the future leader of the country is recovering from a bout of “impostor syndrome” while home from Cambridge University. Panic, by the Smiths, is playing on the jukebox.

It is also a place I know well: like Burnham, I grew up in this quiet Warrington suburb halfway between Manchester and Liverpool, I have spent many nights at the Cherry, and like many locals, I have my own story about him.

Here is mine: 15 years ago I met the then Labour MP for Leigh while drinking with mates in the Cherry. Labour had recently lost the 2010 election, and Burnham had recently lost to Ed Miliband in the race to lead the party in opposition. Home from London for the weekend, I was struggling to get a job, so plucked up the courage for a chat.

As the then shadow education secretary, he talked me through the impact of the Conservatives’ plan to cut Labour’s Building Schools for the Future programme. That £55bn landmark New Labour policy turned cold, leaky 1960s prefab schools around the country into modern buildings of which teachers and pupils could be proud; it rebuilt my secondary, Culcheth high school.

He gave me his mobile number and invited me for a cup of tea in parliament. I expected to be ghosted. But a few weeks later we were sitting in SW1 picking up the conversation over a brew in Portcullis House. Burnham told me Britain’s media and political landscape needed more northern accents like ours.

On Friday, Burnham opened No 10 North, in Manchester; a first step in his promise to rebalance power away from Westminster to deliver “good growth in every postcode”.

This week I travelled back to WA3 to find out what people make of Burnham becoming the first northern prime minister since Harold Wilson 50 years ago. He has spoken with pride of his roots, and how reversing the decimation of Britain’s industrial communities under Margaret Thatcher is a top priority.

Outside the Cherry, one group of friends say it’s at least nice that someone local is in No 10. One of the women lifts her sunglasses and we are transported back a quarter of a century: it’s my old geography teacher, Mrs Crinion.

“I was quite proud seeing him walking down the street,” says one of her friends. “I felt a bit chuffed. I hope he does a good job.” But does having one of our own in high office change anything? “I very much doubt it,” says another.

Earlier this month, Burnham recorded a video for social media arriving “home” from London at Warrington Bank Quay train station. It is far from the most beautiful spot on the railway, in the shadow of an old Unilever soap factory that is up for demolition.

Once the diggers have finished here there are plans for an AI datacentre – a fact deployed by Keir Starmer last month as a symbol of how a “left behind” community could reinvent itself.

But this description elides much of Warrington’s character. The town has its difficulties – not least the boarded-up shops and crumbling, shuttered nightclubs on Bridge Street – but it is more affluent than many other “red wall” communities in this pocket of north-west England.

As a postwar new town, there are miles of suburbia stretching into the Cheshire countryside. There are good transport links, affordable housing, and opportunities for work in high-paying sectors, such as technology and nuclear energy.

This year, the Centre for Cities thinktank suggested Britain could do with a few more towns like Warrington: local disposable incomes have galloped ahead here, growing 2.2 times faster than the UK average since 2013. Perhaps this could influence the Burnham economic blueprint?

Still, many locals feel let down by Labour. Before Burnham replaced Starmer, Reform was predicted to sweep away the party in Warrington’s two constituencies. But many say the new prime minister’s background could help change things.

John Cross, whose family has run a butcher’s stall in Warrington market for five generations, is among them: “I’m made up. That we’ve got someone from the north, rather than someone from down south. There needs to be more balance, how we’re governed in this country. Don’t get me wrong; he’s got an absolute job in front of him. But I think it’s a good thing [that Burnham is prime minister].”

Support is, however, far from uniform, including in Culcheth. Sitting outside McDee’s cafe, Tom says he has little time for politicians – “all a bunch of thieves”. Net zero, failure to invest in defence and prosecutions of British soldiers are his complaints. “It’s Labour, isn’t it? I don’t believe any of them will do anything different.”

Inside the cafe, others are more positive. Veysel Hazar, the manager, seats me at the table where he has served Burnham and his mother, Eileen. He does not do politics, but says of the new prime minister: “Amazing person. I’m happy for Culcheth.”

Eating lunch on the table opposite, the Ollerton family are from nearby Golborne – where Burnham now lives and where coal mining once dominated. They have seen him out running in his retro Everton shirt, and are friends with his nextdoor neighbour on a road a few streets from his new Makerfield constituency.

“You knew he was going to win. Makerfield would have voted Reform if it wasn’t for him,” says Marilyn Ollerton.

“He’s very relatable, rather than just being somebody on the television; somebody from down south that you’ve probably got nothing in common with,” says Lianne Ollerton.

Some places in Warrington – particularly the terraced streets near the town’s old wire factories – rank among the most deprived in England. Burnham’s former Leigh constituency, and his Makerfield one, are among them. Culcheth, though, is seen as “posh”.

Where Burnham grew up, on Common Lane, many homes have gated driveways and easily sell for more than £1m. Locals jokingly call the area “Upper Culcheth” to distinguish it from the rest of the village, including the postwar social housing estate built for officers at the nearby Risley prison.

There is a golf course, parades of neat shops, a butcher, hair and beauty salons and pubs, as well as two Italian restaurants, both of which I worked in as a teenager.

The presence of SUVs and flash cars has steadily increased – in part the spillover from Manchester’s economic renaissance. I do not remember Culcheth being this affluent. It was comfortable, but not in the same league as the footballer-belt Cheshire villages south of Warrington.

But while it does not fit the media stereotype of Coronation Street-style terrace housing, flat caps and spoil heaps, it is still within touching distance of the industrial decline that has crushed this region.

Growing up, the legacy of industry was obvious. I saw the demolition of Parkside colliery’s concrete winding towers – the last deep mine in the Lancashire coalfield – from my bedroom window. A decade earlier, Burnham would pass here on his bus to school – St Aelreds Catholic technology college, now renamed Hope academy, in Newton-le-Willows – and bang on its window to show support to the picket line at the colliery gates during the 1984 miners’ strike.

Born in 1970 at Aintree hospital in Liverpool, Burnham moved from Merseyside to Culcheth at about age one, after his father, Roy, was promoted to a job in Manchester. An engineer at the Post Office, he had once worked at a telephone exchange in the village – opposite the Cherry Tree – and liked the feel of the place.

Raised Catholic, Burnham went to St Lewis primary school, a short walk down Mustard Lane from Croft primary, where I went. He recalls in Head North a “modest” upbringing. There were no holidays abroad. But his family also “didn’t want for anything”, and he went on to study at Cambridge, where he met his future wife, Dutch-born Marie-France van Heel.

Burnham is often in the village playing five-a-side football with his brothers, who are teachers, and their friends, including relatives of another famous son of Culcheth, Roger Hunt, the Liverpool striker and England 1966 World Cup winner.

In the Lords of the North barbershop in Warrington town centre, hairdresser Nicole Egan tells me Burnham’s brother John taught her at school. “If he’s anything like his brother … 10 out of 10. Top family. I’m made up. He seems to be doing some great things already.”

Egan’s mother, Cheryl Good, is cutting a boy’s hair. She says the prime minister went out with her old boss back “when he was a raver” in an Adidas tracksuit.

“He went to a normal school. He wasn’t privately educated where they were told they were special or better than anybody else. So he’s started from the same starting point as everybody else, and he’s done really well for himself.”

Both are Green voters but see Burnham as moving in the right direction, despite hearing “alarm bells” over the rumours that he could allow more North Sea oil and gas drilling. But first impressions matter: addressing the cost of living has cut through in a way that locals say has raised their hopes.

“Working families are struggling,” says Egan. “So the things he’s done at the moment – the [cutting of the] tax on electricity bills, £2 cap on the fares on buses, and that’s only in his first couple of days. I’m very hopeful – what little we have left of that”

Burnham was in Culcheth after a regular football game with his brothers, in his first fortnight as the mayor of Greater Manchester, when he was told of the Manchester Arena bombing on 22 May 2017. It was a moment that would become a turning point for the city, and for Burnham.

People are full of praise for his ability to empathise. Three years ago, Burnham was at the candlelight vigil in his home village for Brianna Ghey, the 16-year-old transgender girl murdered in Culcheth Linear Park.

They also credit him for the economic turnaround of the city along the M62. Manchester – and its resulting “ism” – is central to Burnham’s political and economic blueprint for Britain; founded in the coordination of the private and public sector, and helped by new powers for local areas through devolution.

Grabbing power from Westminster and Whitehall resonates in these parts.

In the market, Neil Kelly, who leads community engagement for the local rugby league team, Warrington Wolves, is having a coffee with his colleague Adam Leah. “There’s been a lot of fights with Whitehall all of the time. So I think devolution is going to work in that sense for Warrington.

“You’ll see for Warrington what it means, and how it can have a real effect, particularly around on the streets and the towns, and the cultures and the communities.”

There are, however, tensions and undercurrents. Warrington is among the most heavily indebted councils in England, with an outstanding pile worth more than £1.5bn. The town’s Labour leadership argues it needed to borrow to invest, to offset Tory austerity directed from Westminster. But critics fear handing over more powers might not be the right answer.

The bus network in Warrington could also show the opportunities and difficulties of local power. Unlike most places, the town never lost control of its buses in the wave of 1980s privatisation.

Buses have long been a Burnham preoccupation, after he overhauled the network in Greater Manchester. The region’s Bee Network, a system of joined-up, accessible transport, has brought buses under local control through franchising. In Warrington, the neon yellow fleet – close in colour to its Manchester equivalent – is fully electric, and locally controlled, but more expensive than many would like, at £5.90 for a day ticket.

In Culcheth there will be tensions with Labour’s national priorities on housing development; in a semi-rural community ringed by green-belt land, many do not want to see more homes built, despite the climbing house prices pushing young people away.

Still, at a Labour party branch meeting at Culcheth library, there is hope that Burnham can square the circle because he knows these issues. Margaret Webber, the branch chair, and Matt Smith, a local Labour councillor who was once my high school form tutor, say that where the person who leads Britain is from has an important bearing.

“He’s got a lot of good will behind him, because he’s saying what a lot of people think.”

Blind date: ‘We were chatting as soon as we sat down’

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 05:00:34 GMT

Jacob, 27, a volunteer manager, meets Sophie, 28, a journalist

What were you hoping for? To meet someone who I could connect with and possibly go on further dates.

First impressions? Sophie was very nice and upbeat.

What did you talk about? Our conversation went all over the place, from both of us having connections to the US to her organising standup comedy nights.

Most awkward moment? There were a couple of moments where the conversation stalled, but overall it flowed nicely.

Good table manners? Yes.

Best thing about Sophie? She was very funny and had me laughing out loud.

Would you introduce Sophie to your friends? I don’t think we are at that stage.

Blind date is Saturday’s dating column: every week, two strangers are paired up for dinner and drinks, and then spill the beans to us, answering a set of questions. This runs, with a photograph we take of each dater before the date, in Saturday magazine (in the UK) and online at theguardian. com every Saturday. It’s been running since 2009 – you can read all about how we put it together here. What questions will I be asked?We ask about age, location, occupation, hobbies, interests and the type of person you are looking to meet. If you do not think these questions cover everything you would like to know, tell us what’s on your mind.

Can I choose who I match with?No, it’s a blind date! But we do ask you a bit about your interests, preferences, etc – the more you tell us, the better the match is likely to be.

Can I pick the photograph?No, but don't worry: we'll choose the nicest ones.

What personal details will appear?Your first name, job and age.

How should I answer?Honestly but respectfully. Be mindful of how it will read to your date, and that Blind date reaches a large audience, in print and online.

Will I see the other person’s answers?No. We may edit yours and theirs for a range of reasons, including length, and we may ask you for more details.

Will you find me The One?We’ll try! Marriage! Babies!

Can I do it in my home town?Only if it’s in the UK. Many of our applicants live in London, but we would love to hear from people living elsewhere.

How to applyEmail blind. date@theguardian. com

Describe Sophie in three words Kind, authentic, humorous.

Did you go on somewhere? No.

If you could change one thing about the evening what would it be? I would have not arrived 15 minutes early. Multiple readings of a menu that I had already looked at online could have been avoided.

From A Useful Ghost to Self Esteem: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 05:00:34 GMT

A woman is reincarnated as a vacuum cleaner in this Cannes prize-winning black comedy, and the uncompromising pop star hits the festival trail

A Useful GhostOut now Winner of best film at Cannes Critics’ Week, this tale of a woman reincarnated as a vacuum cleaner takes you to plenty of unexpected places, even when you discount the sort of unexpectedness suggested by the premise. Part Marxist thriller, part supernatural romance, and taking in foul-mouthed monks and drama with the in-laws along the way, Ratchapoom Boonbunchachoke’s directorial debut is an oddball treat.

On the SeaOut now Made mostly outside the traditional funding mechanisms for UK film, this independent second feature from Helen Walsh is a lovely, graceful depiction of repression and queer desire in a Welsh mussel-harvesting community. Barry Ward gives a fine performance as the married man who finds himself drawn to a younger itinerant worker (Lorne MacFadyen).

Aardman RetrospectiveCinemas nationwide In the run-up to the release of Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom, look out for summer holiday rereleases of a plethora of Aardman classics in cinemas, including A Matter of Loaf and Death, The Curse of the Were-Rabbit and the film that first introduced woolly hero Shaun, A Close Shave.

Pinocchio UnstrungOut now Director Rhys Frake-Waterfield was also behind Winnie-the-Pooh: Blood and Honey and its sequel. This new instalment in what the film-makers call The Twisted Childhood Universe features Robert Englund (Freddy Krueger) as the voice of Jiminy Cricket. Catherine Bray

Camp BestivalLulworth Castle, nr Wareham, 30 July to 2 August Rob da Bank’s enduring family-friendly festival returns with its mix of kids’ activities – bee-keeping has been added this year, alongside skateboard ramp lessons and trampolining – and music from Bastille, Fatboy Slim, Self Esteem and more. Michael Cragg

Elgar’s FirstRoyal Albert Hall, London, 29 JulyThe English composer’s magnificent Symphony No 1 gets top billing, but this concert also features the first major world premiere of the BBC Proms season. The World’s Wife by Brett Dean sets Carol Ann Duffy’s poetry and is performed by soprano Claire Booth and BBC Scottish Symphony Orchestra conducted by Ryan Wigglesworth. Flora Willson

Luke CombsEdinburgh, 25 July; London, 31 July to 2 August The US country music superstar, who scored a UK hit with his cover of Fast Car in 2023, steps up to stadiums. With six albums under his belt, including this year’s deeply personal The Way I Am, expect a setlist brimming with crowd-pleasing self-reflection. MC

Edinburgh Jazz & Blues festivalVarious venues, 25 & 26 July This event consistently embraces international and Scottish artists. Its closing weekend includes folk-inflected sax-led quartet Harben Kay (25 July), Joni Mitchell-inspired singer Michelle Willis (25 July) and multi award-winning jazz/hip-hop sax star Soweto Kinch (26 July). John Fordham

Richard DaddRoyal Academy of Arts, London, 25 July to 25 October Step into a world of fairies and folklore in Beyond Bedlam, a look at the work of the Victorian artist. He remained forgotten by history until the 1960s, when his life in Victorian asylums became a source of inspiration for countless artists.

Michael PinskyMidlands Arts Centre, Birmingham, 25 July to 4 October For The Final Bid, Pinksy has filled this gallery with secondhand chairs, all hung from the ceiling, which visitors are invited to bid on. Each bid drives the chair higher up towards the ceiling, in a strange capitalistic ballet about value and detritus.

Clare WoodsPitzthanger Manor, London, 29 July to 8 November The exhibition, called Garden Without Seasons, sees meditative paintings and collages of the natural world in this Sir John Soane-designed country house, each work pushing the boundary between abstraction and figuration and asking viewers to slow down and contemplate.

Susan HughesMAC, Belfast, 30 July to 18 October This Belfast-based artist and fiddle player travelled around Ireland collecting stories about the mysteries, myths and collective power of traditional music. The result is this show filled with objects, songs and a stage for ad-hoc performances. Eddy Frankel

The World Is Full of Married MenThe Yard theatre, London, to 1 August The great Yard theatre opens its doors after a huge refurb. Its opening season includes a reimagined King Lear with Ian McKellen as well as this brilliantly bizarre adaptation of Jackie Collins’s racy novel, set amid a series of doll’s houses – and performed by dolls. Miriam Gillinson

Mike Reiss25 July to 6 August; tour starts London As part of The Simpsons’ original writing team – and co-showrunner during the programme’s early 1990s glory years – nobody is better placed to unpick the seminal cartoon’s ingenious comic tapestry than Reiss. This tour sees him spill all his Springfield-related secrets and take audience questions. Rachel Aroesti

Matthew Bourne’s The Car ManSheffield Lyceum, 25 July; Sadler’s Wells, London, 28 July to 29 August One of Bourne’s steamiest dance shows is also one of his best dramas. Loosely based on Bizet’s Carmen, but transported to small-town 50s US, a gang of macho mechanics have their close-knit, closed-minded world interrupted when a stranger comes to town. Lust, betrayal, revenge, it’s all here. Lyndsey Winship

Cherry OrchardThe Swan theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon, to 29 August Helen Hunt, Bill Pullman and Kenneth Branagh star in Chekhov’s exquisite final play. The new version has been written by Laura Wade (Posh, Rivals) whose work always manages to be brilliantly entertaining but shot through with real darkness and political bite. MG

FuriousDisney+, 27 July Elizabeth Meriwether (New Girl, Dying for Sex) helms this thriller about an FBI agent whose first case happens to feature that rarest of beasts: a female serial killer. Emmy Rossum – who also came up with the show’s concept – stars as the detective who finds empathy for a devilish criminal.

The RaptureiPlayer & BBC One, 26 July, 9pm Adapted by the performance artist Bryony Kimmings from Liz Jensen’s novel, this drama centres on a forensic psychologist treating a teenage girl with the ability to predict catastrophic events. If that doesn’t sound stressful enough, the whole thing takes place in a heatwave. Ruth Madeley, Iwan Rheon and Ruth Jones star.

Ghosts AustraliaiPlayer & BBC Three, 25 July, 10.30pm Most British comedies get lost in translation when franchised abroad, but this wildly original format is the exception. Following US, French, Greek and German versions, this Aussie spin sees a young couple haunted by an aerobics instructor, a biker, a gold rush miner and a socialite.

Gomorrah: The OriginsNow & Sky Atlantic, 28 July, 9pm Roberto Saviano’s acclaimed Italian mafia drama was described as a darker alternative to The Sopranos when it aired a decade ago. This similarly gritty prequel returns to the mean streets of 1970s Naples to recount the origin story of Camorra boss Pietro Savastano. RA

Halo: Campaign EvolvedPC, Xbox, out 28 July A quarter-century on from the first Halo, the game has been revitalised with new visuals and the original voice actors re-recorded. No competitive multiplayer but you can play cooperatively with one local friend on console, or up to three online.

Mistfall HunterPC, PS5, Xbox, out 29 July Time to learn some new terminology, Gyldhunter. This dark fantasy PvPvE (player-v-player-v-environment) extraction ARPG (action role-playing game) has you (and optional friends) perfecting your weapon stances and combos to kill monsters in an ever-shifting battlefield beneath the Gyldenmist. Gyld luck! Jordan Erica Webber

Nia Archives – Emotional Junglist Out now The Brit-nominated “darling of jungle” follows up 2024’s Top 20 debut Silence Is Loud. Co-produced by her alongside James Ford (Arctic Monkeys) and Ethan P Flynn (FKA twigs), songs such as Boys in Blue expand on her sonic palette, pushing towards 90s electronica and indie.

Baby Queen – I Hope You Don’t Remember Me Out now Inspired by a whirlwind relationship that ended with a ghosting, South Africa-born, London-based alt-pop star Bella Latham returns with a second album that channels emotional turbulence into galloping synthpop on Feel Something, and something far knottier on the frantic Word Vomit.

The Strokes – Reality Awaits Out now Having pulled off a surprising creative and commercial rebirth on 2020’s The New Abnormal, the Strokes return with this seventh album. Produced once again by bearded Zen master Rick Rubin, confounding recent single Going Shopping continues frontman Julian Casablancas’s obsession with Auto-Tune.

Charli xcx – Music, Fashion, Film Out now Despite a recent pivot to acting, Charli returns with her second album of 2026. The follow-up to February’s excellent Wuthering Heights soundtrack dials up the guitars – see snarky lead single Rock Music – while keeping Brat’s potent mix of hedonism and existential dread. MC

Armchair ExplorerPodcast Just in time for the summer holidays, this beloved travel documentary series features deep dives into global cultures and dream itineraries. Highlights include a road trip through Australia’s Northern Territory and a safari in Botswana wilderness.

60 Second DocsInstagram Packing engrossing narrative and fascinating detail into one-minute shorts, this Instagram page is a treasure trove of bite-size curios. Topics range from spoon-playing musical maestros to the art of clay “hug pots” and green-screen tattoos.

James Turrell: Master of LightBBC World Service, 28 July, 4.32am American artist James Turrell’s Skyspaces are large installations that play with natural light. For this edition of In the Studio, Julian May meets Turrell in Denmark as he prepares one of his most ambitious ones to date. Ammar Kalia
