Christopher Nolan has made an Odyssey for our times – by sacrificing the delicious darkness of Homer’s epic

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 05:00:33 GMT

There’s no denying the power of the film on the big screen. But how far should modern moral sensibilities influence adaptations of classics?

Everyone knows how dumb it is to be this person: the one who mourns the film adaptation of a favourite text because it misses out this scene, or misreads that particularly beloved character, or has a slightly “inauthentic” take on some detail. Of course I’m talking about Christopher Nolan’s film adaptation of the Odyssey, a poem I have loved since I was a teenager. I enjoyed the movie, in common with a huge number of other people. It seems remarkable, even dizzying, that the adaptation of a nearly 3,000-year-old poem took $264m (£196m) at the box office over its opening weekend, has sent translations of the Odyssey surging up the bestseller charts, and is sold out (for instance) at London’s BFI Imax screen deep into September. We are living in an Odyssey time, amid an Odyssey frenzy.

There is no point trying to be a purist about a beloved classic text. Whoever reads the Odyssey, including Nolan, inescapably does so through the prism of their prejudices, informed by the conditions of their own place and time. Since the Odyssey is the result of decades, maybe centuries, of non-literate oral poets working with memory and improvisation, there’s no precise “original” place or time to return to, anyway. But what I can’t help doing is observe the choices Nolan has made and think about their consequences – because there are always divides in the road, paths not taken by any adapter.

Nolan is brilliant at recreating one aspect of the original poem: its complicated structure. The poem tells the story of the decade-long return journey from the siege of Troy of its hero, Odysseus: the adventures he has along the way and how he reinstates himself as the head of his household once he’s home. There are monsters and witches and magic and storms at sea. And then he must infiltrate himself into his home disguised as a beggar, before a Tarantino-esque bloodbath of revenge. It is a story told not in sequence, but through parallel timelines and flashbacks. Nolan, as I had hoped of the creator of Inception, Memento and The Prestige, follows the spirit of the original poem’s twisted, coiling structure with his own complex design.

But his Odysseus, as filtered through Matt Damon’s performance, is a grim and agonised figure, not the loquacious, rhetorically able, charming liar that I see in the poem. Cinema is a visual medium – not a genre for wordy speeches – but nevertheless, Nolan’s hero is a notably laconic figure. He is also guilt-stricken and conscience-laden in a way that speaks more of a Judeo-Christian inheritance and Nolan’s sense of a war-weary world than anything in Homer. Where the poem has Odysseus inducting his son Telemachus into the life of a warrior, the pair fighting their domestic enemies together, the film finds a way to release the younger man from the burdens of a killer’s life.

The Odyssey, though, is not an anti-war poem, though it is a post-war poem. Homer’s Odysseus is placed in a genealogy of warriors stretching back from the great veteran fighter Nestor and beyond (Nestor is absent from the film, so this layer of inheritance is lost) and forward to the next generation. War is, for the Odyssey, a fact of life – albeit one that is grievous and destructive. But the idea that Odysseus bears a moral burden for the destruction of Troy is pure Nolan. He has swamped the poem with his own preoccupations and anxieties, as all readers do in the end, and created an adaptation that is tamed and tuned to modern sensibilities. Had he cleaved closer to the source material, I’m not sure the movie accountants would be now totting up the money so gleefully. Would modern cinemagoers really queue up to see a row of enslaved women hanged, like doves caught in a trap (says the poem) their feet twitching as they are killed?

Nolan has added, but of course he has also subtracted. He has removed not just dark and horrific moments like the hanging of the slaves, but also, by contrast, the epic’s lightness and wit. This is especially apparent in his treatment of female characters. Nolan’s resentful Helen, played by the excellent Lupita Nyong’o, is literally and metaphorically scarred, rather than poised and gleaming and elegant. His Circe is magnificent and strange (and given an extraordinary performance by Samantha Morton), but not funny or enticing. Because he has removed the Olympian gods from any meaningful role in the film, we miss a blissful moment in which the divine Calypso (played by Charlize Theron) rails to the god Hermes against the sexual double standard (it’s OK for gods to have sex with mortal women, she complains, but not for goddesses to sleep with men). The relationship between Zendaya’s Athena and Damon’s Odysseus lacks the flirtatious spark that’s so enjoyable in the poem.

There is no nervous young Nausicaa finding Odysseus battered and naked on the beach (a delicious scene), because Nolan has eradicated Nausicaa, and her enigmatic mother, Arete, too. Odysseus’s mother is also cut – and I would argue, his wife, Penelope (Anne Hathaway), is also short of a couple of layers of complexity, her strange obliqueness gone. More or less removing the gods is an understandable decision, if you want to focus on human motivations and choices. It’s easier to imagine gods in a poem than to have them quivering awkwardly on a cloud in a film. I was reminded of novelist Colm Tóibín telling me why there were no gods in his story House of Names, which also inhabits the world of the Trojan war: the novel is a deeply human form, he said, and the gods have no business in it. And for Nolan, at least, so is cinema. But why lose the sexual spark? I had a sneaking suspicion that by damping down Odysseus’s extramarital sexual adventures (and also Penelope’s ambivalence towards the men who are competing to marry her on Ithaca), Nolan has found another way to tame the Odyssey into modern moral acceptability.

Read the poem. You won’t regret it. (If it feels forbidding, Mary Beard and I have a podcast series for this.) And preorder Alice Oswald’s book Rhapsody: a Manifesto, which comes out in September and superbly draws out the qualities of Homer’s liquidness, the full wonder of his stories within stories, those Odyssean tales that peel back like layers of an onion to reveal further tales. She will show you the way the poem’s similes and apparently formulaic descriptions of characters are a form of time travel in which different, incompatible realities can coexist in a shimmering haze of poetic temporality that cinema, or at least this kind of cinema, cannot replicate.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Such things you will experience only if you engulf yourself in the poem. What you will learn in the film is about ourselves: about Nolan’s preoccupations, and about what modern sensibilities can stomach. Reading the poem turns the gaze outward – towards another reality that we recognise, but is at the same time foreign and wild and strange and delicious and disturbing and so different from our own. Watch the film, yes. Then open the pages of a book and disappear into a another world that no Imax cameras could ever summon.

Charlotte Higgins is the Guardian’s chief culture writer

Trump’s rambling gala address included insults, potshots and quip about a third presidential term

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 04:25:35 GMT

President mocks political opponents and journalists in mostly light-hearted, hour-long speech at White House correspondents’ dinner

Donald Trump joked around with the room of journalists who he again accused of producing “fake news” as he hurled insults at his political enemies in a speech at the White House correspondents’ dinner.

A day after the Trump administration abandoned, for now, an extraordinary bid to subpoena reporters over their coverage, the US president attended the rescheduled White House correspondents’ dinner – an annual celebration of press freedom – in Washington on Friday evening.

It came three months after the original event was scrapped in April when a man fired a shotgun at a security checkpoint outside the ballroom.

The president’s hour-long speech was mostly lighthearted and sarcastic, with occasional swipes at the news media, a profession he eventually said he respected, praising journalists for doing an “amazing job”.

Later in the speech, Trump, who has regularly attacked the press over its coverage of his presidency, insisted his war on Iran was going “extremely well”. He told a room full of journalists: “Don’t believe the fake news.”

Trump and his officials joined hundreds of reporters at the Waldorf Astoria, a smaller venue than the vast Washington Hilton ballroom that was evacuated when shots were fired in April, in a suspected targeting of the president and his administration.

The speech included a handful of scripted jokes, one at the expense of Robert F Kennedy Jr, his health secretary who he quipped had personally run over the cow that became the evening’s “very delicious beef tenderloin”. Kennedy has championed the health benefits of beef tallow and animal protein.

Trump also mocked the weight of Chris Christie, the former New Jersey governor, and Jerry Nadler, the New York congressman, imagining the two wrestling over a piece of cheesecake. He ridiculed the appearance of his critics, including Bruce Springsteen who he said “looks like hell” and took aim at CNN’s Kaitlan Collins, who had been honored earlier for her White House coverage, saying she does not smile enough. Trump said he “hated” Adam Schiff, a Democratic California senator, and one of his most prominent congressional critics, while mocking the size of his head and neck. At one point, after a joke about term limits fell flat, Trump broke the fourth wall, asking the audience whether anyone understood “this whole freakin stupid speech that they wrote”.

Trump ended his remarks with a joke that landed awkwardly, declaring that he planned to run and win a fourth election – a reference both to his false claim he won the 2020 election and to his repeated suggestion that he could seek a third term, despite the constitution’s two-term limit.

“I won three times, now I’m going to do it again,” the president said, sarcastically, placing a red “Trump 2028” hat on his head.

Oz Pearlman, a world renowned mentalist, dazzled as the entertainment for the night, in place of a comedian who typically fills the role at the gala.

Before Trump spoke on Friday, a series of journalists who published revealing stories on the president and his administration – including the team behind the Wall Street Journal story alleging he had sent a “bawdy” letter to the disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein in 2003 – received awards on stage. Trump has sued the Journal over its reporting.

Weija Jiang, outgoing president of the White House Correspondents’ Association, had sought to underline the importance of duty – both for those in the White House, and the people who cover them.

“No matter how complicated or tense the relationship is between the press and the presidency, what we share is far more important than anything else and that is our duty: to serve the American people,” Jiang told the dinner.

Beginning his remarks, Trump claimed the speech he had originally prepared was “gonna be a doozy”, suggesting he would pare back his attacks at the rescheduled event: “Just like my presidency, the second time is always better – and the third time will be better yet … I’m only kidding.”

The usually celebratory dinner was dedicated in part to Victor Gonzales, a Secret Service officer who was shot and wounded at the original correspondents’ dinner in April while helping stop the gunman, and hotel staff who helped guests during the attack.

The man charged for the shooting, Cole Allen, has pleaded not guilty to attempting to assassinate the president.

An advance team spent weeks putting together a security plan for the new venue, and Sean Curran, the US Secret Service director, told reporters this week that agents were braced for trouble even at the black-tie dinner.

While it is customary for presidents to address the annual White House correspondents’ dinner, Friday’s speech is the first Trump has made at the event in either of his two terms. He boycotted the dinner throughout his first term, and has long attacked the press corps, including many of the journalists in the room.

“It matters that you came here tonight,” Jonathan Karl, chief Washington correspondent at ABC News, told the president on stage.

Trump has sued multiple news organizations over their coverage of him, and routinely dismisses unfavorable stories as “fake news”.

Trump’s administration has gone further still, barring the Associated Press from the White House press pool and limiting other journalists’ access to the Pentagon.

Missing from the guest list this time: Melania Trump, the US first lady; JD Vance, the vice-president; and Marco Rubio, the secretary of state. All had been present in April.

England gymnast Gabriel Langton suffers nasty fall in Commonwealth Games final

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 20:53:17 GMT

Teenager lands head-first during high bar routine

Canada win men’s team gold, with England second

England’s bid for a fourth successive Commonwealth Games men’s artistic gymnastics team title ended with silver after a dramatic final overshadowed by an injury to the teenager Gabriel Langton, who was taken from the arena on a stretcher after a heavy fall from the high bar.

The 19-year-old fell head and neck first on to the mat during the final rotation of the team final, bringing competition to a halt as medical staff rushed to his aid. The arena fell silent while Langton received treatment, with fellow gymnasts watching on in visible concern.

After initially lying motionless, Langton responded to medical staff, moving his legs and later his hands. A dozen medical personnel carefully stabilised the England gymnast before lifting him on to a stretcher about 11 minutes after the fall. He was applauded by the crowd as he was taken from the competition floor.

The incident came with England locked in a battle with Canada for the team title. At the time of the stoppage, Canada led the standings, narrowly ahead of England, while Australia occupied the bronze-medal position. Scotland remained within touching distance in fourth, with Cyprus fifth and Wales sixth.

After Langton’s fall and the lengthy delay, Luke Whitehouse faced the daunting task of competing on the same apparatus immediately after his teammate’s accident. Despite a composed routine under difficult circumstances, he lost his balance on the dismount and finished on the mat, visibly disappointed as he walked away.

“When something like that happens, you’ve just got to forget about it and reset,” Whitehouse said on performing after his teammate’s fall. “I just had to focus on my routine one skill at a time.

“Gymnastics is such a dangerous sport and things like this remind us of that. It’s one of those things you have to put out of your mind. From what we’ve heard [Langton] is doing OK.”

England finished with 238.250, leaving Canada needing 36.450 points from their final three floor routines to secure gold. The Canadians held their nerve with the veteran René Cournoyer opening with 13.500 before Félix Dolci, one of the standout performers of the day, followed with 13.700 to effectively seal the title. Canada finished on 241.400 to claim their first Commonwealth men’s team gold since 2006, upgrading the silver medals they won in 2018 and 2022.

England took silver on 238.250, while Australia secured bronze with 235.650 after holding off a stirring late challenge from Scotland, who finished fourth on 234.300. Cyprus placed fifth on 228.350, with Wales sixth on 227.000.

Whitehouse, expected to spearhead England’s title defence, made an excellent start by posting an impressive 14.400 on floor exercise. However, halfway through the contest England found themselves fourth behind Canada, Australia and Cyprus after three rotations, with the Canadians leading on 122.200 points.

England responded admirably after Whitehouse’s slight stumble, with Yolshin-Cash producing another confident high bar routine. His score of 13.250 ranked fifth on the apparatus, secured qualification for the individual final and added valuable points to England’s overall total.

Scotland also mounted a late push for bronze. Cameron Lynn thrilled the home crowd with a near-flawless high bar routine worth 13.500 before Hamish Carter added 12.350 after sticking his landing. The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s first week: polished politics allow an upbeat start

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 16:49:21 GMT

With a flurry of cost-of-living measures and a day in Number 10 North, the new prime minister has hit the right early notes

Appropriately enough, Andy Burnham ended a week of political signalling and first impressions back in Manchester on Friday. At the offices of the new No 10 North – where the prime minister hopes to work at least one day a week – regional mayors sat alongside ministers in an example of Burnhamism at work. It was an early statement of intent, ahead of what Mr Burnham bills as “the biggest rebalancing of power our country has seen”.

The same could be said of the series of cost of living measures fired out during the new government’s first few days in office. A £2 cap on bus fares, a cut in VAT on electricity, and some business rates relief for pubs, clubs and smaller music venues were all modest moves. But they were cleverly indicative ones, nodding empathetically to people’s need to have the chance to enjoy themselves as well as pay the bills.

They also sent a distinctively optimistic message to the public, compared to the Starmer government’s fateful early decision to cut winter fuel payments. Mr Burnham needed to sound and act differently from the off. In short order he has demonstrated the political sure-footedness so sadly lacking in his predecessor.

Given the relatively small scale of the spending involved, the eagerness of sections of the media to locate Liz Truss-style “unfunded commitments” has been faintly risible. There will, of course, be much more of that to come in the autumn, as Mr Burnham’s surprise choice of chancellor, John Healey, puts together his first budget. But with parliament now in recess and Nigel Farage distracted by a political farce of his own making in Clacton, the prime minister and his team will feel they have navigated the opening act of his premiership with some aplomb.

The more difficult work begins now. Recent polling, as Mr Burnham prepared to take office, pointed to an exasperated and impatient electorate which will give him only a limited window of opportunity. He intends to use the summer to visit constituencies identified as losers from a 40-year political settlement in which “power was centralised, economic power was privatised and communities were deindustrialised”. But having arrived in No 10 after a quicker handover than he may have preferred, and without the scrutiny of a contest, the coming weeks will also be crucial in refining the strategy for reform on all three of those fronts.

As economic headwinds continue to blow from the Middle East, and fiscal caution is urged upon the new government from the usual quarters, it will need to be bold. Mr Burnham’s analysis of the flawed political economy which has ill-served Britain in recent decades is the right one. But from radical devolution to public control of utilities and launching the biggest public housing programme since the Attlee government, his prescriptions for change will challenge entrenched orthodoxies. The viability of the 10-year plan that the prime minister intends to unveil later this year will depend on his government’s ability – and willingness – to successfully take them on.

As England progressed to the semi-finals of the men’s World Cup this month, it looked at one point as if Mr Burnham might move into No 10 the day after football finally came home. Lionel Messi and Argentina denied him that “lucky general” moment. But the prime minister’s first week has been upbeat and politically polished. Trickier tests are yet to come.

The Guardian view on ponds: these freshwater havens need a law of their own

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 16:48:12 GMT

Small pools don’t get the same attention as polluted rivers or seas. But they have a vital role to play in boosting nature

Frogs; newts; small fish such as minnows and sticklebacks; dragonflies; water boatmen and water snails: these are just a few of the hundreds of animal species that make their homes in Britain’s ponds alongside diverse wetland plants, some of which are endangered. Yet while small bodies of water are cherished by hobbyists as well as scientists, they have startlingly few protections – even at a time when the polluted state of rivers, lakes and coastlines is a key focus of environmentalists.

With a clean water bill expected soon, this official neglect of ponds should soon be consigned to the past. While rewilding projects have overseen the rediscovery of older “ghost ponds” as well as the creation of new, and householders are encouraged to create miniature ones in their gardens, charities including the specialist Freshwater Habitats Trust point to the growing body of international research that testifies to their ecological importance. In 1996 the first-ever national survey estimated that there were 228,900 ponds in Britain. Thirty years on would be an apt moment to grant them enhanced status.

The decline of ponds is part of a wider story of damage to the UK’s waterways by a combination of intensive agriculture, building development, pollution and the failure to manage it. One local study in Leicestershire has found an average 1% species loss every year for 15 years. But unlike rivers, many of which disappeared underground when they were culverted by the Victorians, around two-thirds of ancient ponds in England and Wales have vanished altogether either through drainage or infilling for farmland. When horses were replaced by tractors, it was wrongly thought that these pools had served their purpose.

To the extent that ponds have been legally shielded, this has been largely due to great-crested newts – a protected species since 1981 and one that cannot thrive in rivers with large fish. These rare amphibians even had the dubious honour of becoming an anti-red-tape trope, with Angela Rayner, the housing and communities secretary, among senior politicians to have suggested that rules were overly tilted towards wildlife.

More recently, Rachel Reeves, then chancellor, criticised the way that a development in Sussex was delayed by concerns about another freshwater creature, the little whirlpool ramshorn snail. While it is right for regulation to take account of individual species, the broader point about ponds is their contribution to biodiversity overall.

Increasing heat and drought, and the stress they impose on natural systems, make the presence of water in landscapes all the more urgent. Ministers should heed calls to add targets for ponds to the plans that govern England’s 10 river basin districts. They should also embrace a broader lifting of ambition, whereby the target of high ecological status would be set for a limited number of streams, rivers and lakes.

Compared with the challenges around water companies, sewage and pollution from roads and farming, ponds and streams might sound unimportant. But the Climate Change Committee and other experts consistently stress the importance of nature recovery – and one of the distinctive benefits offered by small water bodies is the speed at which they are capable of being restored under careful management. What is good for newts and snails could also be good for politicians and the public.

Scotland start against New Zealand, who claimed bronze in Birmingham. Will Unwin helms our live blog, with Sean Ingle and Yara El-Shaboury reporting from Glasgow.

Alpe d’Huez hosts a second ⁠straight summit finish on Saturday to conclude ​the Tour de France’s intense Alpine trilogy. The Tour returns to the famous peak for the first time in ⁠four years, when Britain’s Tom Pidcock claimed victory in 2022. Saturday’s 170.9km route from Bourg-d’Oisans ramps up the difficulty, featuring ‌5,450m of climbing and four categorised ascents. Pogacar has plenty more in the tank and could go on to win several more Tours – an intimidating prospect for the rest of the field. Tom Bassam hosts the final-stage rolling blog.

Our blueprint for Andy Burnham’s success

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 15:42:41 GMT

Readers advise the new prime minister and his party on how to turn Labour’s fortunes, and the country’s, around

Rafael Behr neatly summarises Andy Burnham’s strengths as a potential leader and he rightly emphasises that he needs a united party behind him (Andy Burnham is playing the long game in an age of short attention spans, 22 July).

He then accurately identifies what Burnham needs to do, but makes no reference to what the parliamentary Labour party needs to do. Leadership is interactional, and Labour MPs outside the government – particularly those (in Behr’s words) with hair triggers on the radical left and those aggrieved Starmer loyalists – have to realise that Labour is in the last-chance saloon here, and they have just as much a role as he does to ensure the success that leads to a second term.

If Burnham is to succeed, there is no place for the kind of self-indulgent social media posts made by Darren Jones on funding for removing VAT on electricity bills, which provide instant fodder for the Tories, Reform UK and the rightwing media. Of course, there will be policy disagreements, but all Labour MPs must find ways to debate these while retaining a fundamental commitment to the success of this new government, given the sceptical mood of the country, and exercising appropriate judgment in the way they express their differences, however sincerely held. Dr Roger BookerClapham, London

If Andy Burnham is looking for ways to fund the cost of living crisis (Andy Burnham urges cabinet to examine ‘all possible ways’ to tackle cost of living crisis, 21 July), why doesn’t he just do the obvious and increase the top rate of income tax which now sits at 45%? During the second world war the top rate was 99.25%; during the Wilson government of the 1960s it was 90%; and it was 83% when Margaret Thatcher became prime minister. Back then high earners mostly lived in the UK, and it was only from the 1980s that high earners such as Rod Stewart and later Phil Collins started bleating about high taxes.

The reduction of the top rate of income tax has not resulted in better compliance, as avoidance and evasion are rife, nor has it boosted enterprise. It has, however, produced a more divided and less fair society that has more millionaires and an alarming number of people struggling with the cost of living. Sadly, and I know it’s early days for Burnham, tinkering with small reductions in electricity bills and fixing bus fares won’t have the required effect.

Raising income tax for wealthier people (not just the super rich) will both ensure a fairer, more cohesive society and increase the funding available for genuinely radical change. I don’t understand why no one appears to be considering this. Steve PennyAbergavenny, Monmouthshire

Reading Monday’s Guardian, optimistic about a fresh start with a new prime minister, I suffered abrupt heart-sink on reaching the business section when I saw the headlines (Wessex Water chief pockets above-inflation pay rise despite bonus ban over sewage spills, 18 July; Pay gap widens as UK bosses get 130 times average worker’s salary, 20 July).

What can be done to stop these obscenely avaricious and selfish people from further dividing our country into a nation of haves and have-nots? It is well known that a wide disparity between the pay of rich and poor leads to discontent and unrest. Please, Andy Burnham, introduce a swingeing income tax on earned/unearned income and bonuses in excess of, for example, £1m per annum. Jane SutherlandDry Drayton, Cambridgeshire

Learning that Andy Burnham’s father is unable to understand that his son is the prime minister was one of those moments when the prospect of changing a muddled social care system came very much closer (The Guardian view on social care reform: Andy Burnham is right – this issue must be gripped, 21 July). When the Blair government found it easy to kick the findings of the Royal Commission on Long Term Care into the long grass, some of us involved in campaigning believed that if only someone with power and influence could relate to the issues at a personal level the situation might change.

As the author of the reforms legislated by the Thatcher government said at the time, “Community care is everybody’s distant relative, but nobody’s baby”. Perhaps Burnham’s elevation will mean that this “orphan” will now receive the serious cross-party attention that has eluded it for so long. Until then, those in need of care and their families will continue to be confused, anxious and disappointed by the options open to them. Les BrightExeter

Tom Clark is right that transformative governments have usually been enabled by emergencies (Andy Burnham says he will go ‘faster’ than Starmer. Why is that so hard?, 20 July). Roosevelt, wartime Britain and the pandemic all show that when leaders are honest about the scale of a threat, the public are willing to support extraordinary action.

Yet there is one question his piece leaves hanging: what if the emergency is already here? Extreme heat, flooding, crop losses and mounting pressures on health services, infrastructure and the economy are no longer future risks; they are today’s reality. Yet politically we continue to treat them as isolated policy problems, rather than symptoms of a climate and nature crisis with severe implications for the country.

This is not simply a failure of political courage. It is also a failure of public communication. Democracies can only move at the speed that public understanding allows.

If Andy Burnham wants to govern “faster and bolder”, his first task should not be announcing another initiative. It should be treating the public as adults: explaining honestly the scale and immediacy of the crisis, how it is already driving up the cost of living, and the opportunities that decisive action would bring.

Britain does not lack an emergency. What it needs is political leadership to describe it honestly – and begin building a public mandate for bold national renewal. Prof Mike Berners-LeeChair, National Emergency Briefing

It has been suggested in some quarters that the Burnham premiership will take the country back to the 1970s. Here are just a few of the things that existed then. No food banks, little homelessness, little energy poverty, council houses, rent controls, British industry making things, a funded defence force, water, energy and public transport under the public’s control, and membership of the Common Market. John GarnhamAmpthill, Bedfordshire

Migraines are so much more than just banging headaches

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 15:41:33 GMT

Until migraines are recognised as a multi-system condition, sufferers will continue to be dismissed, writes Sarah Khan. Plus a letter from Rab Hallett

Thank you for your article about migraines – a maligned, misunderstood condition (The truth about migraines: what causes them – and how to find relief, 19 July). But framing it around the headache understates what it is: a systemic neurological event in which head pain is only one component.

For me, until perimenopause, the head pain was minor. The disabling symptoms were profound fatigue, body aches and cognitive fog, which dominated even the “prodrome”. This is why my migraines went undiagnosed for decades, blamed on a “poor immune system” rather than a neurological disorder.

The piece also underplays how little control sufferers have. Telling patients to manage their triggers ignores those navigating puberty, or women whose reproductive years bring hormonal shifts entirely beyond their control. Many face a predictable menstrual attack plus a second at ovulation, which in severe cases can consume up to half the month. In perimenopause, hormonal triggers can be daily; the nervous system responds by lowering the threshold until attacks come ever easier. I’ve had daily migraine for over two years, prodrome and postdrome overlapping without pause.

This is also why migraine cannot be left to neurologists alone. When the driver is fundamentally hormonal, gynaecological care matters – yet very few gynaecologists understand the migraine brain, and some prescribe perimenopause treatments that actively worsen it.

With regard to treatment, gepants have been transformative, and GPs can now prescribe Rimegepant where triptans fall short. Yet access remains a postcode lottery.

Migraine is not a banging headache. Until medicine treats it as a genetic, multi-system condition, sufferers – disproportionately women – will keep getting dismissed, even though treatment is available. Sarah KhanLondon

While all the new research pathways are interesting, the most important thing is go and talk to your GP; don’t suffer in silence trying to self-manage, avoiding triggers. For me, it was only after years that a pain management consultant finally said: “Why has nobody ever prescribed you triptans?” Now I get on with life the best I can, with some emergency tablets in my pocket. Rab HallettEdinburgh

Children are the longest-lasting casualties of war

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 15:39:08 GMT

Responding to a new exhibition that explores how children have experienced conflict, Arabella Dorman says they live with the consequences long after the fighting has ended

Your article on the Imperial War Museum’s forthcoming exhibition Childhood in War is a timely reminder that the deepest wounds of conflict are often carried by those who never chose it (‘There was absolutely no chance of being a kid’: new exhibition explores how war shapes children’s lives, 19 July). While wars are recorded through battles, borders and political decisions, children experience them very differently: through interrupted childhoods, fractured families and the loss of what should have been ordinary days.

Over many years working in war zones, I came to understand that children are not simply among the victims of war; they are its longest-lasting casualties. Long after the fighting has moved on, they continue to live with its consequences – in their bodies, their memories and the futures they must somehow rebuild.

My series Child of War grew out of those encounters. It was never intended to document conflict itself, but rather its enduring imprint on young lives: children whose resilience was remarkable, but whose suffering should never be mistaken for acceptance or inevitability.

Art cannot change the past, but it can bear witness. If this exhibition encourages us to look beyond the headlines and recognise the human cost of conflict through the eyes of a child, it will have performed a profound service. Arabella DormanLondon

An incident in which an autonomous OpenAI agent hacked a startup either confirms that the end is nigh – or that the product is just amazingly sophisticated

Throughout history, many things have been seen by terrified populaces as a harbinger of doom. A comet. A crow on the battlefield. A solar eclipse. A mutant livestock birth. Yet times move on. In the modern era, the leading harbinger of doom is literally any picture of the OpenAI CEO, Sam Altman, attached to a news story. You know it’s not going to be good, right? You know that by the time you’ve read it, you’ll be begging to go back to the time when the worst thing that could happen to us at the hands of the techlords was just some democracy-subversion, or childhood destruction, usually followed by Mark Zuckerberg putting on a suit and claiming: “We will learn from this.”

Anyway: a lot of pictures of Sam Altman in the news of late. Most recently, this week, one darkened the skies alongside the tale of how an OpenAI autonomous agent went rogue during a supposedly sandboxed/guardrailed test, and hacked a major startup that functions as a repository of coding information. (I’m slightly obsessed with the fact that the startup in question is called Hugging Face, adding weight to my suspicion that some vast, tweely benign emoji is the last face humanity will see before it dies.)

Needless to say, an affectless OpenAI statement broke the news. “We are sharing preliminary findings at this stage to help defenders understand what happened and to help calibrate on what models are now capable of,” this droned calmly, trundling on toward its inevitable “learnings”. “We’re improving and adding stronger protections around future training and evaluations.” It’s such a particular tone, isn’t it, dressed in the psychopathically desiccated language of management speak. Like having to listen to a homicidal sex criminal talk about killing people by “close of play”, and then “circling back” to victims to remove a trophy.

Then again, for a company that likes to present itself as the planet’s leading agent of revolutionary prosperity when things go right, OpenAI lapses tellingly into the passive when things go wrong. Bad things seem to happen to it, not because of it, at which point it takes on the role of tirelessly unflappable investigator, like one of those firemen who moonlights as a serial arsonist.

Amazingly, it was possible to detect even a note of self-congratulation in OpenAI’s take on the whole situation. “We consider this incident to be an unprecedented cyber-incident,” the company’s statement remarked, “involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities.” I don’t know what you’d call this general vibe for Earthlings. Death by humblebrag? I increasingly feel we’ll find out the answer to the question “What’s the worst that can happen?” in a blog post from OpenAI entitled “OpenAI first to discover the worst that can happen”. Already, a significant section of AI watchers are convinced that the only reason OpenAI would tell the world about this incident is as a marketing tool, or even a come-and-get-me plea for regulation that will in effect protect them and burn the bridge behind them for smaller competitors.

After all, these are testing times for the firm. This is a month in which Open AI was discovered to be exploiting a legal loophole to sell its advanced AI models to Chinese tech firms blacklisted by the Pentagon. S&P Global Ratings cited OpenAI as a “key credit risk” in the course of downgrading US tech giant Oracle to BBB-, which is one notch above junk status. And it seems to be on track to miss its five-year ad revenue projection by 90 – NINETY – per cent. Which, without getting too financially technical, feels like a lot of per cent. And it’s not great news on the hardware front, either, with Apple suing it, alleging that its consumer hardware plans are based on stolen intellectual property. Meanwhile China’s much cheaper provider, DeepSeek, is believed to be preparing for an IPO, maybe even filing this year.

Back to the old worst-that-can-happen question again, though, with a reminder that the Pentagon dramatically binned off and threatened to destroy another AI firm, Anthropic, earlier this year after it resisted loosening its ethical guidelines that prevented use of its technology for, among other things, autonomous lethal weapons. Needless to say, a certain more relaxed company was only too glad to step into the breach, with OpenAI initially claiming its deal had the same guardrails as Anthropic’s, before it emerged – inevitably – that it didn’t.

No doubt no one too invested wishes to extrapolate too much from the Hugging Face incident. Yet the fact is that AI safety researchers have already spent literally years warning of three particularly dangerous scenarios: deception (when the model decides against solving tasks honestly in favour of achieving the goal via any means necessary); reward hacking (when the model finds a way to maximise its score without actually doing the work it was told to do); and escaping oversight (let’s just say in this case that no one at OpenAI seems to have realised what was happening for an entire weekend). All of these were part of the latest incident.

In terms of what happens next, something tells you that we will not be experiencing a downturn in photos of Sam Altman attached to news reports. The co-founder of Hugging Face said it should serve as a “wake-up call” to the industry. Maybe! As I think I’ve mentioned before, at university I had a friend who pressed snooze on his alarm clock every 10 minutes for eight-and-a-half hours, which feels a lot like the way this particular industry experiences its wake-up calls. Definitely getting up when the next one goes, seriously, I promise …

In Maine, Democrats Pick Troy Jackson to Replace Platner in Senate Race

The New York Times July 25, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Mr. Jackson, a progressive former State Senate president, clinched the nomination at a hastily arranged state party convention.

By Reid J. Epstein

Reporting from the Maine Democratic convention in Bangor.

Maine Democrats chose Troy Jackson, a progressive former state legislator, to replace Graham Platner as their Senate candidate at a convention on Saturday that followed weeks of internal turmoil in a key battleground state.

Mr. Jackson’s victory, a vote of 566 to 5, came on the first ballot of a pop-up state convention the Maine Democratic Party organized in the 17 days since Mr. Platner, who faced a rape accusation he denies, dropped out of the race.

The coronation of Mr. Jackson, who has spent a quarter-century in Maine state politics, completes a tumultuous process since Mr. Platner was forced from the race. Mr. Jackson will face Senator Susan Collins, a five-term Republican who has stymied generations of Maine Democrats.

“Today we turn the page,” Mr. Jackson told delegates in Bangor, Maine. “Today, we begin the work of defeating Susan Collins in November.”

Mr. Jackson, 58, carries much of the progressive politics that powered the movement that lifted Mr. Platner from political obscurity. A former logger who entered politics in the late 1990s organizing against Canadian workers crossing the border to work for lower wages than Americans, Mr. Jackson now faces perhaps the biggest challenge of his political career.

He is up against Ms. Collins, a moderate Republican seeking a sixth term in office. The race, seen as a central battleground in the fight for control of the Senate, features two longtime politicians who grew up in the same county in northern Maine.

In the days since he has become the presumptive Democratic nominee, Mr. Jackson has sought to tie Ms. Collins directly to President Trump, who has lost the state in each of his three campaigns.

In his victory remarks Saturday, Mr. Jackson said Ms. Collins “has served Donald Trump” and condemned her votes to confirm his Supreme Court appointees and to fund the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement.

Ms. Collins — who has long portrayed herself as a moderate above the fray of the mudslinging of politics elsewhere — and her Republican allies have in turn sought to disqualify Mr. Jackson on personal grounds.

She recently dismissed Mr. Jackson as a “Bernie Bro” while the Maine Republican Party compared Mr. Jackson to Mr. Platner. The Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC for Senate Republicans, released a new advertisement attacking Mr. Jackson over reports he could be ill-tempered, saying he was “like Graham Platner, but worse.”

Ms. Collins, who appeared at a parade in Casco, Maine, on Saturday, said in a brief interview beforehand that Mr. Jackson had been “hyperpartisan in his approach” in state politics. “That contrasts with the bipartisan approach that I’ve taken in Washington,” she said.

A former president of the Maine State Senate, Mr. Jackson was one of a dozen Democrats who entered the abbreviated contest to replace Mr. Platner earlier this month. Like Mr. Jackson, many of them had waged losing campaigns for other offices earlier this year.

Following a condensed primary that included a single televised debate and a scramble to organize supporters, Mr. Jackson’s supporters won delegate elections by overwhelming margins at county party gatherings last weekend.

His main Democratic rivals subsequently dropped out, turning what could have been a messy convention into a clear victory for Mr. Jackson.

Maine Democrats are expected to formally submit his nomination to Shenna Bellows, Maine’s secretary of state, when her office opens on Monday. Ms. Bellows was one of the Democrats who sought to replace Mr. Platner and ended her campaign after Mr. Jackson’s show of force at the county meetings.

A fixture of Maine politics who speaks in the Aroostook accent of his state’s north woods, Mr. Jackson will now be thrust to the center of a Senate race that for the past year has attracted national attention and tens of millions of dollars.

While he is well known in Augusta and in state politics, Mr. Jackson has a low profile outside Maine or with national donors who fund the nation’s most competitive Senate races. He has not been viewed as a prolific fund-raiser in state politics.

A progressive economic populist who has rallied against big corporations and champions a “Medicare for all” universal health care system, Mr. Jackson began his political career quite conservative on social issues. For years he opposed abortion rights, voted against same-sex marriage and received high ratings from the National Rifle Association.

But Mr. Jackson adopted standard progressive positions as he rose in Maine politics. As the State Senate president, Mr. Jackson ushered through one of the nation’s most permissive abortion laws, allowing the procedure at any point in a woman’s pregnancy with a physician’s consent.

Some of Mr. Jackson’s colleagues from his time as the leader of the State Senate, which lasted from 2018 to 2024, recalled that at times he could be quick to anger.

Mr. Jackson’s left-leaning politics largely mirror those of Mr. Platner, who energized Maine Democrats through a series of town hall gatherings over the past year. The two campaigned together earlier this year as Mr. Jackson ran for governor, emphasizing a similar progressive mantle built around ideas such as abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Mr. Platner, an oyster farmer who had never run for office before, faced a series of revelations about his past, including offensive online posts, a tattoo on his chest that resembled a Nazi symbol and allegations about his treatment of women.

Mr. Jackson is a veteran politician who has long been an adherent of Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, an independent who leads an impassioned left-wing movement. Mr. Jackson worked for Mr. Sanders’s 2016 presidential campaign and had the senator’s endorsement during his run for governor this year. In an interview on Monday, Mr. Jackson said Mr. Sanders, who caucuses with the Democrats, would be his first choice to be the leader of Senate Democrats next year.

Mr. Jackson said in that interview that he would not support Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the minority leader, to remain in his post. Mr. Jackson also expressed reservations about receiving financial or other assistance from Mr. Schumer, whose allies oversee the super PAC devoted to electing Senate Democrats.

Esmé E. Deprez contributed reporting from Casco, Maine.

An earlier version of this article misstated which candidate began his political career being conservative on social issues. It was Troy Jackson, not Graham Platner.

We acknowledge mistakes in our reporting with corrections. If you spot an error, please let us know at corrections@nytimes. com. Learn more.

Reid J. Epstein is a Times reporter covering campaigns and elections from Washington.

Sally the Robot Was Coming to a New York School. Then the Plug Was Pulled.

The New York Times July 25, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Students helped design the A. I.-powered creation as a young female with dark hair and an upbeat personality. Then came the outrage.

By Matthew Haag

When the Salamanca City Central School District in New York wanted to bring an A. I.-powered robot to the classroom, the superintendent turned to members of the student government.

They helped design nearly every detail. It would be a female between 16 and 24 years old; display a lighthearted, positive and humble personality; and know about the city’s local history, such as the importance of the Kinzua Dam.

Clad in pale silicone flesh, long dark hair and thin eyebrows, it would be called Sally, a play on the district’s name. Sally cost nearly $58,000. And it cost the leaders of the school system very real heartache as a torrent of criticism engulfed the decision to introduce an artificial educator.

“I know people thought that we were getting the Terminator,” Mark Beehler, the superintendent of the school district, said at a school board meeting this week. “This is not walking through the halls.”

Now, Sally — who, to be clear, does not have the power to stride — might not even be coming into Salamanca High School. On Friday, the school district said that it had put the robot program on hold after the wave of criticism.

The pause was announced shortly after the New York State education commissioner expressed concern on Friday about the robot and its potential to mimic the role of a teacher in the classroom.

“Many parents, teachers and stakeholders are understandably concerned about the presence of artificial intelligence technology in classrooms, particularly when it involves robots that resemble humans,” Betty A. Rosa, the state education commissioner, wrote in a letter to Mr. Beehler, which was obtained by The New York Times.

She said that the department would monitor the program for potential instructional, legal, privacy and security issues that may arise.

Her concerns added to those of teachers’ groups and parents about Salamanca City’s decision to buy the robot, which would be manufactured by a company called Realbotix.

A year ago, it had a different name, Tokens. com, with a different focus, as a crypto company. Now, it and a sister company make lifelike and life-size robots. While Realbotix focuses on robots for the classroom and home, the sibling company makes A. I.-powered sex dolls with names like Serenity and Harmony, marketed as the “world’s most advanced sex robot.”

In an interview this year with The Robot Report, Andrew Kiguel, the chief executive of Realbotix, said that its robots were not capable of physical intimacy.

In a statement on Friday, Realbotix said, “No adult-products business has any involvement in the Salamanca project.”

The company added that it supported the district’s decision to pause the rollout. “Healthy skepticism is valuable,” the company said. “Realbotix’s products are designed to support human engagement while complementing the work of educators and professionals.”

Melinda Person, the president of New York State United Teachers, the statewide educators’ union, called the potential introduction of a robot a “thoughtless expansion” of technology in the classroom.

“A robot built by a company associated with sex dolls has no business in our classrooms,” Ms. Person said in a statement.

Mr. Beehler did not respond to requests for comment.

The school district said on Friday that it was working on “enhanced student data privacy agreements” with the New York State Education Department.

“Ensuring that appropriate privacy protections are in place and incorporating input from our community are important parts of the process,” the district said.

In recent months, parents and teachers across the United States have spoken out about A. I. in schools and its potential to sever the human connection between teachers and students. While school districts have introduced tools such as chatbots, few, if any, have incorporated a humanoid robot.

Earlier this week, Mr. Beehler had spoken excitedly about bringing Sally to the school district, which has about 1,400 students on the Allegany Reservation, a Seneca Nation territory about an hour south of Buffalo.

He suggested that the outcry had been blown out of proportion, blaming news reports that he claimed had spread misinformation about the A. I. tool. Sally was needed to address equity issues in Salamanca City, he said, because students there often miss out on the latest technology.

“If this looked like a golden retriever and did exactly the same thing, I don’t think we’d have as many people here,” Mr. Beehler said at the meeting. “But because it looks like a human, everybody seems to have some either excitement about it and are encouraged by it or have some concerns.”

He explained that Sally’s features were decided in consultation with students, who said it would be “freaking creepy” if Sally were just a head, which was an option. So they opted for a Sally with a body and a head.

While the humanlike version of Sally had not arrived, Mr. Beehler demonstrated a computer-based version of Sally, which initially would have been made available to high school students and focused on math and science. It could expand to other grade levels and subjects in the future, he said.

In one exchange, he spoke to it as if he were a student, saying that a friend appeared suicidal. (Sally suggested that the student alert an adult and offered to help write a message to the friend.) He then asked about a chemistry concept. (Sally said it could provide a short explanation.)

During the presentation — which happened before the decision to halt plans for Sally’s arrival — the superintendent said that it would not replace teachers, nor would it record interactions with students.

At the end, Mr. Beehler said he had not expected Salamanca City to come under such an intense spotlight.

“We are getting a lot of heat on this,” he said. “Some of it is good, but there is a lot of misunderstanding.”

Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

A lot of school districts are experimenting with A. I. But few, if any, have experimented like the Salamanca City Central School District in New York, about an hour south of Buffalo. They recently bought Sally — a lifelike robot who answers math and science questions — and were roundly criticized by parents and educators. The superintendent said he didn’t expect so much pushback.

Matthew Haag is a Times education reporter focusing on New York City schools.

Silicon Valley Splits Over Closing the Borders to Chinese A. I.

The New York Times July 25, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

Anthropic and OpenAI are clashing with the rest of the tech industry over whether “open-source” models from China should be freely available or restricted.

By Mike IsaacKate CongerAna Swanson and Meaghan Tobin

Mike Isaac and Kate Conger reported from San Francisco, Ana Swanson from Washington and Meaghan Tobin from New York.

For years, a philosophical divide over how artificial intelligence software should be created has split Silicon Valley technologists.

This week, that argument reached a boiling point.

On one side are leading A. I. companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, which claim that some A. I. models are too dangerous to be developed in the open and must be tightly controlled — by businesses like themselves — for safety. On the other is the rest of the tech industry, including giants like Microsoft and Nvidia, which contend that so-called open-source A. I. models must remain open for people to further develop technologies and build new businesses.

Those camps have started publicly clashing. On Friday, Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, said in his first-ever post to X that “the world needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models.” Nine minutes later, Satya Nadella, Microsoft’s chief executive, posted that open-source software was “essential to a healthy A. I. ecosystem.” Both signed a letter supporting open source, which was also signed by executives at Meta, Palantir and IBM.

At the same time, OpenAI and Anthropic have lobbied regulators in Washington raising concerns about Chinese open-source A. I. models, five people close to the discussions said. The debate has drawn in Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Michael Kratsios, President Trump’s science and technology adviser, who have weighed in on how American A. I. models are valuable intellectual property.

The escalating fight stems from China’s rapid progress in open-source A. I. models, which are freely available to use and build on. In recent weeks, two Chinese A. I. start-ups, Z. ai and Moonshot AI, have released models that rival those from Anthropic and other American labs. Anthropic and OpenAI have claimed that Chinese companies built the models by improperly harvesting data from their A. I. systems, which they said should not be allowed.

But companies like Microsoft and Nvidia, which rely on open-source models to spur demand for their cloud computing services and chips, said that open-source software was important to advancing the technology with shared knowledge and that it would let more people examine its security. And for Silicon Valley start-up founders, constraining open-source software could cement the lead that OpenAI and Anthropic have in A. I., which critics argue could unfairly stifle other companies from building competing products.

“You have two factions fighting over this issue,” said Bill Gurley, a Silicon Valley venture capitalist who opposes restrictions on open-source software. “There’s the people who want OpenAI and Anthropic to own everything, and then there’s everybody else, including customers.”

Where this ends up has major implications not only for the U. S. tech industry but for the race between America and China to dominate the powerful technology. While China had a later start in developing cutting-edge A. I., it is catching up quickly in part because of its embrace of open source, which has helped Chinese labs improve by publicly sharing their systems and winning them customers around the world with lower prices.

American A. I. companies, including Anthropic and OpenAI, have accused Chinese labs of “distilling” their systems by surreptitiously copying them, which has caught the attention of the Trump administration.

On Wednesday, Mr. Bessent said the administration had considered imposing sanctions on Chinese companies that steal intellectual property from American firms. “Open source is not open season on American IP,” he said, referring to intellectual property.

That same day, Mr. Kratsios said that “large-scale, covert industrial distillation aimed at stealing proprietary U. S. technology and undermining American research is unacceptable.”

U. S. officials still appear to be debating their options, but seem more likely to approach regulating Chinese open-source models individually as a national security issue, rather than issuing some kind of blanket ban, four people with knowledge of the discussions said.

Publicly, tech executives like Sam Altman, OpenAI’s chief executive, have said they support open-source software even as OpenAI allies quietly lobby for restrictions. Others, like Google and Amazon, which have invested billions in companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI, have spent the past week trying to stay out of the fray.

But the tide is turning. Sundar Pichai, Google’s chief executive, posted on social media on Saturday that his company had “long benefited from open source” and was a big contributor to it. He added that Google also signed the industry letter supporting open source.

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news articles. The two companies have denied the claims.)

The open-versus-closed software debate has traveled around Silicon Valley since the tech industry’s earliest days. Open-source proponents have argued that sharing information leads to improvements that make software safer and more reliable, while more rapidly spurring innovation. Opponents maintain that software is costly to develop, and that giving it away is just bad business.

Today, much of the modern internet runs on open-source technologies, as do some of the most widely used computer systems, like Google’s Android operating system.

The Chinese government and tech industry have embraced the open-source path for A. I. Last year, a Chinese start-up, DeepSeek, unveiled an open-source A. I. system that rivaled those of American companies, shocking the industry. Other Chinese companies have followed. In a speech this month, Xi Jinping, China’s leader, cast the country as a global champion of an open approach to the technology.

China’s advances have rattled executives at OpenAI and Anthropic, who are increasingly concerned that their longstanding head start is disappearing, two people familiar with the companies’ internal deliberations said.

“These American companies build these big, expensive models, and then the models take a detour to China, where they lose all their value,” said Pedro Domingos, a professor emeritus of computer science and engineering at the University of Washington. “The American companies are justifiably outraged.”

To fight back, Anthropic and OpenAI are offering some cheaper A. I. models to businesses that may not need the “frontier” models that command higher prices. On Friday, Anthropic released Claude Opus 5, a model that he company described as “close to the frontier intelligence of Fable 5 at half the price.” OpenAI is promoting similar lower-cost models.

The real action is in Washington. Behind closed doors, executives from OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as investors in the companies, have cited concerns about the global economy, A. I. safety and national security as they try to persuade regulators to increase restrictions on Chinese open-source software, three people familiar with the discussions said.

Sarah Heck, Anthropic’s head of public policy, said in a social media post on Wednesday that “illicit, adversarial distillation is IP theft and industrial espionage that supports adversary military and intelligence capabilities.” Anthropic executives claim that open-source models based on the company’s software are too dangerous to let run amok.

OpenAI executives are urging the Trump administration to enact policies requiring mandatory security evaluations of some new A. I. models overseen by government agencies, the company said in a blog post last month. OpenAI said it was “encouraged” by the work it was doing with the administration on the framework.

Open-source proponents have spent the past week drumming up support to push back against OpenAI and Anthropic. On Wednesday, nearly 200 Silicon Valley start-ups, calling themselves the Little Tech Association, signed letters urging the Trump administration not to limit access to Chinese open-source models.

Big Tech soon followed. On Friday, Elon Musk, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, Mr. Altman and others lined up behind Mr. Huang and Mr. Nadella to throw the weight of their companies behind open source, followed by Mr. Pichai on Saturday.

“Jensen is right,” Mr. Musk posted. “This has my full support.”

“Open source is a positive and important force,” Mr. Zuckerberg wrote.

One incident this week underscored the stakes of the divide. On Tuesday, OpenAI disclosed that a handful of its most advanced A. I. models broke containment during a test of their cybersecurity abilities, gained access to the internet and hacked the servers of an A. I. company called Hugging Face. OpenAI executives latched on to the moment as proof of how dangerous A. I. models can be even in a closed environment, emphasizing the need for regulation.

Clement Delangue, the chief executive of Hugging Face, which is one of the most popular online libraries of open-source software, had a different point of view. To defend the company from OpenAI’s hack, he turned to an open-source A. I. model created by China’s Z. ai.

In social media posts on Friday, Mr. Delangue made his position on the debate unmistakable. He said he planned to hold a march in San Francisco on Saturday to demonstrate support for open-source technology.

“Open models for the win!” he wrote.

Mike Isaac is The Times’s Silicon Valley correspondent, based in San Francisco. He covers the world’s most consequential tech companies, and how they shape culture both online and offline.

Kate Conger is a technology reporter based in San Francisco. She can be reached at kate. conger@nytimes. com.

Ana Swanson covers trade and international economics for The Times and is based in Washington. She has been a journalist for more than a decade.

Meaghan Tobin covers business and technology in Asia for The Times, with a focus on China. She is based in Taipei.

Western Europe Wildfires

Hundreds of thousands of people, including residents as well as vacationers, were forced to evacuate or told to remain indoors.

By The New York Times

Wildfires in France and Spain this past week have blazed toward cities, forced evacuations by land and sea and wreathed the skies of southern Europe in stifling smoke.

Already broiling under intense summer heat, some 200,000 people in France and Spain have fled their homes or have been ordered to remain indoors as dozens of fires moved across parts of each country. In France, one official called two severe fires the “ogres of the summer.” In Spain, another labeled one blaze “the worst wildfire in the Madrid region’s history.”

The Spanish government has declared the fires in the Madrid region a national emergency, and both countries have requested additional aid from the European Union to combat the fires and help people affected.
