Inside the Rushed Effort to Get Trump His New Air Force One

The New York Times July 25, 2026

Trump Administration

Times Investigation

A New York Times investigation found that President Trump’s push to speed delivery of the aircraft led to ballooning costs and trade-offs in safety features.

Times Investigation

A New York Times investigation found that President Trump’s push to speed delivery of the aircraft led to ballooning costs and trade-offs in safety features.

President Trump walked off the new Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews on July 9 after attending a NATO summit in Turkey. A security threat was said to have altered his trip. Credit... Doug Mills/The New York Times

Supported by

By Eric LiptonTyler Pager and Maggie Haberman

Eric Lipton is an investigative reporter. Tyler Pager and Maggie Haberman cover the White House.

President Trump was entranced. It was a few weeks into his second term, and he was on the tarmac of the Palm Beach airport, getting a tour of a luxury Boeing 747-8 that had been flown from Doha for his perusal.

The double-decker jet, which had been outfitted for the Qatari royal family, had a spacious bedroom adorned with leather and wood and a lounge featuring a chandelier and another with suede seats.

Two planes being built by Boeing to replace the aging Air Force One fleet were years behind schedule, and Mr. Trump’s team had asked the Air Force to find a temporary aircraft. This was the one, the president decided.

Mr. Trump’s February 2025 tour of the Qatari jet led to a frantic sprint inside the White House and the Pentagon. The administration sought to upgrade the plane in time to meet his demand for it to be ready by the nation’s 250th birthday this summer, with an accelerated retrofit.

An investigation by The New York Times found that the president’s push to get the luxury aircraft quickly led to ballooning costs and trade-offs in safety features that potentially left Mr. Trump and others who travel with him on Air Force One vulnerable.

Among the findings:

Mr. Trump was personally engaged in making decisions about the retrofitting of the donated plane, giving the final approval on the features and security measures that would be included, according to people familiar with his role. They and others interviewed for this article described the sensitive information about the process and the plane on the condition of anonymity.

Several key security and safety features on the Boeing planes that have been used for decades as Air Force One are not visible on the upgraded jet, including a lower-level exit for high-risk situations, additional backup power capacity and an advanced antimissile system, public Air Force records and photographs examined by The Times show. The planes currently being built to serve as the permanent presidential fleet are all set to have such features, federal records show.

The 747-8 plane was overhauled on a compressed timeline of just about eight months. Experts said the jet would have needed several years for a full upgrade.

Because the Qatari jet was being pushed into service so quickly, some White House officials initially expected it would only be used for domestic travel or to visit allied countries with U. S. military bases.

The government spent hundreds of millions of dollars to purchase equipment needed to train pilots to fly the 747-8 plane so quickly, on top of the approximately $400 million cost of the upgrades that the administration has publicly acknowledged. The Pentagon has tried to mask the total price tag — including from Congress — by taking the funds from a classified budget for nuclear modernization.

The truncated overhaul of the jet came after Qatar agreed to give it to the Defense Department as a gift. It is eventually slated to go to Mr. Trump’s presidential library, an unorthodox donation that has been criticized as a way for the Middle Eastern country to curry favor with the president.

The security trade-offs of the new Air Force One burst into public view when Mr. Trump was forced to fly out of Turkey earlier this month on a different jet, a swap made at the urging of the Secret Service after officials identified a credible threat to him by Iranian proxy forces. The New York Times then reported that the new plane lacks some of the same defensive countermeasures as the previous model.

It is unclear what security measures, including new air-defense technologies, may have been incorporated onto the plane, which the administration has maintained is safe. Nevertheless, the White House announced this week that the Qatari-donated jet would be taken out of service this fall for unspecified “upgrades and enhancements.”

“PLANEMAXXING,” the White House declared in a social media post touting the move.

The reversal exposes the potential risks that the government took to satisfy Mr. Trump’s demand for an aircraft befitting the grandeur he believes should accompany his office. Experts familiar with the Air Force One program said they were surprised Mr. Trump had decided to use the Qatari-donated plane for overseas trips.

“People need to be aware it has a lot of shortfalls compared to Air Force One; they do add a measure of risk,” said Frank Kendall, who supervised the presidential plane modernization project, first as the Pentagon acquisition chief and then the Air Force secretary under President Joseph R. Biden Jr. from 2021 until January 2025.

But for Mr. Trump, having to use decades-old planes that frequently needed repairs was an embarrassment. The two 747 jets had been in service since the early 1990s, when the first of them carried President George H. W. Bush from Washington, D. C., to Topeka, Kansas.

“When you land and you see Saudi Arabia, and you see U. A. E., and you see Qatar and you see all these — and they have these brand-new Boeing 747s mostly, and you see ours next to it, this is like a totally different plane,” Mr. Trump told Sean Hannity during an interview on a flight to the Middle East in May 2025. He added: “And we’re the United States of America. I believe that we should have the most impressive plane.”

Air Force officials have said the rapid retrofitting of the Qatari plane was a success, describing it as safe, secure and equipped with the most advanced technologies.

“A testament to the Air Force’s ability to innovate and rapidly evolve to ensure the continuity of our government under any conditions,” Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach, the Air Force’s chief of staff, said in a statement in May.

The White House has also maintained that the Qatari jet poses no risk the president and his entourage. In a statement this week, Karoline Leavitt, the White House press secretary, called the new plane “fully mission-ready and safe for presidential travel today.” She said the enhancements it was set to receive this fall would “ensure it remains the most advanced, secure and capable aircraft in the world.”

It was December 2016, shortly after Mr. Trump’s first election, and he was being briefed on the lengths that the military goes to harden Air Force One.

In a meeting at Mar-a-Lago, Air Force Gen. Carlton D. Everhart II told the incoming president about the “complex and unique systems” required of the Boeing planes “to ensure survivability and reliability,” according to a copy of a once-secret presentation, reported on earlier by TWZ, a website that covers the Pentagon.

General Everhart described how Air Force One served as a mobile command center for President George W. Bush during the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

Mr. Everhart, who is now retired, said in an interview that Mr. Trump asked about the plans for a modernized Air Force One, expressing confidence about his own expertise.

“I know about my airplane, because I fly all the time,” Mr. Trump told him, as Mr. Everhart recalled, referring to his private plane informally called Trump Force One.

Mr. Trump remained fixated on Air Force One when he regained the White House. Just weeks after his re-election in 2024, Mr. Trump sent the tech entrepreneur Elon Musk to a Boeing airplane hangar in Texas where the two jets were slowly being transformed.

Mr. Musk’s assignment was to find a way to speed up the Boeing effort, as he and others believed the project had gotten bogged down by excessively strict security clearance requirements for some of the workers not involved in sensitive features of the plane.

But the Trump transition team also asked the Air Force for a backup plan, according to former and current Air Force officials: to scour Boeing’s list of all 747-8 airplanes in service to see if there was another in the world that could be quickly procured for Mr. Trump.

Military officials were already concerned about the number of repairs needed for the aging planes in the presidential fleet. The 747-8, the latest model of the Boeing jet, is different than the one that had been used for decades as Air Force One. It has modernized electronic flight controls, a redesigned wing system and engines and a larger cabin and upper deck, among other changes. The Air Force limited the choice to this plane because it has four engines, providing an extra margin of safety if one failed.

But even after locating the Qatari jet, the Air Force knew that it would cost more than $1 billion and take years to install the same features as the planes built to serve as Air Force One, according to Mr. Kendall and other former Air Force officials.

Two auxiliary power units to ensure power for the plane

A lower entryway to allow exit and entry in less secure environments

Multiple self-defense systems, including infrared countermeasure devices

Multiple self-defense systems, including infrared countermeasure devices

A lower entryway to allow exit and entry in less secure environments

Two auxiliary power units to ensure power for the plane

Source: U. S. Air Force.

Arfa Momin and Junho Lee/The New York Times

Pentagon documents show that those Boeing jets must undergo a series of major structural changes to be part of the presidential fleet. Holes must be carefully cut into the fuselage to build a lower entryway, allowing the president to exit and enter in less secure environments. An “autonomous baggage loading” system has to be added to reduce the reliance on foreign ground crews.

Hundreds of miles of electrical wiring and electronic components have to be shielded from an electromagnetic pulse, such as from a nuclear weapon detonation.

The official planes also require a second small engine — known as an auxiliary power unit — to be installed near the rear of the jet to serve as a backup for communication systems and other vital electronics gear. They also need some of the most advanced communications equipment and what the Pentagon has called a “self-defense system.”

The missile defense systems include infrared countermeasures, which can detect, track and jam incoming missile threats and are installed on the plane’s wings near the engines and its tail, according to detailed schematics of the planes prepared for emergency responders.

All the upgrades are “inherently expensive,” one Air Force briefing said, outstripping the roughly $400 million the military initially estimated it would cost just for the two jets.

The latest total estimate: $5.1 billion for the entire modernization effort, now slated to be completed in 2028 — 13 years after the Air Force first decided to rely on 747-8 jets for the project.

Inside the Oval Office, where Mr. Trump displays a model of a gleaming new Air Force One plane, the president was assessing plans to retrofit the Qatari jet.

Over a series of meetings last year, military officials presented him with printouts outlining the various modifications. The president weighed in on choices for the interior décor and exterior paint color and signed off on the security features and communication systems, according to people familiar with the discussions.

Mr. Trump also made it very clear: He wanted the plane in time for America’s 250th birthday, on July 4, 2026.

Early on, White House officials had expected the upgrades would take 18 to 24 months. Once the timeline was truncated, some officials believed Mr. Trump would only use the retrofitted Qatari jet for domestic travel or to allied countries in safe regions.

By the time the Air Force got ownership of the plane in August, it had less than a year.

On Aug. 8, the 747-8 lifted off from Fort Worth, Texas, where it had been stored for months, and landed in Waco, the home of a sprawling complex owned by L3Harris, a military contractor selected to retrofit the Qatari plane. The terms of the contract and the total price have not been made public.

Executives at L3Harris said that even before starting major work on the plane, it was searched for any listening devices or other electronics that might have been installed before the United States took possession of it.

It was “a very rigorous process, really in advance of us even working on it,” said Jason Lambert, the president of L3Harris’s intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance division, in a June interview with Breaking Defense, an industry trade publication. He added that the process was “performed by our electronic warfare experts in conjunction with the U. S. government’s leaders in cybersecurity to fully inspect and ensure that everything within that aircraft was safe for the mission.”

The company assigned as many as 400 employees, working around the clock over three shifts, to supercharge the effort.

A top priority: adding a secure communications system so the plane could serve as a global command center.

But from the start, it was clear there would be some limits on what they could do, Mr. Lambert told Breaking Defense. The interior of the plane would get the presidential seal and new wood and leather furnishings, he said. But major adjustments such as moving bulkheads or fixed structures inside the aircraft were not doable.

Documents examined by The Times show other features were also left out.

For decades, Air Force One has allowed the president to arrive at and depart any airport without having to rely on standard ground equipment.

The plane has had a lower side door with self-contained stairs, which is easier to protect. Mr. Trump used that entrance while boarding the old Air Force One last October after the Secret Service discovered what it suspected was a hunter’s stand hidden at the edge of the Palm Beach, Fla., airport.

Mr. Bush also used the lower stairs on Sept. 11, 2001, when he landed unexpectedly at an Air Force base in Louisiana, with military personnel armed with machine guns helping guard him.

But the retrofitted Qatari jet has no such entrance or a similar rear door with self-contained stairs, according to experts who examined photographs of the plane for The Times.

Administration officials did not dispute that. There was a “reduction of the number of airstairs” for autonomous entry and exit, a Pentagon official told The Times.

Arfa Momin/The New York Times

Photographs of the retrofitted Qatari jet also do not show the infrared countermeasures systems that are installed near the engines of the old Air Force One and documented in the schematics prepared for emergency responders.

Such infrared devices are designed to detect any approaching missile threats, start immediately tracking them and send a high-intensity laser beam into the approaching missile to disrupt its approach, according to one manufacturer.

It is unclear what other self-defense technology may have been added to the Qatari-donated jet. The administration declined to address its security capabilities. A White House official called it “secure and well-protected” and said that officials were always looking for ways to modernize air defense systems.

The Air Force One jets are also supposed to have two auxiliary power units designed to provide electricity if there is a power disruption, even while the plane is in flight.

Only one of these units is visible on the new plane, while two are visible on the old Air Force One. A federal official confirmed that the second unit was not installed on the Qatari jet; the White House did not dispute it was absent.

It is unclear how L3Harris or the Air Force addressed a separate issue that has plagued the Boeing jets: cracks in longitudinal rods that stiffen and support the fuselage skin.

Since 2023, the Federal Aviation Administration has warned the cracks create an “unsafe condition” that “could adversely affect the structural integrity of the airplane.” It ordered owners of 747-8 planes to inspect for such cracks and repair any.

Multiple reports filed with the F. A. A. and Air Force audits detail the expensive and time-consuming efforts to find and fix the cracks in the planes that it is building to serve as Air Force One jets. Some only became apparent when the planes were stripped down to their frames.

Referring to the Qatari-donated plane, the White House official said the aircraft will have those efforts completed as required by the F. A. A., although it did not say if such fixes had been made. L3Harris did not respond to requests for comment.

The plane has another complication: sideways-facing seats. An F. A. A. safety rule mandates that planes with unusual seat arrangements perform special checks with crash-test dummies to ensure that passengers would not be injured during emergency landings.

Documents obtained by The Times show that a subcontractor working on the plane filed paperwork seeking a “special condition” approval from the F. A. A. allowing it to fly.

On July 1, the first day that Mr. Trump was traveling on the new Air Force One, the F. A. A. published a public notice that the request had been approved days earlier.

Similar approvals have been granted for other Boeing 747-8 planes used as luxury carriers. But Sandy Murdock, a former F. A. A. chief counsel, said the approval appeared to be granted just in time for Mr. Trump to fly on the plane.

The White House official said the Air Force had worked with the F. A. A. to ensure the “all Air Force aircraft are safe to fly and operate.”

The rushed process also led to costs far beyond the roughly $400 million in taxpayer money that the Air Force estimated would be spent to retrofit the jet.

During that process, the Air Force had to accelerate training for its pilots, as the 747-8 has a different cockpit than the old jets. To do so, the Air Force leased an Atlas Air cargo 747-8 jet from October until February, a plane that costs hundreds of thousands of dollars a month, to use for “interim pilot qualification training,” records show. The Air Force did not disclose how much it paid for the lease.

Given the tight deadline, the Air Force then moved in December to buy yet another 747-8, this one from Lufthansa to serve as a “dedicated trainer aircraft for aircrew” so that the Pentagon had “immediate operational readiness,” the Air Force said in a statement. It also purchased a second one to supply spare parts. The total cost for both: another $400 million, an Air Force official said.

Both jets will be useful once the new Boeing Air Force One planes are in service. But the need to acquire them so quickly was driven by the arrival of the Qatari jet, the Air Force has said.

The administration has declined to say how the overall project has been financed. But Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink acknowledged in Senate testimony that the government was using funds from a nuclear modernization program called Sentinel. Last summer, $934 million was transferred from that program to an unnamed classified project, as The Times previously reported.

Senator Christopher S. Murphy, Democrat of Connecticut, has repeatedly pressed Trump administration officials for information about the costs and security systems of the temporary Air Force One. He said the funding maneuver was an effort to avoid scrutiny.

“We routinely discuss the cost of the existing Air Force One modifications,” Mr. Murphy said. “But they have declared this work to be a national security secret that cannot be divulged even to appropriators. That is absolutely unacceptable.”

This spring, Mr. Trump’s dream plane finally took to the air again.

At 2:36 p. m. on April 16, just eight months after work began on the jet, it began flying in circles around Texas and Louisiana. Six more test flights followed that month.

By May 1, the Air Force was ready to declare a victory of sorts. “VC-25B Bridge aircraft has officially completed modification and flight testing and is being painted,” the Air Force said in a statement, referring to the formal military name for the retrofitted Qatari jet.

But military officials also acknowledged that they went without certain elements. Overall, the Air Force said, “no risk was taken in security, safety or mission communications, but the collective team made trades on some of the less commonly used mission sets,” without providing details.

The plane was moved to a warehouse to be painted. Rather than using the trademark robin’s egg blue and white design commissioned in 1962 by President John F. Kennedy and Jacqueline Kennedy, Mr. Trump wanted a color scheme of red, white, gold and dark blue.

“The baby blue doesn’t fit with us,” he told Fox News.

The Air Force had previously rejected this change pushed by Mr. Trump in his first term, concluding that the darker color “added heat in certain environments” and potentially disrupt sensitive electronic components installed in the lower part of the plane.

But Mr. Trump overrode those objections. He had been showing off a model Air Force One with the new paint scheme for years, both at his Mar-a-Lago club and even at one of his 2025 inaugural balls.

Mr. Trump was effusive last month as he looked over the retrofitted plane, parked inside a hanger at a military base in Maryland.

Standing below his new jet, the president took out one of his Sharpies and signed his name on a mechanical panel on its belly, while the song “Y. M. C. A.,” a Trump rally anthem, blasted on speakers.

“This is a plane that the United States of America should have,” Mr. Trump said July 1 as he prepared to board to take it on a debut flight to North Dakota.

Days later, he flew the new Air Force One to Turkey to attend a NATO meeting.

While he was in Ankara, the United States resumed airstrikes on the neighboring country of Iran. The war was just 1,000 miles away from the president.

Early in the morning of July 8, a military official shared bad news with Mr. Trump, who was in his suite at the JW Marriott, according to a person familiar with the situation. U. S. officials judged there to be a credible threat that Iranian proxy forces were targeting him. The Secret Service wanted to change the plans for his departure.

That morning, Mr. Trump announced that the Qatari-donated plane would fly ahead to Mildenhall Air Force Base in the United Kingdom so U. S. service members could see it.

The president, who would later get back on the Qatari jet in England, made no mention of the security threat when he announced the change on Truth Social.

For his part, Mr. Trump would fly out of Ankara on the old Air Force One, he wrote, “for old time’s sake.”

Julian E. Barnes, Eric Schmitt, Greg Kendall-Ball and Zolan Kanno-Youngs contributed reporting.

Eric Lipton is a Times investigative reporter, who digs into a broad range of topics from Pentagon spending to toxic chemicals.

Tyler Pager is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.

Maggie Haberman is a White House correspondent for The Times, reporting on President Trump.

After Democratic Shake-Up, Susan Collins Holds Enormous Cash Edge in Maine

The New York Times July 25, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Republicans are pouring huge sums behind the Maine senator through a web of billionaire-funded super PACs. Troy Jackson, picked as the new Democratic nominee, has a lot of catching up to do.

By Bayliss WagnerLisa Lerer and Theodore Schleifer

Bayliss Wagner reported from Portland, Maine.

Even before Graham Platner withdrew from Maine’s Senate race in disgrace this month, he and his Democratic allies were severely outmatched in the race for cash.

Now his replacement, Troy Jackson, inherits a difficult situation: He has just over four months to erect a defense against a towering Republican super PAC apparatus that is intent on re-electing Senator Susan Collins.

Ms. Collins is relying on a web of deep-pocketed outside groups, funded largely by billionaire megadonors, to spend tens of millions of dollars on advertising promoting her and attacking the Democratic nominee. Her campaign, her allies and other groups aligned with Senate Republican leadership have already reserved about $60 million in airtime through the fall, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact.

That is far more than the roughly $24 million that Senate Democrats’ main super PAC and its affiliates have allocated to ads in Maine, though more could be on the way.

With Republicans set to outspend Democrats that drastically, a bruising, asymmetrical battle is about to unfold for a seat that could be pivotal to control of the Senate.

“We’re probably never going to be able to match what the Republicans are going to spend, but we’ve got to have a fight,” said Rufus Gifford, a leading Democratic fund-raiser who hosted an event for donors to Mr. Platner in May. He added, “This is not a level playing field by any stretch of the imagination.”

Mr. Jackson, a former state lawmaker and logger from rural Northern Maine, is a progressive who has railed against billionaires, has few ties to Democratic big donors and has never been a strong fund-raiser.

Democrats chose him to become their new nominee at a state party convention on Saturday. Now, he will have to build an expansive national fund-raising operation and donor list from the ground up even as he works to court voters across Maine.

“I’m going to definitely bust my ass in these next four months to make up the difference” in money, Mr. Jackson said in an interview on Monday with The New York Times. “And in the end, I think I’m on the right side of the issues compared to Susan Collins. So I feel very good about the race.”

He estimated he would need between $40 million and $50 million, but added, “That’s probably not even enough.”

Over nearly three decades as a senator, Ms. Collins has built a deep bench of supporters across the country. And she has had six years to prepare for a tough re-election battle.

She is slated to benefit from the support of outside groups more than any other Republican candidate this cycle, according to advertising data. Including expenditures from during the primary, the Republican ad campaign for her is currently set to cost $113 million in total.

Her allies have set up a deep-pocketed super PAC, Pine Tree Results, that is independent from those controlled by national Republican leaders.

The group poured millions into a series of tough attack ads against Mr. Platner and is planning to spend about $20 million more through Election Day on television and digital ads.

“We plan to welcome Jackson to the N. F. L. quickly,” said Scott Reed, who runs Pine Tree.

Amid the onslaught, Mr. Platner had criticized Pine Tree for relying on out-of-state donors. Of the $16.5 million in contributions the group has received, $5,000 — or 0.03 percent — came from within Maine, according to an analysis of campaign finance reports.

Ms. Collins’s campaign said that the donations from outside Maine were a testament to her experience and her bipartisan record.

“She is receiving support from across the country because, in these tumultuous, highly polarized times, people recognize Senator Collins’s steady, reliable presence in the Senate,” Blake Kernen, a campaign spokeswoman, said in a statement.

Pine Tree has received seven-figure checks from the investor Paul Singer, the hedge fund titan Ken Griffin, the private equity chief Stephen A. Schwarzman and Jim Davis, the owner of the footwear company New Balance. None of them live in Maine, which is known as the Pine Tree State. Mr. Singer is also backing another pro-Collins super PAC called Winning for Women.

Pine Tree has raised $20 million this cycle and had $8 million left in the bank as of June 30, according to the most recent filings, while Winning for Women had nearly $700,000 on hand at that time. Ms. Collins has $12 million in her own campaign accounts, including her leadership fund, Dirigo PAC.

Overall, Ms. Collins and her allied groups collected donations from at least 79 billionaires since January 2025, according to an analysis in June by The Maine Monitor.

Senate Republicans’ main super PAC, the Senate Leadership Fund, is also backing her with tens of millions of dollars. The group released a new advertisement on Saturday attacking Mr. Jackson over reports he could be ill-tempered, saying he was “like Graham Platner, but worse.”

At a time of public anger at inequality, Mr. Jackson may be able to seize on Ms. Collins’s support from billionaires. But allies of Ms. Collins say they have seen such attacks fail before.

“People know her — they know she doesn’t live a lavish lifestyle,” said Lance Dutson, a Republican political strategist who has worked for the senator on her previous campaigns. “There’s just none of the trappings of what someone would see as an associate of the billionaire class.”

In some ways, the Democrats’ candidate switch-up in Maine could help level the playing field.

Democrats have already lobbed millions of dollars’ worth of ads against Ms. Collins. But her operation will now have to devise messaging about a new opponent, after spending months planning how to hammer Mr. Platner over his many controversies.

Those scandals had made some Democratic big-dollar donors hesitant to support his campaign. Mr. Jackson can now try to bring them back into the fold.

But in Mr. Jackson’s previous campaigns, he struggled to raise money. He lagged behind competitors in reported contributions for his unsuccessful primary campaigns for Congress in 2014 (he raised around $300,000) and the governor’s mansion in June (he raised $1.2 million).

After Mr. Jackson’s backers swept delegate elections last weekend, his campaign announced that it had raised $1 million in less than two weeks — a sizable number given the short timeline, but one unlikely to spook Ms. Collins.

Mr. Jackson is likely to have other help, however.

After Mr. Platner withdrew, Senate Democrats’ campaign arm and the Maine Democratic Party established a fund to be transferred to the new nominee. Mr. Jackson is also likely to lean on groups aligned with organized labor, similar to a state PAC that spent nearly $1 million in ads emphasizing his blue-collar bona fides in the governor’s race.

And though Mr. Jackson told The Times on Monday that he would not support Senator Chuck Schumer, the minority leader, the super PAC aligned with Mr. Schumer has kept its millions of dollars in ad reservations in Maine through November.

“Leader Schumer has one message for every Democratic Senate candidate: Just win,” said Allison Biasotti, Mr. Schumer’s spokeswoman.

There will also be no shortage of small-dollar donors, who tend to flock to major Democratic campaigns for Senate, especially at the end. Nearly 25,000 donors have pitched in for Mr. Jackson’s Senate bid so far, according to his campaign.

Money alone does not guarantee victory for either party.

In a state like Maine, which has roughly one million registered voters and just three media markets, strategists say that huge political spending can reach a saturation point for voters. Democrats had high hopes of unseating Ms. Collins after sharply outspending her in 2020 — and she still won.

And there are plenty of signs that Ms. Collins faces an uphill climb to a sixth term in a state Mr. Trump lost in 2024, including concerns about her age and the political headwinds caused by an unpopular Republican president.

But Mr. Jackson finds himself behind in a race to define himself while lacking the infrastructure or money to do so quickly. In that void, Ms. Collins and her backers will lunge to paint him in a negative light.

Democrats have other reasons to be concerned. A Supreme Court ruling late last month that rolled back decades-old restrictions on political-party spending has raised worries in the party about even more spending by big donors.

“National donors are going to have to step up,” said Mr. Gifford, the Democratic fund-raiser, adding, “When you’re going to get millions of dollars spent against you, it’s extremely important to define yourself before they define you.”

Without his own super PAC, Mr. Jackson is also bound by a federal limit of $3,500 per donor per election, making it difficult for him to quickly match Ms. Collins’s numbers.

Ms. Collins has at least eight high-dollar fund-raising events scheduled from late July through December, according to a list reviewed by The Times, including events in Chicago, Nantucket and the Hamptons, and even a birthday reception a month after Election Day.

Some Maine Democrats have speculated behind the scenes about ways of filling the gap, but the options may be limited. Sara Gideon, the Democratic nominee who outspent Ms. Collins in 2020, still has nearly $2.5 million in her campaign account. Mr. Platner, despite being one of the party’s strongest online fund-raisers, had just $1.7 million in the bank as of June 30.

Neither Ms. Gideon nor Mr. Platner has said anything publicly about transferring their money to Mr. Jackson, and neither answered questions from The Times about their plans.

Mr. Jackson and his allies are projecting confidence that the high stakes of the Maine race will motivate donors.

“I’m sure everybody and their brother is going to be trying to jump into this,” he told The Times this week. “And we’re going to just do everything we can to put forward what we’re hoping to do and get support.”

Reid J. Epstein contributed reporting.

Pine Tree Results, the super PAC for Ms. Collins’ allies, is named as such because Maine is called the Pine Tree State. Yet I found 0.03% of its donations came from donors who live in Maine. Democratic super PACs spending in the race are also almost entirely funded by out-of-state donors.

(While I was in Portland, I noticed most Maine license plates say “Vacationland” on them. So maybe next cycle, we’ll get a “Vacationland” PAC.)

Because of an editing error, an earlier version of this article misstated the title of Blake Kernen. Ms. Kernen is a campaign spokeswoman for Senator Susan Collins, not a campaign spokesman.

We acknowledge mistakes in our reporting with corrections. If you spot an error, please let us know at corrections@nytimes. com. Learn more.

Bayliss Wagner is a political reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Lisa Lerer is a national political reporter for The Times, based in New York. She has covered American politics for nearly two decades.

Theodore Schleifer is a Times reporter covering billionaires and their impact on the world.

Lowered Number of Troop Deaths on Pentagon Site Upsets Military Families

The New York Times July 25, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The change in the number to 14 from 18 this week has prompted scrutiny over the Defense Department’s accounting and reporting practices.

By Tim ArangoGeorgia Gee and Pooja Salhotra

A change in the count of those killed as a result of the war in Iran has some veterans, military families and lawmakers expressing outrage and calling for more transparency from the Pentagon.

Earlier this week, the Pentagon had reported on its website that 18 service members had been killed, but that number was later lowered to 14.

The change was made because the four service members killed recently in Jordan and Iraq had died after a cease-fire had been declared by President Trump in April, military officials told The New York Times on condition of anonymity to describe sensitive internal discussions.

President Trump on Wednesday witnessed the return of four young Army soldiers recently killed overseas whose deaths brought the total number of American service members who have died in the war to at least 18.

In comments on Thursday, Mr. Trump compared the toll from other American wars with the war against Iran, saying that even one death “is too many, but it’s 18.”

The acting press secretary for the Pentagon, Joel Valdez, on Thursday attributed the change to “temporary data disruptions” on the website that he suggested would be quickly fixed.

As of Saturday morning, the Pentagon’s website was still listing 14 service members killed.

“It is truly disgusting and disheartening to lower the count of our service members who gave their life for this country,” said Tanya Stamos, a Navy veteran and the founder of Operation R. J. S., a nonprofit in honor of her father, Richard James Stamos, also a veteran, that provides free telehealth counseling and support.

She continued: “As a Navy combat veteran myself, I find it a slap in the face that it is so easy to disregard my brothers and sisters in arms who raised their hand and gave an oath to protect and serve foreign and domestic, all for the government who is choosing to wipe their names from history.”

The brother of Dominic Ascioti, 36, is in the military and has been deployed to the Middle East during the war.

Mr. Ascioti said the change in the count by the Pentagon was either “gross incompetence” or “a deliberate attempt to mislead or mischaracterize reality.”

He said it reminded him of how Russia hides the number of its dead from its war on Ukraine.

“As families we need, to the best of the government’s ability, some transparency,” said Mr. Ascioti, who added that he opposed the war. “We want to know what’s happening with our family, and we want to know what happened to our family if something happened.”

The criticism of the Pentagon over its accounting of American casualties in the war has extended to the halls of Congress. On Thursday, a group of Democratic senators sent a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth requesting a “comprehensive accounting” of the number of service members killed or wounded.

In the week before the recent attacks that killed three soldiers in Jordan, there were three other strikes by Iran that left dozens injured. These casualties were not immediately disclosed by the Pentagon, raising questions about whether the government was meeting its obligation to inform the country about the number of service members who had been either wounded or killed.

The senators wrote: “The American people, Congress, service members, and their families are entitled to a full and accurate accounting of the human costs of war. The information currently available to the public suggests that the Department has not consistently provided timely and comprehensive public casualty reporting throughout the conflict.”

Robyn Wheatley said her son Kyle, 20, joined the Air Force after he graduated from high school and had been deployed in the Middle East since March.

“If he was killed in action while serving in a war zone and his death was covered up, I would be furious, I would be upset,” said Ms. Wheatley, a city councilwoman in Newberg, Ore. “All the servicemen and women need to be honored.”

The criticism of how the Pentagon accounts for the war’s toll and informs the public comes amid renewed fighting after the collapse of the cease-fire.

Jeff Merrick, a retired Air Force master sergeant and a board member of Military Families Speak Out, a group formed in the aftermath of Sept. 11 to oppose the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, said the Pentagon’s accounting of the war dead was emblematic of a larger pattern of obfuscation.

“I don’t know what it shows other than a total disregard for our military and family members,” he said.

Helene Cooper, Lara Jakes and John Ismay contributed reporting.

Tim Arango is a correspondent covering national news. He is based in Los Angeles.

Pooja Salhotra covers breaking news across the United States.

A Summer of Extremes Set the Conditions for Europe’s Wildfires

The New York Times July 25, 2026

Western Europe Wildfires

Advertisement

Supported by

The wildfires are scorching parts of France and Spain that had already faced unusually hot and dry summers.

By Chico Harlan

The wildfires torching Spain and France are a culmination of Western Europe’s extreme summer, in which record-setting heat waves and dry conditions set the stage for vast areas that could easily ignite.

Though it is difficult to connect a single wildfire to global warming, scientists said broiling temperatures last month, which hit both Spain and France, were made likelier because of the burning of fossil fuels. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, the world’s pre-eminent climate science body, said in 2021 that “fire weather” would likely increase across the Mediterranean over the course of the century.

In general, wildfires are closely linked to heat and drought, which sap grasses and forests of moisture. Those conditions allow for fires to spread more quickly — if there is a spark.

“Let me call it the drying out of the European continent,” said Johann Georg Goldammer, the director of the Global Fire Monitoring Center, in Freiburg, Germany. “The vegetation is suffering from this heat and drought stress. And this is accumulating.”

The wildfires were “absolutely” connected to the earlier weather extremes, he said on Saturday.

In western France, firefighters have battled flames in the same area that was a center of earlier heat waves. The city of Bordeaux, where thousands have evacuated from the suburbs, faced its hottest stretch on record in late June, with temperatures reaching 42 degrees Celsius (107.6 degrees Fahrenheit) three days in a row.

Since June 1, Bordeaux has had 20 days with highs of at least 35 degrees Celsius (95 degrees Fahrenheit), compared to five over the same period last year. It has rained only three days, never more than slightly.

Western Europe experienced its hottest June on record, according to Copernicus, the European Union’s climate monitoring service. Copernicus also reported “widespread dry conditions” and soil moisture well below average in Spain and France.

Samantha Burgess, the deputy director of the Copernicus Climate Change Service, said that the heat waves, coupled with warm European waters, posed “growing risks for people, ecosystems and infrastructure.”

To that end, across Europe — the world’s fastest-warming continent — those risks are now playing out in many ways. The Danube River recently reached its lowest water levels in 30 years, partly disrupting shipping. This month, low levels on the Rhine forced cargo ships to cut loads. The Netherlands has declared a water shortage, and much of France is facing water restrictions.

And then there are the fires.

According to the European Forest Fire Information System, France has already recorded its most fires and largest burned area of the last 20 summers. Between 2006 and 2015, France saw 15 fires in a typical year. This year, it has recorded 312 fires, with more than 70,000 hectares burned, and weeks left in summer.

Spain had one of its worst recent fire seasons last year. This year’s destruction is roughly 40 percent of last year’s. Normally, in Europe, wildfire risk is most intense in mid-July and August.

In 2021, the European Environment Agency said that the average yearly burned area in the Mediterranean had decreased slightly since the 1980s because of improved fire management. But, the agency said, wildfires were striking in parts of central and northern Europe “not typically prone to fires.”

Chico Harlan is a global climate correspondent for The Times.

Nolan’s Zero-Eros ‘Odyssey’

The New York Times July 25, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Maureen Dowd

By Maureen Dowd

Opinion Columnist, reporting from Washington

Medievalists must be jealous.

Classicists are having a moment on social media, happily discussing whether Odysseus was “polytropos,” “polymetis” or “polymechanos.” And that’s very cool. Thank you, Mr. Nolan.

Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” is a throwback to the days when Hollywood big shots fearlessly took on literary classics, undaunted by the challenges of bringing vast, thorny tales to the screen.

Conjuring the Civil War in “Gone With The Wind”? Recreating the desert battlefields of World War I in “Lawrence of Arabia”? Depicting the Russian Revolution in “Doctor Zhivago”?

Why not?

Nolan’s portal to ancient Greece has lured audiences back to theaters and spiked book sales of Homer’s “The Odyssey,” over 12,000 lines of dactylic hexameter verse composed in the seventh or eighth century B. C. E. Nolan has turned one of the foundational works of Western literature into an entertaining adventure saga.

Nolan told Stephen Colbert that he used every trick in the book to achieve his stunning visual effects. (The Mediterranean was ready for its close-up!) Yet the director failed to capture the essence of the man of tricks and twists, Odysseus, who delighted in storytelling and feigned identities.

Much of the moral ambiguity has been drained to make Matt Damon’s protagonist more likable. Except for a few mournful appearances by Zendaya’s Athena, who seems more like Odysseus’s conscience than his shape-shifting partner in deception, Nolan doesn’t depict any of the major meddling gods from the story. Besides being rich, fascinating characters, the gods are the framework for everything that happened in the ancient world. If you take the gods out of the picture, you just have people struggling within themselves. You lose the depth and force of the epic.

Nolan’s nearly three-hour master work, the classicist Mary Beard noted, does not have Homer’s “elusive sexiness.” In keeping with Gen Z’s waning interest in sex, the poem’s famous sex scenes have been excised, sapping erotic power from the female characters. As a headline in New York magazine wondered, “Is No One Horny in ‘The Odyssey’?”

Nolan brought the dark spirit of his last hit, “Oppenheimer,” with him to Greece, imbuing Odysseus with shame about his brilliant engineering invention that won the war: the horse that tricked the Trojans. His Odysseus is filled with remorse and haunted by the idea that his actions may lead to the end of civilization as they know it.

Homer’s guy, not so much. After Odysseus and his men sacked Troy, they went across the way and sacked another city.

Emily Wilson, whose popular modern translation of “The Odyssey” inspired Nolan, said the director turned Odysseus into an all-American hero weighed down by anxieties foreign to the ancient Greeks.

“He’s traumatized Jason Bourne,” she said of Damon’s portrayal on Derek Thompson’s podcast. “He’s an action hero who feels bad about being an action hero. He’s not that complicated. Unfortunately, he’s not ‘The Talented Mr. Ripley’ in this film. The Odysseus of the Greek poem is complicated.”

Nolan did not want his Odysseus betraying Penelope and enjoying his sojourns with other women. The director completely cut out the young princess Nausicaa, whom Homer’s Odysseus has a flirtation with, and neuters the text's sexual encounters with Circe and Calypso.

In Homer, Odysseus sails to Aeaea, the island home of the enchanting sorceress Circe, “the nymph with the lovely braids.” (I named my kitten after that Circe.) When Circe drugs Odysseus’s crew and taps the men with her wand, turning them into swine, it’s witchy foreplay.

The messenger god, Hermes, also a trickster, comes down from Olympus to give Odysseus an antidote for when Circe tries to use her magic on him. Hermes also advises Odysseus: “Don’t refuse the goddess’s bed,” because that’s really what Circe wants in return for turning the swine back to men. Under no spell, Odysseus says, “I mounted Circe’s gorgeous bed.” He was so smitten with “the lustrous goddess,” who doted on him with “sides of meat and drafts of heady wine,” he didn’t leave for a year — despite pleas from his homesick men.

Nolan’s Circe, played by Samantha Morton, is like a vindictive feminist hippie making ceramic pots in Vermont, except she’s sculpting pigs. Her romance with Odysseus is scrubbed.

In Homer, Odysseus lands on the island of another luminous goddess, Calypso, and stays seven years. He’s imprisoned, but at the beginning at least, he enjoyed himself, even as Penelope was fending off her boorish suitors back home.

Nolan whitewashes Odysseus’s infidelity here by turning Calypso — played by Charlize Theron — into a fashionable beach therapist who gives him mood-altering lotus flowers to help with his PTSD. In Homer, Odysseus has no need to forget. He cries once over the human cost of the war when he hears a song about Troy’s fall, but mostly he’s proud of his war exploits. And the “scalawag,” as Calypso calls him, doesn’t partake in the lotus; his men become addicted lotus-eaters on a different island.

In the movie, Calypso graciously lets Odysseus go when he comes out of his lotus fog and insists on returning home. In the book, Athena has to ask Zeus to intervene to make Calypso give up her sex slave, and she complains that there’s a double standard, because the male gods have affairs with mortals but interfere when the female gods are similarly romping.

Penelope, a mortal, is expected to be faithful, no matter that Odysseus’s sexual liaisons have added eight years to his 10-year voyage home.

When Homer’s Odysseus finally gets home, there’s a charged scene where he is outraged to see that the marital bed he built, crafted out of an olive tree that grew inside the palace, has been moved. It’s a test by Penelope. Nolan dispensed with that, too.

The director also sanitized Odysseus’s character by skipping the scene near the end when the hero orders his son to round up the 12 female servants who slept with suitors and hack them to death with a sword. Telemachus persuades his father that the women should be hanged instead.

Nolan’s IMAX Odysseus gives up the crown for his son and goes into exile with Penelope to redeem his actions during the war. Homer’s hero? No way!

Homer did not portray a world turning against violence. He limned a profoundly martial universe — interspersed with lots of magic and sex and cavorting, conniving immortals. If you smooth it out and modernize it too much, you lose what made it so important to begin with. And you’re just left with a guy finding his way home.

Give me Kirk Douglas and the Italians in Ulysses any day for a fun movie about Odysseus. Nolan's film was too brooding, reached to far to frame Odysseus in this world, and sucked out all the fun with the story. Nolan wanted his Odyssey to be important instead it became the Oddity and breaking Zeus' prime directive. Nolan sitting around a fire and telling his story would have resulted in the people around yelling, next!

America has gotten increasingly prudish and violent. Nolan is (sadly) reflecting the times.

@Alejandro I have loved The Odyssey for 40 years and LOVED this revisioning. It IS different from what I was taught and what I have imagined. That is what is amazing about it. Dowd should open her mind to the possibility that a 3,000 year old epic could have many minds, just like its eponymous hero.

Time turns violence into a poignant history lesson. The sack of Troy, if it happened, was angry, stupid, violent, and banal, like every sacking was. Odysseus and his crew would have kept going down the coast if they had had more hollow horses.

From Celebration to Escalation: How Trump’s Iran Cease-Fire Collapsed

The New York Times July 25, 2026

War in the Middle East

The U. S. deal with Iran signed in June initially appeared to be a success. It didn’t take long to fall apart.

The U. S. deal with Iran signed in June initially appeared to be a success. It didn’t take long to fall apart.

Credit... Kenny Holston/The New York Times

Supported by

By Michael Crowley

Reporting from Washington

“The Deal with the Islamic Republic of Iran is now complete. Congratulations to all!”

That was how President Trump announced a cease-fire with Iran on June 14 that halted U. S. combat operations and reopened the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping.

Mr. Trump was pleased with the deal, which promised to wrap up a conflict he had promised would be over quickly and ease a spike in U. S. gas prices. “Ships of the World, start your engines. Let the oil flow!” he wrote.

Within a month the agreement was in shambles. U. S. and Iranian forces are again trading strikes, and ships are once more avoiding the strait for fear of Iranian attacks. After a substantial drop in recent weeks, the price of oil again broke $100 on Thursday.

What went wrong? Here is how things unraveled.

Mr. Trump’s deal with Iran, signed on June 17, initially looked to be a success.

The United States stopped bombing and allowed Iran to temporarily sell and ship its oil. Iran at first did not interfere with ships sailing through the strait. Global oil prices plunged as tankers again sailed through the vital waterway.

But analysts warned that the 14-point document establishing the cease-fire was dangerously vague. While Mr. Trump said it restored freedom of navigation in the strait, Iran made clear that it considered itself in control of the international waterway.

On June 21 Vice President JD Vance flew to Switzerland to kick off talks with Iranian officials, outlined by the cease-fire agreement, for a more comprehensive deal that would determine the long-term future of the strait and of Iran’s nuclear program.

But the strait did not quite return to normal.

Iranian mines laid early in the war still posed a threat in the longtime official shipping route through the middle of the strait, rendering that path unsafe. Their removal would take time.

Two alternate routes emerged. Most ships used a southern route close to Oman designated by a U. N. maritime agency. The U. S. military provided guidance and some air support to protect ships from Iranian mines and potential attacks.

But Iran insisted that ships use a northern route along its coast that it had established before the cease-fire. Iran charged fees for sailing those waters but guaranteed safe passage in return.

Under the cease-fire, Iran agreed not to charge vessels only for 60 days. Mr. Trump said his administration would reject any final peace agreement that included fees or tolls for shipping through the strait.

As more shipping vessels began using the southern route, Iranian officials demanded that ships exclusively use the northern route. Only that way, they said, could Iran ensure their safety, in what critics said amounted to a protection racket.

On June 25 and 27, Iran launched drone attacks on commercial ships following the southern route. U. S. forces retaliated against Iranian targets, and Iran in turn lobbed missiles at U. S. bases in Jordan and Bahrain.

A meeting planned for June 28 between U. S. and Iranian negotiators was canceled. The cease-fire was fracturing.

On July 4, Iran held a daylong funeral for its former supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, who was killed in a Feb. 28 airstrike at the start of the war. Huge crowds in Tehran called for revenge and carried at least one giant banner vowing to kill the U. S. president.

Three days later, on July 7, three more tankers were attacked in the strait, an action that the U. S. attributed to Iran. That was enough for Mr. Trump. He declared the cease-fire “over” and revoked Iran’s ability to sell oil on the open market by restoring U. S. sanctions on any buyers.

The fighting escalated. The United States hit dozens of targets along Iran’s coast the next day, and Iran attacked more U. S. military sites in Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar.

Mr. Trump formally notified Congress on July 10 that war with Iran had resumed. But he also wrote on social media that he had agreed to an Iranian request to continue negotiations.

Yet Mr. Trump warned that such talks would be a “waste of time,” complaining that Iran has a history of deceitfully “tapping along” U. S. presidents in negotiations.

On July 11, Iran said it would close the strait “until the end of U. S. interference in the region.”

Two days later, Mr. Trump reimposed the naval blockade on Iranian ports he had lifted as part of the cease-fire deal, cutting off Tehran’s lucrative black market sales, primarily to Chinese buyers, that evade U. S. sanctions.

With most ships again avoiding the strait, the conflict was back to its status before the cease-fire.

Officials in the Trump administration said that an Iran deprived of oil revenue could hold out only for so long against U. S. demands to open the strait and surrender most or all of its nuclear program.

But Iran at a minimum bought itself more time by selling as much as $6 billion of oil during the brief truce, according to the hawkish think tank United Against Nuclear Iran.

By mid-July the two sides were exchanging strikes on a daily basis.

Iranian attacks on U. S. missile defense facilities in Jordan killed three American service members on July 17 and 18. Another American was killed in northern Iraq while disposing of a downed Iranian attack drone.

At a ceremony for the return of the soldiers’ remains, Mr. Trump sought to remind Americans why he had gone to war against Iran. “All of them said very strongly, ‘We cannot let Iran have a nuclear weapon,’” Mr. Trump said, referring to the soldiers. (He did not say how he might have known their views. Mr. Trump has also provided other rationales for the conflict.)

The fatalities raised the war’s U. S. death toll to 18.

More than 1,700 Iranian civilians have been killed in the war, according to estimates.

U. S. forces have struck Iran every day for nearly two weeks. Mr. Trump threatened to respond to more attacks on ships in the strait by striking bridges and power plants in Iran — a potential war crime if the targets have no military function.

Regional mediators, including Qatar and Pakistan, have been trying to secure a new cease-fire. But at the moment, the conflict appears to be further escalating.

Mr. Trump raised the stakes this week by saying that the U. S. would soon attack Pickaxe Mountain, a large underground facility that experts fear Iran could use to reconstitute its nuclear program.

But Mr. Trump is confronting a new threat. Houthi militants in Yemen with close ties to Iran claimed this past week that they attacked two Saudi tankers in the Red Sea and have threatened more such attacks in support of their Iranian allies.

Mr. Trump said he would respond to those attacks with “major military punishment.”

Michael Crowley covers the State Department and U. S. foreign policy for The Times. He has reported from nearly three dozen countries and often travels with the secretary of state.

Why Vance Still Trumps Rubio

The New York Times July 25, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Ross Douthat

By Ross Douthat

Opinion Columnist

For the first year of the second Trump presidency, JD Vance served primarily as the White House’s designated tough guy. Rather than a softener of Trumpian harshness, he was charged with being (or chose to be) tougher than the president himself, whether that meant publicly pressuring Volodymyr Zelensky or defending the Minneapolis immigration crackdown or making a symbolic flight to Greenland, the frozen object of the president’s desire.

In the past several months, Vance’s role has changed. He was the most prominent internal skeptic of the president’s decision to attack Iran and then the would-be diplomatic disentangler of the Iranian knot. (He has also embarked on a — somewhat — culturally conciliatory book tour and welcomed a new son.)

Because I think that the Iran war has been a folly and a snare, I have greatly preferred this version of the Vance vice presidency to the version that seemed subsumed into id-driven conservative politics. By contrast, while I thought that Marco Rubio’s performance in his first year as secretary of state was extremely effective, Rubio’s performance vis-à-vis Iran has often been a profile in evasion, letting other officials take risks to either own the war or seek a peace while he keeps his options open.

Republican Party politics, however, often does not conform to my preferences, and the version of Vance that I’ve preferred is also the version who seems to his internal G. O. P. enemies to be politically weakened. From swarming online attacks to stinging critiques from The Wall Street Journal and Ben Shapiro, there’s a palpable sense in the Vance-skeptical parts of the right that the vice president is unusually vulnerable and that a Rubio scenario for 2028 might actually be viable.

The Vance skeptics have some data on their side. Rubio has crept up on Vance in a new 2028 New Hampshire primary poll and sits not that far below the vice president in betting markets. And you can certainly make a case that being initially right about the Iran war doesn’t offer much political upside to the vice president.

First, even amid growing doubts about the conflict, most of the Republican base doesn’t want to be told that the president made a terrible mistake going to war in the first place, and a vice president can’t campaign that way regardless. And since Vance can’t campaign that way, because he has to defend his boss, his position won’t be fully satisfying to the antiwar right either, whether embodied by Tucker Carlson or Joe Rogan.

This dilemma could have been resolved by a Vance peace deal, letting the V. P. credit Trump with a supposed victory while earning his own credit for deal-making from those who see things clearly. But obviously the efforts to end the war have not succeeded yet, and the June memorandum of understanding between the United States and Iran, mainly negotiated by Vance, is currently bobbing, bullet-strafed, in the Strait of Hormuz. So you could argue that he’s now trapped betwixt and between — a scapegoat for hawks who think the administration hasn’t been tough enough, but not successful enough diplomatically to satisfy conservatives looking for a peacemaker.

But the challenge for the anti-Vance voices is that it’s not enough to have a story where the Iran war has created various political problems for him. You need a story where he is so weakened that Trump himself decides to favor Rubio as a successor — because there’s no way that the secretary of state campaigns against the vice president without Trump’s tacit blessing.

Such a story was imaginable at the start of the war — if it had gone well, Vance’s opposition had looked foolish and Rubio had then positioned himself as the champion of a successful hawkish foreign policy.

But from where we are right now, the position of difficulty and stalemate, there’s no evidence that Trump regards Vance more skeptically because of his initial opposition to the war. Indeed, there’s reporting that the president has warmed to the vice president over the past few months — albeit with Vance’s weight loss given partial credit for the shift. And some of Vance’s most controversy-courting comments on the war, his critiques of Israel’s posture especially, almost certainly reflect the president’s own frustrations.

So how would you get from here to a world where Rubio becomes the heir apparent? If the war grinds on in stalemate and ends in embarrassment for America, I cannot imagine a successful Republican primary campaign being waged on the premise that JD Vance is too dovish or anti-interventionist. If Trump ramps up the hostilities and the war becomes an even bigger debacle, that’s bad for all his would-be heirs, but hardly a boon for a dump-Vance movement.

Which leaves only a scenario where Trump sharply escalates, his vice president opposes the escalation while his secretary of state champions it, and the Iranian regime collapses and gas prices with it, leaving Trump with Rubio to thank for victory and Vance to blame for standing in its way.

That’s the future where I might bet on Rubio for 2028. But it’s also not a future that I would bet on happening.

I hope that Vance is the man---putting aside his pathetic people skills, no winning candidate goes into a race trying to figure out what persona he will project to voters. Say what you want about Trump, as repulsive as his persona is, he never equivocates, he is the Donald. Say what you want about Vance, he never seems to know what persona to project.

The 'coordinated' GOP momentum against JD Vance has a leader, and that is Marco Rubio, who is Trump's heavy-hitter among the conservatives in Congress, and estalishment GOP donors. Vance has loads of money behind him, but is missing the credentials/credibility/gravitas that Rubio will bring tothe contest. Rubio's dual roles, as Secretary-of-State and National Security Advisor, gives him plenty of opportunities to upstage Vance, while preparing to engage in a serious clandestine campaign against the Vice-President. As Trump relies on "Little Marco" to keep the GOP inline and onsides.

Vance and Rubio will both be saddled with their decisions to serve Trump. Even if the Iran war ends, it is likely to leave our economy in worse shape than before the war, and Trump will continue to make missteps, like his new round of inflationary tariffs, that degrade the political prospects of Vance, Rubio and others in his administration, who won't be able to tack away from him unless they leave the administration in early to mid 2027. Obviously Vance is not going to do that. Rubio might, which would boost his chances of winning the primaries. It seems more probable that a non-Trump, non-MAGA Republican would have the best chance to win in 2028 given the continuing train wreck that is the Trump presidency. Right now the expectation is that Trump will back Vance or Rubio, but Trump usually destroys his closest political allies. It probably won't be either of them.
