Blockbuster I. P. O. s Are Creating New Millionaires. Philanthropies Want a Cut.

The New York Times July 25, 2026

SpaceX

Advertisement

Newsletter

As start-ups like Anthropic and OpenAI prepare to go public, nonprofits are hoping for a secondary giving windfall from the new tech ultrawealthy.

By Ian Frisch

As a series of blockbuster I. P. O. s mint a new crop of the ultrawealthy, nonprofits are scrambling to figure out how they can share in the bonanza.

University fund-raising departments are making lists of potential white whales and philanthropy executives are doing napkin math to prepare for a once-in-a-generation windfall that could create hundreds of billions of dollars in new donations.

Some are less optimistic than others. In recent years, a billionaire backlash against charitable giving has emerged, as a subset of the wealthiest people in the world argue that business success, not philanthropy, is the best way to give back.

But the founders of OpenAI and Anthropic — both expected to be among the largest I. P. O. s of all time — have deep links to effective altruism, a philanthropic philosophy that seeks to maximize the impact of giving.

And even those who aren’t feeling particularly generous may be moved by the tax burden that will come with cashing in their highly appreciated shares: If they sold, say, $10 million worth of stock, they could get a tax bill that exceeded $3.5 million.

“It’s common to see vast amounts of low-basis, high-gain stock put in the hands of people that have no clue what an exit strategy is,” said Randy Fox, founder of Two Hawks, a family office consulting firm. “One of the only ways that you can eliminate capital gains taxes is by using charitable vehicles.”

With advisers also having an incentive to collect the fees for setting up charitable trusts and foundations, the nonprofit sector could see an annual infusion of more than $100 billion, according to some estimates.

Nan Ransohoff, the head of public goods at the payment processor Stripe, did the napkin math to figure out how large this windfall could be.

Using current valuations, she figured that the nonprofit OpenAI Foundation, which owns 26 percent of OpenAI, would see about $220 billion become liquid when the company went public.

The seven founders of Anthropic, which is expected to have an enormous I. P. O. as soon as this fall, have each pledged to give away 80 percent of their wealth, which could be about $90 billion. Anthropic also has a philanthropic matching program, which could mean another $60 billion in funds earmarked for giving.

In total, Ransohoff estimated in a Substack post, between $37 billion and $100 billion could become available to charities annually. “You could fully fund the Gates Foundation many times over, and then there’s still more to be spent,” she told DealBook.

And that doesn’t even include OpenAI’s employees. Or the newly rich created by SpaceX, whose I. P. O. spawned an estimated 4,400 millionaires (and some 400 employees now worth more than $100 million). Or the many other IP. O. s on the docket. The value of such public offerings could rise to $160 billion, the biggest year in absolute proceeds ever recorded, according to Goldman Sachs.

Giving money away is a common maneuver to avoid taxes: Up to 74 cents of every dollar donated to charity would have been paid as taxes, according to the Institute for Policy Studies. It reported that charitable giving in 2022 alone had resulted in $73 billion in lost tax revenue.

In California, where both OpenAI and Anthropic are based, and where SpaceX has thousands of employees, some new billionaires may also be in a rush to reduce their net worth before the State Legislature aims to levy a one-time 5 percent excise tax on billionaires. That gives them a double incentive to donate.

Jon Feldhammer, a partner at the law firm Baker Botts, said a client with $300 million worth of stock options at a leading A. I. company set to go public this year was thinking of moving out of the state.

“He has all options on the table,” Feldhammer said. “I have a lot of clients looking at leaving California in a much more serious way and in much larger numbers than I’ve ever seen before.”

Some common donation strategies include donating stock instead of cash to avoid capital gains taxes, and creating a trust that distributes fixed income to both the donor (or the donor’s heirs) and a chosen charity.

Wealth advisers say a donor-advised fund has proved the most popular for young employees bracing for an I. P. O. windfall this year. These nonprofit charitable giving accounts allow the donor to make tax-deductible stock contributions, and then direct funds from the account over time to various charities.

It’s cheap, anonymous and easy, said Paul Tramontano, executive managing director at Cresset Asset Management.

“There are no tax returns, and no filings to do,” he said. “It’s sort of the best of both worlds.”

Some of the most famous philanthropists throughout history — Rockefeller, Gates, Bloomberg — have created private foundations. But that path may not be as appealing to the latest batch of A. I. millionaires and billionaires.

A family foundation “really does require care and feeding,” said Brandon Smith, director of estate planning at LNW Advisors. He has over 10 Anthropic employees as clients, some of them set to make upward of $100 million when the company goes public. “Most of these employees won’t have that kind of time,” he added.

Ransohoff argues that the recipients of windfalls are likely to be interested in expanding beyond traditional philanthropic organizations. Many people who work in artificial intelligence, she said, have fast timelines and appreciate philanthropic organizations that operate more like start-ups. They may be willing to take high-risk, high-reward bets.

“I’ve been thinking about: Should we do a Y Combinator for philanthropic start-ups?” she said.

Stripe recently launched a $500 million fund alongside the OpenAI Foundation, Anthropic, Bill Gates and others, aimed at backing efforts that prevent respiratory infections like the flu and common cold.

Ransohoff’s main worry is that there’s a shortage of organizations that fit the ethos of the employees who stand to benefit from this year’s mega-I. P. O. s.

“At the scale we’re talking about, it’s hundreds of Arc Institutes or thousands of Institutes for Progress,” she said, citing two philanthropic organizations. “It’s sort of an abundance story.”

Many employees of these leading A. I. labs want to enjoy their newfound wealth for at least a few years (even if it’s on paper) before committing to giving a chunk of it away.

“They’re having a harder time grasping what the dollar value actually means in their lives,” said Frank Alvarez, a financial consultant at Tidemark Financial Partners. He has 26 clients who work at SpaceX, he said, and also advises employees from Anthropic and OpenAI.

“The psychological transition of becoming a world steward, rather than an accumulator, is the hardest aspect,” Alvarez added.

But Feldhammer said the best tax strategy was one that began long before a company went public. “There are a lot of ways to drastically change your estate tax situation long before the company is worth something,” he said.

For example, rapidly appreciating private shares could be placed into a Roth I. R. A. — and therefore avoid taxes entirely without having to leverage charity.

“It’s so sad when people come to us when they I. P. O.,” Feldhammer added. “The economics never really work out such that you’re ahead — unless you’re charitably minded.”

Sarah Kessler contributed reporting.

A word from Andrew

Good morning. Andrew here. We may be on the cusp of a $100 billion giveaway: With SpaceX and Anthropic creating a new class of wealth, the nonprofit world is salivating. DealBook contributor Ian Frisch goes inside the frenzy. Also: Lauren Hirsch discusses the latest implications of the regulatory battle over the proposed merger of Paramount with Warner Bros. Discovery. And get out your popcorn for this week’s quiz.

President Trump’s tariffs changed again. As a previous round of tariffs expired, new levies of at least 10 percent went into effect on Friday for 80 countries. The tariffs were issued under a provision that targets allegations of lax enforcement of forced labor bans, and experts say they’re more durable than the tariffs that the Supreme Court struck down in February. Within hours, small businesses challenged the legality of the tariffs.

Inflation fears are on the rise. The new tariffs, plus rising oil prices amid the war with Iran, have reignited worries about rising prices. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note, a rate that underpins most commercial loans, topped 4.7 percent on Thursday before retreating on Friday.

Google’s A. I. spending spree worried investors. The company reported $112 billion in quarterly profit, up fourfold from a year earlier. But it also raised its capex forecast for the year to as much as $205 billion and reported negative quarterly free cash flow, prompting a big drop in its stock price.

More big deals: New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, appointed Lina Khan, a former chair of the Federal Trade Commission, and Anthony Shorris, a partner at McKinsey & Company, to lead the city’s Economic Development Corporation. OpenAI models went rogue and hacked into the digital library Hugging Face. And LeBron James will sign with the Philadelphia 76ers for $4 million a year.

The proposed $111 billion merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery hit a bump this week when a federal judge paused the deal to consider a lawsuit brought by 12 states that argue the deal violates antitrust laws.

The merger has cleared most other major roadblocks, including the Justice Department and the European Commission. The interference by attorneys general is the latest test of a new trend as states try to expand their role in antitrust enforcement.

DealBook asked Lauren Hirsch, who has been covering Paramount’s deal for Warner Bros. Discovery for The Times, how the shift is changing dealmaking and what is next for the blockbuster merger.

Are attorneys general becoming a bigger factor as companies consider deals?

A dealmaker recently described the current antitrust landscape to me as “Whac-a-Mole.” Federal enforcers are now more willing to usher deals through, but state attorneys general are increasingly looking to fill that gap.

Just this week, the Justice Department announced it is speeding its review of certain deals and reducing the amount of information they request. And then you have states like Colorado, which have created new paperwork requirements for proposed mergers.

The key question is how far states can take matters into their own hands, because they have vastly fewer resources than the federal government. (Some states, like California, have been looking to expand their budgets for antitrust enforcement.)

The success of the states in going up against Paramount will be a huge test of that.

Are dealmakers doing anything differently as a result of attorney general scrutiny?

If a deal involves a company that is particularly high profile or strikes a particular political nerve, like affordability, they know it is likely to attract attention from the states.

They’re also careful to not draw focus from the states while they’re pursuing federal approval. A number of deals, including HPE’s acquisition of Juniper, were criticized for interference of lobbyists and political appointees.

Many companies are now making an extra effort to get support from staffers at the Justice Department — or at least appear they got support. David Ellison had a long meeting with the Justice Department that included staffers about the proposed deal in May. But attorneys general pounced after The Wall Street Journal reported that the Justice Department’s decision to approve the deal took staffers by surprise.

Paramount has agreed to pay Warner Bros. shareholders $650 million for each quarter the deal doesn’t close, starting in October. Is there a point at which Paramount gives up rather than keeps paying?

To start with, Paramount is contractually obligated to use its best efforts to get the deal closed. And the deal is existential for Paramount — they need the scale that WBD provides them.

Sometimes, long delays in closing a deal can create pressure from the investors who have committed to finance it. But, in this case, David’s father, Larry Ellison, has personally guaranteed the deal. (Still, it is worth noting Oracle, the primary source of Larry’s wealth, has been under significant pressure over its data center costs.)

And walking away has costs, too: Paramount agreed to pay Warner Bros. Discovery $7 billion if the deal falls apart over regulatory concerns. Not to mention it already paid Netflix $2.8 billion to make it go away.

What happens next?

Yesterday brought a curveball: Paramount said it had agreed to halt the deal until June 2027 at the latest, while they proceed with a full trial before the federal Judge. (The merger agreement expires if the deal has not closed by June 4, 2027.)

The big question is why Paramount made that decision. Paramount cast it as a win, calling it “the fastest and clearest way” to make its case in a full-fledged trial. But some on Wall Street are wondering whether Paramount opted to move straight to a trial, rather than facing the possibility of losing an Aug. 3 hearing over whether the judge would impose a court-mandated pause

If Paramount loses, it could still appeal. And there’s always the possibility that the two sides strike some sort agreement to avert a lengthy delay, though California has indicated it wants significant concessions.

Up next: scheduling the trial.

This question comes from a recent Times article. Click an answer to see if you’re right. (The link will be free.)

“The Odyssey” sold $124.5 million worth of tickets last weekend, making it the biggest domestic opening of the year for a live-action film. And that doesn’t even include the revenue from … popcorn buckets.

These ornate special-edition snack holders, which cost as much as $70, have become a surprisingly strong revenue generator for movie theaters.

How much revenue does AMC Theatres expect to generate from popcorn buckets this year?

$20 million

$75 million

$100 million

$150 million

Karl-Anthony Towns Knows the Knicks’ Win Was Bigger Than Basketball

The New York Times July 25, 2026

The Interview

The Interview

Credit... Devin Oktar Yalkin for The New York Times

Supported by

By David Marchese

When the New York Knicks acquired Karl-Anthony Towns from the Minnesota Timberwolves in 2024, it was in the hope that the star center would help the team get over the hump from good to great. Well, that worked out nicely. Towns, a native New Jerseyan who grew up rooting for the Knicks, was a crucial contributor to the team’s glorious, joy-inducing championship run this past spring, and arguably its most important player not named Jalen Brunson.

If there’s one area in which Towns, who is engaged to the actress and influencer Jordyn Woods, is unequaled among his teammates, it’s his willingness to display his emotion both on and off the court. The eloquence and honesty with which he spoke during the finals about being motivated by the loss of his mother, and also his naked displays of elation and frustration as he dueled against the San Antonio Spurs’ phenom Victor Wembanyama, further endeared him to fans. We spoke about that, as well as his path to the N. B. A., the team’s interpersonal dynamics and what it means to win a championship for the long-suffering Knicks faithful.

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Amazon | iHeart

You know, even on the way into the studio for this interview, there were people congratulating you and wanting to shake your hand. And when I’ve been talking to Knicks fans, people say, “I can’t believe that happened.” I still can’t believe it.

How does winning feel to you now, about a month after? Growing up, seeing the Knicks not be able to win the championship and then to be in a Knicks jersey and be the one to do it — it’s an honor, it’s a blessing. I still can’t fathom that we’ve done it. People call me champ and I’m like, I don’t know why they keep calling me that. But it’s something that we’ve earned and the city has earned: the right to call ourselves champions.

I want to do some pure relive-the-magic fan service with you right now. Game 4 of the finals —— I don’t know what happened in that game. [Laughs]

No one knows what happened in that game! But that’s the game that people are going to be talking about years from now. In the first half, you guys were getting your butts kicked. Talk to me about what you were thinking and feeling late in that half when you were down almost 30. We were getting our ass kicked. They’re hitting shots. We’re not hitting many shots. They were bringing more physicality to the game than us. I’ve seen what we can accomplish when all the odds are against us. Last year we had the same situation in Boston Game 1 and Game 2. At halftime I told the guys: We have experience coming back from these moments, especially in the playoffs. Just trust our experience, trust each other. Let’s go out there and let’s swing for the fences. At least give ourselves a chance. And if not, at least we’ll have a different standard walking into the next game. We build off of this game, get ready for Game 5. But this team, man, they’re special, they have no quit in them.

And then when in the second half, do you think, All right, this might happen? Is it early in the fourth that you hit the three falling down? Oh yeah, the step back? Was that not a foul? No, I’m just playing with you. Don’t answer that.

I know you were trying to get a foul. Don’t answer that, don’t answer that, don’t answer that. I thought we had a good chance of winning when I walked in the building.

Oh, come on. I told Jordyn — I told everybody — I felt really, really good about the game. Obviously, as the first half was going on, I was like, Man, maybe I was wrong. But in the second half, as soon as we got it into that 15-point range, I felt good about our team finding a way to win.

When you’re starting to claw back, do you feel the Spurs tightening up? Sometimes when you’re a young team, you look to not lose the game, and we were looking to win the game. That was what made us bring such aggression. I think they were trying to protect the lead, and if you look at our playoff run, you’ve seen us get a lead, and instead of protecting the lead, we’re trying to build the lead.

I think there was one stretch where the Spurs took something like nine three-pointers in a row. Maybe a more mature team takes a different approach. This is my first time hearing that they took nine threes. Even if it was six, seven, eight, we weren’t aware of that, because we’re so locked into the game just trying to find a way to get a stop, go back down the court and make a bucket. You’re not really thinking about what type of shots they’re shooting. They had some shots at the end, but we did such a great job as a team just sticking with it, finding ways to make that one bucket, get that one stop. And of course the right hand of God came through, OG getting a tip in.

You need to tell me about OG’s play. Where were you on the court? I’m right next to him. I was gonna dunk it in. I see OG flying in the sky and I’m like, if he tries to tip the ball back in and it goes off the front rim, I’m going to dunk it back in. OG made it. It was something special. The play was designed to go to me, and then two people guarded me. We finally got the ball to J. B. [Jalen Brunson], and J. B. took a quick pull-up three, and OG, who was inbounding the ball, found himself with no one on him, and he crashed to the board and got the offensive rebound, which was the tip-in, and found a way to make the bucket. It’s going to go down as one of the greatest plays in New York history. One of the great plays in N. B. A. finals history.

When you see that ball go through the hoop, what is that feeling? Are you even having thoughts? No. When you see me in the game, it’s so loud I didn’t hear the whistle. I just see people running on the court so my first reaction is to tell everyone to get off the court right now and stay focused on the game, but then I look back and see the ref grabbing the ball and I’m like, Oh, it’s a timeout. I see OG, and OG is very, uh, OG.

He doesn’t have a lot to say. New York all knows how OG is. I saw him, and it was one of those things — you want to hype him up and stuff. I have such a close friendship with OG. I was like, Nah, you’re gonna get a hug for this one. This is a career-changing bucket for all of us. And he gave us a chance. We still had to get a stop, and he gave us a chance to get that stop.

Did OG have more to say about that play in the locker room? No. OG has no reaction, no emotion on his face whatsoever. And he was just like, Yeah, I guess I made it. [Laughs]

There’s another moment from the series I want to ask you about. You had just scored against Wemby. You’re coming off the court, and the camera caught you saying something like — we’re not supposed to curse here — he can’t “fudge” with me. What was that in response to? I was just being competitive. I have tremendous confidence in my ability and what I do and the work I put in. It’s the finals, and you’re on the biggest stage against one of the best players in the world, and I wanted to prove again, after all these years, where I stand in the N. B. A.

You had to take it a little personally, just as a competitor, to hear how much people were talking up Wemby before the finals. He deserves it — he’s a generational player. He’s extremely tall, and he’s God-gifted with intangibles that none of us were able to get. I mean, I’m seven feet, thank God, but 7-foot-4 would’ve been cool, too. He deserved it, but I’ve earned my stripes in this league, too.

You know, you’re known for being a sweet guy. Even just talking to you now, you smile easily, you were joking around in the green room. But I can imagine that being a professional basketball player pushes you toward a kind of —— Aggression?

Aggression or hardness. Is that something that came naturally, or did you have to develop that side of yourself? I was definitely more aggressive when I was younger. I had a mean streak, because I understood what it was to be the young kid playing with the older kids. There’s no respect given to the young kid. I had to go earn it. Every day I learned how to earn it when I was 13 playing U-16 basketball, U-17 basketball, going out there and competing against the best of the best at age groups way higher than mine. And when you’re doing that, you understand you’ve got to bring that kind of aggression to the game. As I got older, I had the finesse, I learned the physical attributes, I got my strength and my maturity going and I also learned how to maintain it. My mom taught me really well how to take that aggression and utilize it to my advantage.

You spoke very movingly about your mom in an on-court interview after Game 1. You lost her during Covid, and you talked about how she was there with you. Did you think during the playoffs, I am here trying to commemorate my mother? You know, I’ve dedicated my life to this game. Precious time I could have been hanging out with her, enjoying life with her — I spent it in the gym working on my game, working on my craft, getting treatment on my body, getting ready for the next game, mentally not always being 100 percent present because I’m thinking about that opponent coming up. I’ve sacrificed so much for this game. It would be a disservice to her if I didn’t try to capitalize on this opportunity as much as possible. I wanted to make her proud.

Did you find yourself thinking about her at moments during the games? I think about her all the time. It’s not just basketball. My life doesn’t revolve around basketball — it’s just my job. I still have a whole life outside, and I think about her with the basketball in my hand and not.

After you guys won, who was most meaningful for you to celebrate with in terms of remembering your mom? Jordyn. The next-closest woman in my life was there and able to celebrate that moment with me and seeing all the trials and tribulations it took to get there — traded from Minnesota to New York, coming up short last year, all the trade rumors this year. And my father as well, who has been with me every step of the journey since birth. I think the most meaningful one was Patrick Ewing. Just to see all those years of misery and that exhale he had. I could tell he had the weight of the world on his shoulders, and finally, for the first time, he could breathe. We had talked about this moment since I got here. I know while he may have been disappointed that he was not the one in the jersey bringing it home, he is the Knicks culture. He is the Knicks team. He’s the most recognized Knick of all time, and just to see him finally get that moment to hold the trophy, I knew how much it meant to him.

In news conferences and on the court interviews after the game, the way that you’re willing to show your emotion and be vulnerable is not something that we necessarily encourage in professional athletes. Did you consciously decide to put yourself out there in that way? No. I’m just myself. I’m not trying to be anybody. I’m just trying to answer the questions as honestly as I can. And in doing that, I guess my personality shows itself sometimes. I’m not going to say sorry for any of it, because that’s how my mother raised me. She told me to be comfortable in my skin and to never diminish my light.

I want to ask some questions about the internal dynamics of the team. One of the big changes between last year and this year was the coaching change from Tom Thibodeau to Mike Brown. Something that people pointed to as a key difference between Thibs and Coach Brown is a certain flexibility or willingness to have back-and-forth with players. Both coaches did an amazing job. One took us to the Eastern Conference finals, and we came up short. The other took the same team that Thibs did an amazing job with, was able to watch from afar and see what he could do to help us. And we found a way to win a championship. That’s not a testament to Thibs not being the guy or Thibs not being good enough. He’s always been good enough. Thibs is an amazing coach, an amazing person too, and to see his growth as a person from when I was with him in Minnesota to when I got here to the Knicks has been amazing. Thibs gets a lot of credit for this.

I’m not trying to throw shade on Coach Thibs or anything, but from your perspective, what was the biggest change that Coach Brown brought to the team to help you guys get to that next step? He just built off of an amazing foundation that Thibs had set and added his own swag and flavor to it. I think he did a great job of finding the right combinations that worked. Landry Shamet was huge in the playoffs, and shout-out to Ariel Hukporti too. He had some big moments when we really, really needed him. And Mitchell Robinson, Jose Alvarado, you could go down the list. Mohamed Diawara — all these people had an amazing impact on the game, especially Tyler Kolek during the year when J. B. got hurt, played some amazing basketball. So I think Mike did a great job of finding at the right time and the right place where he needed to put certain players into the game and not put them in the game. Amazing chess game he played.

In the first round of the playoffs, you’re down 2-1 to the Hawks, and then it seems like there’s a strategic decision made to run more of the offense through you. Talk to me about that from a basketball perspective and also from a psychological perspective. What did it unlock? For us as a team, being the hub, it drew out their five man or their four man and it put us in a great spot where the four man, if he was guarding me, their five man would have to guard OG or Josh [Hart], which with that speed advantage, I was able to utilize my passing ability to get guys easy buckets, whether it was me getting an assist or me making the pass that led to the assist. It was making it easier on our offense. It took so much pressure off of J. B. having to dribble, dribble, dribble and figure out what’s gonna happen, and it made it easier for him to score, less energy expended and gave us more energy to do other things. And for me as a competitor, as a player, it was something I asked for all year. My teammates trusted me, Mike trusted me, the coaching staff trusted me at a vital point in our season. Probably the most vital point. I’m just glad I was able to repay their trust with some amazing games.

So you’d had that idea earlier in the season? I wanted to maximize what we could do all year. And we’d done a great job getting to that point and pulling out another chess piece.

Does unlocking that feel like something that you’re going to bring into the upcoming season? We’ll see. The opponents will have to see, they’ll have to figure it out.

My advice would be: Do that. [Laughs] I think the way we did it this year worked out well.

That’s true. So, obviously, as a professional player, you can only control what you can control. But you had the experience in Minnesota of playing with the same team for nine years and then getting traded. Lots of us can’t control every aspect of our jobs, but the idea of somebody just tapping you on the shoulder one day and saying, Hey, you’ve got to go work in some other city, it’s not your choice — that’s kind of wild. What is most challenging about that experience? Your world changes. An away game becomes a home game all of a sudden. You’re living a whole different lifestyle. You go from living in a big house, you built a life there, you know this whole house like the back of your hand, and then all of a sudden you’re in an apartment with much less space, you’re in a city now. It’s a totally different way of living. But this is the life we chose and there ain’t no crying about it. Getting traded, it sucks. It’s never good. But to get traded back home to a team I rooted for my entire life and for a team that gave my father his only chance in the N. B. A. — I couldn’t have gone to a better situation for me and my family. And on top of that, Jordyn always wanted to live in New York. So the wife was happy, the family was happy, I was happy.

When you get the call that you’re traded —— No, I didn’t get a call. I got told.

So when you got told that you’re traded, what’s the first call that you then make? I remember having to call Jordyn in Paris. She was having a good time, and I said, “Take me off speaker right now.” I didn’t have to call my dad. He was there. He heard the news as I heard it, and he was shocked, and I was shocked. The second call was to my agent and having that conversation about what I was just told, because even she didn’t know at the time.

Did Kevin Garnett talk to you after you were traded? I talk to K. G. all the time — that’s my vet, that’s my mentor.

Can you talk about some of the advice that he gave you? I was under his wing just learning about how he became a Hall of Famer, one of the best forwards of the game ever.

He must have given you a hard time about defense though, right? I mean, I was guarding him well when he was there, but he’s a competitor. Me and him are really fierce competitors. So we had fun at practice, talking smack to each other.

But Karl-Anthony, I’m saying this with love: The reason I bring up defense is that sometimes I watch, and you do those, like, 30-feet-away-from-the-basket fouls. And you’re near the top of the league for fouls per game every year. That means I’m being physical.

It’s so different from your offensive game, which to me always feels so —— Finesse-y?

Explain to me the disparity. I’m a Jersey boy like Kyrie, it’s all reaction.

So you’re just swiping on defense? I mean, I’m getting a lot of steals. What were we in defense this year? Top 3? And what’s the No. 1 thing done in the N. B. A. right now? Probably isos and pick-and-rolls. I’m involved in all of them. So we did a pretty damn good job at it, thank you.

All right, that’s my one constructive criticism: less reaching. [Laughs] No one said that in the playoffs when it was working.

My wife was watching a lot of the playoffs, and she watched you do interviews and then watched Jalen Brunson do them, and she was like, Jalen’s the dad of the team, and KAT is the mom. You’re more open emotionally, more expressive. He’s kind of buttoned down. Is that how it plays out behind the scenes? That’s intriguing. I’m going to say that to J. B. I don’t think it’s too far off. Aren’t we both like our parents? He gives Rick energy, and I give Jacqueline energy, and that’s beautiful. That shows great parenting. Shout out to Rick and J. B.’s mom, and shout out to my mom and my dad for leading us to, one, be men that people respect. That’s the most important thing as a parent. You want to have kids that people will respect more than anything. And two, giving us those personalities.

Let me ask you some league questions. Giannis Antetokounmpo went to the Heat. Kawhi Leonard looks like he’s gonna go to the Raptors. Jaylen Brown went to the Sixers. Who are you most worried about in the East? The Knicks. That’s all I need to worry about.

Do you get why Jaylen Brown is now on the Sixers? Of all the teams for him to end up on, the Celtics trade him to one of their biggest rivals! It’s pretty fun. Like I said, control the controllables. If I worried about all the uncontrollables in my life, I’d be lost in the sauce.

But of course, your buddy Mitch Robinson is now on the Celtics. That was a tough one.

In good conscience, could the team do hack-a-Mitch if you were playing the Celtics? That would be heartbreaking. I don’t even know if I could look at Mitch with a Celtics jersey on after everything, so I’ll just have to start laughing at Mitch when we see each other. He owes me a pickup truck.

For what? I don’t know, I just want a pickup truck.

Watching him shoot free throws as a fan is the most emotional roller coaster experience. It’s an emotional roller coaster, watching a man shoot free throws?

Because you want him to succeed so badly! It’s not like walking up to a woman at a bar.

That’s easier! What is the experience for the teammates watching Mitch shoot free throws? Oh, we love it. One, it gets a foul and puts us closer to the bonus. Two, every time it happens, it gives us breaks to reset. And three, we believe in Mitch. We believed in everyone on that team, one through 15. We see each other put the work in. So when he goes up there, we’re excited because we can’t wait to talk junk if he makes it.

To be able to represent joy for people in New York City seems like such a privilege. Talk about what that means to you. To bring so much joy to families, especially those families that have previous generations of Knicks fans who have been begging for a chance to be in the N. B. A. finals, let alone winning the N. B. A. finals after 53 years — I feel like a “Love Island” character getting back my phone after the playoffs and seeing these reels and these videos and these Instagram posts about the grandfather celebrating with his son’s kid and passing that kind of Knicks fandom down to the kid, or the father who grew up watching the disappointment of 1999, or families who have lost loved ones going to the cemetery to celebrate the Knicks win with them. I know how special it is because I saw people in Brooklyn cheering, and they got their own N. B. A. team! [Laughs] It just shows New York is so unified with each other when you give them something to be unified for. And to reach the mountaintop and give so many people something to cheer for and to have hope for? Inspiring hope is one of the hardest things to do, and for us to be able to do that is something special.

So, last question: The margins in professional sports between winning and losing are so slim. One small decision changes everything.

Last year, for example, you guys were up big in the playoffs against the Pacers in the fourth quarter, and they pulled off a comeback against you. This year, OG tips in a shot that if he missed —— I am dunking that.

I know you’re saying you would have dunked it. I’m telling you, I’m dunking it.

But OG’s was a miraculous shot. And then just the level of intensity and focus that winning takes, it seems almost unbelievable that you can do it once. Does it seem even more daunting to think about winning it again? Well, my competitive spirit says, That’s what we’re planning to do. We were always the underdogs in every series. We’ve got to be ready to be looked at as the favorites. And that’s not something we like a lot, so we’re going to have to go out there and continue to have that underdog mind-set. We’re going to have to be an even better version of ourselves, even though a lot of y’all say we were one of the best ever in the playoffs. We’ve got to find another level, because people are going to be ready for us this year.

All right, I’m going to say it: back to back. I ain’t going to say that. I’m gonna say we’re going to do our best.

Thanks, champ. [Laughs] Appreciate it.

This interview has been edited and condensed. Listen to and follow “The Interview” on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, iHeartRadio or Amazon Music. Follow us on Instagram and TikTok.

Director of photography (video): Sean Mattison

Working with David on The Interview comes with perks, but his chat with KAT was special. Our colleagues were SO excited to have the beloved Knicks center at the New York Times — people were clapping and cheering as he walked through the newsroom. New Yorkers are still riding high on that championship, and Towns’ reflection on what it means is so genuine. I was especially struck by how quickly he came to the defense of former coach Tom Thibodeau, who didn’t get the team as far as current coach Mike Brown. Towns clearly gives Thibodeau a lot of credit.

David Marchese is a writer and co-host of The Interview, a regular series featuring influential people across culture, politics, business, sports and beyond.

How a Housing Bill Trump Spurned Became Law

The New York Times July 25, 2026

Despite partisan differences, intraparty feuds and the president’s lack of interest, Congress delivered the first major housing bill in a generation.

Despite partisan differences, intraparty feuds and the president’s lack of interest, Congress delivered the first major housing bill in a generation.

The high cost of housing has been a burden in Democratic cities for years but since the pandemic, conservative states like Idaho and Montana also experienced increases in rents and home prices. Credit... Ariana Drehsler for The New York Times

Supported by

By Ronda Kaysen

Ronda Kaysen, who covers real estate, reported from Washington.

When Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts went to her fellow Democrats last year during their weekly lunch to suggest working with Republicans on a major new housing bill, she was met with trepidation and doubt.

Members of her party had long wanted to tackle the housing crisis, but most assumed that there was no way they could overcome deep divisions with Republicans to agree on the kind of landmark legislation Ms. Warren envisioned.

“There was kind of this sense of, ‘Yeah, you’ll put it together, and then we’ll all look at it, we’ll say yay, I’m a co-sponsor of a bill that will go nowhere,’” Ms. Warren said in an interview in the Capitol, reflecting on the improbable process that had led to the enactment of the measure this month.

“They’ve been taught around here that it will all be for nothing, that the bills that you put together are just kind of for show,” she added. “Especially on the Democratic side, when Republicans are in control.”

Instead, against seemingly impossible odds, the bill succeeded and won bipartisan support, overcoming the polarization of Congress, G. O. P. infighting, the bitter politics of the midterm campaign season and an utter lack of enthusiasm from President Trump, who ultimately refused to sign it. At a time when bipartisan legislating has become a lost art, its proponents managed to push through the biggest piece of housing legislation in three decades, assembling a broad coalition across both houses of Congress to address an affordability issue that is front and center for voters.

It very nearly did not happen. This account of how the 21st Century Road to Housing Act became law after several near-death experiences was drawn from interviews with a dozen lawmakers and aides who played key roles.

It started with an unlikely partnership between Ms. Warren, the progressive top Democrat on the Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs Committee and Senator Tim Scott, Republican of South Carolina, the panel’s ultraconservative chairman. They had forged a rapport sitting side by side on the dais of the panel, chatting quietly when a meeting would drag on, or when a witness had something compelling — or obnoxious — to say.

“Everyone else comes and goes, except for the witnesses and the two of us,” Ms. Warren said. “So you end up whispering a little in between. Someone will say something and it triggers a thought. And I’d lean over and say, ‘You know, it makes me wonder why we couldn’t do this,’ or, ‘What a jerk.’”

Mr. Scott, whose mother bought her first home at age 40, shared Ms. Warren’s zeal for a big new housing bill — Congress had not passed one since 1990 — and as the chairman of the Senate Republicans’ campaign arm, he had a powerful political incentive to try to make it happen before the midterm elections.

Mr. Scott declined to comment.

The politics were tricky: Republicans would never agree to Democrats’ goals of pouring major new spending into housing programs and expanding the Department of Housing and Urban Development, and it would be a tough sell to get them to accept Ms. Warren’s priority of rewarding communities that were building housing with funds for infrastructure.

Democrats would have to embrace a housing bill with limited money for housing programs in it. And, they would have to be willing to hand Republicans a victory they could cite in their fight to keep control of Congress.

But there were upsides for both parties. The high cost of housing had been a relentless burden in heavily Democratic cities like New York, Boston and Los Angeles for years. But since the pandemic, conservative states like Idaho and Montana had also experienced stratospheric increases in rents and home prices, transforming what had been a regional issue into a national one.

By last October, Mr. Scott and Ms. Warren had an agreement and hatched a strategy to speed it through the Senate in a way they thought would guarantee its quick enactment. They attached it to the annual defense policy bill, which is considered a must-pass item, in a bid to prod the House to accept it without changes.

The move touched off a feud within the G. O. P. Representative French Hill, the Republican chairman of the Financial Services Committee who had been focused on banking legislation, was blindsided.

He called Mr. Scott and told him he needed to pump the brakes.

“The process was premature,” Mr. Hill, of Arkansas, said in an interview. Over a series of conversations, he said he told Mr. Scott, “You know, if you’d like to negotiate and take House input, I’d be happy to do that.”

But the senator was not interested in making changes.

“Well, this is what I’ve got in the Senate, and this is the way it’s going to be, and this what I can do,” Mr. Hill recounted Mr. Scott telling him. “And I said, ‘Well, I can’t support that.’”

House Republicans stripped the housing measure from the defense bill, dealing it a major setback.

In early January, Mr. Trump provided an opening to revive it. He posted on social media that he planned to curb the role institutional investors play in the single-family housing market, addressing an issue that was a priority for Senate Democrats and riles home buyers, particularly in markets like Atlanta and Charlotte, N. C., where people are often outbid by investors making all-cash offers on starter homes.

She saw an opening to get ahead of the president, with a bill shaped by Democrats that would drive the debate.

“I was electrified,” Ms. Warren said, adding, “If I’d been a cartoon, there would have been a lightbulb above my head.”

The next morning, Ms. Warren was on the phone with Democrats,, working to pull together a proposal that could be introduced before Mr. Trump’s State of the Union address.

Soon, the White House was negotiating directly with Mr. Scott and Ms. Warren.

But the House was working on its own, far narrower, housing bill, which it passed in February with overwhelming bipartisan support.

The next month, the Senate passed a measure that was meant to merge the two chambers’ bills, including the new private equity piece, by a lopsided margin of 89 to 10.

Mr. Trump, with his attention focused on the war in Iran, a White House ballroom and a sweeping voting restriction bill, largely ignored the process. But once again, House Republicans balked.

Responding to a wave of criticism from the building industry, they said they could not accept a provision in the Senate bill that set strict limits on single-family homes built as rentals.

“Now it has a fatal problem,” Mr. Hill said.

Mr. Hill and Representative Maxine Waters of California, the ranking Democrat on the Financial Services Committee, called for bicameral negotiations. But once again, senators refused to engage, noting the overwhelming support their measure had drawn in the otherwise polarized chamber.

The only alternative, Mr. Hill said, was yet another round of legislative “pingpong.” And so in May, the House passed yet another version of the bill that watered down the private equity provision.

Ms. Warren saw it as catastrophic because Senate Democrats would not support a bill that failed to meaningfully address private equity in the housing market.

“They just ripped the heart out of it,” Ms. Warren said. “I thought, ‘Oh, now we’ve lost something that really matters.’”

The standoff finally broke when, over a series of phone conversations in early June, Ms. Warren and Ms. Waters began hashing out a deal to satisfy both chambers.

“The real breakthrough came when Elizabeth Warren and I got together,” Ms. Waters said in an interview. “And then we got Tim Scott to say yes.”

While their compromise softened the build-to-rent provisions, it still targeted the private equity industry by capping at 350 the number of single-family homes an investor could own. With more than 50 provisions, the final legislation addressed the housing crisis by boosting supply, which is considered the crux of the crisis, with rules that aimed to ease federal regulations, to make it easier to borrow money and to update federal programs to encourage development.

On June 23, the House gave final approval to the bill, clearing it for Mr. Trump. Republican leaders quickly arranged for a celebratory signing ceremony the next morning at the Capitol. But as industry and congressional leaders arrived at the Capitol and as Ms. Warren was being interviewed on CNBC crowing about the bill, Mr. Trump announced in a social media post that he would not sign it after all.

“I thought it was a joke,” Ms. Warren said.

The president singled her out in the post, referring to her with a derisive nickname and describing the legislation as “the Elizabeth ‘Pocahontas’ Warren centric housing bill, which is of minor importance.”

Mr. Hill, walking into a news conference when he saw the social media post, took the turn of events in stride.

“I play the cards as they’re dealt out on the table,” he said. “We moved on to yet another twist in the story of this legislation.”

The next day, Mr. Hill and Speaker Mike Johnson went to the White House to meet with Mr. Trump. They urged him to sign the legislation and made it clear that the House had the votes to override a veto. The president, Mr. Hill said, “was aware of the strengths of the feelings about that bill in both chambers.”

Mr. Trump ultimately refused to sign the measure, but allowed it to become law, which it did automatically and without fanfare at midnight on July 11.

“I’m still disappointed he didn’t sign it,” Mr. Hill said.

Three days later, Ms. Warren again went before Democratic senators at their weekly luncheon at the Capitol, this time to celebrate the bill’s enactment.

“I said, ‘Start thinking about Road 2.0,” she said, “because we’re going to do this again.’”

Robert Draper contributed reporting.

Ronda Kaysen, a real estate reporter for The Times, writes about the intersection of housing and society.

A Global Economy Jolted by an Oil Shock Now Gets a Tariff Reminder

The New York Times July 25, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

Tariffs are back, but this time there is a war in the Persian Gulf and oil has hit $100 a barrel.

By Patricia Cohen

Patricia Cohen, the global economics correspondent in London, has been has been writing about trade policy for more than a decade.

We’ve all been down this road before.

President Trump issues a blitz of punitive tariffs on allies and rivals, straining trade, rattling bond markets, raising prices and injecting more uncertainty into the global economy.

The difference now is that the United States is at war with Iran, key trade and energy routes in the Persian Gulf region are blocked and the global oil price is near $100 a barrel. When Mr. Trump unveiled his original cold blanket of tariffs, on April 2, 2025, oil had been around $70 a barrel.

“These new trade tensions come at a moment in which the global economy, due to higher energy prices, is in a weaker spot than on Liberation Day last year,” said Carsten Brzeski, an economist at the Dutch multinational bank ING, referring to the day President Trump announced the specific rates.

The new import taxes on more than 80 countries, including members of the European Union, are Mr. Trump’s latest bid to reimpose tariffs after the U. S. Supreme Court struck down many of his previous levies in February.

The tariffs, which use trading partners’ unfair labor practices as a rationale, replace a similar, temporary set he imposed right after the court ruling. More tariffs are expected to follow.

Mr. Brzeski and other analysts said the economy had already absorbed much of the inflationary impact of Mr. Trump’s trade war.

“The worst of the tariff-related goods inflation is probably behind us,” said Carl Tannenbaum, chief economist for Northern Trust, a global financial institution based in Chicago. Companies raised prices last year and didn’t roll back those increases after the Supreme Court’s decision.

Both the tariffs and their erratic implementation tend to hamper long-term planning, dent investment and drag down growth as businesses are forced to spend time and resources figuring out how to adapt their production and supply chains.

Even so, at the moment, the escalating war with Iran, which began five months ago with attacks by the United States and Israel, is having a much greater impact on the health of the global economy than tariffs are. In Japan, the government cabinet office said on Friday that companies might be passing on increased costs caused by the war in Iran at an ever faster pace than they did after the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the last great global energy shock.

Key energy trade routes in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea continue to be disrupted. Oil prices jumped again this week, as the Iranian-backed Houthi militia group in Yemen escalated its confrontation with Saudi Arabia and opened a second front in the region’s conflict.

The spike in oil prices sent jitters through the market, leading to a sell-off of government bonds and weighing down stocks. In the United States, gas prices hit $4 a gallon and mortgage rates ticked up.

“The situation in the Middle East is to me, and from what I can see from the data, very much more worrying for the global economy than this fireworks of tariffs,” said Paola Subacchi, a professor at Sciences Po, Paris. On the trade front, she said, “it’s more or less the same story.”

Perhaps no region in the world has been hit harder by the double whammy of tariffs and the war than Asia, where economies are heavily reliant on both exports and imported energy.

Several major Asian countries have already negotiated aggressively to secure trade agreements with Washington. It’s not yet entirely clear how the new tariffs imposed by Mr. Trump will affect those deals, but representatives from several foreign governments said they had privately been told that tariff rates would be the same as those negotiated last year.

Japan promised $550 billion in American investments as part of a trade deal in exchange for a reduced tariff rate of 15 percent. South Korea has similarly committed tens of billions of dollars toward shipbuilding and battery manufacturing, while Taiwan has promised tens of billions to expand advanced semiconductor production.

So far, economies in Asia have performed better than expected. “The biggest takeaway for me has been how resilient these economies have been to all these shocks,” said Sonal Varma, an economist at Nomura, Japan’s largest investment bank and brokerage firm.

Companies have either absorbed costs, passed them on to consumers or rerouted shipments through other countries. And since the Iran war, despite shortages, governments have offered supplies and subsidies to help businesses and consumers deal with rising fuel prices.

Yet even as the bigger picture has been more positive than expected, there are divergences across the region.

Countries participating in the boom in artificial intelligence, through semiconductors, data centers or other parts of the ecosystem, have fared better than those that are more exposed to energy shocks.

The Philippines, which declared a national energy emergency in March and has continued to grapple with rising fuel prices, has been left behind in the A. I. boom and is experiencing an economic slowdown.

By contrast, an increase in semiconductor exports helped South Korea’s economy grow faster than expected this spring, offsetting declines in other sectors like construction.

How negotiations play out between the United States and China is perhaps the most important arena in Mr. Trump’s renewed trade wars.

“The main event in all of this is U. S. v. China,” said Mr. Tannenbaum at Northern Trust.

“China has shown itself to be a very formidable trade bargainer,” he said. “They have been preparing for this for a long time, and they know exactly where our vulnerabilities are.”

Xi Jinping, China’s leader, is planning a state visit to Washington in September. And he has already shown his willingness to withhold minerals that are critical to America’s tech and defense industries to pressure the Trump administration on trade.

Mary E. Lovely, senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics, recently met with Chinese analysts as part of a regular exchange program. She said China’s leaders “are very confident that their chokehold on permanent magnets and rare earths will prevent President Trump from really going much higher than where he already is” on tariff levels.

That could mean China ends up with lower tariffs than some of its neighbors, giving it an economic edge over competitors.

The prize — easier access to the gigantic American market — is more valuable than ever. American consumers have an enormous appetite for goods and have increased their spending at a faster pace than those in Europe or in China.

River Akira Davis contributed reporting from Tokyo, and Alexandra Stevenson from Hong Kong.

Patricia Cohen writes about global economics for The Times and is based in London.

In Rush to Track Down Leaks, Justice Dept. Reversed Its Own Process

The New York Times July 25, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

A judge’s remarks on subpoenas to reporters cast attention on two administration officials under consideration for powerful cabinet posts, Todd Blanche and Jay Clayton.

By Devlin BarrettJonah E. BromwichGlenn Thrush and William K. Rashbaum

Devlin Barrett and Glenn Thrush reported from Washington, and Jonah E. Bromwich and William K. Rashbaum from New York.

The hearing had just started and Judge Arun Subramanian was no longer allowing Manhattan federal prosecutors to finish their sentences.

Instead, he pressed a top prosecutor, Sean Buckley, for an explanation: Why had the U. S. attorney’s office issued subpoenas to New York Times reporters — typically the final step in a leak investigation — just two days after the publication of an article about the security concerns of the president’s plane?

“Doesn’t that turn the law and the regulations on their head?” Judge Subramanian asked.

Mr. Buckley did not supply the answer immediately. But after an hour of questioning, he and the other prosecutors voluntarily withdrew the subpoenas, a tacit acknowledgment that the judge was poised to rule the government had not followed the law.

The episode underscored the administration’s hasty effort to identify the sources of The Times’s reporting as part of a powerful push by Mr. Trump and his top aides to crack down on the news media. The judge’s remarks raised questions about the role of not only Mr. Buckley but also of two high-level Justice Department officials who are under consideration for leading cabinet positions.

The acting attorney general, Todd Blanche, and the current U. S. attorney in New York, Jay Clayton, both testified this month that the issuance of the subpoenas had been in keeping with laws and regulations.

“We followed the processes that we were required to follow,” Mr. Clayton, nominated to be the director of national intelligence, insisted in sworn testimony before a Senate committee, adding, “I’m confident that the procedures that we have in place — to protect the First Amendment and protect the freedom of the press and not result in intimidation of journalists or the like — were followed.”

Mr. Blanche, appearing at his own confirmation hearing last week, told members of the Senate Judiciary Committee that the Justice Department was “not targeting reporters.”

“They’re material witnesses, just like a reporter would be a material witness to a car crash,” added Mr. Blanche, who said he had authorized the subpoenas.

The hearing also threatened to cast a shadow over the incoming leader of the Manhattan prosecutor’s office, which like others has faced President Trump’s tightening grip over the department overall. James M. McDonald, who is expected to take over from Mr. Clayton, was one of the select group of prosecutors involved in the inquiry, according to people with knowledge of the matter.

During the hearing, Manhattan federal prosecutors repeatedly denied any intentional wrongdoing. A spokesman for the U. S. attorney’s office for the Southern District of New York declined to comment. The Justice Department did not respond to a request for comment.

The investigation stemmed from two articles published in early July by The Times about the vulnerabilities of an Air Force One jet that Qatar had given to Mr. Trump. On July 10, two days after the first article, the F. B. I. director, Kash Patel, was summoned to the White House, where he spent about eight hours overseeing the investigation into the leak, according to people familiar with the day’s events. That evening, three Times reporters whose names appeared on the articles were served with subpoenas to testify about their sources before a federal grand jury.

Mr. Clayton and Mr. Blanche have said any actions the department has taken were motivated only by the need to protect national security secrets and to quickly root out leakers who might be jeopardizing Mr. Trump’s safety at a time of heightened threats.

They have pushed back against the claim that the subpoenas were a strong-arm effort by the White House to intimidate journalists and chill officials who step forward with information in the public interest.

After Thursday’s hearing, the Justice Department accused Judge Subramanian of threatening its prosecutors, saying the judge’s conduct disregarded “longstanding principles and common sense.”

“Make no mistake, this investigation remains ongoing, and we will pursue justice against those threatening national security by leaking classified information, a serious federal crime,” the department said in a statement.

Mr. Clayton’s exact role in the inquiry remains unclear. In his Senate hearing, Mr. Clayton said that his office had consulted with officials in Washington in demanding reporters’ testimony. The decisions were made “collectively,” he said, without elaborating on who had been involved.

Mr. Clayton’s signature has been on most of the legal filings, but he has delegated the details to a small group of mostly senior lawyers. In court on Thursday, Mr. Buckley said that he personally had overseen the inquiry since it began.

The investigation has also involved Amanda Houle, the chief of the office’s criminal division, and Kevin T. Sullivan, a career prosecutor in the office’s national security unit who was also questioned fiercely by the judge on Thursday. Mr. Sullivan had omitted relevant details from a request asking to keep private a subpoena to a phone provider, and Judge Subramanian summoned him to the front of the courtroom to answer for it.

“Mr. Sullivan, when you affirmed in your July 14 application to a judge in this court, under penalty of perjury, that the investigation was not public, that was false, correct?” he asked.

“The wording was imprecise,” Mr. Sullivan said.

Judge Subramanian said during the hearing that if lawyers had behaved this way in a civil case, he would consider whether to punish them. After the hearing, the judge asked that prosecutors send him all internal communications regarding the application for the nondisclosure order.

The U. S. attorney’s office does not appear to have followed longstanding Justice Department practice.

A typical investigation into the leak of classified information begins with a referral known as a “crimes report” from the victim agency, or the agency whose information was disseminated, such as the C. I. A. or Defense Department.

There has not yet been any indication as to whether a similar report was created before the subpoenas were issued in the Times inquiry.

For years, under administrations of both parties, including in Mr. Trump’s first term, the Justice Department has used a set of 11 questions, to be answered by the victim agency, to determine whether to proceed with a criminal investigation.

The third question asks: “What are the specific statements that are classified?”

A letter dated Monday from Mr. Clayton’s office to a federal judge seemed to hedge on that basic point, saying that the Times articles “indicated potential leaks of classified or national defense information.”

The sixth question in the report asks whether the disclosed information “previously appeared in an open source publication.” Days before The Times’s July 8 article about the plane’s security issues, The Associated Press reported that photographs of the new plane “show that it is not equipped with at least some of the same missile detection and countermeasure systems as the outgoing Cold War-era jets.”

In a standard classified leak investigation, a trial attorney in the counterintelligence section of the Justice Department would have a discussion with that agency to evaluate the answers after he or she received the agency’s crimes report, according to David Laufman, who once led the department’s counterintelligence and export section, which oversees classified leak investigations.

But Mr. Trump was angry and embarrassed by The Times’s reporting about the security vulnerabilities in an aircraft he had long championed as proof of his deal-making prowess, people close to him have said.

Even before the July 8 article published, a senior F. B. I. official called a Times reporter and editor, asking them not to publish the information and asking them to identify their sources.

In 2012, the Justice Department issued subpoenas for the phone records of reporters at The Associated Press, which had reported on a C. I. A. operation to disrupt a Qaeda plot to bomb a commercial airliner. The department did so nine months after the article in question was published, and only after conducting more than 500 interviews and reviewing tens of thousands of documents.

In March, the Trump administration issued subpoenas to reporters at The Wall Street Journal nine days after it published an article about a Pentagon official warning about the risks of military action against Iran. The Trump administration eventually abandoned those subpoenas, after a federal judge in Virginia signaled in sealed proceedings that she was likely to quash them, according to people familiar with that case who spoke on condition of anonymity.

Since Mr. Trump’s return to office, judges appear to have blocked subpoenas more regularly. Still, the hearing on Thursday dealt a blow to prosecutors who lead what has long been considered the most prestigious U. S. attorney’s office in the country.

Even Judge Subramanian, who has been on the bench for three years, seemed in disbelief at the government’s responses, as when Mr. Buckley said that he had not reviewed the application his subordinate had made to the other judge.

“How did you not review the nondisclosure if you were overseeing the investigation?” Judge Subramanian asked.

“Because I don’t review every piece of paper, Judge,” Mr. Buckley replied. His answer would be the same for other missteps in the process, he said.

“Help me understand here,” Judge Subramanian said. “The inadvertent errors and the ‘in hindsight we should have done things differently,’ these things are piling up. Under these circumstances, are you still unwilling to withdraw these subpoenas?”

About 20 minutes later, the government conceded.

Devlin Barrett covers the Justice Department and the F. B. I. for The Times.

Jonah E. Bromwich covers criminal justice in the New York region for The Times. He is focused on political influence and its effect on the rule of law in the area's federal and state courts.

Glenn Thrush covers the Department of Justice for The Times and has also written about gun violence, civil rights and conditions in the country’s jails and prisons.

William K. Rashbaum is a Times reporter covering municipal and political corruption, the courts and broader law enforcement topics in New York.

Why Lettuce Is Always Making People Sick

Wired July 22, 2026

Salad is usually synonymous with healthy eating. Except now, as the US grapples with an expanding outbreak of cyclosporiasis that’s sickened more than 7,100 people in Michigan alone, likely caused by iceberg lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms.

In fact, leafy greens are frequently implicated in instances of foodborne illness. There was a 2022 multistate E. coli outbreak tied to romaine served on Wendy’s sandwiches and 173 cases of norovirus linked to Illinois eatery D. C. Cobb’s. In 2021, BrightFarms recalled packaged salad greens sold in several states after 31 people got salmonella. And in 2019, a total of 167 people were infected with E. coli after eating romaine harvested from the Salinas Valley region in California. This isn't even the first cyclospora outbreak linked to lettuce: In 2020, Fresh Express salad kits were linked to more than 700 cases of people afflicted with the parasite.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that produce is responsible for almost half of the reported foodborne illness cases, with leafy vegetables topping the list. So what is it that makes lettuce a major source of America’s foodborne tummy troubles?

One big reason is simply because lots of people eat it. Lettuce is the second-most-consumed vegetable in the US behind potatoes. (The latest outbreak ensures potatoes will remain the king of US veggies. Plus, french fries.) Wraps, subs, tacos, you name a fast food sandwich and it’s almost certainly got lettuce on it. Salad-slinging chains are fixtures across the US. Grocery store coolers are stocked with salad kits, on top of the unadorned heads of iceberg lettuce and containers of spinach.

Those ready-to-eat salads and blends of spring mix pose a particularly acute risk because they contain multiple types of leafy greens, which can come from different farms and locations. If one type of lettuce in the mix is contaminated, it can contaminate the whole bag. And because that contaminated lettuce gets packaged into lots and lots of bagged salad, it has the potential to spread germs far and wide.

How lettuce is grown can also expose it to a wide array of pathogens. A 2025 study by researchers at Cornell University who studied E. coli outbreaks in romaine lettuce found that a lot of contamination originates from irrigation with untreated surface water applied through overhead spray irrigation systems. There are ways to lower that risk, including switching to irrigation systems that do not directly touch the leaves, but that would require upgrades and downtime.

Lettuce’s satisfying crunch is also what makes it prone to pesky pathogens. Since it’s eaten raw—really, who wants wilted lettuce?—there’s no opportunity to cook off any lingering contaminants. Like other raw fruit and produce, leafy greens don’t go through what’s known as a “kill step”—heating, pasteurization, or freezing—which is designed to eliminate pathogens during the food manufacturing process.

The texture of lettuce is an additional factor in its ability to spread disease.“Many lettuce types have a lot of crevices and folds,” says Jeanne Marrazzo, CEO of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. “It’s very easy for these tiny pathogens to get in there.”

Even prewashing procedures at manufacturing facilities don’t always remove microbes, which can cling tightly to leaves. In the case of cyclospora, the parasite has thick outer walls, making it highly resistant to most food sanitizers. Experts say vigorous washing that involves scrubbing is the best way to get rid of cyclospora.

“If you don't wash these products well, you're going to end up ingesting whatever is on the lettuce,” says Amira Roess, an epidemiologist at George Mason University.

The White House Is Trying to Figure Out What to Do About Chinese AI

Wired July 22, 2026

The Trump administration is split over how to respond to the rapid rise of China’s leading AI models, according to multiple people familiar with deliberations.

The debate is broadly divided between parts of the White House, which has pushed for stricter controls on Chinese AI that may soon rival the most powerful US models, and the Commerce Department, which has viewed those restrictions as unworkable.

The conundrum has become the latest flash point for the administration over AI, after China’s Moonshot AI lab last week released its Kimi K3 model that rivals the top US models from Anthropic and OpenAI.

In recent days, senior White House officials have discussed possible measures to stop China’s AI labs from developing their models by training them on US models, a practice known as distillation, the people say.

The White House is expected to take some sort of presidential action after Anthropic last month alleged the Chinese tech company Alibaba had carried out the “largest known distillation attack” against it to date. This action is not currently expected to take the form of an executive order, according to one of the people.

A White House spokesperson did not comment on the reporting in this story.

The White House has been taking distillation attacks especially seriously. It announced on Wednesday that Moonshot had developed Kimi K3 by distilling Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 model, and Treasury secretary Scott Bessent told Fox Business that covert distillation could lead to sanctions, describing it as “IP theft.”

While proposals have been making the rounds inside the White House, no formal request for input has been transmitted yet to the Commerce Department, which has its own ideas, according to two people familiar with deliberations.

The Commerce Department has increasingly emerged as an influential part of the intra-administration split over AI, in part because it oversees export controls through the Bureau of Industry and Security.

Lutnick has contemplated ways to create incentives for top US labs to create their own open weight models to counterbalance China, and has spoken with leaders at a number of AI labs in recent weeks, the people add.

Lutnick appears to be straddling a middle ground of regulation—he imposed export controls on Anthropic to bring them to heel—but has been more freewheeling than Cairncross, one of the people said.

Earlier this month, the biggest AI issue for the administration was Anthropic’s Claude Mythos and Fable 5 models, because of their ability to find vulnerabilities in government systems and critical infrastructure.

But policy headaches with AI have only escalated with the rise of so-called open weight models from China—models that have few to no safeguards to prevent hacking government systems and can be downloaded and used by anyone.

The Odyssey’s Success Is Inspiring Unprecedented Levels of Cope

Wired July 22, 2026

For months, Elon Musk and the right-wing cranks he caters to on X have whipped themselves into a raging froth over the supposed desecration of an ancient Greek poem by one of the most successful movie directors alive.

Now that their manufactured backlash has bombed, they’re searching for ways to cope with the reality that they are increasingly divorced from popular opinion.

Christopher Nolan’s artistic crimes in bringing The Odyssey to the screen, according to Musk and others in a furor, were instances of what they called “historical inaccuracy” in a lavish fantasy teeming with monsters, witches, and undead spirits—mainly the casting of Lupita Nyong'o, who is Black, as Helen of Troy, and Elliot Page, who is trans, as Sinon. The grand total of approximately 10 minutes of screen time between these actors in a three-hour saga, combined with the general hysteria over “wokeness” in Hollywood, a rejection of Americanized dialog, and lingering misogyny regarding scholar Emily Wilson’s 2017 translation of Homer’s epic (the first by a woman), resulted in countless teeth-gnashing posts and calls for a boycott that never materialized.

Instead, the mythic drama hauled in a staggering $264 million as it opened this past weekend, sailing toward continued box office dominance and, in all likelihood, a slew of awards. A few conservative commentators, including Ben Shapiro—no fan of DEI or “woke” values—acknowledged it as a landmark achievement. But while some who had predicted its doom knew enough to move on from this battle to other fronts in the culture war, many sank deeper into denial.

“BREAKING,” blared one anonymous X account on Monday. “The Odyssey is FAKING ticket sales by buying up theaters/seats (Fraud) to make the movie look like a success (already $400 million in the hole) moviegoers are reporting having to take terrible seats (because full) but when they show up the theaters are mostly empty.” The post included screenshots of unverifiable anecdotes from Reddit about quiet cinemas and no-show ticket holders.

What Universal Pictures, the studio behind the film, would stand to gain by spending millions beyond a $250 million production budget and $125 million in marketing costs to astroturf a flop was not exactly clear. Then again, these are the same conspiracists who find it suspicious that the critics’ reviews tend to all be published at the same time.

Musk, for his part, seemed to be inspired by an X user who posted three minutes of AI-generated scenes in which characters from The Odyssey are all white and speak in British accents. Commenting on the clip, which at best resembles a montage from a hokey 1970s adaptation, the richest man in the world declared: “Before this year ends, Grok Imagine will make a full-length movie of The Odyssey that is historically accurate and true to the art of Homer.”

Those familiar with Musk know that when he vows to reach a milestone by year’s end, it basically never happens. The promise of a Grok-animated Odyssey, though minor compared to most of his ambitions—he even speculated in 2025 that the xAI model might “discover new technologies” within several months—is sure to fall by the wayside as well. Not only is it a tiresome idea with zero appeal to the mainstream moviegoer (who has or will soon see Nolan’s version), it’s also unoriginal: The AI studio Fountain 0 is planning the online release of an artificially generated feature titled Odyssey: The Fall this summer.

Moreover, both ill-conceived projects misunderstand the lesson that the entertainment industry seems to be taking from Nolan’s latest blockbuster. At a moment when executives imagine that AI is the key to cutting costs and turbocharging output, the director has shown once again that the practical craft of filmmaking beats out what he himself has disparaged as “slop.”

So, will this aggrieved little cadre of internet reactionaries ever be able to accept that they don’t understand what audiences want? Or that they have deluded themselves, thanks to skewed algorithms and bogus amplification, into thinking they possess an influence they never had? Please. They’re not capable of conceding a loss. And there’s always another outrage down the road.
