The Best Fitbit Depends on Your Goals. Here’s How to Choose

Wired July 22, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

It’s been five years since Google officially acquired Fitbit for a reported $2.1 billion, grabbing hardware and software teams that also absorbed assets from Pebble, which Fitbit itself acquired in 2016. So, how have things changed? Well, for starters, Fitbit is now Google Fitbit. It’s not the most imaginative of name changes, and it hasn't stuck in consumers’ minds, but the good news is that Fitbit devices remain some of the most user-friendly and welcoming fitness trackers available. This is especially true if you're just starting, or reigniting, your fitness journey.

Fitbit’s dominance has waned slightly in the face of countless alternatives, but its affordable approach, user-friendly interface, and great styling make it one of the best wearable fitness brands. If you’re looking for a reliable step-counting, sleep-tracking monitor, you’re in for a treat—and thanks to Google’s stewardship, you can now even find a smartwatch with features to rival the competition. Here are my picks of the best Fitbit trackers, whatever your wearable needs are.

For more wearable recommendations, check out our guides to the Best Fitness Trackers, Best Smart Rings, and Best Garmin Watches.

Updated July 2026: I've added the Google Fitbit Air and incorporated pros and cons to all of our recommendations. Product information, links, and prices were also updated.

Google

Amazon

Google Store

Google Store

Google

Google

If you don't need another screen competing for your attention, the Google Fitbit Air is the one I'd recommend to most people. At just 12 grams, it's the lightest Fitbit—you'll forget you're wearing it—yet it quietly tracks everything that matters: heart rate, sleep, daily activity, skin temperature variations, and menstrual health (to name a few). And instead of constantly checking stats on your wrist, you'll find all insights in the Google Health app, where your data is presented in an easy-to-understand format.

The Air nails the basics. Battery life stretches to about a week, and a five-minute top-up gets you roughly a day's worth of wear. Automatic workout detection can occasionally mistake one activity for another, and some of the AI guidance can feel generic, but those are minor trade-offs for a wearable that's comfortable enough to wear all day and night. Its $100 price also makes it one of the most affordable ways to get comprehensive health tracking. The biggest downside of the Air is also its biggest strength; there's no screen, so if you prefer having a display, go with the Fitbit Charge 6. But for most people, the Fitbit Air strikes the best balance of price, comfort, and everyday health tracking.

Fitbit

Amazon

Google Store

Best Buy

Launched in 2023, the Charge 6 remains the best fitness tracker for beginners. It's the same slim build as its predecessor (the Fitbit Charge 5), maintaining the bright AMOLED touchscreen, with an optional always-on display, and fortunately bringing back the physical side button. It monitors your heart rate, blood oxygen, and skin temperature, and it offers ECG and electrodermal activity scans to measure irregular heart rhythms and stress level insights. The largest upgrade on the functionality front is the new ability to connect Fitbit's heart rate sensor to particular gym equipment like the NordicTrack treadmill or Peloton bike. In testing, its heart rate sensors held up well against the Oura ring. Battery life is also fantastic, with up to a week per charge.

The built-in GPS support doesn't rival dedicated sports watches for accuracy, but it's useful enough for outdoor activities. Plus, unlike those wearables, Fitbit dishes out detailed sleep data that is both insightful and actionable. Google’s presence has increased on the Charge with the useful additions of Google Maps and Google Wallet. You get all of this and more for less than the cost of Fitbit's smartwatches.

Fitbit

Google Store

Amazon

Best Buy

Along with its budget price, the Inspire 3 also offers the longest battery life of the Fitbit lineup. A full charge will last you up to 10 days, depending on how much you use it. It is pretty similar to the Charge 6, except that it lacks a built-in GPS, and it only features 20 exercise modes (as opposed to Charge 6's 40 modes, which I found to be excessive anyway). You also miss out on some of the other premium features, such as Bluetooth compatibility with certain gym equipment, the EDA Scan app for stress management, and NFC technology. If none of those qualities matter to you, I would opt for the Inspire 3, which is just as accurate as the Charge 6.

Fitbit

Google Store

Best Buy

The first Fitbit Ace landed in 2018, offering kids ages 8 and above the ability to track their steps and sleep and to be in constant pursuit of virtual badges. The Fitbit Ace LTE ditches the fitness band form for a smartwatch one, instantly giving it more grown-up kids appeal. The Ace LTE is built for ages 7 to 14 and comes with a design perhaps best described as a more child-friendly Versa. There’s a sizable OLED screen with Gorilla Glass 3 to fend off scratches, and unlike the first Ace, it can be submerged in water up to 50 meters deep.

There are some familiar fitness tracker sensors in place, including an optical heart rate monitor and motion sensors to track movement, though Fitbit has ditched the sleep-tracking support that was available on the original Ace. It has LTE connectivity so parents and children can make calls to each other, and it also taps into Google Maps to give it location-tracking smarts. Payments are on the way for the watch, too.

There are also games to play, including a very Fitbit take on a Tamagotchi that’s sure to appeal. There is the matter of a $10 per month subscription fee to get the complete Ace experience; it isn’t a cheap kids’ smartwatch either. But it’s easy to use, and it gets the balance of fun and fitness just right to make it a good fit for kids. —Michael Sawh

Fitbit

Google Store

Amazon

Best Buy

Now that the Google Pixel Watch 4 actually exists, the fate of Fitbit’s own smartwatches feels up in the air. But if the idea of owning a Pixel Watch doesn’t appeal and you’re interested in a more Fitbit-centric experience with better battery life, the Versa 4 is the one to go for. You get a smartwatch with a gently curved design; it’s almost identical to the original Versa, but with the welcome return of a physical button. There’s a large, vibrant, 1.5-inch AMOLED display touchscreen and a battery performance that can really stretch over the promised six days if you don’t leave the screen on 24/7.

As for sports, the Versa 4 is designed with a built-in GPS to track outdoor runs and rides and motion sensors to track indoor swims, though not with sports-watch-rivaling accuracy. Fitbit’s PurePulse heart rate sensor is a better fit for day-to-day heart rate stats than it is for a CrossFit class. And third-party app support has been replaced by native Google apps, like Maps, with Google Assistant joining Amazon’s Alexa. As a device that lets you check your phone notifications, keep an eye on step counts and sleep, and forget about constantly charging it, the Versa 4 has plenty to like. —Michael Sawh

Fitbit

Google Store

Amazon

Best Buy

The Fitbit Sense 2 was meant to attract the kind of people who were looking at the Apple Watch. It's designed with an electrocardiogram (ECG) sensor that’s been approved in the US to help wearers detect potential signs of atrial fibrillation. A skin temperature sensor can monitor temperature changes during the night to spot any trends, and a SpO2 sensor goes to work when you’re sleeping to detect breathing disturbances. While it’s not a regulatory-approved feature, it can detect potential warning signs of a sleep disorder, like sleep apnea.

An electrical cEDA sensor captures on-the-spot and continuous measurements of galvanic skin response that Fitbit uses as a marker of stress. Fitbit needs to work on delivering information on potential stressors in a useful way, but it’s a start. The Sense 2 also grabs all of the cheaper Versa’s fitness-tracking and sports-tracking features, including built-in GPS, and uses a PurePulse heart rate sensor to keep track of your Active ZoneMinutes when you’re upping the intensity. You do need Fitbit Premium ($10 per month) to unlock the most valuable health insights.

What Is Fitbit Premium?

Fitbit Premium is a subscription service that costs $10 a month or $80 a year, and gives you perks not available in the free version of the Fitbit app. For example, you get access to a library of recipes, mindfulness sessions, and workouts led by Fitbit's trainers and partner brands (Peloton, Calm, Aura Health, Breethe, and Ten Percent Happier). In addition to your sleep score, with Fitbit Premium, you'll receive more detailed sleep insights, including a monthly analysis of your sleep profile. Similarly, you also get a personalized stress analysis.

Whether the premium membership is worth it boils down to how much information you'd like to receive. It's relatively cheaper than most wearables' subscription models; plus, if you buy a new Fitbit, you'll get a free six-month trial to test it out yourself.

Are Fitbits Waterproof?

All of the latest Fitbit products, including the Charge 6, Sense 2, and Inspire 3, can be submerged in water up to 50 meters deep. Where supported, some Fitbits do offer the ability to track swimming, though only in an indoor pool, where it uses motion sensors to track your movements.

Note that while the Fitbit pebble itself is water-resistant, not all of Google's accessory bands or third-party bands are waterproof.

Can Fitbits Connect to Strava?

Yes, although the Strava app that was previously on some older models has been removed from the Fitbit Gallery. If you have a Pixel Watch, you can download the Strava Wear OS app. If you don’t have a Pixel Watch, you can use the strava. fitbit. com link and follow the steps to start sharing your exercise data between the two apps.

Can Fitbits Measure Blood Pressure?

No. While the Fitbit app previously supported the ability to manually log blood pressure readings, that is no longer the case. Google allows you to connect Fitbit to its Health Connect app to consolidate health, fitness, and wellness data in one place; if you use a blood pressure monitor and app that offers support for the Health Connect app, that’s currently the main way to bring the two platforms together.

Can Fitbits Detect Sleep Apnea?

Fitbits, like most activity trackers, aren't designed to diagnose sleep apnea, but they can help detect potential warning signs through their sleep-monitoring capabilities.

The Sense 2 and Versa 4 both offer a snore- and noise-detection feature, thanks to their built-in microphones. Unfortunately, they're not the most accurate, as they can pick up the snoring of someone next to you. They also work best with no background noise, which can be an issue for users who sleep with white noise or ambient soundscapes.

Which Fitbit Has an ECG sensor?

An ECG sensor is considered one of the most accurate ways to monitor heart rate activity and measures the electrical activity from the heart. That’s different from the way that photoplethysmography (PPG) sensors gather heart rate information; PPG sensors can be a little more susceptible to disruptions like increased movement that can affect data accuracy.

Fitbit introduced an ECG sensor to the Sense in 2020, and it’s now available in the Sense 2, the Charge 6, and the entire Google Pixel Watch lineup. Using the accompanying Fitbit ECG app, users can take on-the-spot ECG measurements, analyzing heart rhythm to help detect—not diagnose—signs of atrial fibrillation, which could be an indicator of a serious health condition.

Should I Get a Fitbit or an Apple Watch?

Fitbit and Apple remain the two biggest names in the activity tracking business. Fitbit offers more form factors to choose from, while Apple is led by its Apple Watch, with the Watch Ultra appealing to endurance athletes. Fitbit’s trackers and watches have a more beginner-friendly feel and can offer longer battery life between charges compared to Apple’s collection of smartwatches.

If you care about daily-activity tracking, both offer motivational features to keep you moving throughout the day. Fitbit doesn’t get you to close those rings like Apple does, but it will nudge you to get up. The majority of its stats and metrics are geared toward telling you how active or inactive you’ve been.

Both are serious about health tracking, offering ECG, SpO2, and optical heart rate monitors on most devices for useful and possibly life-changing insights. The Apple Watch has more strengths as a sports tracker; the richer app store gives it the edge here, though the growing presence of Google’s apps on Fitbit’s wearables is a step in the right direction. But for a variety of designs, ease of use, and sheer range of metrics and data across health, fitness, and mental well-being, Fitbit still certainly holds its own.

States Want ICE Agents to Show Their Faces. The Trump Administration Is Blocking Them

Wired July 22, 2026

The Trump administration has sued at least five states and the city of Philadelphia over laws that supporters say would hold law enforcement—including Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers—accountable for misconduct on the job. The specifics of the laws vary, but the Trump administration takes particular issue with the fact that the laws would prohibit ICE officers from wearing masks during immigration raids, and require them to wear some sort of individual identifier.

Having to show their faces, lawyers for the Trump administration argue, would put ICE officers in danger.

In complaints filed against New York, Virginia, Connecticut, New Jersey, and Philadelphia, attorneys for the federal government claim that people take photos of ICE officers to “run them through facial recognition applications that search social media and doxing sites,” specifically calling out an art project called ICESpy. (California was subject to a similar lawsuit months before the other states, but the DOJ did not mention ICESpy in that complaint.)

There's just one problem, according to ICESpy’s creator, artist Kyle McDonald: the art project's face-recognition software cannot recognize most, if any, ICE agents currently in the field.

ICESpy is based on photos, job titles, and names of people who self-identified as ICE nearly a decade ago on LinkedIn. WIRED viewed a version of the list, which had just over 700 entries, and found that the most common title was “assistant chief counsel,” and many of the people appeared to have executive, administrative, or legal roles. Only 39 people on it had “deportation officer” in their title, and an additional 27 had related titles such as “enforcement and removal assistant” or “immigration enforcement agent.”

Many deportation officers joined the agency well after the data was collected. In January, ICE announced that it had more than doubled its number of agents and officers in just a few months, from 10,000 to 22,000. None of those additional people would be in the database, unless they had another job with ICE in 2018 (and posted about it online).

“They make this claim that people are using this site and others to search for family members. They offer no evidence of this in the filing,” McDonald tells WIRED. “The idea that someone could use a site like ICESpy and find an active ICE deportation officer in 2026 is absurd.”

ICE did not respond to a request for comment.

Data issues aside, ICESpy is not popular. WIRED reviewed activity logs for ICESpy between June 30 and July 6, which showed there were only 84 page views that week—a remarkably small number, even for a niche art project website. Only two face-match attempts were made, and the results of both were so bad that McDonald says they could not possibly be a match of anyone in his dataset of 2018 LinkedIn users.

“Like, I'm sure people were playing with it at some point?? But it is not an active threat to ANYBODY lmao,” McDonald says in a text message.

Attorneys for the federal government also blame another site, ICE List, for aiding people interested in "doxing" ICE agents. ICE List describes itself as an accountability initiative, and keeps track of people involved with ICE and other agencies involved in deportation efforts, along with vehicles used on the job and incidents that occur during enforcement actions.

Individual agent pages on ICE List typically include the person’s name and general information about what their job title is, the field office they are associated with, and any incidents they might have been involved in along with links to public sources that corroborate the claims on the page. When WIRED analyzed the site in January, we found that it too relied mostly on data that self-described ICE employees had posted on LinkedIn. It also doesn't have any sort of public-facing way for visitors to try to computationally analyze photos, though some agent pages include headshots.

Dominick Skinner, ICE List’s maintainer, says the site has a small, dedicated group of people who try to use face recognition, but their success with the technology so far has been “overblown,” and the site mostly relies on manual research.

“I wish we had a tool good enough to take away the work 😂” Skinner tells WIRED via text message.

The group of ICE List users was recently credited for identifying David Brouillette, the ICE agent and former Army veteran who allegedly shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a 25-year-old Colombian living in Maine. In that case, the website put out a request for information from people in Bangor, Maine, and Skinner says two people close to Brouillette came forward. Brouillette’s ex-wife later told the Portland Press Herald that she had previously reported concerns about Brouillette’s mental health to his superiors in the US military. Brouillette did not respond to a request for comment.

Skinner says that ICE List doesn’t fit the traditional definition of doxing—it does not post agents’ home addresses or that of their family—and that data broker sites post far more intimate information about agents but don’t face the same level of scrutiny. Older guidance from the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, advises people to request to remove their personal data from such sites.

It’s unclear how many ICE agents have actually been identified because of ICESpy or ICE List. The Department of Justice, which is litigating the cases, did not put specific numbers in its complaints.

DOJ spokesperson Kiersten Pels says that “individuals have used facial recognition and doxxing tools to identify and harass federal law enforcement officers, and these sites frequently change domains, shut down, and reappear under new names.”

Pels did not respond to WIRED’s request for a concrete example of a protester using ICESpy to identify an ICE agent.

Meanwhile, state lawmakers say their laws requiring ICE agents to identify themselves are trying to address very real issues around democracy and justice, and the federal government should prioritize other work that’s within its remit.

“Instead of challenging these reasonable restrictions, the Department of Justice should seek accountability for the actions of poorly trained ICE agents, release the Epstein files, and investigate the Trump organization’s unprecedented corruption,” says Virginia state senator Saddam Salim, where the federal government successfully won an injunction pausing SB 352, the state’s new law that prohibits law enforcement in the state from wearing masks, among other restrictions.

ICE officers weren’t wearing congressionally mandated body cameras when they fatally shot two people in Maine and Texas this month, making it more difficult to investigate what happened. Federal officials refused to produce evidence to Minnesota investigators related to the fatal shootings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti for nearly half a year until they were compelled by the courts. WIRED recently reported that ICE's Office of Professional Responsibility, an internal watchdog that investigates employee misconduct, is busy looking into civilians who post criticism online about the federal government and its immigration policies.

“States have a right and an ability to be able to react and respond to what we see as unconstitutional behavior by our federal government,” says Bob Duff, a Connecticut state senator who worked on a law for his state that is now being challenged. “And we have a right and responsibility to protect our own residents in the state.”

An FDA Panel Just Endorsed These Unproven Peptides

Wired July 23, 2026

Peptides are inching closer to the mainstream.

A panel of experts on Thursday narrowly recommended that the Food and Drug Administration reclassify four popular peptides—including one endorsed by podcaster Joe Rogan—to allow certain pharmacies to legally dispense them.

In an at-times emotionally charged meeting that lasted more than 11 hours, members of an FDA advisory committee heard data presentations from FDA staff on four unapproved peptides—BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, and MOTs-C—as well as testimony from health care practitioners, patients, pharmacies, and clinics.

Members voted eight to six, with one abstention, to add three of the four peptides to the agency’s bulks list, meaning compounding pharmacies can use them to create custom medications for patients. (The fourth peptide—MOTs-C—received a seven-to-five vote in favor, with two abstentions.) The advisory panel, which includes several members tied to peptide-related businesses and telehealth clinics, will consider three more peptides on Friday.

Peptide therapies have been growing in popularity thanks to the endorsement of podcasters, wellness influencers, and Health and Human Services secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has said he’s a “big fan.” Essentially smaller versions of proteins, peptides are being touted for everything from skin rejuvenation and hair growth to gut health and injury recovery despite a lack of scientific evidence to back up these claims.

Many peptides currently exist in an unregulated gray market after the Biden administration banned compounding pharmacies from producing 20 peptides out of safety concerns in 2023. They can be legally sold online for “research use only” and “not for human consumption,” yet their marketing heavily implies otherwise. China and India are major suppliers of peptides, with some crypto-funded fentanyl labs switching gears to produce them.

During the meeting, the FDA’s own scientists recommended against allowing compounding pharmacies to produce any of the seven peptides being considered due to a lack of evidence showing they are safe and effective. Peptide proponents meanwhile testified that US compounding pharmacies should be able to produce them so that patients can access safer, regulated options with a prescription.

“I'm not going to tell you that the evidence for BPC-157 is strong. It isn't, and I won't overclaim it," said Anant Vinjamoori, chief medical officer of telehealth provider Hims & Hers. “What I'd ask is that you not read thin as non-existent.” The company is actively preparing to launch peptide treatments in anticipation of the FDA greenlighting some peptides.

Among the peptides approved, two are particularly popular with podcasters and influencers. BPC-157 and TB-500 are paired as part of a so-called “Wolverine stack” to help improve recovery after injuries. Committee members were asked to evaluate BPC-157, which is thought to promote tissue repair, for ulcerative colitis. The World Anti-Doping Agency says BPC-157 poses a risk to athlete health because it has not been studied extensively in humans.

Some health care providers testified that patients of theirs had turned to the gray market to buy peptides and ended up with products that were laced with illicit substances. But while FDA approval may help reduce some of those risks, other commenters said it could create new ones.

John Hertig, chair of the Collaborative for Evidence-Based Medicines, said allowing compounders to make these peptides sends the message that the FDA is approving them. “That gets very confusing for our patients,” he said, adding that the existence of a gray market isn’t a reason to allow compounders to make these peptides.

He argued that there will still be a gray market even if the FDA allows for compounding of these peptides, citing that patients still seek out gray market GLP-1 drugs despite several FDA-approved drugs on the market.

Adriane Fugh-Berman, a physician and professor at Georgetown University, also challenged the idea that allowing legal versions would eliminate this gray market. “Would the government endorse companies manufacturing heroin because it would be cleaner than what's sold on the street?” she said. “Just because the market is large, doesn’t mean it should be legalized. It means that a product should be studied.”

The experts who voted against adding these four peptides to the bulks list cited a lack of data to support their use.

Elizabeth Rebello, an anesthesiologist at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, was one of the committee members who voted against allowing the four peptides to be compounded, citing unknowns around safety and confusion for the public.

“I'm just concerned that we're entering a Pandora's box here,” she said.

For now, the panel’s recommendations are just that. A formal FDA decision will likely not come for several months.

Meta’s New Feel-Good AI Ad Uses a Song About the World Ending

Wired July 23, 2026

On Thursday morning, Meta published an ad to its official Instagram account with the message that artificial intelligence will not “make us less connected” or “leave us behind.” It was set to the 1972 David Bowie track “Five Years,” which is about, among other things, the end of the world.

“Call us optimists, call us dreamers, call us whatever the hell you want—but we’re betting on people, and we like those odds,” the narrator says, as a toddler plays with a butterfly, two parents laugh with their infant, and Jalen Brunson waves at the Knicks Championship Parade. (The ad also takes special care to highlight use cases for its controversial smart glasses that are not, say, harassing women while surreptitiously recording them.)

The snippet of “Five Years” used in the ad includes the following lyrics:

I heard telephones, opera house, favorite melodies

I saw boys, toys, electric irons and TVs

My brain hurt like a warehouse, it had no room to spare

I had to cram so many things to store everything in there

And all the fat, skinny people

And all the tall, short people

And all the nobody people

And all the somebody people

I never thought I'd need so many people

Perhaps understandably, it skips other parts of the song, including the opening:

News had just come overWe had five years left to cry inNews guy wept and told usEarth was really dying

When reached for comment, Meta spokesperson Francis Brennan said he “would like to highlight what David Bowie himself said about ‘Five Years’ and its meaning: having optimism for the future.” Brennan sent along a 1972 quote about the song that he sourced to BowieBible. com.

“People are so incredibly serious and scared of the future that I would wish to turn the feeling the other way, into a wave of optimism,” reads the quote, which is itself sourced from NME Magazine. “If one can take the micky out of the future, and what it is going to be like … It’s going to be unbelievably technological.”

Nevertheless, BowieBible. com also notes that the song “speaks of a dystopian nightmare in which Earth enters its final five years, for reasons undisclosed, and the ensuing panic, violence, and attempts at redemption.”

BowieBible. com also quotes from a 2018 interview with drummer Mick Woodmansey: “Well, we chatted about it, and we knew it was about the end of the world and pretty depressing,” Woodmansey said of the song. “I remember when we recorded it, he was actually in tears. He was doing the vocal and he was actually crying.”

According to Jeremy D. Larson, the deputy director of Condé Nast sister publication Pitchfork, taking songs out of context for commercials is a time-honored tradition. He points to a Carnival Cruise ad that uses an Iggy Pop song about heroin addiction. (He also says that since Warner Chappell Music owns Bowie’s catalog, they are the ones with discretion over where his songs end up.)

“Meta choosing this specific song where the context for human connection is the apocalypse seems either really ignorant or really insidious,” Larson tells WIRED over Slack. “I don't know, maybe in that context it's genius.”

“Hearing [Bowie’s] work used for AI just feels especially and specifically nonconsensual,” he adds. (CEO Mark Zuckerberg, in a post about the ad, wrote that the company was “focused on giving every person the tools to reach your full potential and making sure the benefits of technology are distributed to everyone.”)

Over the past few years, tech companies have made several heavy-handed attempts to assuage people’s fears about their technology making the world worse. Just a few weeks ago, Anthropic released its own lofty ad, “There’s hope in hard questions.” It opens with a clip of a burning building and asks, “Who’s gonna hit the brakes if we need to?” before flashing over dozens of graves. The tone of the ad gradually shifts toward optimism, and ends with vague questions like, “What if we started to be more human again?” over images of families and a humpback whale.

In 2024, Google released a baffling ad about a father teaching his daughter, an aspiring athlete, how to hurdle. The father decides that he should use Gemini to draft a letter, from the perspective of his daughter, so that she can send it to decorated hurdler Sydney McLaughlin-Levrone. And during the 2022 Super Bowl, FTX aired a now-notorious ad starring Larry David, playing various Larry-esque characters, dismissing useful inventions throughout history—the toilet! the fork! the lightbulb!—before ultimately dismissing FTX.

“Don't be like Larry,” reads the text overlay at the end of the ad. “Don't miss out on crypto, on NFTs, on the next big thing.”

FTX filed for bankruptcy about nine months later.

Of course, it’s understandable that tech companies would use every tool at their disposal to increase goodwill. But the ads also demonstrate that many tech companies are failing to sell products that independently convince people that they are not actively making the world worse.

For Taylor Swift, Madison Square Garden’s Controversial Cameras Briefly Went Dark

Wired July 23, 2026

Madison Square Garden owner James Dolan has insisted that the face-recognition system and array of surveillance cameras deployed at his venues is “very, very useful for security”—a big reason why MSG “is the most secure venue in the country.”

On the night of July 2, security in and around the Garden was particularly intense. Roughly 130 cops were deployed to the area. New York City officials were preparing to shut down the surrounding blocks to both vehicles and pedestrians the next day for a major, major event.

July 2 was, of course, the kickoff to Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce’s wedding celebration, an approximately 100-person rehearsal dinner at Madison Square Garden’s Infosys Theater. And yet, on that extremely sensitive evening, Dolan’s MSG locked nearly all of its security team out of the network of surveillance cameras inside the arena, according to an internal document reviewed by WIRED. The move functionally prevented MSG security from fully operating the venue’s controversial face-recognition program that evening, two sources familiar with the Garden’s operations say.

While the shutdown order reviewed by WIRED applied only to July 2, those sources add that they were told the lockout was repeated on July 3, Swift and Kelce’s wedding night, which drew roughly 1,000 of the biggest names in media, music, business, and sports.

At every stage of their planning, Swift’s and Kelce’s teams went to extraordinary lengths to keep private what happened inside the Garden. Guests had to sign a nondisclosure agreement before they could receive a digital invitation. Tents were set up for cars to park in, so people could move in and out in relative secrecy (and, presumably, avoid the biometric surveillance gear positioned at the standard entrances). Wedding attendees were told there was a no-phone policy. The only detailed description of the event posted by a wedding night guest was quickly deleted.

According to the internal document, an MSG executive ordered on July 2 a seven-hour lockdown of the Garden’s video management system, made by the security tech company Genetec, “due to a client privacy request.” Security staffers who ordinarily monitor the building’s internal cameras and the accompanying face-recognition software were barred from doing so. The memo states that only a handful of company leaders and engineers were allowed into their Genetec accounts. The rest were “disabled.”

“If you somehow still have access to cameras after 3PM, you will be forcibly logged off,” the document warned MSG security personnel.

Since 2018, Dolan’s company has experimented with biometric surveillance at its venues, which include Radio City Music Hall and the Beacon Theater in New York, as well as the Sphere in Las Vegas. The organization contends that the technology is a security measure, but there are many publicly documented cases where the face-recognition system appears to have been for something else: retribution.

Fans who’ve been critical of Dolan have had their faces captured and then put on watch lists. A lawyer representing a cop was banned in April because his client is suing MSG. A mom trying to take her then 9-year-old Girl Scout to a Christmas show at Radio City Music Hall had her face flagged and was blocked from entering. The reason: She was an attorney, and her firm was in a legal dispute with one Dolan-controlled entity.

Genetec’s software serves as the backbone for MSG’s video security system, monitoring feeds from the various cameras and allowing security personnel to manage the applications that rely on those feeds, including face recognition. Cameras at the guest entrances are tied into a face-recognition system made by eConnect. If someone’s face triggers an alert, Genetec then allows that person to be easily tracked across the camera network. According to a person familiar with the security surveillance setup, “This makes it much easier to track a person, because we can jump from camera to camera in real time and follow them.”

As WIRED previously reported, Garden security used these systems to monitor a transgender woman second-by-second when she was in the arena. The cameras even noted when she went in and out of a bathroom.

Attendees at the Swift-Kelce pre-wedding celebration were spared such prying eyes. Civil libertarians say they understand why the couple might not want Dolan’s surveillance system deployed in full. But those activists see the accommodation as more than a one-off. It’s a preview of “a future where privacy is a luxury for the elite few, and the rest of us are subjected to pervasive surveillance everywhere we go,” says Evan Greer, director of the digital rights group Fight for the Future.

MSG’s venues host private events not infrequently. NBCUniversal takes over Radio City Music Hall every year to preview its shows for the next season; Warner Bros. Discovery goes to other Dolan-owned properties. But those customers did not ask to disable any aspect of the Garden’s security system, according to a source with direct knowledge of the matter. “It has never been done,” the source says, reflecting on their years at MSG, “and the request wouldn’t have been entertained.”

Even when the New York Police Department takes over Madison Square Garden, the cameras have stayed on. The NYPD regularly holds its graduation ceremonies from the Police Academy within the arena. As WIRED previously reported, the MSG face-recognition system contained a photograph apparently taken from one of those events. It shows an officer in his Police Academy dress uniform.

Which would make this celebration an outlier.

There’s the argument that Swift and Kelce, two of the planet’s most famous people, bought some modicum of privacy for themselves and their guests when they spent the estimated $1.2 to $1.6 million to book the Garden. It’s a venue with “some unique advantages,” former NYPD intelligence official John Miller noted for CNN. “The Garden has no windows, is covered by a roof, and access to the venue can be tightly controlled. That limits the ability of paparazzi, helicopters with powerful, long-distance cameras, or drones to capture the kinds of images they have at other celebrity weddings in outdoor venues.” Of course, for that money, they could have reserved any number of islands more private than Manhattan and an event space more discreet than the so-called “World’s Most Famous Arena.”

“People who have their wedding at Madison Square Garden don’t make that choice for privacy,” says a security professional who is deeply familiar with the venue.

Early July was a particularly hectic time. The city was considered to be in a “heightened threat environment” by the New York Police Department because of the America 250 celebrations and ongoing war with Iran. (That threat estimate is presumably one reason why the cameras outside the Garden—which can be accessed by the NYPD—stayed on, according to the memo.) Swift’s presence, of course, amped up the stakes enormously. In May, a man was sentenced to 15 years in prison for planning an attack at her concert in Vienna, Austria.

The Garden’s interior camera network is supposed to help in those situations, and more. What if someone snuck into the ultra-exclusive event? What if that person was a real threat to the people inside? Dolan, in a 2023 interview, told a local news anchor that the combination of surveillance cameras and face recognition did important work to keep such dangerous people out: “Are you someone who is on this list? If you’re a terrorist it’ll say, ‘That’s a terrorist.’”

But the NYPD supplies no such data to the Garden, a department spokesperson previously told WIRED. While some photographs from the FBI’s most-wanted list have been uploaded into the system, a lawsuit from a former MSG security staffer contends that was done to establish “an after-the-fact false narrative” that the face recognition was primarily geared toward stopping hostile actors rather than individuals Dolan perceived to be personal threats.

“Clearly the technology is not that helpful if it wasn’t needed at one of MSG’s highest-profile events of the year,” Michelle Dahl, executive director for the Surveillance Technology Oversight Project, said in a statement.

That said, there are indications that some cameras were rolling during the event. A notice near the Garden’s entrance alerted visitors that there would be “photography and videography” on the premises from June 29 to July 3—the date of the wedding—and that, by entering, guests agreed that their images and voices could be used in “any and all manner, format, and media.”

The Garden has long had a reputation for being the epicenter of global entertainment, a place that attracts the very brightest stars. But the Garden’s handling of its high-profile visitors has come under scrutiny recently, after the hacker collective ShinyHunters posted an internal MSG database of more than 39,000 VIPs. MSG sued WIRED for defamation for its reporting on the database; in the lawsuit, MSG confirmed that the “spreadsheet-like export” was stolen after an employee’s credentials were compromised by a social-engineering attack and that it no longer employed that individual. The lawsuit also confirmed that a small subset of those celebrities were designated some sort of “risk.” Among the 400 or so found by WIRED are the actor and musician Jamie Foxx; former “Real Housewife” Ubah Hassan; Shang-Chi star Simu Liu; Formula One driver Lewis Hamilton; and Achraf Hakimi, the captain of Morocco’s World Cup team.

Sources previously indicated to WIRED that these risk scores could reflect internal assessments of whether the VIPs might say something less than positive about Dolan and the Garden’s management or become involved, even indirectly, with some sort of public relations issue. MSG acknowledged that it maintains a “Threat Management notes field” for VIPs that might address, among other things, “prior incidents at MSG venues, the conduct or intensity of an individual’s fanbase or associates, or identity-verification concerns.” There was “a separate database” for “genuine security risks,” the lawsuit noted.

The celebrity database also included fields for race, gender, and sexual orientation, as MSG confirmed in its suit. The actor Elliot Page and the beauty influencer Emira D’Spain, for instance, were two of the 93 VIPs marked as “LGBTQIA,” as were the singer Avery Wilson and the designer Zac Posen.

“James Dolan has serious questions to answer. First, why is he so obsessed with us?” Tony Simone, an openly gay New York state lawmaker whose district includes midtown Manhattan, posted on July 9.

The company, for its part, states that its “support for the LGBTQIA community is indisputable.” The sexual orientation field, MSG added in its lawsuit against WIRED, was used for “inclusion-oriented outreach, including Pride events, community engagement, sales opportunities, and donations.”

Page, D’Spain, Posen, and Wilson also received a “risk” designation in the Garden database, albeit a “low” one. (In its lawsuit, MSG notes that only 4 percent of the celebrities it “tagged with an orientation of ‘LGBTQIA’” have threat-management notes.) Some of Swift and Kelce’s guests were also given risk scores, including Selena Gomez; her husband, the producer Benny Blanco; the broadcaster and former football player Michael Strahan; the actress Mariska Hargitay; the singer Benson Boone; and the rapper Ice Spice.

Representatives for Swift and Kelce did not respond to requests to comment for this story. In an email, a spokesperson for MSG declined to comment “due to the fact that we are in active litigation with WIRED.”

While face recognition is pervasive at Dolan-owned venues, it is not universal. The iconic Chicago Theater, for example, doesn’t collect biometric data, because private entities are forbidden to do so under an Illinois law that prohibits such surveillance without written consent. In its lawsuit against WIRED, the Garden highlighted at least two statements from current and former lawmakers that discussed WIRED’s reporting along with “existing and proposed biometric-data legislation.” WIRED’s coverage was damaging to the organization, the Garden added, because the public’s reaction to it would increase “the foreseeable regulatory and political consequences to MSG.”

Attempts to rein in MSG’s face-recognition system in New York City and state long predate WIRED’s reporting. A multiyear inquiry by the state liquor authority into the Garden’s use of face recognition ended this week with a “slap on wrist,” in the words of The New York Times. A recent measure in the State Assembly targeting biometric surveillance in public spaces (like MSG) was cosponsored by Simone and Zohran Mamdani, who now serves as New York’s mayor. It’s not hard to imagine why event planners intent on privacy would want to disable the controversial MSG camera system for their ultrahigh-profile clients. “I don’t blame them for turning it off, but let’s be clear,” said Dahl. “Privacy shouldn’t just be afforded to the rich and famous.”

The EU Fines Google $1 Billion for Prioritizing Its Own Services in Search

Wired July 23, 2026

The European Commission has levied a $1 billion penalty against Google over alleged competition law violations.

An EC investigation found that Google had abused its dominance in the European Union’s search and app store markets to funnel people toward its own apps and services, in violation of the EU’s Digital Markets Act.

The body has ordered Google to refrain from giving preferential treatment to its own services—such as shopping, accommodations, transport, and flights—in search rankings. Google must also allow app developers to communicate and transact with users outside the Play Store, where it takes a commission on sales.

“The best products should succeed because they’re better, not because they’re owned by the company running the search engine,” says Teresa Ribera, an executive vice president at the EC. “European consumers have a right to be told by app developers where to sign up to the best offers, even when the app store owner does not get a cut.”

In a statement to WIRED, Google said it would consider appealing the penalty.

“This isn't fair competition; it’s product degradation driven by a small group of self-serving complainants, with European businesses and consumers taking the hit,” says Kent Walker, president of global affairs at Google.

Tech industry trade associations argue that heavy-handed enforcement of the Digital Markets Act is self-defeating. “Reducing the quality of what Europeans have access to is not a positive outcome,” Daniel Friedlaender, senior vice president at trade organization CCIA Europe, tells WIRED.

The EU has brought numerous multi-billion-dollar fines against Google in the last decade over a medley of antitrust violations. In early July, a European court upheld a record $4.1 billion fine brought against Google in 2018 over agreements that required phone makers to install Google Search and the company’s Chrome web browser on their devices.

“Certainly, the stakes are really high for companies. How they are ranked affects their businesses a great deal,” says Kathryn McMahon, an associate professor of law at the University of Warwick. “The way EU competition law looks at it, firms in a dominant position—like Google—have a special responsibility not to distort competition.”

To address the latest complaints, Google has proposed alterations to the way it administers the Play Store and presents its products in search rankings, which the EC has characterized as "progress towards compliance.”

Recently, US president Donald Trump vowed to impose steep new tariffs on European countries that seek to restrict American technology companies. The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

The latest penalty is “quite a strong response, in the context of the transatlantic complaints—the way that Trump can leverage fines,” says McMahon. “It shows the commission is willing to be tough.”

Welly

Amazon

Target

First-aid kits are college-dorm essentials. There are lots of options from Welly that are bright and easy to find. Make sure your kit is always stocked with bandages, antibiotic ointment, antiseptic wipes, over-the-counter pain relief, plus some cold and flu medicine. I also recommend including Tums, Pepto-Bismol, cough drops, and Narcan. It's better to be safe than sickly (and unprepared).

LectroFan

Amazon

This top-recommended sound machine is compact and offers classic fan noise as well as different-colored noises. There may be nights when you're homesick or when you accidentally study-chugged too many energy drinks, and your mind is racing. This little machine may help you relax and get some quality shut-eye.

HoMedics

Homedics

Dorm rooms are notoriously dry and drafty. Putting a small humidifier like this one on your nightstand may help you breathe easier and may even help with dry skin. The humidifier also includes a nightlight, plus a place to add essential oils, if you want to scent the air.

Keurig

Keurig

Amazon

Walmart

For coffee drinkers who prioritize speed in their machine of choice, this pod-style coffee maker is an excellent option, with readily available refills. It has a built-in milk frother, so you can make your own specialty beverages without paying $8 for the same at the local chain coffee spot. The machine is easy to clean, and the water reservoir is large.

Zojirushi

Amazon

Wayfair

Students who want to consume caffeine by the pot rather than by the cup might consider our favorite affordable drip coffee maker. The entire brewing process is automatic with basically zero bells or whistles, but the resulting coffee is flavorful and consistent every time. It also doesn't take up much counter space.

Hatch

Amazon

Hatch

The Hatch Restore 3 is a popular sunrise alarm clock that doubles as a sound machine. Some of the features are paywalled behind a monthly subscription that costs $5 per month or $50 per year, but you don't need to subscribe to get good use out of the device. The alarm can help reinforce positive sleep and wake-up routines, and the Hatch even has fun features (not paywalled) like guided meditation, which stands to help around finals season.

All of us at WIRED have complicated desk setups that make working from home easier. You don't have to go that hard for a dorm room, and you probably only have so much space to spare anyway. See our full work-from-home guide for more options, but these are some of our favorite desk accessories worth considering—plus some more options for around your dorm room.

Aecooly Chic Touch Control Desk Fan: I tested this fan all summer last year for our Best Fans guide, and my friend's son took it to school for his first year at the University of Colorado. It's going to be hot for move-in week, and this fan is not only powerful, but its 8-inch-tall body fits in a suitcase, it’s USB-C rechargeable, and it’s quiet enough (36 decibels on low) that it won’t bother roommates or interfere with studying. —Kat Merck

Ruggable Pamir Ivory Washable Rug: I like this washable rug because it's durable, it looks great, and it's supremely easy to clean. A rug is one of the easiest ways to make a room feel more grown-up, and this one won’t break the bank.

AmazonBasics 3-Tier Utility Cart: I use this utility cart in my kitchen, and I'm about to get another for my bathroom. It's easy to put together and makes good use of vertical storage space. Use it to organize school supplies, toiletries, accessories, or whatever else is taking up space in your half of the dorm room.

BenQ ScreenBar Computer LED Lamp: WIRED editor Julian Chokkattu swears by this desk lamp, which only works if you have an external monitor on your desk. It hangs over the top of the screen and illuminates your workspace. Best of all, it takes up zero space on your desk!

Monoprice Extra Wide Length Microfiber Desk Mat: This mat is soft and doubles as a mouse pad, which is great for students who use a separate keyboard and mouse.

Ikea Skubb Underbed Storage Case: When former WIRED reviewer Medea Giordano lived in a tiny NYC apartment, she stowed four of these storage bins under her bed to hold every item of clothing that her closet couldn't accommodate. The same tack works well for college beds, which generally have ample room underneath. These cases can hold off-season clothing, shoes, or anything else you may need, like party supplies. Amazon has a bunch of similar options.

Dalykate Backpack Laundry Bag: One reality of dorm life is that you may need to hike your dirty laundry down a few flights to the laundry room. This hamper has a pocket to hold your detergent and backpack straps for portability, and it’s not as bulky as a laundry basket. It's what WIRED editor Julian Chokkattu uses to head to his laundromat.

Crocs Classic Clogs: You need a pair of shower shoes. Trust me when I say that you do not want to deal with athlete's foot in a college dorm. These Crocs are my favorite for shared showers—they're not fussy to walk in, easy to slide out of when you're balancing on one leg to wash your feet, and they dry quickly, too. Alternatively, you could go with a dedicated pair of flip-flops or slides. And don’t forget a shower caddy for your toiletries!

Govee RGBIC LED Light Strip: String lights are cute, but this light strip from Govee is much more fun. You can easily adjust the colors and brightness using the smartphone app, and you can trim down the lights to suit the space.

Basic Cleaning Supplies: I didn’t realize how much stuff I was forgetting when I first moved into my dorm. Make sure you remember household essentials, like laundry detergent, paper towels, dish soap, disinfectant wipes, and washcloths. You might also want a little broom and dustpan.

The Best Vacuums for Pet Hair

Wired July 23, 2026

Amazon

Amazon

Amazon

Amazon

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The best vacuum for pet hair is one that actually sucks up the fur—which is a more difficult ask than you may imagine. Pet fur is particularly tough to clean up. If it’s short and coarse, like my cat Basil’s, it gets easily embedded in fabrics and carpet; if it’s long and fluffy like my cat Clover’s, it flies away to accumulate in hard-to-reach corners. But whatever your situation, there’s a vac for that!

A few of my pet-owning colleagues and I have tested over a dozen vacuums—from traditional corded models to cordless, handheld, robotic, and even 2-in-1 vac/mop combos—to find out which is actually the best vacuum for pet hair. My consistent favorite cordless option for pet hair has been the Dyson Gen5 Detect ($800), because of its illuminating light that lets you see hairs normally naked to the human eye. I'm not usually the biggest fan of corded vacuums, because of their limitations, but I was also seriously impressed with the amount of deep dirt, dander, and embedded fur the cheap Bissell Pet Hair Eraser Allergen Lift-Off Vacuum ($200) got out of my high-pile carpet.

We recommend our favorites here, but we’re continually testing more, so check back often. And be sure to check out our related guides, like the Best Handheld Vacuums, Best Cordless Vacuums, Best Robot Vacuums, and How to Live With a Pet If You're Allergic.

Updated July 2025: I've added the Eufy Omni C28, 3i P10 Ultra, Riccar R65 Cordless Stick Vacuum, and Smoture VAC01 Cordless Vacuum Cleaner. I've also updated links and prices throughout.

Dyson

Amazon

Best Buy

I am completely obsessed with this cordless vacuum. Dyson’s Gen5Detect packs all the punch you’d get from a corded vac while also being lightweight and convenient. It also doubles as a handheld vac with a crevice tool and smaller hair screw tool when you want to do a quick or tight job like stairs or corners. Dyson claims it has the most powerful HEPA filtration of any cordless vac on the market. It even has a digital screen that shows just how much gross stuff you’re vacuuming up, tracking particle size—microscopic, like allergens; fine, like skin flakes; medium, like dust mites; and coarse, like sugar.

There’s a Digital Motorbar cleaner head for carpets—with 56 detangling vanes, hair never gets stuck in the bar—and pet hair gets sucked straight into the back for a mess-free clean. There’s also a Fluffy Optic cleaner head for hard floors. It has a super-soft rotating material and an angled green blade of light to illuminate invisible pet hair and dust invisible to the human eye. With 70 minutes of run time and excellent attachments that work for pet hair (and dust and dander) on a myriad of surfaces, this versatile vac is one of my favorite products I’ve ever tested.

Bissell

Amazon

Bissell

It has three power levels and a big headlight on the front to make it easy to spot fur and cat litter, and it performs well on hardwood, carpet, rugs, and tile. And it turned my cat tree from hairball hell into nearly brand-new. All you need to do is push a button to switch between suction modes; a light indicates the level. It's easy to pop the dust cup off and empty it, plus the canister sits on the outside of the bar, which makes it less likely to lean while cleaning.

WIRED reviewer Nena Farrell's favorite part of the vac was the FurFinder Tool, which looks like a mini vacuum head. It's 6 inches wide, about half the size of a regular cordless vacuum head, but it's a fantastic size to vacuum upholstery and platforms on a cat tree. There's also a crevice tool with a brush extension included, and she was impressed with the suction power to easily pull up all types of fur and dust.

Shark

Amazon

Best Buy

Walmart

Shark

This lightweight (just under 3 pounds) handheld vac from Shark is specifically designed to tackle pet hair: It has powerful suction with two cyclonic airstreams, and a motorized self-cleaning power brush sucks the hair back so it doesn't get wrapped around the brush (my biggest complaint with vacuuming pet hair). It also has an extra-large capacity for pet hair, dander, and dust, and it has a button to easily (and cleanly) dispense the hair and debris from the XL dust cup. It also has surface and crevice attachments to tackle pet hair on a myriad of surfaces, and has a washable filter for easy cleanup that also helps with longevity. WIRED reviewer Nena Farrell liked using this vacuum for various messes around the house, including her toddler’s spilled Cheerios and debris from a home renovation, but she wasn’t the biggest fan of its somewhat short battery life.

Bissell

Amazon

Wayfair

Best Buy

Bissell

This lightweight, 3-pound hand vacuum is specially designed to target pet hair with three attachments: a powerful motorized brush lifts pet hair from a myriad of surfaces, including fur embedded in fabric and carpet; a super-skinny crevice tool sucks debris from in between cushions; and a flat, wide attachment works well for surface upholstery vacuuming. After prolonged testing, I realized that hair gets tangled in this bar more easily, and the brush isn’t the easiest to clean. I mostly use the crevice tool now, which has become my go-to for sucking up pet hair in tight, hard-to-reach places like the corners of my pets’ cat tree and between my bed and the wall.

Roborock

Amazon

Roborock

This high-end robot vacuum/mop combo uses AI to identify up to 108 obstacles, plus it has a 20,000-Pa suction, a fast-charging and intelligent recharging dock, and extended clean time. This vacuum has a high-efficiency washable filter that captures 99.97 percent of dust, pollen, and allergens down to 0.3 microns in size. There's hot-water washing for the mop, a flexible arm, and a main brush that splits in two to make it easier to clean. You can use voice commands via Alexa, Apple Siri Shortcuts, and Google Home, and the robovac can navigate smartly around your home on its own with multi-floor mapping, using its StarSight Autonomous System 2.0 with lidar, ToF sensors, RBG cameras, and AI.

Former WIRED reviewer Adrienne So loved the vacuum's AI mapping capabilities to avoid sucking up her daughter's toys or her elderly dog’s accidents. It also has pet-friendly smart navigation, pausing its main brush and moving aside to avoid frightening your pet, and you can identify the locations of pet supplies like dog beds or food bowls to make sure the robovac deep-cleans those areas. Although this is a pricey upgrade, I’d argue that the ability to never have to manually vacuum or mop again is priceless.

Eufy

Amazon

Eufy

This model from my colleague Nena Farrell has replaced my previous 3i P10 Ultra pick (below, in “Others Tested”) for the best cheap robovac after I had trouble finding replacement bags for the model. It also started missing large areas of my small apartment, especially in corners where pet hair accumulates. However, I advise every pet owner to invest in a combo robovac/mop, since one of the best ways to fight pet allergies is with consistent mopping to reduce dander and microscopic dust.

Robovac-mop models, especially those with multi-mapping capabilities, often hover in the four figures. This robovac/mop model is super affordable for its expansive capabilities. It has 15,000-Pa suction power, a self-cleaning roller mop that keeps things more hygienic than mop pads, and retractable detangling brushes to clean hard-to-reach corners. It also has multifloor mapping, which is a valuable feature that many cheaper robovacs don't have. Its battery life needs charging after each floor, but it does charge fairly quickly, hiking back up to 57 percent battery after just 20 minutes in its docking station. It uses a laser distance sensor and laser line to navigate and map multiple floors, and it has the ability to mop and vacuum the whole home—this model is the best you can buy at this price point.

Dyson

Amazon

Dyson

I will preface this by saying now that technology has expanded and cordless vacs are just as powerful as upright vacuums and easier to use, I rarely go back to corded options. However, this Dyson is literally engineered to pick up pet hair with a large bin capacity, a Motorbar cleaner head with detangling hair-removal vanes, and three different power modes: one for deep- and medium-pile carpets, one for low-pile carpets and large debris, and one for hardwood floors and ground-in dirt.

With the Extra, there’s also a tangle-free turbine tool (for removing pet hair and dirt from upholstery) and a grooming tool for pets with medium or long hair that removes loose hairs, allergens, and dead skin from your animal—plus the included combination tool and stair tool. When we tested, the canister never clogged up with wads of fur, the motor-bar cleaner head remained free of tangled hair, and the vacuum worked well on both hardwood floors and carpet. Our only complaint is that it's heavy and loud—my exact gripe with corded vacs.

Bissell

Amazon

Bissell

This isn't the corded vacuum of yesteryear. With an easily detachable pod and hose with a crevice tool and a super-powerful motorized, rotating upholstery tool, this vacuum is ready for all types of pet messes. In fact, it's designed to combat pet hair, fur, dust, and microscopic dander with multiple modes. It has settings to adjust for high and low pile carpet, and you switch between hardwood, where the motor bar doesn't rotate, and carpet modes, where it does. It was super easy to assemble, the dust bin was incredibly easy to pop off and empty, and the washable filter twisted out for easier cleaning. The mini rotating upholstery tool (and crevice tools) attach to a long hose, and the pod can be unattached for easier cleaning on things like furniture or cat trees.

I live in a small apartment with three humans and two furry cats, and I vacuum every day with various vacs I test. So I was shocked at how well this sucked up deeply embedded fur in my high-pile carpet and the huge amounts of microscopic dirt and dust that no other model had been able to suck up so efficiently.

Levoit

Amazon

Walmart

Levoit

I love cordless vacuums for so many reasons, including portability and how easy they are to use. But, the downfalls of cordless vacs are frustrating and sometimes yucky emptying, and awkward charging ports. This self-emptying stick vac from Levoit fixes all of that. With a convenient upright auto-cleaning and -charging station and a bin that self-empties, all you have to do is press a button to change power levels or self-empty when in the station. There, the vacuum opens from the bottom, and the yucky fur, dirt, and dander are sucked into the bag without you ever needing to touch it. It's perfect for pet parents who don't want to deal with emptying the pet messes that the vacuum powerfully sucks up.

The five-stage HEPA filtration system claims to capture 99.97 percent of particles (as small as 0.3 microns), making it ideal for pet parents who want to lessen pet allergens around the home. It also doubles as a hand vacuum for easier, lightweight cleaning and comes with a slew of handy attachments for sucking fur or hair in hard-to-reach places, including crevice and combination tools, a mini motorized brush, and an extension hose for longer reach. It works excellently on both high- and low-pile carpets, pulling up microscopic dust and dirt that passes with other vacuums didn't get. Although beware, it isn't nearly as effective on hardwood floors.

Riccar

Riccar

This cordless vacuum is the tool I'd recommend for a pet owner with a limited budget who wants an upholstery cleaner, handheld vacuum, and vacuum for both hardwood and carpet all in one. Although the battery life isn't the longest (at only 40 minutes run time with two hours of charge time), and the dust canister is very small—you'd really only need this one versatile vacuum for all types of pet messes.

The vacuum comes with tons of attachments that are valuable for cleaning up pet dander and fur on hard and soft surfaces, as well as furniture like couches and cat trees. It has a dusting brush and upholstery tool, a crevice tool that extends to almost 17 inches (ideal for in between cushions or in hard-to-reach places where fur accumulates), another dust brush for cushions or fabric, and a rotating dusting brush that also helps to sweep up lightweight fur. If those weren't enough additional attachments, Riccar also sent me a pet and upholstery power tool ($56) attachment specifically designed to suck up pet fur and dander that gets embedded in fabric and carpet, and a bare floor nozzle ($95) specifically designed for hardwood or tile floors.

In addition to the short run time and small dust bin, I also didn't love that it needs to be on a stand to charge. In my small New York apartment, every square inch of space counts, and I much prefer models with an attachable battery that can be simply plugged in and tucked away. Still, I appreciated the illuminating lights and various attachments that can suck up pet hair and dander on literally every surface and corner of your home.

Smoture VAC01 Cordless Vacuum Cleaner for $150: This vacuum surprised me with how powerfully it was able to pick up fur and dust from hardwood floors, carpet, and furniture. Its dust cup was easy to open and empty, and it comes with a bunch of attachments to easily convert to a handheld vacuum and upholstery cleaner. It has 55,000 Pa of max suction power, with a 650-watt brushless motor to suck up embedded fur and hair in my high-pile carpet. It has an LED touchscreen where you can switch between eco, standard, boost, and auto modes, where it runs for up to 70 minutes in eco mode and 15 minutes in max mode. In auto mode, the vacuum intelligently adjusts suction power depending on the surface to conserve battery. It has a wall-mounted dock, or you can just plug in the detachable battery if you live in a small home like me. It comes with a 3-plus-foot flexible hose for crevices, a motorized upholstery brush, and a dual dust brush and crevice tool. It also stands upright on its own (which is a convenient plus), its dust canister is easy to empty, and the various attachments are easy to change—a gripe I've had as my Dyson ages and the attachments get harder to change out. For this price point, it's a super solid vacuum, especially with its attachments for reaching pet hair on lots of different surfaces.

Simplicity Vacuums Flash Mini Handheld Vacuum for $45: This handheld vacuum gets power through an electrical cord, which I'm not usually the biggest fan of since it limits mobility around the house. But it's still one of the most powerful and efficient handheld vacuums I've ever tested. It has a 2-foot-long flexible hose to suck up pet fur and dander in hard-to-reach places, and comes with a myriad of attachments like a crevice tool (with an optional brush tip), upholstery brush, and dusting brush. I loved the attachments, which helped to brush fur up, and the hose helped me suck up hair that had settled in hard-to-reach spots. It was also able to suck up embedded fur in multiple high- and low-pile carpets around the house that others I've tested weren't able to. It has dual filters, a washable dust cup filter for larger debris, and a foam exhaust filter for finer particles like dust and dander, which can lead to pet allergy symptoms. The only downside is that the vacuum is quite loud and a little clunky.

Ryobi 18V One+ HP Advanced Stick Vacuum Kit for $399: It has powerful suction with cyclonic filtration, a brushless motor, an easily removable roller bar, and lights on the vacuum head to better see the debris. The dual plush (for hard floors) and brush rolls (for carpet) move together to suck the pet hair up into the dust cup without getting tangled. There's also an easily removable roller bar, which makes dealing with fur tangles easier. Plus, the dust cup is also super convenient to empty. It can also be used as a handheld vac, which comes with crevice tools and a dust brush. This model is a bit heavier with its battery positioned right behind the handle, but the vacuum stands upright unsupported.

Tineco Go Pet Cordless Vacuum for $176: As when I tested the Tineco Go Mini ($180) for my handheld vacuums guide, I was a bit underwhelmed by this vacuum specifically for pets. It has a slot for easy brush removal if hair gets stuck around the bars, which is a helpful thing to have when you’re dealing with pet (and human) hair. The lever and the angle of the lid for emptying are counterintuitive, and the first few times I emptied it, the debris went everywhere. It’s hard to distinguish between eco and power modes, and the vac blinked red and the brush stopped rotating when transitioning between surfaces. (It especially had a hard time on my thin runner rug.) It felt a bit heavier and clunkier than others as well. But it does have handy lights to illuminate debris and comes with attachments to make handheld cleaning a breeze.

Mova P50 Pro Ultra Robot Vacuum for $799: This robot vacuum-mop combo has extendable side brush and mop pads to reach tight corners, a self-emptying dock station that empties dust and debris, and self-cleans and dries mop pads. It also uses an RGB camera and “intelligent dirt detection system” whose sensors identify messes to clean deeper and avoid objects on the ground. The robovac generates 3D maps of your home and identifies things like furniture and even pets. Through the app, you can customize cleanings, and there’s also synced video and voice interaction to allow you to talk to your pets, schedule cleanings, and more, and it is compatible with Alexa and Google Home. When first mapping my small apartment, the vac didn’t want to go past certain rooms, and it took several days to get it to create a complete cleaning map. It has a hard time going over small thresholds, eventually avoiding cleaning the rooms altogether, and has thrown itself off my stairs twice, causing the mop pads to pop off. Despite having intelligent object detection, it still often tried to suck up or roll over small objects on the ground, like shoes and pet toys. I love that this combo vac-mop self-cleans and empties, but for nearly $1,000, I wish the smart features were smarter and the mapping were more accurate.

Dyson Car + Boat Handheld Vacuum for $247: Former WIRED reviewer Brenda Stolyar liked this handheld vacuum, designed specifically for sucking up dirt and debris from your car and boat, plus bedding, furniture, and other awkward spaces. (Read our full review here).

3i P10 Ultra for $400: This AI-enabled, self-emptying robovac with auto-extending mop pads spins at 220 rpm, and the vac has 18,000-Pa suction power. It uses lidar scans to 3D-map your home and AI to identify pets and maneuver around objects, increasing suction around things like pet food bowls and extra mopping for dirtier areas, like around litter boxes. It also has smart carpet detection, which boosts suction, and because it self-empties and cleans, the only thing you have to do is empty the dirty water and refill clean water in the tank. You can adjust the settings in the app, for things like customized cleaning schedules, routes, order, wetness, and suction power. Plus, it's compatible with Alexa and Google Assistant. One problem I've faced is that I can't share the app with anyone else in the home, so when they want to run it, they have to manually turn it on and off.

Hoover HL4 Pet Upright Vacuum Cleaner for £130: While it is only available in the UK, Hoover’s HL4 successfully removed lots of cat hair from my home. I live with a trio of cats, two of them long-haired, so a powerful vacuum is essential. The HL4 is sadly corded (7.6 meters), but at around 240 air watts it was powerful enough to lift dust and hair that my lightweight cordless vac and robot vac had missed. The smart design easily converts into a portable vacuum, and it comes with a pet tool and crevice tool. The pet tool proved adept at lifting hair from the couch, stairs, and cat beds, though it didn’t quite have the grunt to remove every strand. There’s a handy vent to reduce suction for mats and blankets. The 1.2-liter bin is easy to remove and empty, though not without releasing a dust cloud, and the Anti-Twist floor head seems to collect considerably less tangled hair than other vacuums. —Simon Hill

Eufy RoboVac 11S Max for $150: Our esteemed competitors at places like the Strategist and Wirecutter loved this cheap robovac, so I bought one for myself before moving into my new apartment with two cats. And I have to say, I don't agree with them. Yes, this robovac is significantly cheaper than most others and has generally good ratings, but I have nothing nice to say about it besides that it is able to go under furniture and suck up pet hair I otherwise wouldn’t be able to. Its navigation system is random, it doesn't have an app (but it does come with a remote control to direct it to a specific spot or schedule cleanings), it’s loud, and it tends to be attracted to cords. It has extreme difficulty traversing even minor height differences, like the small panel of wood between the hallway and bathroom door. But most of all, it is needlessly hard to empty the bin, and nearly impossible to detangle all of the hair and fur from the bar or spinning brush beneath. There’s gross hair that will probably still be wrapped around the mechanism until the day I am put into the ground. This cursed thing will outlive us all, I fear.

How We Tested

I tested these pet hair vacuums for a week, if not more (I’ve been using both the Dyson cordless and handheld for months now), and I’ve used them on nearly every surface in my house—including the cat trees and behind my two cats’ litter box. When testing began, I lived in a large house with three cats and a dog (more hair in a larger area), and for the latter half of testing, I lived with two cats in a small apartment (slightly less hair in a smaller area with fewer places for hair to hide).

I also tested every attachment on problem areas like carpeted stairs, crevices of air vents, a high-pile rug, and hardwood floors. Not all pet hair vacuums are created alike, and they vary quite a bit in their effectiveness on different surfaces and with different attachments. I set these up, charged ’em, and vacuumed with them until they died, noting run time, power, effectiveness, and ease of emptying the bin and cleaning the filter.

What to Look For

It seems like a lot of brands will slap the words “pet hair” onto a product and market it as such without really specifying why or how it’s effective for pet hair. Of course, I tested those to see if they put their metaphorical vac mouths where their money was. On the flip side, I also tested some that were well rated for overall efficacy but not marketed toward pets—like the Roborock Saros 10R, a pricey robovac that uses AI mapping and can identify pets nearby and quiet its motor.

Speaking of, vacuums and pets are inherently antithetical. Vacuums are a necessary evil to combat pet hair, but your pets will likely be scared of them. If my cat Basil had opposable thumbs, I know he’d be leaving hate comments on this article. Aside from the robovac picks (which for some reason my cats don’t mind), my cat Basil had a mild cardiac event each time I tested the other vacs on this list. So along with effectiveness and suction, I also took into consideration loudness, as well as how easy the product is to handle.

Generally though, when shopping for a pet hair vacuum, look for suction power, bin capacity, attachments, and type of bristle or Motorbar—figure out what’s going to be doing the actual picking up of dust, dander, and pet hair. I found that conical bars like the ones on certain Dyson models work well to not get tangled, and dual brushes like on the Ryobi work together to effectively pick up more. Also read reviews from real people with real, furry pets, but know that no two pets are alike. Take into consideration what kind of shedder you live with, and what type of space needs cleaning; a robovac may not be best for a house with multiple flights of carpeted stairs.
